Exclusion of viral and autoimmune etiologies strengthens the likelihood of a drug-induced cause.

reasoning.content: The histological evaluation reveals well-formed, non-necrotizing epithelioid granulomas in portal tracts [Image 1], a hallmark of granulomatous hepatitis. The absence of necrosis reduces the likelihood of infectious granulomas (e.g., tuberculosis). Expanded, hypercellular portal tracts with fibrous septa [Image 2] and a mixed inflammatory infiltrate including lymphocytes, plasma cells, neutrophils, and notably eosinophils [Image 3] suggest a chronic inflammatory process with features of hypersensitivity. Eosinophils in particular are often associated with drug reactions. The patient has no evidence of viral hepatitis or autoimmune disease based on serology, eliminating major differential diagnoses. Critically, liver enzymes improved after stopping allopurinol, confirming a temporal and causal relationship. Given the patient’s long-term allopurinol use, absence of other new medications, and resolution of liver injury upon discontinuation, the constellation of histological, serological, and clinical findings strongly supports allopurinol as the causative agent.
reasoning.conclusion: The patient’s granulomatous hepatitis is most likely induced by allopurinol, representing a rare but plausible adverse drug reaction characterized by non-necrotizing granulomas, mixed portal inflammation, and clinical resolution upon drug withdrawal.

question:
In a study assessing histopathological changes in rat intestinal tissue following hypoxia-reoxygenation (H/R) and treatment with low-dose (LDAT) or high-dose atropine (HDAT), histopathological examination was performed on four groups of rat pups: Group I (control), Group II (H/R), Group III (LDAT), and Group IV (HDAT). Tissue sections were stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and examined at 200× magnification. The histopathological injury score (HIS) was calculated based on epithelial and architectural changes.

- In the first experiment, intestinal tissue from Group I (control) was analyzed.
- In the second experiment, intestinal tissue from Group II (H/R) and Group IV (HDAT) was analyzed.
- In the third experiment, intestinal tissue from Group III (LDAT) was analyzed.
- In the fourth experiment, HIS values were quantified for each group, yielding mean scores of 1.14 in the LDAT group, 1.84 in the H/R group, and 1.86 in the HDAT group.

What conclusions can be drawn from these findings, and how do the results across experiments support this conclusion?

input_logic_chain.research_context: Assessment of histopathological changes in rat intestinal tissue following hypoxia-reoxygenation (H/R) and treatment with low-dose (LDAT) or high-dose atropine (HDAT), with evaluation of epithelial integrity and injury severity using histopathological scoring (HIS).

experiments.experimental_setting: Histopathological examination of intestinal tissue from rat pups in four experimental groups: Group I (control), Group II (H/R), Group III (LDAT), and Group IV (HDAT). Tissue sections were stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and examined at 200× magnification. The HIS was calculated based on epithelial and architectural changes.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate the extent of intestinal mucosal injury across experimental groups using histopathological analysis.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Image 1 shows well-preserved intestinal villi architecture, continuous epithelial lining, uniformly sized columnar cells with basal nuclei, intact crypts, and no inflammatory infiltration or structural disruption [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The absence of cellular swelling, vacuolation, or architectural distortion indicates normal intestinal mucosal histology, consistent with minimal or no injury.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Group I (control) exhibits no significant histopathological injury, serving as a baseline for comparison.

experiments.experimental_setting: Same histopathological analysis as above, focusing on Group II (H/R) and Group IV (HDAT) intestinal tissue sections stained with H&E at 200× magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To identify pathological changes induced by H/R injury and assess whether HDAT treatment modifies these changes.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Image 3 shows epithelial cells with cytoplasmic swelling, pale vacuolated cytoplasm, nuclear displacement toward the periphery, and reduced eosinophilic staining; villi architecture is partially preserved but with disrupted cellular organization [Image 3]. Image 4 shows similar cytoplasmic vacuolation, nuclear displacement, reduced eosinophilia, and mild mononuclear infiltration in the lamina propria, with irregular villus height and localized epithelial distortion [Image 4].
experiments.interpretation: Cytoplasmic vacuolation and swelling with nuclear displacement are characteristic of hydropic degeneration, a form of reversible cellular injury due to cellular swelling from impaired ion transport, commonly seen in ischemia-reperfusion injury. The presence of mild inflammatory infiltration in Image 4 suggests a low-grade immune response.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Both H/R (Group II) and HDAT (Group IV) groups exhibit grade II histopathological injury, primarily due to epithelial hydropic degeneration, indicating persistent mucosal damage despite HDAT treatment.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histopathological analysis of intestinal tissue from Group III (LDAT), treated with low-dose atropine, using H&E staining at 200× magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To determine whether LDAT treatment attenuates H/R-induced intestinal injury.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Image 2 shows well-preserved villi with continuous epithelial lining, regular crypt architecture, normal columnar epithelial cells with basal nuclei, and only sparse inflammatory cells in the lamina propria without architectural distortion [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: The preservation of epithelial structure, absence of cytoplasmic vacuolation, and minimal inflammatory infiltration indicate significantly reduced cellular injury compared to H/R and HDAT groups.
experiments.sub_conclusion: LDAT treatment is associated with markedly less histopathological damage, suggesting a protective effect against H/R-induced intestinal injury.

experiments.experimental_setting: HIS values were calculated for each group and compared using the Mann-Whitney U test. Mean HIS values were reported as 1.14 (LDAT), 1.84 (H/R), and 1.86 (HDAT), with p < 0.001 [Context].
experiments.experiment_goal: To statistically compare the severity of histopathological injury across treatment groups.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The mean HIS values are lower in the LDAT group compared to H/R and HDAT groups [Context].
experiments.interpretation: A significantly lower HIS in the LDAT group indicates reduced overall histopathological injury, corroborating the visual findings of preserved mucosal architecture.
experiments.sub_conclusion: LDAT treatment results in a statistically significant reduction in intestinal injury score compared to both H/R and HDAT groups.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: Control group (Group I) shows no histopathological injury, establishing a baseline for normal intestinal histology.
H/R and HDAT groups exhibit grade II epithelial hydropic degeneration, indicating significant mucosal injury.
LDAT group shows preserved mucosal architecture and minimal injury, suggesting a protective effect.

reasoning.content: The histopathological evaluation reveals a clear contrast between treatment groups. Images 1 and 2 demonstrate intact mucosal architecture in control and LDAT-treated animals, respectively, with no signs of cellular degeneration. In contrast, Images 3 and 4 from H/R and HDAT groups show definitive features of hydropic degeneration—cytoplasmic vacuolation, nuclear displacement, and reduced eosinophilia—indicating cellular swelling and injury. The preservation of tissue structure in the LDAT group, supported by a significantly lower mean HIS (1.14 vs. ~1.85), demonstrates that low-dose atropine mitigates H/R-induced intestinal damage. The lack of improvement in the HDAT group suggests a dose-dependent or potentially adverse effect at higher doses. Together, the visual and statistical evidence indicate that LDAT, but not HDAT, provides a protective effect against experimental intestinal injury in neonatal rats.
reasoning.conclusion: Low-dose atropine treatment significantly reduces histopathological injury in rat pups following hypoxia-reoxygenation, as evidenced by preserved mucosal architecture and lower histopathological injury scores, whereas high-dose atropine does not confer protection and results in injury comparable to untreated H/R controls.

question: The use of formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue samples enables multimodal diagnostic analysis, including immunohistochemistry (IHC) and electron microscopy (EM), to correlate histopathological and ultrastructural features of viral infection, specifically SARS-CoV-2 in tracheal epithelial cells. Serial sections from FFPE tracheal tissue were prepared; one section was subjected to IHC using antibodies against SARS-CoV-2 and visualized by light microscopy. A scale bar of 20 μm is present in the image. Targeted regions from the FFPE block, corresponding to areas identified on adjacent sections, were processed either by on-slide embedding or biopsy punch extraction, deparaffinization, and epoxy resin embedding for transmission electron microscopy (TEM). In the electron micrograph, a scale bar of 200 nm is present. EM analysis was performed on both on-slide and biopsy punch-processed FFPE samples to compare ultrastructural preservation. In these samples, viral particles appeared smaller than typical coronavirus size and with reduced clarity of subcellular details, particularly in on-slide preparations. What can be concluded from these findings?

experiments.sub_conclusion: IHC successfully identifies focal areas of SARS-CoV-2 antigen expression in ciliated epithelial cells of the trachea, providing a spatial target for subsequent EM analysis.

These are observed in proximity to ciliary structures within a granular matrix. [Image 2]
experiments.interpretation: The size (~75 nm), spherical morphology, central lucency (suggesting nucleocapsid), dense outer layer (viral envelope), and surrounding fuzz (consistent with peplomers) are morphological hallmarks of coronaviruses, though reduced in size due to processing-induced shrinkage.
experiments.sub_conclusion: EM reveals structures with morphological features consistent with SARS-CoV-2 virions in extracellular spaces adjacent to IHC-positive ciliated epithelial cells, despite compromised ultrastructure.

experiments.experimental_setting: EM analysis was performed on both on-slide and biopsy punch-processed FFPE samples to compare ultrastructural preservation.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess the impact of FFPE processing on viral morphology and detectability.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Viral particles appear smaller than typical (closer to 75 nm than 100 nm), with degraded surrounding tissue architecture and reduced clarity of subcellular details, particularly in on-slide preparations. [Context]
experiments.interpretation: Multiple processing steps—formalin fixation, paraffin embedding, deparaffinization, staining, drying, and epoxy embedding—induce shrinkage and ultrastructural degradation, leading to reduced particle size and loss of fine morphological detail.
experiments.sub_conclusion: FFPE-derived samples exhibit compromised ultrastructure, necessitating cautious interpretation of viral morphology, but retain sufficient features for presumptive identification when correlated with IHC.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: IHC successfully localizes SARS-CoV-2 antigen to ciliated epithelial cells in tracheal tissue, defining regions of interest for EM.
EM of IHC-targeted areas reveals extracellular particles with coronavirus-like morphology, including size, core-rim structure, and peplomer-like projections.
Processing artifacts from FFPE workflow reduce viral particle size and ultrastructural fidelity, but do not preclude identification when combined with orthogonal data.

reasoning.content: The integration of IHC and EM on serial sections of FFPE tracheal tissue enables targeted ultrastructural investigation of SARS-CoV-2 infection. IHC first identifies antigen-positive ciliated epithelial cells [Image 1], guiding precise sampling for EM. Subsequent TEM of these regions reveals numerous ~75 nm spherical particles in the extracellular space near ciliated surfaces [Image 2], exhibiting a central electron-lucent core, dense outer rim, and fuzzy surface projections—features morphologically consistent with SARS-CoV-2 virions. Although the reduced size and degraded ultrastructure (compared to glutaraldehyde-fixed samples) are attributed to FFPE processing artifacts, the morphological coherence of these particles—especially their uniform size, localization to IHC-positive areas, and structural complexity—supports their identification as viral. The correlation between positive immunostaining and the presence of morphologically characteristic particles strengthens diagnostic confidence. However, due to potential mimics and processing-induced changes, definitive identification requires expert evaluation and cautious terminology (e.g., 'virus-like' when criteria are incomplete).
reasoning.conclusion: A multimodal approach combining IHC and EM on FFPE tissues allows accurate localization and morphological characterization of SARS-CoV-2 in tracheal epithelium, despite processing-induced ultrastructural compromise, enabling reliable correlation of histopathological and ultrastructural features of infection when interpreted with expert knowledge and orthogonal validation.

question:
A 47-year-old woman died of rapidly progressive liver failure eight months after being diagnosed with microinvasive ductal carcinoma in situ (DCISM) and undergoing mastectomy, sentinel lymph node biopsy, and immediate reconstruction, without adjuvant systemic therapy. To understand the nature and biological behavior of the metastatic lesions, the following investigations were performed:

- Histological examination of liver tissue was conducted using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining.
- Immunohistochemical staining of the liver tissue was performed for hormone receptors and HER2 using chromogen-based detection.
- Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) analysis of the liver tissue was carried out using DNA probes targeting the HER2 gene and a control locus, with fluorescence microscopy.
- The primary tumor pathology from the mastectomy specimen and sentinel lymph node biopsy was reviewed, revealing microinvasive foci measuring up to 0.1 mm; the DCIS component was high-grade, multicentric, and extensive (approximately 8 cm); tumor cells were negative for estrogen and progesterone receptors; HER2 status was not assessed in the microinvasive foci due to their small size; and sentinel lymph nodes showed isolated tumor cells but no macrometastases.

What can be concluded from these findings regarding the biological behavior and clinical implications of this case of DCISM?

input_logic_chain.research_context: To determine the nature and biological behavior of metastatic lesions in a patient who died of rapidly progressive liver failure eight months after being diagnosed with microinvasive ductal carcinoma in situ (DCISM) and treated with mastectomy, sentinel lymph node biopsy, and immediate reconstruction, but without adjuvant systemic therapy.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological examination of liver tissue obtained at autopsy using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess the histopathological features of the liver lesions and determine whether they represent metastatic carcinoma.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Disrupted tissue architecture with dense cellular clusters and infiltrative growth patterns lacking organized trabecular or glandular structures typical of normal liver; pleomorphic, hyperchromatic nuclei with high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio; presence of mitotic figures; scant eosinophilic cytoplasm with occasional clear vacuolation; tumor cells arranged in poorly defined nests or diffusely scattered; minimal stromal fibrosis with one area showing dense fibrous tissue suggestive of desmoplastic reaction [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The architectural disarray, nuclear atypia, high mitotic activity, and infiltrative growth pattern are characteristic of malignant neoplasia. The presence of a desmoplastic reaction supports an invasive epithelial tumor, commonly seen in carcinomas. These features are inconsistent with benign or reactive processes.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The liver contains diffuse metastatic carcinoma with high-grade histological features.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining of liver tissue for hormone receptors and HER2 using chromogen-based detection.
experiments.experiment_goal: To determine the receptor status (estrogen, progesterone, HER2) of the metastatic tumor cells and compare it with the primary tumor characteristics.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Clusters of irregular epithelial cells arranged in gland-like structures with strong, intense brown chromogen staining localized to the cell membrane, showing continuous, circumferential, or patchy patterns at cell-cell junctions. Minimal background staining in stroma or non-target cells. The letter 'B' is visible in the lower-left corner [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: The strong, membranous brown staining pattern is diagnostic of HER2 protein overexpression in tumor cells. This staining is specific and uniform across tumor cell aggregates, consistent with HER2 positivity by immunohistochemistry (IHC) 3+.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The metastatic tumor cells in the liver are HER2-positive.

experiments.experimental_setting: Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) analysis of liver tissue using DNA probes targeting the HER2 gene and a control locus, with fluorescence microscopy.
experiments.experiment_goal: To confirm gene amplification of HER2 in the metastatic tumor cells.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Blue-stained nuclei (DAPI) with superimposed red fluorescent signals appearing as discrete punctate dots or small clusters within nuclei. The number of red signals varies between cells, with some showing multiple foci. The letter 'C' is visible in the lower-left corner [Image 3].
experiments.interpretation: The red fluorescent signals represent HER2 gene copies. The variability in signal number, including cells with multiple red foci, indicates HER2 gene amplification. A high HER2/CEP17 ratio (implied by signal abundance) confirms amplification, consistent with a FISH ratio >10 as mentioned in the text.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The metastatic tumor exhibits HER2 gene amplification.

experiments.experimental_setting: Review of primary tumor pathology from mastectomy specimen and sentinel lymph node biopsy, including receptor status and extent of microinvasion.
experiments.experiment_goal: To correlate the biological characteristics of the primary DCISM with the metastatic disease and understand the clinical course.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Microinvasive foci measuring up to 0.1 mm; DCIS was high-grade, multicentric, and extensive (approx. 8 cm); tumor cells negative for estrogen and progesterone receptors; HER2 status not assessed in microinvasive foci due to size [Context]. Sentinel lymph nodes showed isolated tumor cells but no macrometastases [Context].
experiments.interpretation: Despite minimal microinvasion (<1 mm), the tumor was biologically aggressive, with hormone receptor-negative phenotype. The presence of isolated tumor cells in sentinel nodes suggests early dissemination. The inability to test HER2 in microinvasive foci left a critical biomarker unknown.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The primary DCISM was high-grade, hormone receptor-negative, with minimal invasion and nodal micrometastatic spread, but HER2 status was undetermined.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The liver contains widespread metastatic carcinoma with histological features of high-grade malignancy.
The metastatic tumor is HER2-positive at both protein and gene levels.
The primary tumor was hormone receptor-negative and had minimal invasion but showed early nodal spread.

reasoning.content: The autopsy revealed diffuse liver metastases with histological features of aggressive carcinoma, including architectural disruption, nuclear pleomorphism, and mitotic activity [Image 1]. Immunohistochemistry showed strong membranous HER2 staining [Image 2], and FISH confirmed HER2 gene amplification [Image 3], establishing the metastatic tumor as HER2-positive. Although the primary DCISM had microinvasion ≤1 mm and was classified as T1mic, it was high-grade, hormone receptor-negative, and had spread to sentinel nodes as isolated tumor cells. The absence of HER2 testing in the microinvasive component meant this aggressive phenotype was not identified at diagnosis. Despite no adjuvant systemic therapy, the rapid development of fatal liver metastases within eight months indicates high biological aggressiveness. The metastatic tumor’s HER2 positivity, confirmed by both IHC and FISH, suggests that the primary microinvasive component likely harbored the same HER2-amplified clone, which was not detected due to sampling or testing limitations. This case demonstrates that DCISM, even with minimal invasion, can have metastatic potential when associated with aggressive molecular features such as HER2 amplification and hormone receptor negativity.
reasoning.conclusion: DCISM with hormone receptor-negative and HER2-amplified biology can exhibit aggressive metastatic behavior despite minimal microinvasion and absence of macrometastases in sentinel lymph nodes, indicating that molecular subtype, not just anatomical extent, determines clinical outcome.

question:
A 49-year-old female nonsmoker with stage IV lung adenocarcinoma harboring an ALK gene rearrangement was treated with crizotinib, which failed to induce a response, suggesting primary resistance. Subsequent plasma NGS revealed an EGFR exon 19 deletion, and treatment with the EGFR-TKI icotinib led to partial response, indicating a possible molecular transformation or co-occurrence of EGFR mutation contributing to primary resistance to ALK inhibition.

To investigate this case, the following experiments were conducted:

1. A needle core biopsy of a lung mass was obtained and processed for histopathological evaluation using Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) staining.

2. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) was performed on tumor tissue to detect ALK gene rearrangement using a split-signal probe design, with nuclei counterstained with DAPI and ALK signals labeled with red fluorophores.

3. ARMS assay (AmoyDx) was used on tumor tissue DNA to detect common EGFR mutations, including exon 19 deletions and L858R. The test result indicated wild-type EGFR.

4. Next-generation sequencing (NGS) was performed on circulating cell-free DNA from plasma (GeneSeeq One platform, Illumina HiSeq 4000) to detect somatic mutations after progression on crizotinib. The test detected an EGFR exon 19 deletion.

5. Chest CT scans were performed at baseline, during crizotinib treatment, and after initiation of icotinib to assess tumor response using RECIST 1.1 criteria. Initial CT showed a right lung mass and pleural metastasis. After crizotinib, CT demonstrated increased tumor size and metastatic burden. After icotinib, CT showed decreased tumor size.

What conclusions can be drawn from the integration of these findings, and what do they imply about the mechanisms of primary resistance to ALK inhibition in this patient?

Although tumor heterogeneity or a minor pre-existing EGFR-mutant subclone undetected by tissue testing could explain this, the clinical response to EGFR inhibition strongly supports a functional role of the EGFR mutation in driving resistance. question: The case report aims to confirm the diagnosis of a renal mass as inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor (IMT) based on histopathological and immunohistochemical findings, distinguishing it from renal cell carcinoma and other malignant or benign renal tumors. To evaluate the architectural and cytological features of the tumor, a histopathological examination of the resected renal tumor was performed using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining, viewed under light microscopy at low and high magnification. To assess cellular morphology and architectural patterns in greater detail, high-magnification H&E staining was used. Additionally, immunohistochemical staining was performed using antibodies against epithelial membrane antigen (EMA), actin, and other markers, with visualization via chromogenic detection. What can be concluded from these experiments regarding the nature and diagnosis of the renal mass?

input_logic_chain.research_context: The case report aims to confirm the diagnosis of a renal mass as inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor (IMT) based on histopathological and immunohistochemical findings, distinguishing it from renal cell carcinoma and other malignant or benign renal tumors.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histopathological examination of the resected renal tumor using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining, viewed under light microscopy at low and high magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess the architectural and cytological features of the tumor for diagnostic characterization.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: A thick, pink-stained, eosinophilic collagenous fibrous capsule is visible on the left side of the image, adjacent to a myxoid zone with a pale, bluish, gelatinous matrix containing scattered inflammatory cells. Centrally, there is a cellular region with spindle-shaped cells arranged in interlacing fascicles [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The eosinophilic capsule indicates a well-encapsulated tumor. The myxoid stroma with inflammatory infiltrate and the fascicular arrangement of spindle cells are characteristic of IMT, which typically shows a triphasic histologic pattern including fibrous, myxoid, and cellular zones.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The tumor exhibits histological features consistent with a well-encapsulated mesenchymal neoplasm showing myxoid and cellular zones with inflammatory infiltrate, supporting a diagnosis of IMT.

experiments.experimental_setting: High-magnification H&E staining of the tumor tissue to evaluate cellular morphology and architectural patterns.
experiments.experiment_goal: To identify specific cytological features such as nuclear atypia, mitotic activity, and stromal composition that help differentiate IMT from sarcomatoid or other spindle cell tumors.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Densely packed spindle-shaped cells arranged in parallel and interlacing fascicles with occasional whorled patterns. Cells have elongated, hyperchromatic nuclei, high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, minimal extracellular matrix, and occasional mitotic figures. No necrosis or epithelial structures are present [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: The fascicular and whorled growth of uniform spindle cells with minimal atypia and low mitotic rate, in the absence of necrosis or epithelial differentiation, is typical of IMT. This contrasts with high-grade sarcomas or sarcomatoid carcinoma, which usually show marked atypia, frequent mitoses, and necrosis.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The absence of high-grade malignant features and the presence of a fascicular spindle cell pattern support a benign or low-grade neoplastic process such as IMT rather than a high-grade sarcoma or renal cell carcinoma.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining of tumor tissue using antibodies against epithelial membrane antigen (EMA), actin, and other markers, with visualization via chromogenic detection (likely DAB, brown precipitate).
experiments.experiment_goal: To determine the immunophenotypic profile of the spindle cells and confirm their myofibroblastic origin while excluding other spindle cell neoplasms.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Brownish cytoplasmic staining of variable intensity in spindle-shaped cells arranged in interlacing fascicles and whorls. Staining is heterogeneous, with clusters of strongly positive cells and others showing weak or no staining. No glandular structures are present [Image 3].
experiments.interpretation: The brown cytoplasmic staining indicates positive immunoreactivity for a marker expressed in myofibroblasts. Given the context, this corresponds to focal positivity for actin and EMA, markers of myofibroblastic differentiation. Vimentin positivity (diffuse) further supports mesenchymal origin. Absence of cytokeratin, desmin, CD34, etc., rules out carcinomas, rhabdomyosarcoma, and vascular tumors.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The immunohistochemical profile—vimentin diffuse (+), actin and EMA focal (+), and negative for epithelial, melanocytic, and vascular markers—confirms the myofibroblastic nature of the tumor and supports the diagnosis of IMT.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The tumor is well-encapsulated and composed of spindle cells in a variable stromal background with inflammatory infiltrate, consistent with IMT histology.
The spindle cells show a fascicular and whorled pattern without necrosis, significant atypia, or epithelial differentiation, ruling out high-grade sarcoma or carcinoma.
The immunophenotype confirms myofibroblastic differentiation and excludes other spindle cell tumors.

reasoning.content: The histological examination reveals a well-encapsulated tumor with a characteristic zonation: fibrous capsule, myxoid stroma with inflammation, and a cellular spindle cell component. This architectural pattern aligns with the myxoid-vascular and compact spindle cell patterns described by Coffin et al. for IMT. The absence of necrosis, low mitotic activity, and lack of epithelial markers argue against renal cell carcinoma or sarcomatoid variants. Immunohistochemistry demonstrates vimentin positivity (mesenchymal origin), focal actin and EMA expression (myofibroblastic differentiation), and absence of cytokeratin, desmin, and other lineage-specific markers, effectively excluding carcinoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, angiomyolipoma, and other mimics. Together, these findings confirm a diagnosis of IMT, a benign-appearing but locally aggressive tumor that clinically mimics malignancy.
reasoning.conclusion: The renal mass is definitively diagnosed as inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor (IMT) based on its encapsulated architecture, spindle cell morphology with inflammatory background, and immunohistochemical profile confirming myofibroblastic origin, despite initial clinical suspicion of renal cell carcinoma.

question: Evaluation of the extent and histopathological characteristics of neuroendocrine lesions in the resected gastroduodenal specimen, including identification of tumor architecture, invasion depth, and metastatic potential, was performed. To identify and characterize all neuroendocrine lesions in the stomach cardia and duodenum, including those not visible macroscopically, histologic mapping of the entire resected specimen was carried out with 217 tissue sections processed into 109 formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded blocks, followed by microscopic examination and immunohistochemical staining for synaptophysin and chromogranin A. To determine the histological growth pattern and cellular features of the neuroendocrine tumors, histopathological examination of H&E-stained sections from the resected specimen was performed, focusing on architectural patterns and cellular morphology. To assess the histological features of the metastatic lesion and compare them with the primary tumors, a lymph node metastasis in station 3 was examined using H&E staining. To confirm neuroendocrine differentiation of the identified lesions, immunohistochemical analysis for synaptophysin and chromogranin A was performed on representative tumor sections, which showed positive immunoreactivity for both markers. To determine the T stage according to the AJCC 8th edition TNM classification, tumor invasion depth in the stomach and duodenum was assessed using histological sections from the mapped specimen, revealing that all duodenal lesions were located in the mucosa or submucosa, with the largest measuring 0.8 × 0.8 × 0.3 cm, and gastric lesions were in the lamina propria or submucosa, with the largest measuring 0.3 × 0.2 × 0.2 cm. To determine tumor grade according to WHO classification, Ki-67 index and mitotic count were evaluated in representative tumor sections, showing a Ki-67 index < 1% and mitotic activity < 1 per 10 high-power fields. To assess nodal metastasis for N staging, lymph node dissection and histological evaluation of 30 regional lymph nodes were performed, revealing metastasis in one lymph node in station 3, measuring 0.4 mm. What can be concluded from these findings regarding the nature, classification, and staging of the neuroendocrine lesions in this case?

input_logic_chain.research_context: Evaluation of the extent and histopathological characteristics of neuroendocrine lesions in the resected gastroduodenal specimen, including identification of tumor architecture, invasion depth, and metastatic potential.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histologic mapping of the entire resected specimen with 217 tissue sections processed into 109 formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded blocks, followed by microscopic examination and immunohistochemical staining for synaptophysin and chromogranin A.

experiments.visual_phenomenon: Microscopic examination revealed 14 neuroendocrine lesions in the duodenum and 5 in the stomach cardia, with only 3 of the 19 lesions visible macroscopically as submucosal nodules in the duodenum [Context].
experiments.interpretation: The majority of neuroendocrine lesions were microscopic, indicating that macroscopic inspection alone is insufficient for detecting early or small neuroendocrine tumors.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Neuroendocrine lesions in this case are predominantly microscopic and widely distributed in both the duodenum and stomach cardia.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histopathological examination of H&E-stained sections from the resected specimen, focusing on architectural patterns and cellular morphology.
experiments.experiment_goal: To determine the histological growth pattern and cellular features of the neuroendocrine tumors.

The stroma is fibrous and eosinophilic, with thin vascular channels and no necrosis [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The ribbon-like architectural pattern with uniform cytology and absence of necrosis is characteristic of well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumors (NETs), typically associated with low-grade behavior.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The duodenal neuroendocrine tumors exhibit a well-differentiated, low-grade histological pattern consistent with Grade 1 NET.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histopathological examination of a lymph node metastasis in station 3, stained with H&E.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess the histological features of the metastatic lesion and compare them with the primary tumors.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: In Image 2, the lymph node section shows nests, trabeculae, and gland-like structures of small to medium cells with hyperchromatic nuclei, finely granular chromatin, high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, and occasional mitoses. There is necrosis, hemorrhage, and infiltration into lymphoid tissue with residual follicles at the periphery [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: The disorganized, infiltrative growth with necrosis and mitotic activity in a nodal metastasis indicates a neuroendocrine neoplasm with malignant potential, though the cytology remains relatively uniform, supporting a well-differentiated NET rather than a poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The lymph node metastasis represents a well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor with malignant behavior, consistent with nodal spread of the primary disease.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical analysis for synaptophysin and chromogranin A on representative tumor sections.
experiments.experiment_goal: To confirm neuroendocrine differentiation of the identified lesions.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Positive immunoreactivity for synaptophysin and chromogranin A in tumor cells [Context].
experiments.interpretation: Expression of synaptophysin and chromogranin A confirms neuroendocrine lineage of the tumor cells.
experiments.sub_conclusion: All identified lesions are of neuroendocrine origin.

experiments.experimental_setting: Assessment of tumor invasion depth in the stomach and duodenum using histological sections from the mapped specimen.
experiments.experiment_goal: To determine the T stage according to the AJCC 8th edition TNM classification.

experiments.interpretation: Tumor invasion limited to mucosa or submucosa without deeper penetration corresponds to T1 stage in both stomach and duodenum.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The primary tumors in both stomach and duodenum are classified as T1.

experiments.experimental_setting: Evaluation of Ki-67 index and mitotic count in representative tumor sections.
experiments.experiment_goal: To determine tumor grade according to WHO classification.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Ki-67 index < 1% and mitotic activity < 1 per 10 high-power fields [Context].
experiments.interpretation: Low proliferative activity meets the criteria for Grade 1 neuroendocrine tumor.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The tumors are histologically low-grade (Grade 1).

experiments.interpretation: Presence of regional lymph node metastasis, even if small, qualifies for N1 staging.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: Neuroendocrine lesions are numerous and predominantly microscopic, located in both duodenum and stomach cardia.
The primary tumors exhibit well-differentiated histology with ribbon-like architecture and no necrosis, consistent with Grade 1 NET.
The lymph node metastasis shows infiltrative growth with necrosis but retains well-differentiated cytology, confirming malignant potential within a low-grade framework.
Immunohistochemistry confirms neuroendocrine origin of all lesions.
Tumor invasion is limited to mucosa/submucosa in both organs, supporting T1 staging.
Low Ki-67 and mitotic rate confirm Grade 1 classification.
Regional lymph node metastasis is present, leading to N1 staging.

reasoning.content: The histologic mapping revealed a high burden of microscopic neuroendocrine lesions in both the duodenum and stomach cardia, most of which were not detectable macroscopically. The primary tumors in the duodenum and stomach display classic features of well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumors, including uniform cells, ribbon-like or nested architecture, and low proliferative activity. Image 1 illustrates the typical organoid growth pattern of Grade 1 NET in the primary site, while Image 2 demonstrates that the metastatic deposit, though showing infiltrative growth and necrosis, retains neuroendocrine differentiation and lacks overt anaplasia. The presence of lymph node metastasis, even in a small focus, confirms regional spread. Combined with T1 invasion depth and Grade 1 morphology, the tumors meet the criteria for Stage T1, N1, Grade 1 in both locations. The absence of vascular, lymphatic, or perineural invasion in the primary tumors does not negate nodal metastasis, which is a known feature of some low-grade NETs.
reasoning.conclusion: The patient has multifocal, well-differentiated Grade 1 neuroendocrine tumors of the stomach and duodenum, staged as T1, N1, with widespread microscopic disease and regional lymph node metastasis, indicating early malignant behavior despite low-grade histology.

question: A 61-year-old woman presents with abnormal genital bleeding and is found to have a pedunculated cervical tumor, which is excised via a vaginal approach. Histological examination of the tumor specimen involves hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining and light microscopy analysis at low magnification, revealing a densely cellular tissue with cells arranged in sheets, nests, and irregular clusters, exhibiting architectural disorganization. The cells are polygonal to round with abundant cytoplasm that appears glassy and finely granular, ranging from pale pink to lavender, and contain dark purple, round to oval, centrally located nuclei that are hyperchromatic with vesicular chromatin and prominent nucleoli. Mitotic figures and foci of necrosis are identified, and the fibrous stroma is infiltrated by inflammatory cells. Cellular cohesion is reduced, with indistinct borders and a syncytial pattern. Higher magnification (400×) analysis of the same H&E-stained section shows tightly packed, disorganized epithelial cells with minimal stroma, a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, and nuclei that are pleomorphic, hyperchromatic, and variably shaped, some with prominent nucleoli. The cytoplasm is scant to moderate, eosinophilic, and in some cells has a pale, finely granular, glassy appearance. Cellular borders are indistinct, creating a syncytial growth pattern, and occasional mitotic figures are observed. Following these histological evaluations, imaging studies including MRI and 18-FDG PET/CT are performed, which show multiple hypermetabolic lymph nodes in the retroperitoneal and supraclavicular regions, with no residual tumor mass detected in the uterine cervix or body. What is the most appropriate diagnosis, and how do these findings collectively support this diagnosis?

input_logic_chain.research_context: Diagnosis of glassy cell carcinoma (GCC) of the uterine cervix based on histopathological features and clinical presentation in a 61-year-old woman with abnormal genital bleeding and metastatic disease.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological examination of a pedunculated cervical tumor specimen excised via vaginal approach; tissue sections were stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and analyzed under light microscopy at various magnifications.
experiments.experiment_goal: To determine the histological characteristics of the excised tumor and establish a diagnosis.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Densely cellular tissue architecture with cells arranged in sheets, nests, and irregular clusters, exhibiting disorganization and loss of normal structure. Polygonal to round cells with abundant, glassy, homogeneous, finely granular cytoplasm (pale pink to lavender). Nuclei are dark purple, round to oval, centrally located, hyperchromatic, with vesicular chromatin and prominent nucleoli. Mitotic figures and foci of necrosis are present. Stroma is fibrous and infiltrated by inflammatory cells. Cellular cohesion is reduced, with indistinct borders and syncytial pattern. [Image 1]
experiments.interpretation: The glassy, finely granular cytoplasm is a hallmark of GCC and results from abundant glycogen or mucin accumulation. Hyperchromatic, pleomorphic nuclei with prominent nucleoli indicate high-grade malignancy. Reduced cellular cohesion and architectural disarray suggest aggressive behavior. Lymphoplasmacytic stromal infiltration is a characteristic feature of GCC and supports the diagnosis.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The histological features observed are consistent with a diagnosis of glassy cell carcinoma of the cervix.

experiments.experimental_setting: Higher magnification (400×) analysis of the same H&E-stained tumor tissue section.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess cellular morphology and nuclear features in greater detail for diagnostic confirmation.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Tightly packed, disorganized epithelial cells with minimal stroma. High nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, hyperchromatic and pleomorphic nuclei of variable size and shape. Some nuclei show prominent nucleoli. Cytoplasm is scant to moderate, eosinophilic, and in some cells appears pale and finely granular, imparting a glassy appearance. Cellular borders are indistinct, creating a syncytial pattern. Mitotic figures are occasionally seen. [Image 2]
experiments.interpretation: The high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, nuclear pleomorphism, and frequent mitoses indicate rapid proliferation and poor differentiation. The glassy cytoplasmic appearance, even at high magnification, confirms the presence of abundant intracytoplasmic material typical of GCC. The syncytial growth pattern reflects loss of intercellular bridges, a known feature of GCC.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The high-magnification histological findings further confirm the diagnosis of poorly differentiated adenosquamous carcinoma with glassy cell features.

experiments.experimental_setting: Imaging studies including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and 18-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography (18-FDG PET/CT) performed after initial histological diagnosis.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate the extent of disease and detect residual or metastatic tumor.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Multiple hypermetabolic lymph nodes in retroperitoneal and supraclavicular regions on PET/CT; no residual tumor mass in the uterine cervix or body on MRI or PET/CT. [Context]
experiments.interpretation: The presence of FDG-avid lymph nodes indicates metabolically active metastatic disease. The absence of a primary tumor mass post-excision suggests complete removal of the visible lesion but confirms systemic spread at diagnosis.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The patient has primary metastatic GCC with no residual local tumor but widespread nodal metastases.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The tumor exhibits classic histopathological features of glassy cell carcinoma, including ground glass cytoplasm, prominent nucleoli, and stromal lymphoplasmacytic infiltration.
The disease is metastatic at presentation, with no residual local tumor but distant nodal involvement.

reasoning.content: The histological examination of the excised tumor reveals key diagnostic features of GCC: abundant glassy cytoplasm, nuclear pleomorphism, prominent nucleoli, reduced cellular cohesion, and stromal inflammatory infiltration—features consistently observed in both low- and high-magnification images [Image 1, Image 2]. These morphological characteristics align with the established diagnostic criteria for GCC. The absence of intercellular bridges and the syncytial growth pattern further support its poorly differentiated nature. Imaging studies confirm that despite complete excision of the primary lesion, the patient has widespread metastatic disease, as evidenced by hypermetabolic lymphadenopathy in retroperitoneal and supraclavicular regions. This indicates that the tumor was already systemically disseminated at diagnosis, classifying it as primary metastatic GCC. Together, the histopathological and imaging findings confirm both the rare histological subtype and the advanced clinical stage.
reasoning.conclusion: The patient has primary metastatic glassy cell carcinoma of the uterine cervix, diagnosed based on characteristic histopathological features and confirmed by imaging evidence of distant nodal metastases in the absence of residual local tumor.

question:
A 43-year-old woman was found to have a mediastinal mass on chest imaging, and a diagnostic core biopsy followed by surgical excision was performed. To confirm the diagnosis of the mediastinal mass as paraganglioma based on histopathological and immunohistochemical features, the following studies were conducted:

- Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining was performed on tissue sections obtained from the diagnostic core biopsy and subsequent surgical excision of the mediastinal mass. Representative high-magnification images of the H&E-stained sections are available for evaluation.

- Immunohistochemical staining for chromogranin A and synaptophysin was performed on the same tumor tissue section. Representative images of the immunohistochemical stains are also available for review.

Based on these investigations, what can be concluded regarding the nature and diagnosis of the mediastinal mass? Provide a detailed pathological reasoning process to support your conclusion.

input_logic_chain.research_context: To confirm the diagnosis of the mediastinal mass as paraganglioma (PGL) based on histopathological and immunohistochemical features.

experiments.experimental_setting: Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining was performed on a tissue section of the mediastinal mass obtained via diagnostic core biopsy and subsequent surgical excision.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate the histological architecture and cytological features of the mediastinal tumor.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The tissue shows well-defined, rounded nests of polygonal to round cells with granular cytoplasm and centrally located, round to oval nuclei, arranged in a zellballen pattern, separated by delicate fibrovascular stroma containing thin-walled capillaries. The cells are densely packed with uniform nuclear morphology and low mitotic activity. No necrosis is evident [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The zellballen pattern—characterized by cellular nests surrounded by sustentacular cells and vascular stroma—is a hallmark histological feature of paragangliomas. The uniform nuclei, low mitotic rate, and absence of necrosis suggest a benign or low-grade neuroendocrine neoplasm.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The histological architecture and cytology of the mediastinal mass are consistent with paraganglioma.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical (IHC) staining for chromogranin A and synaptophysin was performed on the same tumor tissue section.
experiments.experiment_goal: To confirm neuroendocrine differentiation of the tumor cells.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: A diffuse, intense brown chromogenic signal is observed in the cytoplasm and membranes of the tumor cells, with no staining in the stromal components [Image 3 and Image 4].
experiments.interpretation: Chromogranin A and synaptophysin are specific markers of neuroendocrine cells. Their strong and diffuse expression in tumor cells confirms neuroendocrine origin.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The tumor cells exhibit definitive neuroendocrine immunophenotype, supporting the diagnosis of paraganglioma.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The tumor exhibits classic zellballen architecture and uniform cytology typical of paraganglioma.
The tumor cells express neuroendocrine markers chromogranin A and synaptophysin diffusely and intensely.

reasoning.content: The H&E-stained sections demonstrate the characteristic zellballen pattern of paraganglioma, with nests of uniform neuroendocrine cells surrounded by vascular stroma [Image 1 and 2]. This architectural pattern, combined with low mitotic activity and absence of necrosis, is diagnostic of paraganglioma. Furthermore, immunohistochemical staining reveals strong cytoplasmic and membranous expression of chromogranin A and synaptophysin in the tumor cells [Image 3 and 4], which are definitive markers of neuroendocrine differentiation. The specificity of staining—limited to tumor cells with no background stromal reactivity—confirms the neoplastic cells' neuroendocrine lineage. Together, these findings fulfill the histopathological and immunohistochemical criteria for paraganglioma.
reasoning.conclusion: The mediastinal mass is histopathologically and immunophenotypically consistent with paraganglioma.

question: A 43-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis developed new-onset skin lesions after 10 months of infliximab therapy, presenting with erythematous, scaly plaques on the trunk, limbs, and scalp, along with palmoplantar pustules. To determine whether these lesions represent paradoxical psoriasis, a skin biopsy was performed from a plaque on the trunk or limb, fixed in formalin, embedded in paraffin, sectioned, and stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E), then examined under light microscopy at 100x magnification. A second examination of the same H&E-stained section was performed at 400x magnification to assess the dermal inflammatory infiltrate. Clinically, after switching from infliximab to adalimumab, there was worsening of palmoplantar scaling, an increase in erythematous scaly plaques, and new pustules on the lower limbs within two weeks. Following discontinuation of adalimumab, the patient was treated with cyclosporine, which led to clinical improvement, but the drug was later discontinued due to hypertension. Methotrexate was initiated at 7.5 mg/week, with dose escalation, but no improvement occurred. Six weeks after reintroducing leflunomide, the skin lesions went into remission. Based on these findings, what can be concluded about the nature and etiology of the skin lesions, and how do the histopathological and clinical data together support this conclusion?

input_logic_chain.research_context: To determine whether the skin lesions in a patient receiving anti-TNF therapy for rheumatoid arthritis represent paradoxical psoriasis, based on histopathological and clinical evidence.

experiments.experimental_setting: Skin biopsy from an erythematous, scaly plaque on the trunk or limb, fixed in formalin, embedded in paraffin, sectioned, and stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E). Examination performed under light microscopy at 100x magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate epidermal architecture and keratinization abnormalities consistent with psoriasis.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Epidermal thickening with elongated and undulating rete ridges, diminished or absent stratum granulosum, thickened stratum corneum with retained nuclei (parakeratosis), and scattered dark cells with dense nuclei within the stratum corneum [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: Epidermal hyperplasia with elongated rete ridges and loss of the granular layer are hallmark features of psoriasiform hyperplasia. Parakeratosis with intracorneal neutrophils (identified as small, dark, dense nuclei) indicates Munro microabscess formation, a characteristic finding in psoriasis.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The histopathological features observed are diagnostic of psoriasis vulgaris.

experiments.experimental_setting: Same H&E-stained skin biopsy section examined under light microscopy at 400x magnification to assess the dermal inflammatory infiltrate.
experiments.experiment_goal: To characterize the composition and distribution of the dermal inflammatory infiltrate to support a diagnosis of psoriasis and evaluate for drug-induced etiology.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Dense perivascular inflammatory infiltrate composed of small round dark nuclei (lymphocytes), multi-lobed nuclei with granular cytoplasm (neutrophils), and cells with bilobed nuclei and bright pink cytoplasmic granules (eosinophils), clustered around blood vessels [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: The presence of lymphocytes and neutrophils aligns with typical inflammatory patterns in psoriasis. The notable presence of eosinophils in the perivascular infiltrate is not typical in classic plaque psoriasis but is frequently associated with drug-induced or paradoxical psoriasis, suggesting a hypersensitivity or immune-mediated drug reaction.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The inflammatory infiltrate supports a diagnosis of psoriasis and suggests a possible drug-induced (anti-TNF) origin due to eosinophilic component.

experiments.experimental_setting: Clinical follow-up of skin lesions after switching from infliximab to adalimumab (both anti-TNF agents), with photographic documentation and physical examination over a two-week period.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess whether switching within the same class of biologic agents affects the severity of skin lesions.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Worsening of palmoplantar scaling, increase in erythematous scaly plaques, and new pustules on the lower limbs two weeks after initiating adalimumab [Context].
experiments.interpretation: The clinical worsening after switching to another anti-TNF agent suggests that the phenomenon is not specific to infliximab but likely reflects a class effect of TNF inhibition.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Paradoxical psoriasis in this patient is likely due to a class effect of anti-TNF drugs rather than an idiosyncratic reaction to infliximab alone.

experiments.experimental_setting: Treatment with cyclosporine (200 mg/day) after discontinuation of adalimumab, followed by methotrexate (7.5 mg/week, later increased) and finally reintroduction of leflunomide, with clinical monitoring of skin lesions.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate the response of paradoxical psoriasis to non-anti-TNF systemic therapies and determine effective management strategies.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Clinical improvement with cyclosporine, followed by worsening after its discontinuation due to hypertension; no improvement with methotrexate; remission of skin lesions six weeks after reintroduction of leflunomide [Context].
experiments.interpretation: Cyclosporine is effective in controlling paradoxical psoriasis but carries significant side effects. Methotrexate failed in this case, possibly due to inadequate dosing or resistance. Leflunomide, a non-biologic DMARD, ultimately induced remission, suggesting control of the underlying immune dysregulation without TNF inhibition.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Non-anti-TNF immunomodulatory agents can resolve paradoxical psoriasis when anti-TNF drugs are discontinued, especially if the underlying rheumatologic disease can be controlled by alternative means.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The histopathological features are diagnostic of psoriasis, confirmed by psoriasiform hyperplasia, parakeratosis with neutrophilic microabscesses, and characteristic inflammatory infiltrate.
The presence of eosinophils in the infiltrate and the temporal association with anti-TNF therapy suggest a drug-induced (paradoxical) etiology rather than pre-existing psoriasis.
Worsening of lesions upon switch to another anti-TNF agent indicates a class effect, not a drug-specific reaction.

Resolution of lesions with leflunomide after failure of other systemic therapies indicates that discontinuation of anti-TNF agents and use of alternative immunomodulators can lead to remission when the underlying disease is controllable.

reasoning.content: The patient presented with new-onset skin lesions during anti-TNF therapy for rheumatoid arthritis. Histopathological examination revealed classic features of psoriasis, including epidermal hyperplasia, loss of stratum granulosum, parakeratosis with neutrophilic microabscesses [Image 1], and a dermal perivascular infiltrate rich in lymphocytes and neutrophils [Image 2]. The presence of eosinophils in the infiltrate [Image 2] is atypical for idiopathic psoriasis but commonly reported in drug-induced or paradoxical forms, supporting a medication-triggered pathogenesis. The clinical course further supports this: lesions emerged after infliximab initiation, worsened after switching to adalimumab, and only resolved after discontinuation of all anti-TNF agents and reintroduction of leflunomide. The lack of improvement with methotrexate and cyclosporine’s partial efficacy followed by withdrawal due to toxicity highlight the therapeutic challenge. The ultimate remission with leflunomide indicates that controlling the underlying autoimmune condition without TNF inhibition allowed resolution of the paradoxical skin manifestation. This sequence confirms that the psoriasis was induced by anti-TNF therapy and that its management required both withdrawal of the causative drug class and effective alternative control of rheumatoid arthritis.
reasoning.conclusion: The patient developed paradoxical psoriasis as a class effect of anti-TNF inhibitors, confirmed by histopathological findings and clinical course, which resolved only after discontinuation of all anti-TNF agents and successful control of rheumatoid arthritis with non-biologic immunomodulatory therapy.

question: In a retrospective study of patients with early gastric cancer (EGC) who underwent gastrectomy with lymphadenectomy, histological evaluation was performed to assess the presence of lymph node metastasis (LNM) based on examination of resected lymph nodes. The specimens were serially sectioned into 3-mm-thick slices and stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E). Two experienced pathologists independently examined the slides immediately after resection under light microscopy at 20× and 200× magnification. Based on this research context and experimental setting, what conclusions can be drawn regarding the presence of lymph node metastasis in these patients, and what reasoning supports such conclusions?

Dense aggregation of cells with high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, arranged in irregular clusters, nests, and nodular formations of varying size and shape [Image 1]. Nuclei exhibit hyperchromasia, pleomorphism, and mitotic figures [Image 1]. Scattered clear spaces or vacuoles within cellular regions and eosinophilic stromal elements at periphery [Image 1].
