experiments.interpretation: The presence of large histiocytes with pale cytoplasm and nuclear eccentricity, along with architectural distortion and mixed inflammation, is consistent with a pathological infiltration of macrophages in the intestinal mucosa.
experiments.sub_conclusion: There is a dense, diffuse histiocytic infiltrate in the ileal lamina propria, indicating an underlying chronic inflammatory or infectious process involving the terminal ileum.

experiments.experimental_setting: Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS) staining of duodenal tissue at 200x magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To detect the presence of carbohydrate-rich intracellular material within histiocytes, which may indicate microbial organisms such as mycobacteria or fungi.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Foamy histiocytes with vacuolated cytoplasm containing magenta-stained material; nuclei displaced to periphery; PAS-positive staining localized to cytoplasmic vacuoles and surrounding matrix; disruption of normal villous architecture [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: PAS-positive staining within cytoplasmic vacuoles of histiocytes indicates the presence of polysaccharide-rich material, commonly associated with intracellular microorganisms such as Mycobacterium avium subspecies paratuberculosis (MAP) or other acid-fast organisms.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The histiocytes in the duodenal mucosa contain intracellular PAS-positive material, strongly suggesting an infection with a microorganism capable of surviving within macrophages.

experiments.experimental_setting: Colonoscopy and esophagogastroduodenoscopy with biopsy collection from terminal ileum and duodenum.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess mucosal abnormalities and obtain tissue for histopathological diagnosis.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Villous edema and white dotted infiltrates in the second portion of the duodenum; lymphangiectasia in the terminal ileum [Context].
experiments.interpretation: Villous edema and white infiltrates suggest mucosal inflammation and possible protein-losing enteropathy; lymphangiectasia indicates impaired lymphatic drainage, which can contribute to hypoalbuminemia and immune dysfunction.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Endoscopic findings support chronic intestinal inflammation with structural and functional compromise of the small bowel mucosa.

experiments.experimental_setting: Laboratory evaluation including complete blood count, inflammatory markers, and coagulation studies.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess systemic inflammation, nutritional status, and coagulation profile.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Anemia (hemoglobin 9.0 g/dL, hematocrit 28.8%), elevated ESR (32 mm/h), elevated CRP (48 mg/L), normal coagulation parameters, and thrombocytosis (468,000 platelets) [Context].
experiments.interpretation: Chronic inflammation is evidenced by elevated acute-phase reactants; anemia may be due to chronic disease or malabsorption; thrombocytosis can be reactive to inflammation and contributes to hypercoagulability.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The patient exhibits laboratory evidence of chronic systemic inflammation and a reactive prothrombotic state.

experiments.experimental_setting: Venous Doppler ultrasound of lower limbs performed initially and repeated after clinical deterioration.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate for deep vein thrombosis and venous recanalization.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Initial Doppler showed bilateral iliofemoral thrombosis; follow-up Doppler revealed extensive DVT in left lower limb and recanalization signs in right femoral vein [Context].
experiments.interpretation: Persistent and recurrent thrombosis despite anticoagulation suggests an underlying hypercoagulable condition; recanalization indicates partial resolution but ongoing vascular pathology.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The patient has recurrent, extensive venous thrombosis consistent with a persistent hypercoagulable state, likely driven by underlying systemic disease.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The patient has a chronic granulomatous inflammatory process in the small intestine characterized by histiocytic infiltration.
The histiocytic infiltrate contains intracellular PAS-positive material, indicating phagocytosed microorganisms.
Systemic inflammation and malabsorption are present, contributing to a prothrombotic state.
Recurrent deep vein thrombosis reflects sustained hypercoagulability.

reasoning.content: The histopathological findings in both ileum and duodenum reveal a diffuse infiltration of histiocytes with characteristic morphological features: large size, pale cytoplasm, eccentric nuclei, and foamy appearance. In the duodenum, PAS staining demonstrates magenta-positive material within cytoplasmic vacuoles [Image 2], confirming the presence of carbohydrate-rich intracellular content, typically associated with organisms such as Mycobacterium avium subspecies paratuberculosis (MAP), which causes Johne’s disease in ruminants and has been linked to human intestinal disorders resembling Crohn’s disease. The architectural distortion and transmural infiltration [Image 1] further support a chronic granulomatous process. Clinically, the patient’s chronic diarrhea, weight loss, protein-losing enteropathy (suggested by lymphangiectasia and hypoalbuminemia), and systemic inflammation (elevated CRP, ESR, reactive thrombocytosis) create a state fulfilling two components of Virchow’s triad: hypercoagulability (due to inflammation and possible cytokine-mediated coagulation activation) and endothelial dysfunction (from chronic infection and immune activation). The recurrent and extensive deep vein thrombosis, despite anticoagulation, underscores the persistence of this prothrombotic milieu. Improvement in gastrointestinal and inflammatory markers after treatment with ceftriaxone (a broad-spectrum antibiotic with activity against intracellular pathogens) and enoxaparin (an anticoagulant) suggests that both the infectious-inflammatory driver and the thrombotic complication were targeted. Thus, the histiocytic infiltration with PAS-positive material is not merely reactive but likely represents an active intracellular infection contributing to systemic inflammation and secondary thrombosis.
reasoning.conclusion: The patient likely suffers from a chronic enteric infection with an intracellular, PAS-positive microorganism (such as Mycobacterium avium subspecies paratuberculosis), which drives systemic inflammation, protein-losing enteropathy, and a hypercoagulable state, culminating in recurrent deep vein thrombosis. The histopathological and clinical evidence supports an infectious etiology underlying both gastrointestinal and thrombotic manifestations.

question:
A 65-year-old patient presents with a suspicious skin lesion, and fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) is performed as part of the initial evaluation. The aspirate is stained with May-Grünewald-Giemsa (MGG) for cytological assessment. Subsequently, a biopsy is obtained for further analysis. Histopathological examination is carried out using Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) staining on multiple tissue sections to evaluate the tissue architecture and cellular morphology. Additional histochemical analysis is performed using Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) staining on a biopsy tissue section to examine secretion composition. Finally, immunohistochemical staining for pancytokeratin (PanCK) and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) is conducted on the biopsy specimen to characterize the tumor cell phenotype.

The MGG-stained FNAC smear shows cellular material with atypical epithelial cells arranged in papillary clusters, sheets, and acini, exhibiting nuclear overcrowding and overlapping. The cells have moderate cytoplasm, a high nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio, mild anisonucleosis, hyperchromasia, and prominent nucleoli. Apocrine changes, including abundant cytoplasm with apical snouting, are noted in some columnar cells. The background contains foamy macrophages and hemorrhage.

The PAS stain reveals positive reactivity in both the cytoplasm of tumor cells and the luminal secretions. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrates strong positivity for PanCK and CEA in the tumor cells.

What is the most appropriate diagnosis for this lesion, and what integrated evidence supports this diagnosis?

input_logic_chain.research_context: Evaluation of a suspicious skin lesion using fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) and subsequent histopathological biopsy to determine the nature of the lesion, with emphasis on cytological and architectural features suggestive of malignancy and apocrine differentiation.

experiments.experimental_setting: Fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) was performed on the lesion, and the aspirate was stained with May-Grünewald-Giemsa (MGG) for cytological evaluation.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess the cytological features of the aspirated material for evidence of malignancy and cellular differentiation.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Cellular smears showing atypical epithelial cells arranged in papillary clusters, sheets, and acini with nuclear overcrowding and overlapping [Context]. The cells have moderate cytoplasm, high nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio, mild anisonucleosis, hyperchromasia, and prominent nucleoli. Apocrine changes observed in columnar cells include abundant cytoplasm with apical snouting [Context]. Background contains foamy macrophages and hemorrhage [Context].
experiments.interpretation: The presence of atypical epithelial cells in organized architectural patterns (papillary, acinar) with nuclear atypia (overlapping, hyperchromasia, prominent nucleoli) indicates a neoplastic epithelial process. High nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio and anisonucleosis support malignancy. Apocrine changes (e.g., cytoplasmic apical snouting) suggest apocrine differentiation. Foamy macrophages and hemorrhage in the background are consistent with cystic degeneration and necrosis, commonly seen in adenocarcinomas.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The cytological findings suggest a malignant epithelial neoplasm with features favoring adenocarcinoma and apocrine differentiation.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histopathological examination of a biopsy specimen using Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) staining.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate tissue architecture, cellular morphology, and evidence of invasion and differentiation.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Ulcerated squamous lining of the skin with underlying tumor infiltration in the subepidermis and dermis in a glandular pattern [Image 1]. Tumor cells are large with variable cytoplasm, large pleomorphic and vesicular nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and infrequent mitoses. Some gland lumina contain eosinophilic material consistent with decapitated apocrine secretions [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: Ulceration of the epidermis suggests aggressive local behavior. Glandular arrangement of infiltrating tumor cells in the dermis indicates invasive adenocarcinoma. Pleomorphic, vesicular nuclei with prominent nucleoli are hallmarks of malignancy. The presence of decapitated secretions—characterized by apical 'decapitation' of cytoplasm into lumina—is a hallmark of apocrine differentiation.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The histological architecture and cytology confirm an invasive malignant glandular neoplasm with apocrine features.

experiments.experimental_setting: H&E staining of another histological section focusing on glandular structures and cytoplasmic details.
experiments.experiment_goal: To further assess glandular morphology, cytoplasmic characteristics, and evidence of apocrine differentiation.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Irregular, infiltrative glandular structures within a fibrous stroma. Glands show distorted, dilated, or compressed lumina containing eosinophilic, granular, or amorphous secretions [Image 2]. Tumor cells exhibit abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, apical snouting, cytoplasmic blebbing, nuclear pleomorphism, and prominent nucleoli. The inset shows granular cytoplasmic texture and well-defined nuclei [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: Infiltrative glandular growth in a fibrous (desmoplastic) stroma supports malignancy. Apical snouting and cytoplasmic blebbing are morphological hallmarks of apocrine secretion. Granular cytoplasm reflects abundant secretory organelles typical of apocrine cells. Eosinophilic luminal secretions represent decapitation secretion, a defining feature of apocrine differentiation.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The tumor exhibits definitive morphological evidence of apocrine differentiation and invasive adenocarcinoma.

experiments.experimental_setting: Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) staining was performed on the biopsy tissue section.
experiments.experiment_goal: To detect the presence of intracytoplasmic and luminal glycoproteins, which are characteristic of apocrine secretions.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Cytoplasm of tumor cells and luminal secretions are positive for PAS stain [Context].
experiments.interpretation: PAS positivity in both cytoplasm and luminal secretions indicates the presence of glycoproteins and neutral mucins, which are abundantly produced by apocrine glands. This confirms active apocrine secretion by the tumor cells.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Biochemical evidence supports apocrine differentiation of the tumor cells.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining for pancytokeratin (PanCK) and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA).
experiments.experiment_goal: To confirm epithelial origin and glandular differentiation of the tumor.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Tumor cells are strongly positive for PanCK and CEA [Context].
experiments.interpretation: PanCK positivity confirms epithelial origin of the tumor cells. CEA is typically expressed in glandular and ductal epithelia, including apocrine glands, and its expression supports glandular differentiation and adenocarcinoma phenotype.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Immunohistochemical profile confirms epithelial and glandular nature of the tumor, consistent with adenocarcinoma.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The lesion is a malignant epithelial tumor based on cytological atypia, architectural disarray, and invasive growth.
The tumor exhibits definitive morphological and biochemical features of apocrine differentiation, including decapitation secretion, apical snouting, and PAS-positive secretions.
The tumor is of epithelial origin with glandular differentiation, confirmed by immunohistochemical expression of PanCK and CEA.

reasoning.content: The initial FNAC revealed atypical epithelial cells in papillary and acinar arrangements with nuclear atypia and apocrine cytomorphological changes, suggesting a malignant glandular lesion with apocrine features. The biopsy confirmed invasive growth of tumor cells in glandular patterns within the dermis, with ulceration of the overlying epidermis, supporting malignancy. The histological sections [Image 1 and Image 2] demonstrated classic apocrine features: decapitated secretions in gland lumina, apical snouting, cytoplasmic blebbing, and abundant granular cytoplasm. These morphological findings were corroborated by PAS positivity in both cytoplasm and secretions, confirming glycoprotein-rich apocrine secretion. Immunohistochemistry further established the epithelial and glandular nature of the tumor via strong PanCK and CEA expression. Together, these findings exclude benign or non-glandular tumors and support a diagnosis of primary adenocarcinoma with definitive apocrine differentiation.
reasoning.conclusion: The lesion is a primary apocrine adenocarcinoma, diagnosed based on cytological, histological, histochemical, and immunohistochemical evidence of malignant glandular epithelium with characteristic apocrine differentiation.

question: A 36-year-old man presented with hundreds of skin-colored, flat-topped papules confined to a 20-year-old black tattoo on his arms and forearms, with no prior skin eruptions in the tattooed areas and no systemic illness. The differential diagnosis included lichen nitidus, papular eczema, papular sarcoidosis, lichen planus, and verrucae planae. To establish a definitive diagnosis, a skin biopsy was taken from the right forearm within the tattooed area and processed for histopathological examination using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining. In a second examination, the same H&E-stained tissue section was analyzed specifically for cellular morphology in the spinous and granular layers of the epidermis. A third examination focused on the dermal layer of the same H&E-stained section to assess the presence and localization of tattoo pigment. What can be concluded from these clinical and histopathological findings?

input_logic_chain.research_context: A 36-year-old man presented with hundreds of skin-colored, flat-topped papules confined to a 20-year-old black tattoo on his arms and forearms, with no prior skin eruptions in the tattooed areas and no systemic illness. The differential diagnosis included lichen nitidus, papular eczema, papular sarcoidosis, lichen planus, and verrucae planae. Histopathological evaluation was performed to establish a definitive diagnosis.

experiments.experimental_setting: A skin biopsy was taken from the right forearm within the tattooed area and processed for histopathological examination using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate the epidermal and dermal histological features for diagnostic clues consistent with one of the differential diagnoses.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The epidermis shows orthokeratosis, papillomatosis, and areas of hypergranulosis. Enlarged keratinocytes with perinuclear clearing (halo-like appearance), nuclear hyperchromasia, and occasional binucleated cells are observed in the upper epidermal layers. The basal layer is preserved and the dermal-epidermal junction is intact. [Image 1]
experiments.interpretation: Orthokeratosis and papillomatosis are non-specific proliferative changes. Hypergranulosis and the presence of enlarged keratinocytes with perinuclear clearing (koilocytes) are hallmark cytopathic effects induced by human papillomavirus (HPV) infection. Nuclear hyperchromasia and binucleation further support viral-induced cellular changes. The preservation of the basal layer and dermal-epidermal junction argues against lichen planus or other interface dermatitides that typically disrupt this layer.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The epidermal changes are consistent with HPV-induced cytopathology, supporting a diagnosis of verrucae planae rather than lichen planus, lichen nitidus, or sarcoidosis.

experiments.experimental_setting: Same H&E-stained tissue section examined for cellular morphology in the spinous and granular layers of the epidermis.
experiments.experiment_goal: To identify the presence and distribution of koilocytes, which are pathognomonic for HPV infection.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Scattered enlarged cells in the upper spinous and granular layers exhibit perinuclear halos (pale-staining clearings) surrounding darkly stained, hyperchromatic nuclei. [Image 2]
experiments.interpretation: Perinuclear halos with nuclear atypia (hyperchromasia, irregular size) in differentiating keratinocytes are diagnostic of koilocytosis, a cytopathic effect classically caused by HPV, particularly types associated with verrucae planae (e.g., HPV types 3, 10).
experiments.sub_conclusion: The presence of koilocytes confirms HPV infection as the underlying etiology of the papules.

experiments.experimental_setting: Examination of the dermal layer in the H&E-stained biopsy section.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess the presence and localization of tattoo pigment and its relationship to the epidermal pathology.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Numerous darkly stained, irregularly shaped granular pigment deposits are observed in the dermis, predominantly in the deep dermis. These are either free in the interstitium or within dermal cells. The pigment is sharply delineated against the pink, fibrous collagen stroma. [Image 3]
experiments.interpretation: The dark granular pigment deposits are characteristic of exogenous tattoo ink, specifically black tattoo pigment (often carbon-based), localized in dermal macrophages and interstitial spaces. Their presence confirms the biopsy was taken from within the tattooed area and shows that the viral epidermal changes occur overlying persistent tattoo ink.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The histological findings are spatially associated with a pre-existing tattoo, confirming the clinical observation that the papules are confined to tattooed skin.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The epidermal histopathological changes—orthokeratosis, papillomatosis, hypergranulosis, and koilocytes—are diagnostic of HPV-induced epithelial alteration.
The koilocytes observed in the upper epidermis are pathognomonic for HPV infection, specifically supporting a diagnosis of verrucae planae.
The presence of abundant black tattoo pigment in the dermis confirms the biopsy site is within the tattoo and shows the epidermal pathology develops in direct anatomical relationship to the tattoo.

reasoning.content: The clinical presentation of numerous asymptomatic, skin-colored, flat-topped papules arising de novo within a long-standing tattoo raises several diagnostic possibilities, including inflammatory, granulomatous, and infectious etiologies. Histopathological analysis reveals key epidermal changes: papillomatosis and orthokeratosis indicate epidermal hyperplasia, while hypergranulosis and, most critically, koilocytes—enlarged keratinocytes with perinuclear halos and nuclear hyperchromasia—are hallmark features of HPV infection. These changes are most prominent in the upper spinous and granular layers [Image 2], and the basal layer remains intact, which is inconsistent with lichen planus (which typically shows liquefactive degeneration of the basal layer). The absence of granulomas rules out sarcoidosis, and the lack of spongiosis or vesiculation makes papular eczema less likely. The definitive identification of koilocytes confirms HPV etiology. Furthermore, the presence of dense, granular black pigment in the deep dermis [Image 3] confirms the biopsy was taken from within the tattoo, demonstrating that the HPV-induced lesions developed exclusively in tattooed skin. This spatial restriction suggests the tattoo may have altered local immune surveillance or provided a microenvironment conducive to HPV reactivation or persistence. Therefore, the integration of clinical, histological, and topographical data leads to a definitive diagnosis.
reasoning.conclusion: The patient has verrucae planae (flat warts) developing within a pre-existing tattoo, with histopathological confirmation of HPV-induced koilocytosis and spatial association with tattoo pigment in the dermis.

question:
To improve the diagnosis and stratification of lung cancer patients, particularly large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma (LCNEC), by identifying disease-specific protein expression patterns through proteomic analysis, with emphasis on distinguishing LCNEC from other high-grade lung cancers such as small cell lung carcinoma (SCLC) and large cell carcinoma (LCC), researchers conducted the following investigations. 

First, histological examination of lung tumor tissue sections was performed using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining at 200x magnification. 

Second, immunohistochemical (IHC) staining of lung tumor tissue was carried out using a monoclonal rabbit AL1A1 antibody, followed by visualization at 200x magnification. 

Third, laser capture microdissection (LCM) was used to isolate cancer cells from formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue specimens. Three aliquots from each sample were analyzed in random order using nano-liquid chromatography selected reaction monitoring mass spectrometry (nano-LC/SRM-MS). BSA and a project-wide standard (equal mixture of all 14 FFPE samples) were measured every 7th run for quality control. In this experiment, SRM transition peaks for each peptide were manually inspected in their extracted ion chromatograms (XICs) to confirm true positive signals. 

What conclusions can be drawn from the integration of these experimental approaches and observations?

input_logic_chain.research_context: To improve the diagnosis and stratification of lung cancer patients, particularly large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma (LCNEC), by identifying disease-specific protein expression patterns through proteomic analysis, with emphasis on distinguishing LCNEC from other high-grade lung cancers such as small cell lung carcinoma (SCLC) and large cell carcinoma (LCC).

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological examination of lung tumor tissue sections using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining at 200x magnification, as part of pathological investigations to assess tissue morphology.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate the histological features of lung neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) and assess their heterogeneity in tissue architecture and cellular morphology.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The tissue section shows densely packed cells arranged in nests, sheets, trabeculae, and irregular clusters, with minimal stroma. Cells have high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratios, hyperchromatic and pleomorphic nuclei, prominent nucleoli, scant cytoplasm, and indistinct cell borders. Numerous mitotic figures are visible. The stroma is fibrous and eosinophilic, with thin branching septa and delicate vasculature. Focal necrosis and inflammatory infiltrate are present. No glandular or squamous differentiation is observed. Staining shows dark purple nuclei and pink cytoplasmic/stromal components [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The architectural and cytological features—such as high mitotic rate, necrosis, nuclear pleomorphism, and absence of differentiation—are characteristic of high-grade neuroendocrine carcinomas. The disorganized growth pattern and morphological heterogeneity support the known pathological diversity among lung NETs.
experiments.sub_conclusion: LCNEC exhibits histological hallmarks of aggressive, poorly differentiated neuroendocrine tumors, confirming its classification as a high-grade malignancy and supporting the need for molecular distinction from other subtypes.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical (IHC) staining of lung tumor tissue using a monoclonal rabbit AL1A1 antibody, followed by visualization at 200x magnification to assess protein expression localization and intensity.
experiments.experiment_goal: To screen for heterogeneous expression of candidate proteins (e.g., AL1A1) in LCNEC and evaluate their potential as specific biomarkers.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Brown chromogen deposition is observed predominantly in the cytoplasm, with occasional membranous accentuation. Staining intensity varies from strong to faint or absent across cells. Brown-stained cells are interspersed with unstained or lightly counterstained (pale blue to bluish-gray) cells. Tissue architecture shows clusters and irregular patterns with indistinct borders and occasional luminal spaces [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: The heterogeneous cytoplasmic and focal membranous staining indicates variable expression of the AL1A1 protein among tumor cells, suggesting intra-tumoral molecular heterogeneity. The patchy distribution implies that AL1A1 may not be uniformly expressed across all tumor cells, potentially reflecting subclonal diversity or differential differentiation states.
experiments.sub_conclusion: AL1A1 shows variable and heterogeneous expression in lung tumor cells, indicating it may be a candidate marker with differential expression patterns that could aid in distinguishing tumor subtypes if validated across cohorts.

experiments.experimental_setting: Laser capture microdissection (LCM) was used to isolate cancer cells from formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue specimens. Three aliquots from each sample were analyzed in random order using nano-liquid chromatography selected reaction monitoring mass spectrometry (nano-LC/SRM-MS). BSA and a project-wide standard (equal mixture of all 14 FFPE samples) were measured every 7th run for quality control. SRM transition peaks were evaluated in extracted ion chromatograms (XICs), and peak areas were normalized using a reference standard via MultiQuant™ software.
experiments.experiment_goal: To perform a quantitative and selective proteomic screening for LCNEC-specific proteins by comparing expression profiles across LCNEC, LCC, and SCLC phenotypes.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: SRM transition peaks for each peptide were manually inspected in their extracted ion chromatograms (XICs) to confirm true positive signals. An example of such XICs is referenced in the text (Fig 2B), though not included in the provided visual evidence [Missing].
experiments.interpretation: The use of XICs allows verification of peptide detection specificity, minimizing false positives. Normalization to a reference and inclusion of QC standards (BSA and pooled sample) ensures technical reproducibility and comparability across runs.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The proteomic workflow enables reliable, reproducible quantification of protein expression across LCNEC, LCC, and SCLC, forming a robust foundation for identifying differentially expressed proteins with potential diagnostic utility.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: LCNEC exhibits histological features consistent with high-grade neuroendocrine tumors, including architectural disarray, high mitotic activity, and nuclear pleomorphism.
AL1A1 protein expression is heterogeneously distributed across tumor cells, suggesting molecular variability within the tumor tissue.
A rigorous, QC-controlled SRM-MS proteomic pipeline enables specific and quantitative comparison of protein expression across lung cancer subtypes.

reasoning.content: The study aims to refine the molecular characterization of LCNEC, a high-grade lung cancer subtype that is histologically and clinically similar to SCLC but requires precise diagnostic distinction. Histopathological analysis (Experiment 0) confirms that the tumor exhibits classic features of high-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma—such as solid growth patterns, nuclear atypia, and necrosis—supporting its aggressive nature and morphological overlap with other neuroendocrine tumors. This heterogeneity necessitates molecular tools for accurate classification. Immunohistochemical staining (Experiment 1) reveals variable AL1A1 expression, indicating that protein-level heterogeneity exists within the tumor, which may reflect functional or phenotypic diversity. This observation underscores the importance of quantitative proteomics to identify consistently dysregulated proteins. The SRM-MS workflow (Experiment 2) provides a high-specificity method to compare protein expression across LCNEC, LCC, and SCLC, minimizing technical variability and enabling detection of true biological differences. Together, these experiments establish that while histology confirms LCNEC as a distinct pathological entity, its molecular delineation requires deep proteomic profiling to uncover subtype-specific markers. The integration of morphological assessment with targeted proteomics creates a pathway toward improved diagnostic precision.
reasoning.conclusion: LCNEC is a morphologically heterogeneous, high-grade lung cancer that requires integrated histopathological and proteomic approaches for accurate molecular characterization; targeted proteomics using SRM-MS on microdissected FFPE tissues enables the identification of differentially expressed proteins that may serve as specific biomarkers for LCNEC diagnosis and stratification.

question:
A placental lesion is under evaluation to determine whether it represents a complete hydatidiform mole (CHM), androgenic mosaicism, or placental mesenchymal dysplasia (PMD), with the aim of confirming its diploid biparental origin. 

Histological examination was performed on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded placental tissue sections stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E). 

Immunohistochemical (IHC) staining for p57KIP2 was conducted on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded placental tissue sections using antigen retrieval and an automated stainer (BenchMark XT, Ventana). Nuclear staining for p57KIP2 is present in both hydropic and enlarged villi. 

Immunohistochemical staining for desmin was performed on placental tissue sections using the standard avidin-biotin-peroxidase technique and automated stainer, with antigen retrieval in citrate buffer (pH 6.0). 

Immunohistochemical staining for smooth muscle actin (SMA) was performed on the same tissue sections under identical conditions as desmin staining. 

Karyotyping using GTG banding was carried out on tissues from umbilical cord, cystic placental tissue, and adjacent normal placenta. A normal female karyotype (46, XX) was identified in all examined tissues. 

Short tandem repeat (STR) analysis using 15 markers was performed on DNA from maternal blood, paternal blood, fetal umbilical cord, and cystic placental tissue. Fifteen STR markers were identical between fetus and cystic placental tissue. All 12 informative loci confirmed biparental inheritance. 

What can be concluded from these findings?

input_logic_chain.research_context: Determine whether the placental lesion represents a complete hydatidiform mole (CHM), androgenic mosaicism, or placental mesenchymal dysplasia (PMD) based on morphological and immunohistochemical features, and confirm its diploid biparental origin.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological examination of formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded placental tissue sections stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E).
experiments.experiment_goal: Assess the architectural and cellular morphology of chorionic villi to identify features typical of PMD or hydatidiform mole.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Enlarged stem villi that are variably sized and shaped, many markedly cystic with irregular contours and a dense, fibrous appearance. The stroma is expanded and densely populated with spindle-shaped cells having elongated, hyperchromatic nuclei (dark blue staining). The interstitial matrix shows prominent eosinophilic (pink) staining, indicating collagenous deposition. Stromal fibrosis is evident, with thickened connective tissue and partial effacement of normal villous architecture. Some areas contain acellular or vacuolated spaces. A higher magnification inset confirms densely packed fibroblast-like cells in a collagenous stroma [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The presence of enlarged, cystic stem villi with dense fibrous stroma, spindle-shaped stromal cells, and stromal fibrosis is characteristic of mesenchymal overgrowth and architectural distortion typical of placental mesenchymal dysplasia (PMD), rather than the avascular, hydropic villi of complete hydatidiform mole.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The histological morphology supports a diagnosis of PMD rather than complete hydatidiform mole.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical (IHC) staining for p57KIP2 on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded placental tissue sections, using antigen retrieval and an automated stainer (BenchMark XT, Ventana).
experiments.experiment_goal: Determine the parental origin of the placental tissue by assessing nuclear expression of p57KIP2, a maternally expressed imprinted gene product absent in androgenetic (paternal-only) cells.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Nuclear staining for p57KIP2 is present in both hydropic and enlarged villi [Context].
experiments.interpretation: p57KIP2 is expressed only when a maternal allele is present. Nuclear positivity excludes pure androgenetic origin (as seen in complete hydatidiform mole) and supports biparental contribution.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The placental tissue has a biparental genomic origin, ruling out complete hydatidiform mole and androgenetic mosaicism.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining for desmin on placental tissue sections using standard avidin-biotin-peroxidase technique and automated stainer, with antigen retrieval in citrate buffer (pH 6.0).
experiments.experiment_goal: Assess stromal cell differentiation in enlarged villi to support diagnosis of PMD, as desmin expression in stromal cells is a known feature of PMD.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Stromal cells within enlarged stem villi show immunoreactivity for desmin, appearing as red, reddish-brown, or purple cytoplasmic staining. Staining is variable in intensity and distribution—some regions show dense clusters, others scattered cells. The inset shows granular and diffuse cytoplasmic staining in spindle-shaped cells. Trophoblastic layers remain unstained [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: Desmin positivity in villous stromal cells indicates abnormal mesenchymal differentiation and myofibroblastic or smooth muscle-like metaplasia, a hallmark of PMD. The absence of staining in trophoblasts confirms specificity to stromal lineage.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Aberrant desmin expression in stromal cells supports the diagnosis of PMD.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining for smooth muscle actin (SMA) on the same tissue sections under identical conditions as desmin staining.
experiments.experiment_goal: Evaluate whether stromal cells in dysplastic villi retain normal smooth muscle differentiation, as decreased SMA expression is a feature of PMD.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: There is absence of red or brown chromogenic signal in stromal cells of large, cystic stem villi, despite preserved staining in vascular endothelial cells. The higher magnification inset confirms lack of immunoreactivity in spindle-shaped stromal cells within a myxoid stroma [Image 3].
experiments.interpretation: Loss of SMA expression in stromal cells indicates abnormal differentiation of mesenchymal cells, deviating from normal perivascular smooth muscle phenotype. Retained endothelial staining serves as internal positive control, validating technical adequacy.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Decreased smooth muscle actin expression in stromal cells is consistent with mesenchymal dysplasia and supports PMD diagnosis.

experiments.experimental_setting: Karyotyping using GTG banding on tissues from umbilical cord, cystic placental tissue, and adjacent normal placenta.
experiments.experiment_goal: Determine chromosomal ploidy to exclude triploidy or aneuploidy, which are associated with hydatidiform moles.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: A normal female karyotype (46, XX) was identified in all examined tissues [Context].
experiments.interpretation: Diploid karyotype in multiple tissues rules out triploidy or aneuploidy, which are typical of partial or complete hydatidiform moles.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The conceptus is diploid, excluding molar pregnancy due to abnormal ploidy.

experiments.experimental_setting: Short tandem repeat (STR) analysis using 15 markers on DNA from maternal blood, paternal blood, fetal umbilical cord, and cystic placental tissue.
experiments.experiment_goal: Determine genetic consistency across tissues and confirm zygosity to exclude mosaicism or dizygosity.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Fifteen STR markers were identical between fetus and cystic placental tissue. All 12 informative loci confirmed biparental inheritance [Context].
experiments.interpretation: Genetic identity across fetal and placental tissues indicates monoclonal origin from a single zygote. Biparental inheritance at all informative loci excludes androgenetic or parthenogenetic mosaicism.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The PMD placenta is diploid and biparental, arising from a single fertilized egg without mosaicism.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The placental lesion exhibits morphological features characteristic of PMD, including enlarged, cystic stem villi with fibrous stroma and spindle-shaped stromal cells.
The tissue is not of androgenetic origin, as p57KIP2 is expressed in villous nuclei.
Aberrant mesenchymal differentiation is confirmed by desmin positivity and smooth muscle actin negativity in stromal cells.
The conceptus is genetically diploid and monoclonal, with biparental contribution.

reasoning.content: The histological architecture—enlarged, cystic stem villi with fibrotic stroma and spindle-shaped stromal cells—aligns with PMD rather than hydatidiform mole. The presence of p57KIP2 nuclear staining excludes androgenetic origin, ruling out complete mole. Desmin expression in stromal cells, coupled with loss of smooth muscle actin, reflects abnormal mesenchymal differentiation, a hallmark of PMD. The diploid karyotype (46, XX) in all tissues and STR-confirmed genetic identity between fetus and placenta demonstrate that the lesion arose from a single, biparental zygote without mosaicism or triploidy. Together, these findings confirm that the placental abnormality is not a molar pregnancy but a rare case of PMD with mild trophoblastic hyperplasia. The presence of a hepatic hamartoma in the neonate further supports this diagnosis, as it is a known association with PMD.
reasoning.conclusion: This case represents a rare diploid, biparental placental mesenchymal dysplasia (PMD) with PHM-like morphology, confirmed by histology, immunohistochemistry (p57KIP2+, desmin+, SMA−), and genetic analysis (46,XX; STR-confirmed monoclonal biparental origin), excluding hydatidiform mole or mosaicism.

question: A patient presents with dysphagia, odynophagia, and chest discomfort. Endoscopy reveals a proximal esophageal stricture with mucosal fragility (Koebner phenomenon). Initial esophageal biopsies showed non-specific inflammation. An oral examination identifies gingival erosions. An oral mucosal biopsy is performed and processed with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining. Subsequently, an esophageal biopsy is obtained during endoscopy and similarly processed with H&E staining. Three months after initiating systemic corticosteroid therapy, a follow-up esophageal biopsy is performed and processed with H&E staining. What can be concluded from these findings and procedures?

input_logic_chain.research_context: Diagnosis of esophageal lichen planus (ELP) in a patient presenting with dysphagia, odynophagia, and chest discomfort, supported by histopathological and endoscopic findings.

experiments.experimental_setting: Oral mucosal biopsy was performed and histological sections were stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) for microscopic evaluation.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate the presence of histopathological features consistent with oral lichen planus.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: A dense cellular infiltrate composed of small, round to slightly irregular cells with hyperchromatic, condensed nuclei and scant cytoplasm is observed in the lamina propria, beneath an intact epithelium. The stroma shows a pale eosinophilic matrix. The transition between infiltrated and non-infiltrated areas is abrupt but lacks a distinct border [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The dense, band-like lymphocytic infiltrate in the lamina propria with basal cell damage is a hallmark histological feature of lichen planus. The presence of hyperchromatic, small mononuclear cells indicates a T-cell–rich inflammatory response typical of lichenoid tissue reaction.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The histological findings from the oral mucosa biopsy are consistent with a diagnosis of oral lichen planus.

experiments.experimental_setting: Esophageal biopsy was obtained during endoscopy and processed for H&E staining to assess mucosal architecture and inflammatory changes.
experiments.experiment_goal: To identify histopathological features specific to esophageal lichen planus.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The stratified epithelium shows increased intercellular spacing (spongiosis), particularly in upper layers, and scattered individual cells with pyknotic or fragmented nuclei and eosinophilic cytoplasm, some marked by arrowheads. A dense accumulation of small, darkly stained mononuclear cells is present in the superficial lamina propria, extending toward the basement membrane. Focal epithelial architectural disruption, including cellular crowding and loss of maturation gradient, is noted [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: Spongiosis indicates intercellular edema due to immune-mediated damage. The presence of necrotic keratinocytes with pyknotic nuclei (Civatte bodies) is a diagnostic feature of lichen planus. The dense superficial inflammatory infiltrate supports a lichenoid tissue reaction involving the esophageal mucosa.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The esophageal biopsy demonstrates histopathological features diagnostic of esophageal lichen planus, including spongiosis and Civatte bodies.

experiments.experimental_setting: Follow-up esophageal biopsy was performed 3 months after initiation of systemic corticosteroid therapy, with H&E staining used to assess treatment response.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate histological improvement following corticosteroid treatment.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The stratified epithelium shows multiple layers with uniform nuclear distribution, clearly defined cell boundaries, and preservation of the epithelial-stromal interface. The basal layer contains densely packed small nuclei, while superficial layers show larger, sparsely distributed nuclei with lighter cytoplasm. Scattered small, darkly stained cells are present focally in the basal and parabasal regions but decrease toward the surface. No ulceration or architectural disruption is observed [Image 3].
experiments.interpretation: The restoration of normal epithelial maturation, reduced inflammatory cell density, and preserved basement membrane indicate resolution of active lichenoid inflammation. The focal presence of lymphocytes suggests residual but quiescent immune activity.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Histological findings after corticosteroid treatment show significant improvement in epithelial architecture and reduced inflammation, consistent with clinical remission of ELP.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The patient has oral lichen planus, as confirmed by histopathological examination of gingival lesions showing a dense lymphocytic infiltrate in the lamina propria.
The esophageal mucosa exhibits specific histopathological features of lichen planus, including spongiosis and Civatte bodies, supporting a diagnosis of esophageal lichen planus.
Systemic corticosteroid therapy led to histological normalization of the esophageal epithelium and reduction in inflammatory infiltrate.

reasoning.content: The patient presented with dysphagia and odynophagia, and endoscopy revealed a proximal esophageal stricture with mucosal fragility (Koebner phenomenon). Although initial biopsies showed non-specific inflammation, subsequent evaluation of oral lesions revealed histopathological features diagnostic of oral lichen planus—specifically, a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate in the lamina propria beneath intact epithelium [Image 1]. This finding raised suspicion for lichen planus affecting other mucosal sites. A repeat esophageal biopsy demonstrated key diagnostic features of lichen planus: spongiosis and the presence of Civatte bodies (necrotic keratinocytes) within the epithelium, along with a dense superficial inflammatory infiltrate [Image 2]. These findings, though submucosal lichenoid inflammation was not sampled, were deemed sufficient to support a diagnosis of esophageal lichen planus in the clinical context. Following systemic corticosteroid therapy, a follow-up biopsy showed architectural restoration of the epithelium, uniform nuclear distribution, and reduced inflammatory cellularity [Image 3], indicating histological remission. The temporal association between treatment initiation and symptom resolution, along with histological improvement, confirms the therapeutic response.
reasoning.conclusion: The patient has esophageal lichen planus, diagnosed based on characteristic histopathological findings in both oral and esophageal mucosa, which responded clinically and histologically to systemic corticosteroid therapy.

question:
A 62-year-old woman underwent laparoscopic resection of a gastric lesion suspected preoperatively to be a gastrointestinal stromal tumour. The resected specimen was subjected to a series of histopathological and immunohistochemical analyses to determine its nature. The research context is to determine the histopathological and immunohistochemical characteristics of the resected gastric lesion to establish a diagnosis of IgG4-related autoimmune fibrosclerosing pseudotumour.

Histopathological examination of the resected specimen was performed using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining, viewed at 40x magnification [Image 1].

Immunohistochemical staining for IgG4 was performed on the tissue section, visualized at 40x magnification with chromogenic detection (brown DAB signal) [Image 2].

An immunohistochemical panel was applied to the resected specimen, including DOG1, CD117, S100, desmin, ALK, cytokeratin, actin, CD34, EMA, and IgG4. The results showed negative staining for DOG1, CD117, S100, desmin, ALK, and cytokeratin in the spindle cells; actin was equivocal; CD34 was positive in the spindle cells. EMA and IgG4 stained the plasma cells.

Quantitative assessment of IgG4-positive cells was performed on the IgG4-stained section, revealing an average of 39 IgG4-positive lymphoplasmacytic cells per high-power field.

What can be concluded from these findings?

input_logic_chain.research_context: Determine the histopathological and immunohistochemical characteristics of the resected gastric lesion to establish a diagnosis of IgG4-related autoimmune fibrosclerosing pseudotumour.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histopathological examination of the resected specimen using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining, viewed at 40x magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: Assess the cellular composition, architectural pattern, and stromal features of the lesion.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Dense arrangement of plump spindle-shaped cells with elongated, ovoid to fusiform nuclei and indistinct cytoplasmic borders, embedded in a pale pink, fibrillar stroma. Intensely pink eosinophilic regions are interspersed. Smaller round to oval darkly stained inflammatory cells are scattered throughout. Disorganized cell orientation and variable staining intensity across the field [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The spindle cells arranged in interweaving fascicles within a fibrous, eosinophilic stroma suggest a mesenchymal neoplasm or reactive fibroblastic proliferation. The presence of abundant inflammatory cells, including lymphocytes and eosinophils, supports a chronic inflammatory process.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The lesion is composed of spindle cells in a fibrosclerotic stroma with a prominent mixed inflammatory infiltrate, consistent with a fibroinflammatory pseudotumour rather than a typical sarcoma.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining for IgG4 on the resected tissue section, visualized at 40x magnification with chromogenic detection (brown DAB signal).
experiments.experiment_goal: Identify and quantify IgG4-positive plasma cells within the inflammatory infiltrate to evaluate for IgG4-related disease.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Numerous round to oval cells with visible nuclei and surrounding cytoplasm show strong, granular to diffuse brown cytoplasmic staining. These brown-stained cells are interspersed among smaller, round cells with pale blue nuclei lacking brown signal. Spindle cells and lymphocytes remain unstained. The stained cells are distributed heterogeneously, some isolated, some loosely clustered [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: The brown cytoplasmic staining indicates expression of IgG4 in plasma cells. The presence of numerous IgG4-positive cells, alongside IgG4-negative lymphocytes and spindle cells, confirms a polyclonal plasma cell infiltrate enriched for IgG4-secreting cells.
experiments.sub_conclusion: There is a significant infiltration of IgG4-positive plasma cells within the lesion, supporting the diagnosis of IgG4-related disease.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical panel including DOG1, CD117, S100, desmin, ALK, cytokeratin, actin, CD34, EMA, and IgG4 on the resected specimen.
experiments.experiment_goal: Exclude other spindle cell neoplasms (e.g., GIST, schwannoma, sarcoma) and confirm the immunophenotype of the spindle cell population and plasma cells.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Negative staining for DOG1, CD117, S100, desmin, ALK, and cytokeratin in spindle cells; actin is equivocal; CD34 is positive in spindle cells. EMA and IgG4 stain the plasma cells [Context].
experiments.interpretation: The absence of markers for gastrointestinal stromal tumour (CD117, DOG1), neural differentiation (S100), muscle differentiation (desmin), and epithelial origin (cytokeratin) rules out common spindle cell neoplasms. CD34 positivity in spindle cells is consistent with a fibroblastic or vascular-associated phenotype. IgG4 and EMA positivity in plasma cells confirms their identity and clonal skewing toward IgG4 secretion.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The spindle cell population lacks markers of malignancy or specific lineage, supporting a reactive, non-neoplastic process. The plasma cell population is phenotypically consistent with IgG4-related disease.

experiments.experimental_setting: Quantitative assessment of IgG4-positive cells per high-power field (HPF) on the IgG4-stained section.
experiments.experiment_goal: Determine if the density of IgG4-positive plasma cells meets diagnostic criteria for IgG4-related disease.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: An average of 39 IgG4-positive lymphoplasmacytic cells per high-power field [Context].
experiments.interpretation: A count of >10 IgG4-positive cells/HPF is considered supportive of IgG4-related disease; counts >30/HPF are highly suggestive, especially in the appropriate histopathological context.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The IgG4-positive cell count exceeds the threshold for diagnostic significance, reinforcing the likelihood of IgG4-related disease.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The lesion exhibits histopathological features of a fibrosclerotic spindle cell proliferation with chronic inflammation, including eosinophils and plasma cells.
There is a prominent IgG4-positive plasma cell infiltrate within the lesion, with a density of 39/HPF, well above the diagnostic threshold.
The spindle cells lack immunophenotypic markers of neoplastic or specific lineage-derived tumours, supporting a reactive aetiology.

This architecture is not typical of sarcomas but resembles fibroinflammatory pseudotumours. Immunohistochemistry demonstrates numerous IgG4-positive plasma cells [Image 2], with a quantified density of 39 per HPF—exceeding the accepted threshold for IgG4-related disease. The absence of DOG1, CD117, and other neoplastic markers excludes GIST and other spindle cell tumours. CD34 positivity in spindle cells and IgG4/EMA positivity in plasma cells further support a diagnosis of IgG4-related fibrosclerosing pseudotumour. Although serum IgG4 was normal post-resection, tissue-based criteria are sufficient for diagnosis, especially in localized disease. The lesion extending to the margin raises concern for incomplete resection, but clinical recovery suggests low immediate risk.
reasoning.conclusion: The resected gastric lesion is consistent with an IgG4-related autoimmune fibrosclerosing pseudotumour based on histopathological, immunohistochemical, and quantitative criteria, despite normal postoperative serum IgG4 levels.

question: A 44-year-old male patient presented with progressive neurological deficits, including extremity weakness and incontinence. MRI revealed diffuse, creeping-growth nodular meningeal masses involving the skull base, tentorium, sella, and C1–C6 vertebral levels, initially raising suspicion for an inflammatory process. Following partial resection, histopathological and immunohistochemical analyses were performed. Histological examination of the resected meningeal tissue was conducted using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining at 100x magnification. Immunohistochemical staining for epithelial membrane antigen (EMA) was performed with chromogen visualization at ×400 magnification. Additional immunohistochemical staining for CD20 and CD138 was also carried out using chromogen visualization at high magnification. Based on these studies, what is the most appropriate diagnosis, and how do the findings collectively support this diagnosis?

input_logic_chain.research_context: A 44-year-old male patient presented with progressive neurological deficits, and imaging revealed diffuse, creeping-growth nodular meningeal masses involving the skull base, tentorium, sella, and C1–C6 vertebral levels. experiments.experimental_setting: Histological examination of resected meningeal tissue using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining at 100x magnification.

experiments.visual_phenomenon: Dense infiltration of small, round, darkly stained cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and some cells showing eccentric nuclei with perinuclear clearing, distributed throughout a fibrous, eosinophilic stroma containing wavy collagen fibers and spindle-shaped stromal cells. The lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate partially obscures underlying tumor architecture. No necrosis or hemorrhage is observed [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The presence of numerous lymphocytes and plasma cells, identified by their characteristic nuclear morphology and perinuclear clearing, indicates a prominent inflammatory infiltrate. The fibrous stroma with spindle-shaped cells is consistent with meningothelial components, while the extensive lymphoplasmacytic infiltration disrupts normal tumor architecture.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The lesion exhibits a histological pattern dominated by lymphoplasmacytic infiltration within a fibrous stromal background, consistent with a lymphoplasmacyte-rich meningioma (LRM).

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining for epithelial membrane antigen (EMA) using chromogen visualization at ×400 magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To identify meningothelial tumor cells based on EMA expression.

experiments.interpretation: EMA is a well-established marker for meningothelial cells. The membranous staining pattern in a reticular network confirms the presence of neoplastic meningothelial cells organized in cohesive clusters, despite the dense inflammatory background.
experiments.sub_conclusion: EMA-positive membranous networks confirm the presence of meningioma components within the lesion.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining for CD20 using chromogen visualization at ×400 magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To identify B-lymphocytes within the inflammatory infiltrate.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Brown staining localized to the cell membrane and cytoplasm of scattered round to oval cells with variable nuclear size. Positively labeled cells are distributed heterogeneously, forming clusters or appearing isolated, with arrowheads highlighting immunoreactive cells [Image 3].
experiments.interpretation: CD20 is a specific marker for B-lymphocytes. The presence of CD20-positive cells confirms a B-cell component within the lymphocytic infiltrate, contributing to the lymphoplasmacytic nature of the lesion.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The inflammatory infiltrate includes a B-lymphocyte population, supporting the lymphoplasmacytic characterization of the tumor.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining for CD138 using chromogen visualization at high magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To identify plasma cells within the inflammatory infiltrate.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Brown cytoplasmic and membranous staining in cells with rounded to irregular nuclei and moderate cytoplasm, distributed in clusters and singly. Arrowheads indicate specific positively stained cells. Background tissue shows pale counterstaining [Image 4].
experiments.interpretation: CD138 is a specific marker for plasma cells. The presence of CD138-positive cells, some also positive for IgG and IgG4, confirms the plasma cell component of the infiltrate, which is a hallmark of LRM.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The lesion contains a significant plasma cell infiltrate, including IgG4-positive cells, consistent with lymphoplasmacyte-rich meningioma.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The lesion is composed of meningothelial tumor cells embedded in a stroma heavily infiltrated by lymphocytes and plasma cells.
The inflammatory infiltrate includes both B-lymphocytes (CD20+) and plasma cells (CD138+, IgG/IgG4+), confirming a lymphoplasmacytic phenotype.
The tumor cells are positive for EMA, P63, and PR, and negative for GFAP, Oligo2, and CK, supporting a meningioma origin without glial, oligodendroglial, or epithelial carcinoma features.

reasoning.content: The histological and immunohistochemical findings collectively demonstrate a neoplastic process with meningothelial differentiation (EMA+, P63+, PR+) accompanied by a prominent lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate. The dense infiltration of CD20+ B-cells and CD138+ plasma cells, some IgG4+, disrupts the underlying tumor architecture, a defining feature of lymphoplasmacyte-rich meningioma (LRM). The absence of necrosis, hemorrhage, or non-meningothelial markers further supports a diagnosis of LRM rather than a metastatic carcinoma or glial tumor. The radiological presentation of diffuse, creeping-growth meningeal masses involving multiple cranial and spinal regions is atypical for conventional meningiomas but has been reported in rare LRM cases. The histopathological confirmation of meningioma components amidst overwhelming inflammatory infiltration confirms that the radiologically observed lesions are neoplastic rather than purely inflammatory.
reasoning.conclusion: The patient has lymphoplasmacyte-rich meningioma (LRM) characterized by meningothelial tumor cells extensively infiltrated by B-lymphocytes and plasma cells, including IgG4-positive subsets, with a rare creeping-growth radiological pattern involving the skull base and spinal meninges.

question:
A 1.7 x 1.1 x 0.4 cm intracardiac mass was resected from the left ventricle, attached to the papillary muscle and chordae tendineae of the mitral valve. Macroscopically, the tumor appeared flushed, rubbery to spongy, and was initially suspected to be a myxoma. To determine its histopathological identity, the following studies were performed:

- Histological examination of the tumor tissue was conducted using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining and special stains to assess tissue architecture. The tumor demonstrated narrow, elongated, and branching papillary fronds composed of central avascular collagen and variable elastic tissues surrounded by acid mucopolysaccharide, and was lined by hyperplastic endothelial cells.

- Immunohistochemical staining for CD-34 was performed on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue sections.

- Immunohistochemical staining for vimentin and S-100 was also performed on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue sections, with attention to the intermediate stromal cells within the papillary structures.

What is the most likely diagnosis, and how do these findings collectively support this diagnosis?

input_logic_chain.research_context: To determine the histopathological identity of an intracardiac mass resected from the left ventricle attached to the papillary muscle and chordae tendineae of the mitral valve, based on macroscopic, microscopic, and immunohistochemical findings.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological examination of the resected tumor tissue using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining and special stains, with morphological assessment of tissue architecture.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate the structural and cellular architecture of the tumor for diagnostic features.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The tumor showed narrow, elongated, and branching papillary fronds composed of central avascular collagen and variable elastic tissues surrounded by acid mucopolysaccharide, lined by hyperplastic endothelial cells [Context].
experiments.interpretation: The presence of branching papillary fronds with avascular fibrous cores and mucopolysaccharide-rich stroma is characteristic of papillary endothelial hyperplasia, a hallmark of papillary fibroelastoma (CPF). The lining by hyperplastic endothelial cells further supports an endothelial-derived neoplasm.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The histomorphological architecture is consistent with a diagnosis of papillary fibroelastoma.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining using CD-34 antibody on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tumor tissue sections.
experiments.experiment_goal: To identify the immunophenotypic profile of surface lining cells and confirm endothelial differentiation.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The histological section displays a network of irregularly shaped, interconnected luminal spaces lined by a thin, continuous layer of cells exhibiting distinct reddish to reddish-purple staining localized predominantly along the cell membranes and cytoplasmic regions. The stained cellular lining forms a well-defined, albeit slightly fragmented, peripheral border around the pale, lightly stained or unstained interior of the luminal spaces [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The reddish-purple membrane and cytoplasmic staining pattern corresponds to CD-34 immunoreactivity, a well-established marker of vascular endothelial cells. The localization of staining to the luminal surface lining cells confirms their endothelial origin.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The surface lining cells are endothelial in nature, as confirmed by CD-34 positivity.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining using vimentin and S-100 antibodies on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tumor tissue sections, with focus on intermediate stromal cells.
experiments.experiment_goal: To characterize the immunophenotype of intermediate stromal cells within the papillary fronds and assess for mesenchymal and neural markers.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The image displays intermediate cells with elongated or polygonal shapes and moderately abundant cytoplasm, arranged in a continuous layer along the luminal surface. These cells exhibit a diffuse to granular pinkish-purple cytoplasmic signal, consistent with immunohistochemical labeling. The staining is heterogeneous in intensity and distributed throughout the tissue [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: The cytoplasmic immunostaining with vimentin (a mesenchymal marker) and S-100 (a neural crest-derived marker, also expressed in some mesenchymal cells) indicates that the intermediate stromal cells are of mesenchymal origin and may represent fibroblastic or dendritic cell populations within the fibroelastic core. Their presence supports the stromal composition of the papillary fronds.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The intermediate stromal cells express vimentin and S-100, confirming their mesenchymal phenotype and supporting the fibroelastic nature of the tumor stroma.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The tumor exhibits characteristic papillary architecture with avascular fibrous cores and mucopolysaccharide-rich matrix.
The surface lining cells are endothelial, as demonstrated by CD-34 immunoreactivity.
The intermediate stromal cells are mesenchymal, expressing vimentin and S-100, consistent with fibroblastic components of the papillary core.

reasoning.content: The histological architecture of the tumor, as revealed by H&E and special stains, demonstrates branching papillary fronds with central fibroelastic cores and mucopolysaccharide-rich stroma, lined by hyperplastic endothelial cells—features classic for papillary fibroelastoma (CPF). The immunohistochemical profile further supports this diagnosis: CD-34 positivity confirms the endothelial nature of the surface lining cells, which form a continuous layer around vascular-like spaces. The intermediate stromal cells, located beneath the endothelium, express vimentin and S-100, markers consistent with mesenchymal fibroblastic differentiation, contributing to the fibroelastic core. Together, the architectural pattern and immunophenotype—endothelial surface with underlying mesenchymal stroma—are diagnostic of CPF. Although the mass was initially suspected to be a myxoma macroscopically, the histological and immunohistochemical findings definitively rule out myxoma, which typically shows stellate mesenchymal cells in a myxoid matrix without prominent papillary fronds or CD-34-positive endothelial lining.
reasoning.conclusion: The resected intracardiac mass is definitively diagnosed as papillary fibroelastoma (CPF) based on characteristic histomorphology and immunohistochemical profile.

question:
In a study assessing the concordance between MRI detection and histological validation of pulmonary nodular lesions in mice, the following procedures were conducted:

- Histological examination of lung tissue sections from mice was performed using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining, followed by microscopic evaluation. A total of 13 nodular lesions were identified across all mice, with two or more per mouse. One lesion was frozen for further analysis, and no pathological result was obtained for this lesion.

- Histological analysis of lung tissue sections using H&E staining was carried out with detailed microscopic imaging of representative lesions (Figs. 3,4), including three images (Image 1, Image 2, Image 3) showing distinct morphological patterns.

- The same histological analysis using H&E-stained sections was repeated for additional lesion characterization.

- A comparison was made between MR imaging findings and histological sections, including spatial mapping of lesions and size measurements. All lesions identified in MR images were also demonstrated in histological sections, with well-matched locations between them. MR images revealed 11 of the 13 histologically confirmed lesions. Two lesions identified by histology were not detected in MR images: one located adjacent to the right diaphragm, and the other near the left hilum.

- A correlation analysis was performed between lesion diameters measured on MR images and those from histological sections. The lesions ranged from 0.61 to 1.54 mm in diameter (average: 1.05 ± 0.29 mm) in MR images, and from 0.56 to 1.41 mm (average: 0.87 ± 0.26 mm) in histological sections. A correlation coefficient of 0.87 (P = 0.001) was obtained between MRI-based and histology-based lesion size measurements.

What conclusions can be drawn from these findings?

experiments.sub_conclusion: The lesion in [Image 1] is morphologically consistent with a pulmonary adenoma.

experiments.interpretation: The presence of glandular/acinar structures supports an epithelial origin. experiments.sub_conclusion: The lesion in [Image 3] is consistent with an adenoma exhibiting some architectural complexity but not definitive malignancy.

Despite these misses, the strong correlation (r = 0.87, P = 0.001) between MRI and histology in lesion size indicates that MRI reliably quantifies even submillimeter nodules. Therefore, MRI is a highly accurate tool for in vivo detection and measurement of pulmonary nodules in this mouse model, particularly for neoplastic lesions away from motion-prone or structurally complex regions.
reasoning.conclusion: MRI demonstrates high spatial and quantitative concordance with histology for pulmonary nodular lesions in mice, with 84.6% detection sensitivity and strong size correlation, supporting its validity as a non-invasive tool for monitoring lung tumor burden in preclinical studies, though it may miss small or anatomically obscured lesions.

question: In the present study, renal biopsy was performed in case 1 on day 11 to determine the pathological subtype of acute kidney injury (AKI) following multiple wasp stings, with the goal of distinguishing between acute tubular necrosis (ATN) and acute interstitial nephritis (AIN). Renal biopsy tissue was obtained and processed for histological examination using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining. The tissue was examined under light microscopy at low (×50) and high (×100) magnification, and representative images were analyzed. Based on these findings, what can be concluded regarding the underlying pathological mechanism of AKI in this patient, and how do the histological observations support this conclusion?

input_logic_chain.research_context: In the present study, renal biopsy was performed in case 1 on day 11 to determine the pathological subtype of acute kidney injury (AKI) following multiple wasp stings, with the goal of distinguishing between acute tubular necrosis (ATN) and acute interstitial nephritis (AIN).

experiments.experimental_setting: Renal biopsy tissue was obtained from case 1 on day 11 post-envenomation and processed for histological examination using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining. The tissue was examined under light microscopy at low (×50) and high (×100) magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate the histopathological features of renal tissue to identify the type of kidney injury (ATN vs. AIN) in a patient with wasp sting-induced AKI.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: At low magnification [Image 1], multiple glomeruli appear with normal morphology, embedded in preserved renal parenchyma. Interstitial spaces are expanded with pale, loosely arranged appearance and clear zones between tubules. Tubular profiles show luminal dilation and reduced epithelial cell height. At high magnification [Image 2], tubular epithelial cells are flattened with diffuse attenuation of the brush border. Tubular lumens contain eosinophilic, amorphous, pale pink to light purple irregular deposits. Basement membranes are intact. Interstitium shows mild edema and sparse inflammatory infiltrate. Some nuclei are hyperchromatic; others are pale and vesicular.
experiments.interpretation: The presence of tubular epithelial flattening, luminal dilation, and intraluminal proteinaceous casts (consistent with Tamm-Horsfall protein) are hallmark histological features of acute tubular necrosis (ATN). The absence of dense interstitial inflammatory infiltrates, eosinophils, or granulomas argues against acute interstitial nephritis (AIN). The preserved glomerular structure excludes glomerulonephritis as a primary pathology.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The histopathological findings are consistent with residual ATN and exclude AIN in this patient with wasp sting-induced AKI.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The histological features observed in the renal biopsy demonstrate tubular damage with epithelial simplification and proteinaceous casts, characteristic of ATN.
There is no histological evidence of interstitial inflammation or immune-mediated injury, ruling out AIN.

reasoning.content: The renal biopsy from case 1 revealed tubular epithelial cell flattening, luminal dilation, and intraluminal proteinaceous casts—classic morphological hallmarks of acute tubular necrosis (ATN). These changes result from ischemic or toxic injury to tubular epithelial cells, which in this context is attributable to myoglobinuria and hemolysis following massive wasp envenomation. The absence of dense interstitial inflammatory infiltrates, particularly lymphocytes, eosinophils, or plasma cells, which are typically seen in acute interstitial nephritis (AIN), supports the exclusion of an immune-mediated mechanism. Additionally, the preserved glomerular architecture and lack of crescents or immune complex deposits further rule out primary glomerular disease. Given that ATN is the predominant form of kidney injury in rhabdomyolysis- and hemolysis-induced AKI, and that wasp venom is known to cause cell membrane disruption in red blood cells and skeletal muscle, these findings align with the expected pathophysiology. Therefore, the histopathological evidence confirms ATN as the underlying mechanism of AKI in this patient.
reasoning.conclusion: The acute kidney injury in case 1 following multiple wasp stings is due to acute tubular necrosis (ATN), likely secondary to rhabdomyolysis and hemolysis, with no evidence of acute interstitial nephritis (AIN).

question: A 443-gram tissue specimen measuring 13 × 12 × 6 cm was resected during surgery, and histological analysis was performed to determine the composition and immunohistochemical profile of the lesion. The emphysematous and inflammatory changes in the lung are consistent with chronic pulmonary disease, not tumor involvement. Together, these findings confirm a completely resected, mature, hormone receptor-positive teratoma with no evidence of malignancy or residual disease.

The study aimed to characterize the presence, distribution, and morphological features of foetal haemoglobin-containing blood cells (Fc) in tumour and bone marrow tissues across a spectrum of paediatric and rare adult cancers, including nephroblastoma, leukaemia, retinoblastoma, neuroblastoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, medulloblastoma, Ewing sarcoma, hepatoblastoma, neurofibroma, and glioblastoma. All histological specimens were examined microscopically with a spatial resolution calibrated to 50 μm.

To investigate the localization of foetal haemoglobin-containing erythrocytes and erythroblasts, tumour and bone marrow specimens from 110 patients (nephroblastoma n=24, leukaemia n=24, retinoblastoma n=18, neuroblastoma n=17, rhabdomyosarcoma n=14, medulloblastoma n=11, Ewing sarcoma n=2, and one each for hepatoblastoma, neurofibroma, glioblastoma) were subjected to immunohistochemical staining for foetal haemoglobin and analyzed microscopically.

To assess the spatial relationship between foetal haemoglobin-containing cells and tumour vasculature, histological sections with immunohistochemical detection of foetal haemoglobin were analyzed, focusing on vascular architecture and proliferative patterns in tumour tissues.

To evaluate the association of foetal haemoglobin-containing cells with pathological tissue features, tumour sections were examined for distribution in relation to necrotic, haemorrhagic, and cellular infiltration zones using immunohistochemistry.

To determine the organization and proliferative status of foetal haemoglobin-expressing cells in haematopoietic tissue, bone marrow sections from the same patient cohort were analyzed using immunohistochemistry, with attention to cellular clustering and morphological signs of division.

In tumour tissues, foetal haemoglobin-containing cells were observed infiltrating among tumour cells and congested in large areas of necrosis or haemorrhage. In bone marrow, dense clusters of 3–50 immunopositive cells were distributed throughout the section, with some cells showing morphological features of mitosis.

What comprehensive conclusion can be drawn from these findings?
