reasoning.content: The histological analysis ([Image 1] and [Image 2]) reveals a structurally heterogeneous tumor with a well-defined viable rim and central necrosis, a hallmark of rapidly growing neoplasms. This spatial organization directly informs the interpretation of NMR data: the measured T1 and T2 relaxation times represent a weighted average of signals from regions with differing cellular integrity, water content, and macromolecular environment. Viable tumor tissue, with high cellular density and intact membranes, is expected to exhibit shorter T2 due to restricted water mobility, while necrotic regions, with lysed cells and increased extracellular fluid, likely contribute longer T2 components. The presence of residual viable cells near vessels in necrotic zones further adds complexity to the signal. Since melanin is absent, it does not influence proton relaxation, simplifying the interpretation. The experimental NMR setup, with optimized pulse sequences and signal averaging, ensures that these heterogeneous contributions are captured with high fidelity. Therefore, the NMR signal is not representative of a uniform tissue but reflects the underlying histopathological heterogeneity.
reasoning.conclusion: The NMR signal obtained from the Cloudman S91 melanoma in mouse tails is a composite signal arising from both viable and necrotic tumor compartments, with the spatial distribution and histological heterogeneity of these regions directly influencing the measured relaxation parameters. This necessitates careful interpretation of in vivo NMR data in the context of tumor architecture.

question:
To determine whether BDA-labeled axonal terminals form synaptic connections with WGA-HRP-labeled premotor neurons in the rat brainstem, and to characterize the ultrastructural features and distribution of these synapses, the following experiments were conducted:

1. Electron microscopy was performed on brainstem tissue sections from rats that were dual-labeled with BDA (to trace axonal terminals) and WGA-HRP (to label premotor neurons). Tissue was processed for ultrastructural analysis using standard electron microscopy protocols to visualize subcellular structures and tracer localization. The images were acquired at high resolution with scale bars indicating measurements between 0.35 μm and 0.5 μm.

2. High-resolution electron micrographs were analyzed for synaptic junctions between BDA-labeled terminals and WGA-HRP-labeled dendrites or somata in brainstem regions including PCRt, MdD, MdV, Vsup, and PBN.

3. Ultrastructural analysis was conducted in the parvicellular reticular nucleus (PCRt) across five tissue sections to quantify the proportion of BDA-labeled boutons forming axo-dendritic versus axo-somatic synapses with WGA-HRP-labeled neurons. It was found that 88 out of 120 BDA-labeled boutons formed synapses with dendrites of WGA-HRP-labeled neurons, while 32 formed synapses with somata.

4. Ultrastructural analysis was conducted to examine the morphology of synaptic vesicles and synaptic architecture in BDA-labeled terminals forming synapses with WGA-HRP-labeled neurons.

5. Electron micrographs were examined for synaptic contacts involving unlabeled terminals or unlabeled dendritic elements in the same tissue sections. It was observed that some BDA-labeled boutons formed synapses with dendrites or spines lacking WGA-HRP labeling, and some unlabeled boutons synapsed onto WGA-HRP-labeled dendrites or somata. Some unlabeled terminals contained dense-core vesicles.

Based on these experiments, what can be concluded about the synaptic connectivity between BDA-labeled axonal terminals and WGA-HRP-labeled premotor neurons in the rat brainstem?

input_logic_chain.research_context: To determine whether BDA-labeled axonal terminals form synaptic connections with WGA-HRP-labeled premotor neurons in the rat brainstem, and to characterize the ultrastructural features and distribution of these synapses.

experiments.experimental_setting: Electron microscopy was performed on brainstem tissue sections from rats that were dual-labeled with BDA (to trace axonal terminals) and WGA-HRP (to label premotor neurons). Tissue was processed for ultrastructural analysis using standard electron microscopy protocols to visualize subcellular structures and tracer localization.
experiments.experiment_goal: To identify BDA-labeled axonal terminals and WGA-HRP-labeled premotor neurons at the ultrastructural level and to detect synaptic contacts between them.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: BDA-labeled terminals appear as dark, electron-dense profiles with fine granular reaction product and contain numerous small, spherical synaptic vesicles [Image 1], [Image 2], [Image 3], [Image 4], [Image 5], [Image 6]. WGA-HRP-labeled dendrites and somata exhibit lighter, granular cytoplasm with punctual or crystalline electron-dense clumps [Image 1], [Image 2], [Image 3], [Image 4], [Image 5], [Image 6].
experiments.interpretation: The electron-dense granular appearance in BDA-labeled terminals is consistent with the known ultrastructural signature of BDA reaction product, which localizes in the cytoplasm and on organelle membranes. The crystalline or punctual electron-dense clumps in dendrites and somata are characteristic of WGA-HRP labeling, confirming successful retrograde tracing of premotor neurons.
experiments.sub_conclusion: BDA and WGA-HRP labeling are ultrastructurally distinguishable, enabling unambiguous identification of presynaptic (BDA+) terminals and postsynaptic (WGA-HRP+) neuronal compartments.

experiments.experimental_setting: High-resolution electron micrographs were analyzed for synaptic junctions between BDA-labeled terminals and WGA-HRP-labeled dendrites or somata in brainstem regions including PCRt, MdD, MdV, Vsup, and PBN.
experiments.experiment_goal: To determine if BDA-labeled terminals form direct synaptic connections with WGA-HRP-labeled premotor neurons.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Close apposition between BDA-labeled terminals and WGA-HRP-labeled dendrites or somata is observed, with visible synaptic clefts and asymmetric membrane thickenings (postsynaptic densities) on the WGA-HRP-labeled side [Image 1], [Image 2], [Image 3], [Image 4], [Image 5], [Image 6].
experiments.interpretation: The presence of a synaptic cleft, closely opposed membranes, and a thickened postsynaptic density is diagnostic of an asymmetric synapse, which is typically excitatory in nature. The pre- and postsynaptic elements are differentially labeled, confirming the identity of the synaptic partners.
experiments.sub_conclusion: BDA-labeled terminals form asymmetric synaptic junctions with dendrites and somata of WGA-HRP-labeled premotor neurons, indicating direct synaptic connectivity.

experiments.experimental_setting: Ultrastructural analysis was conducted in the parvicellular reticular nucleus (PCRt) across five tissue sections to quantify the proportion of BDA-labeled boutons forming axo-dendritic versus axo-somatic synapses with WGA-HRP-labeled neurons.
experiments.experiment_goal: To determine the relative distribution of synaptic contacts (axo-dendritic vs. axo-somatic) made by BDA-labeled terminals onto labeled premotor neurons.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: In PCRt, 88 out of 120 BDA-labeled boutons form synapses with dendrites of WGA-HRP-labeled neurons, while 32 form synapses with somata [Context].
experiments.interpretation: The numerical data indicate a strong preference for axo-dendritic synapses over axo-somatic ones, with a 73% to 27% distribution. This suggests dendritic integration is the dominant mode of input from these terminals onto premotor neurons.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The majority of synaptic inputs from BDA-labeled terminals to premotor neurons occur on dendrites rather than on cell bodies.

experiments.experimental_setting: Electron micrographs were examined for the ultrastructural morphology of synaptic vesicles and synaptic architecture in BDA-labeled terminals forming synapses with WGA-HRP-labeled neurons.
experiments.experiment_goal: To characterize the type of synapses (asymmetric vs. symmetric) and the nature of presynaptic vesicles.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Presynaptic terminals contain small, clear, spherical synaptic vesicles. Postsynaptic membranes show overt thickening and specialization, consistent with asymmetric synapses [Image 1], [Image 2], [Image 3], [Image 4], [Image 5], [Image 6].
experiments.interpretation: Small, clear, spherical vesicles and asymmetric postsynaptic densities are hallmarks of excitatory glutamatergic synapses in the central nervous system.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The synapses formed by BDA-labeled terminals onto premotor neurons are predominantly excitatory in nature.

experiments.experimental_setting: Ultrastructural analysis included examination of synaptic contacts involving unlabeled terminals or unlabeled dendritic elements in the same tissue sections.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess the specificity of labeling and to identify non-specific or unlabeled synaptic interactions in the neuropil.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Some BDA-labeled boutons form synapses with dendrites or spines lacking WGA-HRP labeling, and some unlabeled boutons synapse onto WGA-HRP-labeled dendrites or somata [Image 6]. Some unlabeled terminals contain dense-core vesicles [Image 6d].
experiments.interpretation: The presence of unlabeled synaptic partners indicates that not all inputs to or from premotor neurons are captured by the tracers used, and that diverse neurotransmitter systems (e.g., peptidergic, based on dense-core vesicles) may be involved.
experiments.sub_conclusion: While BDA-labeled terminals specifically synapse onto premotor neurons, these neurons also receive inputs from unlabeled sources, and BDA-labeled terminals contact unlabeled postsynaptic targets, indicating network complexity beyond the labeled pathway.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: BDA and WGA-HRP labeling produce distinct ultrastructural signatures that allow unambiguous identification of presynaptic and postsynaptic elements.
Direct synaptic contacts exist between BDA-labeled terminals and WGA-HRP-labeled premotor neurons, characterized by asymmetric synaptic junctions.
The majority of synaptic inputs from BDA-labeled terminals to premotor neurons target dendrites rather than somata.
These synapses exhibit ultrastructural features consistent with excitatory neurotransmission.
The synaptic circuitry includes both labeled and unlabeled elements, indicating partial pathway tracing and complex local connectivity.

reasoning.content: The experimental evidence demonstrates that BDA-labeled axonal terminals form direct, asymmetric synapses with WGA-HRP-labeled premotor neurons in the rat brainstem. The differential electron density and morphological features of the tracers allow clear identification of pre- and postsynaptic compartments. Synaptic junctions are characterized by close membrane apposition, synaptic clefts, and prominent postsynaptic densities, confirming synaptic connectivity. The predominance of axo-dendritic synapses (73%) over axo-somatic ones (27%) suggests dendritic integration is the primary mode of input. The presence of small, clear, spherical vesicles and asymmetric architecture indicates excitatory synaptic transmission. Although the labeled pathway reveals a specific projection, the presence of unlabeled synaptic partners underscores the complexity of the local network. Together, these findings establish a direct, excitatory, and predominantly dendritic synaptic input from BDA-labeled axons to premotor neurons in brainstem regions including PCRt, MdD, MdV, Vsup, and PBN.
reasoning.conclusion: BDA-labeled axonal terminals form direct, asymmetric (excitatory) synapses predominantly onto dendrites of WGA-HRP-labeled premotor neurons in the rat brainstem, with a smaller proportion of axo-somatic contacts, indicating a specific and functionally excitatory connectivity pattern within the brainstem premotor network.

question:
A 35-year-old female patient presents with a skin-colored nodule on the toe clinically suggestive of a fibroma. Histopathological and immunohistochemical analyses were performed to determine the nature of the dermal tumor composed of stellate and spindle-shaped cells in a myxoid and collagenous stroma.

Histopathological examination was performed on a formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded skin biopsy from the toe, stained with hematoxylin and eosin, analyzed at 20x magnification.

High-magnification histopathological analysis (H&E, 400x) was conducted on the superficial portion of the tumor.

Immunohistochemical staining for CD34 was performed on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue, visualized at 20x magnification with chromogen detection (brown DAB signal).

Immunohistochemical staining for CD99, Factor XIIIa, S100, and EMA was performed on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue sections. The results showed focal positivity for CD99, scattered Factor XIIIa-positive cells, and no expression of S100 or EMA.

What is the most likely diagnosis, and how can it be justified based on the histopathological and immunohistochemical findings?

input_logic_chain.research_context: A 35-year-old female patient presents with a skin-colored nodule on the toe clinically suggestive of a fibroma. Histopathological and immunohistochemical analyses were performed to determine the nature of the dermal tumor composed of stellate and spindle-shaped cells in a myxoid and collagenous stroma.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histopathological examination of a formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded skin biopsy from the toe, stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E), analyzed at 20x magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess the overall architecture, location, and cellular morphology of the dermal lesion.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The lesion appears as a nodular, well-circumscribed mass in the dermis with a distinct boundary from surrounding tissue. The epidermis is intact with mild acanthosis and a wavy rete pattern. The tumor is composed of stellate and spindle-shaped cells within a myxoid stroma and between collagen bundles. Deeper portions show nodular growth with infiltration into surrounding stroma. Mast cells are visible in the stroma [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The well-circumscribed but focally infiltrative nodular architecture in the dermis, along with the presence of stellate and spindle cells in a myxoid background, suggests a mesenchymal neoplasm rather than a reactive process. The presence of mast cells is a supportive feature in certain dermal fibroblastic/myofibroblastic tumors.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The lesion is a dermal mesenchymal tumor with a mixed fascicular and nodular growth pattern, showing focal infiltration and myxoid stroma, consistent with a benign fibroblastic neoplasm.

experiments.experimental_setting: High-magnification histopathological analysis (H&E, 400x) of the superficial portion of the tumor.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate the cytological features and spatial arrangement of tumor cells.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Stellate and spindle-shaped cells are arranged in fascicles forming parallel or slightly interwoven bundles. Cells have elongated, hyperchromatic nuclei aligned with the cellular axis, mild nuclear pleomorphism, and eosinophilic cytoplasm. The stroma contains wavy collagen bundles and myxoid areas creating cleft-like spaces between cellular fascicles. Nuclear basophilia and cytoplasmic eosinophilia are evident [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: The fasciculated growth of spindle cells with tapered nuclei and alignment along collagen bundles is characteristic of fibroblastic or myofibroblastic differentiation. The cleft-like spaces in the myxoid stroma are typical of mucin-rich environments seen in tumors like glomus tumors or fibrohistiocytic lesions, but the cell morphology does not support glomus differentiation.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The tumor exhibits fibroblastic differentiation with a fasciculated architecture and myxoid stromal changes, further supporting a diagnosis within the spectrum of fibroblastic tumors.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining for CD34 on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue, visualized at 20x magnification with chromogen detection (brown DAB signal).
experiments.experiment_goal: To determine the immunophenotypic profile of the tumor cells and aid in differential diagnosis.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Diffuse brown chromogenic staining is present throughout the tumor cells, appearing widespread and uniform, with a reticular pattern outlining cellular membranes and cytoplasmic processes. The staining is strong and consistent across the densely cellular areas. Unstained regions correspond to extracellular matrix [Image 3].
experiments.interpretation: The diffuse and strong membranous and cytoplasmic CD34 expression is a hallmark of certain dermal dendrocytic and fibroblastic tumors. CD34 positivity is commonly seen in dermatofibroma, solitary fibrous tumor, and atypical fibroxanthoma, but the pattern and context help differentiate. In this case, the widespread positivity supports a CD34-positive fibroblastic tumor.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The tumor shows diffuse strong CD34 expression, supporting a diagnosis of a CD34-positive mesenchymal tumor of the skin, such as a cellular dermatofibroma or solitary fibrous tumor.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining for CD99, Factor XIIIa, S100, and EMA on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue sections.
experiments.experiment_goal: To further narrow the differential diagnosis by excluding other spindle cell tumors.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Focal positivity for CD99 is noted [Context]. Scattered Factor XIIIa-positive cells are present [Context]. S100 and EMA are negative [Context].
experiments.interpretation: Focal CD99 expression can be seen in various mesenchymal tumors but is not specific. Factor XIIIa is typically positive in dermal dendrocytes and is strongly expressed in dermatofibroma; however, only scattered positive cells are seen here, which is atypical for classic dermatofibroma. S100 negativity excludes melanocytic and nerve sheath tumors. EMA negativity argues against perineurioma or solitary fibrous tumor with epithelial differentiation.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The immunoprofile (CD34+, Factor XIIIa scattered+, S100-, EMA-) supports a CD34-rich, Factor XIIIa-poor spindle cell tumor, which is inconsistent with typical dermatofibroma but overlaps with atypical fibroxanthoma or CD34-positive fibroblastic tumors.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The tumor is a dermal-based mesenchymal neoplasm with spindle and stellate cells in fascicles and nodules within a myxoid and collagenous stroma, showing focal infiltration.
The tumor cells show strong and diffuse CD34 expression, indicating a CD34-positive fibroblastic or dendrocytic lineage.
The immunoprofile (CD34+, Factor XIIIa scattered+, S100-, EMA-) rules out melanocytic, neural, and epithelial tumors and suggests a fibroblastic tumor with atypical immunophenotype.

reasoning.content: The histopathological features—stellate and spindle-shaped cells in fascicles and nodules, myxoid stroma, and mast cells—are characteristic of certain fibroblastic tumors. While classic dermatofibroma typically shows strong Factor XIIIa positivity and patchy CD34, this tumor demonstrates the inverse: strong CD34 and only scattered Factor XIIIa. This immunophenotypic pattern is more consistent with a cellular CD34-positive fibrous tumor, such as a superficial CD34-positive fibroblastic tumor (formerly called 'atypical fibroxanthoma of the dermis' or 'dermal corkscrew fibroma'). The acral location (toe), age of patient, and myxoid stroma further support this entity. The absence of S100 and EMA rules out melanocytic and perineural differentiation. The focal CD99 positivity is nonspecific but may be seen in such tumors. Collectively, the architecture, cytology, and immunoprofile point away from common mimics like dermatofibroma, neurofibroma, or solitary fibrous tumor.
reasoning.conclusion: The tumor most likely represents a CD34-positive dermal fibroblastic tumor, possibly within the spectrum of superficial CD34-positive fibroblastic neoplasms, sometimes referred to as 'acral fibroblastic tumor' or 'CD34-positive fibroma'.

question:
A 52-year-old multiparous woman presents with a reducible mass protruding from the introitus, initially suspected on imaging to be either a nabothian cyst or a cervical fibroid with multicystic degeneration. To determine the histopathological nature of the large cervical cystic mass, the following investigations were performed:

- Histopathological examination of the excised cystic mass was conducted using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining, with microscopic evaluation at 100x and 400x magnification.
- A separate histopathological assessment focused on the inner cyst wall using H&E-stained tissue sections visualized at 400x magnification.
- Macroscopic examination of the excised mass was carried out to evaluate its size, surface characteristics, and internal structure. The mass measured 9.5 cm × 8.0 cm, had a multiloculated cut surface with cystic spaces of varying sizes filled with mucinous material, and showed focal epidermidization with an ulcer on the external surface.
- Microscopic evaluation was performed to assess for cellular atypia, mitotic activity, and stromal invasion in H&E-stained sections. No nuclear atypia, no increased mitotic figures, and no evidence of stromal invasion were observed in either epithelial layer.

What can be concluded from these findings, and how do they collectively inform the diagnosis of the cervical mass?

input_logic_chain.research_context: To determine the histopathological nature of a large cervical cystic mass initially suspected to be either a nabothian cyst or a cervical fibroid with multicystic degeneration, based on clinical and imaging findings.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histopathological examination of the excised cystic mass using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining, with microscopic evaluation at 100x and 400x magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To identify the epithelial lining and structural characteristics of the cyst wall for definitive diagnosis.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The outer cyst wall is lined by a thickened layer of keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, with multiple cellular layers, dense eosinophilic cytoplasm, and flattened, dark nuclei toward the luminal surface; underlying stroma consists of fibrous connective tissue with spindle-shaped cells [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The presence of a thickened, keratinized stratified squamous epithelium on the outer wall indicates squamous metaplasia covering the original glandular epithelium, a hallmark of nabothian cyst formation due to obstruction of endocervical glands.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The outer epithelial lining is consistent with squamous metaplasia, supporting the diagnosis of a nabothian cyst.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histopathological examination of the inner cyst wall using H&E-stained tissue sections visualized at 400x magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess the nature of the inner epithelial lining of the cyst for evidence of glandular or respiratory-type epithelium.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The inner cyst wall is lined by a single layer of ciliated low columnar epithelium with vertically oriented nuclei, pale cytoplasm, and visible cilia projecting into the lumen [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: Ciliated low columnar epithelium is characteristic of normal endocervical glandular epithelium, confirming that the cyst originated from entrapped endocervical glands whose secretions accumulated due to ductal obstruction.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The inner lining corresponds to native endocervical epithelium, confirming the cyst's origin from obstructed endocervical glands.

experiments.experimental_setting: Macroscopic examination of the excised mass, including assessment of size, surface features, and internal structure.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate gross morphological features suggestive of benign versus malignant processes.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The mass measured 9.5 cm × 8.0 cm, had a multiloculated cut surface with cystic spaces of varying sizes filled with mucinous material, and showed focal epidermidization with an ulcer on the external surface [Context].
experiments.interpretation: Large size and multiloculation are consistent with long-standing retention cysts; mucinous content reflects secretory activity of endocervical epithelium; focal epidermidization suggests squamous metaplasia, while ulceration may result from trauma due to prolapse.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Gross features support a benign, chronic cystic lesion of cervical glandular origin.

experiments.experimental_setting: Microscopic evaluation for cellular atypia, mitotic activity, and stromal invasion in H&E-stained sections.
experiments.experiment_goal: To exclude malignancy in the cyst wall and epithelial lining.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: No nuclear atypia, no increased mitotic figures, and no evidence of stromal invasion are observed in either epithelial layer [Image 1, Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: Absence of cytological atypia and destructive growth patterns indicates a non-neoplastic, benign process.
experiments.sub_conclusion: There is no histological evidence of malignancy.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The outer wall exhibits squamous metaplasia, a key feature in the pathogenesis of nabothian cysts.
The inner lining is composed of normal ciliated endocervical epithelium, confirming glandular origin.
Gross morphology is consistent with a long-standing benign retention cyst.
Absence of atypia or invasive growth rules out malignancy.

reasoning.content: The dual epithelial lining—outer keratinized stratified squamous epithelium and inner ciliated low columnar epithelium—demonstrates that the cyst formed when proliferating squamous epithelium covered the orifices of endocervical glands, leading to obstruction and accumulation of secretions. This process, known as squamous metaplasia, is a well-documented mechanism in nabothian cyst formation. The multiloculated structure filled with mucinous material further supports chronic retention. The lack of cytological atypia or invasive features confirms a benign etiology. Together, these findings are pathognomonic for a nabothian cyst, despite its unusually large size. The clinical context—no tumor marker elevation, reducible prolapsing mass, and confirmation via biopsy—further supports this diagnosis.
reasoning.conclusion: The histopathological and gross features confirm the diagnosis of a huge benign cervical nabothian cyst arising from obstructed endocervical glands due to squamous metaplasia.

question: To determine the neurotropism of Pseudorabies virus (PRV) in naturally and experimentally infected animals, particularly focusing on the localization of PRV antigen in the central and peripheral nervous systems, immunohistochemical (IHC) analysis was performed on brainstem tissue sections from PRV-infected dogs using specific antibodies against PRV and chromogenic visualization followed by hematoxylin counterstain. Additionally, histopathological examination using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining was conducted on brainstem tissue sections from PRV-infected dogs. What can be concluded from these experiments regarding the interaction of PRV with the brainstem in infected animals?

input_logic_chain.research_context: To determine the neurotropism of Pseudorabies virus (PRV) in naturally and experimentally infected animals, particularly focusing on the localization of PRV antigen in the central and peripheral nervous systems.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical (IHC) analysis was performed on brainstem tissue sections from PRV-infected dogs. The tissue was processed for antigen detection using specific antibodies against PRV, followed by chromogenic visualization (likely DAB), counterstained with hematoxylin.
experiments.experiment_goal: To identify the cellular localization of PRV antigens in the brainstem of infected animals.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Neurons and glial cells in the brainstem exhibit punctate to granular brownish-orange immunoreactive deposits localized within their cytoplasm, against a pale neuropil background. The tissue architecture is preserved without inflammatory changes [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The brownish-orange deposits represent PRV antigens detected by immunohistochemistry, indicating active viral protein expression within neurons and glial cells. The absence of inflammatory changes suggests that antigen presence precedes or occurs independently of overt inflammation in this stage.
experiments.sub_conclusion: PRV antigens are present in neurons and glial cells of the brainstem, confirming neurotropism of the virus in this region.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histopathological examination using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining was conducted on brainstem tissue sections from PRV-infected dogs.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess inflammatory changes and histological lesions in the brainstem associated with PRV infection.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Section A shows perivascular cuffing with mononuclear cells and a neuron containing an eosinophilic intranuclear inclusion body. Section B displays denser perivascular infiltrates, microgliosis (small dark nuclei in neuropil), and disrupted tissue architecture [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: Perivascular cuffing and parenchymal infiltration by mononuclear cells indicate nonsuppurative encephalitis. The intranuclear inclusion body is a hallmark of herpesviral infection. Microgliosis reflects activation of resident immune cells in response to neuronal damage.
experiments.sub_conclusion: PRV infection induces nonsuppurative encephalitis in the brainstem, characterized by inflammatory infiltrates, microgliosis, and viral inclusion bodies.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: PRV infects neurons and glial cells in the brainstem, as evidenced by cytoplasmic antigen deposition without immediate inflammation.
PRV infection leads to inflammatory brain lesions in the brainstem, including perivascular cuffing, microgliosis, and intranuclear inclusion bodies.

reasoning.content: The immunohistochemical findings in Image 1 demonstrate that PRV antigen is localized specifically within neurons and glial cells of the brainstem, confirming the neurotropic nature of the virus. This antigen presence occurs in structurally preserved tissue, suggesting early or direct viral invasion without immediate host inflammatory response. In contrast, H&E-stained sections (Image 2) reveal hallmark features of viral encephalitis: perivascular cuffing, microgliosis, and intranuclear eosinophilic inclusion bodies—consistent with active herpesvirus replication. These two lines of evidence together indicate a progression from initial viral entry and replication in neural cells to subsequent immune-mediated inflammation and tissue damage. The co-localization of antigen and pathology in the brainstem aligns with clinical and pathological reports of neurological disease in PRV-infected animals.
reasoning.conclusion: PRV exhibits strong neurotropism for the brainstem, where it replicates in neurons and glial cells and induces nonsuppurative encephalitis, contributing to the neurological manifestations of Aujeszky's disease.

question: A 77-year-old Japanese woman presented with heart failure, purpura, leg ulcer, rapidly progressive renal failure, and multiorgan dysfunction. Autopsy revealed histopathological changes in coronary arteries and visceral organs, prompting investigation into systemic vasculitis. Histopathological examination of a small- to medium-sized coronary artery was performed using Elastica van Gieson (EVG) staining, with a scale bar indicating 100 μm. Histopathological analysis of thyroid tissue was conducted using haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining. Gross autopsy examination of the coronary arteries and abdominal organs was carried out, revealing that the coronary arteries were patent without aneurysms, but small- to medium-sized coronary arteries showed inflammatory changes, narrowing, and occlusion associated with myocardial necrosis. Laboratory testing for perinuclear antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (p-ANCA) showed normal levels. What is the most likely underlying pathological process explaining this patient’s clinical and pathological findings?

input_logic_chain.research_context: A 77-year-old Japanese woman presented with heart failure, purpura, leg ulcer, rapidly progressive renal failure, and multiorgan dysfunction. Autopsy revealed histopathological changes in coronary arteries and visceral organs, leading to the investigation of underlying systemic vasculitis.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histopathological examination of a small- to medium-sized coronary artery using Elastica van Gieson (EVG) staining, which specifically highlights elastic fibers in black and collagen in pink, allowing detailed visualization of vessel wall architecture.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess structural integrity and pathological changes in the coronary artery wall.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The lumen is irregular and reduced in diameter, surrounded by a thickened intima composed of densely packed pink-staining material with small, dark nuclei. The internal elastic lamina appears dark and fragmented. The media contains concentric smooth muscle cells with interspersed collagen, and the adventitia blends into surrounding connective tissue [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: Intimal thickening with collagen deposition and cellular infiltration indicates chronic vascular injury and repair. Fragmentation of the elastic lamina is characteristic of inflammatory destruction of the vessel wall. Luminal narrowing suggests ischemic potential due to impaired perfusion.
experiments.sub_conclusion: There is evidence of active vasculitis affecting small- to medium-sized coronary arteries, with luminal compromise due to inflammation and intimal proliferation [Image 1].

experiments.experimental_setting: Histopathological analysis of thyroid tissue using haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining, which differentiates nuclei (blue-purple) from cytoplasm and extracellular matrix (pink), enabling assessment of tissue architecture and inflammatory infiltration.
experiments.experiment_goal: To identify signs of systemic vasculitic involvement in non-cardiac parenchymal organs.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: A central region of amorphous, intensely eosinophilic, glassy, and structureless material is surrounded by concentric layers of spindle-shaped cells and a dense infiltrate of small dark nuclei (lymphocytes and plasma cells). The surrounding stroma shows swirling collagen and fibroblasts, with preserved peripheral connective tissue [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: The central eosinophilic zone represents fibrinoid necrosis—a hallmark of immune-mediated vascular injury. The surrounding inflammatory infiltrate and reactive spindle cells indicate an active host response to tissue damage, consistent with necrotizing vasculitis.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Thyroid tissue exhibits fibrinoid necrosis with perivascular inflammation, confirming systemic involvement of small- to medium-sized vessels [Image 2].

experiments.experimental_setting: Autopsy-based gross examination of coronary arteries and abdominal organs, including visual and tactile assessment for aneurysms, occlusions, and tissue necrosis.
experiments.experiment_goal: To rule out atherosclerotic or aneurysmal disease and identify macroscopic features of systemic vasculitis.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Coronary arteries were patent without aneurysms; however, small- to medium-sized coronary arteries showed inflammatory changes, narrowing, and occlusion associated with myocardial necrosis [Context].
experiments.interpretation: Patency of major epicardial arteries rules out acute thrombotic occlusion as cause of myocardial injury. However, microvascular or mid-vessel inflammation leading to occlusion suggests an alternative mechanism—namely, vasculitis.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Myocardial necrosis is secondary to occlusive vasculitis in small- to medium-sized coronary arteries, not atherosclerosis or embolism [Context].

experiments.experimental_setting: Laboratory testing for perinuclear antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (p-ANCA), which are serological markers associated with certain types of vasculitis such as microscopic polyangiitis.
experiments.experiment_goal: To differentiate polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) from ANCA-associated vasculitides.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: [Missing]
experiments.interpretation: Normal p-ANCA levels help exclude ANCA-associated vasculitides (e.g., microscopic polyangiitis), supporting a diagnosis of PAN, which is typically ANCA-negative.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Absence of p-ANCA positivity supports classification of the vasculitis as PAN rather than other small-vessel vasculitides.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: Histopathology of the coronary artery shows luminal narrowing, intimal thickening, and fragmented elastic lamina, indicative of necrotizing inflammation in medium-sized arteries.
Fibrinoid necrosis in thyroid gland with surrounding inflammatory infiltrate confirms systemic necrotizing vasculitis affecting visceral organs.
Occlusion of small- to medium-sized coronary arteries with resulting myocardial necrosis, despite patent large arteries, points to vasculitic etiology rather than atherosclerosis.
Normal p-ANCA levels rule out ANCA-associated vasculitis, narrowing differential diagnosis toward PAN.

reasoning.content: The patient presented with multiorgan failure involving the heart, kidneys, skin, and gastrointestinal organs. The histopathological findings in the coronary artery [Image 1] demonstrate structural disruption typical of necrotizing vasculitis—specifically, intimal hyperplasia, luminal stenosis, and fragmentation of the internal elastic lamina. These changes are not consistent with atherosclerosis, which typically shows lipid-laden plaques and calcification, nor with embolic disease. Concurrent fibrinoid necrosis in the thyroid gland [Image 2], characterized by acellular eosinophilic debris surrounded by inflammatory cells, confirms systemic involvement of small- and medium-sized vessels. The absence of aneurysms on gross examination does not exclude PAN, as segmental necrotizing arteritis may not always form aneurysms. The occlusion of coronary vessels led to ischemic myocardial damage, explaining the echocardiographic findings of apical hypokinesis and reduced ejection fraction, despite negative troponin—possibly due to chronic supply-demand mismatch rather than acute infarction. Rapidly progressive renal failure, purpura, and leg ulcer are clinical manifestations consistent with systemic vasculitis. The normal p-ANCA level excludes ANCA-associated vasculitides, which often affect smaller vessels and present with glomerulonephritis. Together, these findings meet the diagnostic criteria for polyarteritis nodosa (PAN), as outlined in the supplementary guidelines: necrotizing vasculitis of medium-sized arteries without glomerulonephritis, multiorgan involvement, and exclusion of ANCA-mediated disease.
reasoning.conclusion: The patient had polyarteritis nodosa (PAN), a systemic necrotizing vasculitis of small- to medium-sized arteries, which caused multiorgan failure including cardiomyopathy, renal failure, and skin lesions, ultimately leading to fatal cardiovascular collapse.

question:
A 50-year-old woman presented with a long-standing abdominal lump and altered bowel habits. Imaging and histopathological studies were conducted to determine the nature and origin of the lesion in the mesentery.

Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen was performed to evaluate the anatomical location, size, and characteristics of the abdominal mass. The scan revealed a large well-defined cystic lesion on the left side of the mesentery, close to the psoas muscle, with enhancing walls and peripheral, ill-defined, irregular, enhancing solid components. The lesion closely abutted the jejunal loop. Perilesional mesenteric fat stranding was observed. No lymphadenopathy or organ invasion was noted.

Histopathological examination of the excised tumor was performed using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining on tissue sections.

Immunohistochemical (IHC) analysis was performed on tumor tissue sections using antibodies against vimentin, smooth muscle actin (SMA), desmin, S100, CD117, and CD34.

What can be concluded from these findings?

input_logic_chain.research_context: A 50-year-old woman presented with a long-standing abdominal lump and altered bowel habits. Imaging and histopathological studies were conducted to determine the nature and origin of the lesion in the mesentery.

experiments.experimental_setting: Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen was performed to evaluate the anatomical location, size, and characteristics of the abdominal mass.
experiments.experiment_goal: To determine the morphological features and spatial relationship of the lesion with adjacent structures.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: A large well-defined cystic lesion on the left side of the mesentery, close to the psoas muscle, with enhancing walls and peripheral, ill-defined, irregular, enhancing solid components. The lesion closely abutted the jejunal loop. Perilesional mesenteric fat stranding was observed. No lymphadenopathy or organ invasion was noted [Context].
experiments.interpretation: The well-defined cystic nature with enhancing walls and solid enhancing components suggests a neoplastic process. Perilesional fat stranding indicates local inflammatory or reactive changes, commonly seen with aggressive or growing tumors. The proximity to the jejunum without invasion suggests mesenteric origin rather than primary intestinal tumor.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The lesion is a well-circumscribed, locally aggressive mesenteric mass with features suggestive of a malignant neoplasm of mesenchymal origin.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histopathological examination of the excised tumor was performed using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining on tissue sections.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess the cellular architecture, cytological features, and mitotic activity of the tumor.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The tumor comprises alternating fascicles of spindle cells with high mitotic activity, marked pleomorphism, and intranuclear inclusions. Bizarre tumor cells and tumor giant cells are present. Perivascular accentuation, hemorrhage, and necrosis are evident. Mitotic count exceeds 10 per 10 high power fields [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: Spindle cells arranged in intersecting fascicles with nuclear pleomorphism, hyperchromasia, and high mitotic rate are hallmark features of high-grade sarcomas. question: An investigation was conducted into histopathological and gross pathological changes in the bursa of Fabricius in broiler flocks infected with very virulent infectious bursal disease virus (vvIBDV), including structural alterations, cellular responses, and molecular detection of IBDV. A 45-year-old male with a history of hepatitis B virus-induced cirrhosis underwent liver transplantation for a large right lobe liver tumor. Two months post-transplant, he developed progressive respiratory symptoms including dry cough, chest tightness, shortness of breath, and hypoxemia, with imaging showing interstitial lung changes, pleural effusion, and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. To determine the histopathological and immunohistochemical characteristics of the resected liver tumor and understand its biological behavior, including rare metastatic patterns such as pulmonary lymphangitic carcinomatosis, the following investigations were performed:

1. A histopathological examination of the resected liver tumor specimen was conducted using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining. The tissue was obtained from the right lobe of the liver during transplantation surgery.

2. Immunohistochemical staining for cytokeratin 19 (CK19) was performed on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded liver tumor tissue, with visualization using a brown chromogen and hematoxylin counterstain.

3. Immunohistochemical staining for cytokeratin 7 (CK7) was performed on the same liver tumor tissue, using brown chromogen and hematoxylin counterstaining, at 100× magnification.

4. An immunohistochemical panel was carried out on the liver tumor tissue, including alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), hepatocyte marker, CD34, CD19, CD10, synaptophysin, chromogranin A, and pan-cytokeratin.

The results of the immunohistochemical panel showed the following: AFP positive, hepatocyte marker positive, CD34 positive, CD19 positive, CD10 focally positive, synaptophysin negative, chromogranin A negative, and pan-cytokeratin positive.

What can be concluded about the nature of the liver tumor based on these findings, and how do the results collectively inform the diagnosis?

This study was designed to compare bone healing after application of two osteoconductive graft materials (ABB and β-TCP) in experimentally induced bone defects in rabbit calvaria. 

Histological analysis of bone defects in rabbit calvaria grafted with ABB, β-TCP, or left untreated (control) was performed using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining, evaluating new bone formation and residual graft material. 

Additionally, quantitative histomorphometric analysis of new bone formation and residual graft material in the same defect models was conducted. The mean percentage of new bone formation was 16.83 ± 11.07% in the ABB group, 30.83 ± 14.29% in the β-TCP group, and 14.00 ± 8.17% in the control group. The mean percentage of residual material was 36.50 ± 8.43% in the ABB group and 24.17 ± 14.01% in the β-TCP group.

question:
In a study on calves with respiratory disease, lung, nasal, conjunctival, and auricular swab samples were collected from 23 calves and tested for Mycoplasma bovis using PCR, bacterial culture, and immunohistochemistry (IHC). M. bovis was detected in 78.26% of lung samples (18/23), with PCR and culture identifying the pathogen in 65.2% (15/23) and IHC in 73.9% (17/23) of lung samples. Most calves positive by PCR were also positive by IHC, with only one discordant case. Extrapulmonary detections occurred in nasal (11/18), conjunctival (6/18), and auricular (4/18) swabs, and most of these calves also had pulmonary infection.

Additionally, immunohistochemistry was performed on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded lung tissue sections using anti-M. bovis antibodies, with detection visualized at a microscopic resolution of 50 µm. The staining revealed specific labeling patterns in lung lesions associated with caseonecrotic foci.

Based on these findings, what can be concluded about the role and distribution of M. bovis in the respiratory pathology of these calves?

input_logic_chain.research_context: Detection and localization of Mycoplasma bovis in calves with respiratory disease, including assessment of anatomical distribution and diagnostic method performance.

experiments.experimental_setting: Lung, nasal, conjunctival, and auricular swab samples were collected from 23 calves. Detection of M. bovis was performed using PCR, bacterial culture, and immunohistochemistry (IHC).

experiments.sub_conclusion: M. bovis antigens are concentrated at the margin of caseonecrotic lesions, suggesting active bacterial presence at the advancing edge of inflammation.
