question:
A 35-year-old male presents with a painful femoral lytic lesion and systemic symptoms. To determine the histopathological and immunophenotypic characteristics of the neoplastic cells in the femoral lytic lesion and establish a diagnosis of anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL), ALK-positive, based on morphological, immunohistochemical, and clinical findings, the following investigations were performed.

A femoral bone biopsy was examined using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining under standard light microscopy. The histological evaluation revealed large, atypical cells arranged in solid sheets with round to oval irregular nuclei, nuclear indentations, coarse to vesicular chromatin, prominent nucleoli, and moderate basophilic to eosinophilic cytoplasm. Kidney-shaped hallmark cells were identified. Mitotic figures were frequent. The neoplastic cells were seen replacing bone trabeculae, with associated dead bony fragments, osteoclast-type giant cells, and reactive bone formation. Skeletal muscle and fibro-adipose tissue were infiltrated.

Immunohistochemical staining for Leukocyte Common Antigen (LCA) was performed on the tissue section using chromogen-based detection. The large neoplastic cells showed membranous positivity of variable intensity.

CD20 immunostaining was performed on the same tissue section, which demonstrated no immunoreactivity in the tumor cells.

CD3 immunostaining revealed weak membranous positivity in the large neoplastic cells.

CD30 immunostaining showed diffuse, strong, and uniform immunoreactivity in the large cells, localized to the membrane and Golgi zone.

An immunohistochemical panel including CD2, CD4, CD5, CD7, CD8, CD138, c-MYC, P63, and pan-cytokeratin was performed on the biopsy tissue, and all markers were negative.

In-situ hybridization (ISH) for Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) encoded RNA (EBER) was performed on the biopsy tissue and was negative.

ALK and MUM1 immunohistochemical stains were also performed on the biopsy specimen.

Based on all the above findings, what is the most likely diagnosis, and what is the full pathological reasoning supporting this diagnosis?

The kidney-shaped nuclei are a hallmark of anaplastic large cell lymphoma. Bone and soft tissue invasion confirms aggressive local behavior and extraosseous spread.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The histomorphology is consistent with a diagnosis of anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL), with features of aggressive infiltration into bone and adjacent soft tissues.

experiments.interpretation: LCA (CD45) positivity confirms that the neoplastic cells are of hematopoietic origin, supporting a diagnosis of lymphoma rather than a carcinoma or sarcoma.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The tumor is of lymphoid lineage, consistent with a lymphoma.

experiments.visual_phenomenon: CD20 immunostain is negative. [Context]
experiments.interpretation: Absence of CD20 expression rules out a B-cell lymphoma, such as diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The neoplasm is not of B-cell origin.

experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate T-cell lineage.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: CD3 shows weak membranous positivity. [Context]
experiments.interpretation: Weak CD3 expression suggests T-cell differentiation, though it may be downregulated in anaplastic lymphomas. This supports a T-cell lymphoma diagnosis.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The tumor likely arises from T-cells.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining for CD30 on the femoral biopsy, using chromogenic detection.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess expression of CD30, a hallmark marker of ALCL.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Diffuse, strong, and uniform immunoreactivity in the large cells, localized to the membrane and Golgi zone. [Context]
experiments.interpretation: Strong and diffuse CD30 positivity is a defining feature of anaplastic large cell lymphoma, supporting the diagnosis.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The immunophenotype is consistent with ALCL.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining for ALK protein on the biopsy tissue, visualized with a chromogenic substrate at 200x magnification [Image 1].
experiments.experiment_goal: To determine ALK expression, which distinguishes ALK-positive ALCL from ALK-negative variants.

experiments.interpretation: The diffuse nuclear and cytoplasmic ALK staining indicates expression of the ALK fusion protein, typically resulting from chromosomal translocations (e.g., NPM-ALK). This is characteristic of ALK-positive ALCL.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The tumor is ALK-positive, confirming a specific subtype of ALCL with distinct molecular pathogenesis.

experiments.sub_conclusion: MUM1 positivity further supports the diagnosis of ALCL.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical panel including CD2, CD4, CD5, CD7, CD8, CD138, c-MYC, P63, and pan-cytokeratin on the biopsy tissue.
experiments.experiment_goal: To exclude other lymphoid and non-lymphoid malignancies.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: All markers are negative. [Context]
experiments.interpretation: The absence of cytokeratin rules out carcinoma. CD138 negativity excludes plasmacytoma. c-MYC negativity suggests no double-hit or highly aggressive B-cell lymphoma. T-cell marker variability is common in ALCL due to aberrant antigen loss.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The tumor does not show features of carcinoma, myeloma, or other lymphoma subtypes, supporting ALCL as the most likely diagnosis.

experiments.visual_phenomenon: EBV ISH is negative. [Context]
experiments.interpretation: Absence of EBV suggests the lymphoma is not driven by viral oncogenesis, which is typical for ALK-positive ALCL, as opposed to some EBV+ T-cell lymphomas.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The lymphoma is not associated with Epstein-Barr virus.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The neoplasm is a high-grade lymphoid malignancy with characteristic morphology of ALCL, including hallmark cells and destructive bone infiltration.
The tumor is of T-cell lineage and not of B-cell or epithelial origin.
The immunophenotype is defined by CD30 and ALK positivity, with MUM1 expression and absence of other lineage markers, confirming ALK-positive ALCL.
The absence of EBV rules out viral-driven lymphomas, supporting a diagnosis of de novo ALK-positive ALCL.

reasoning.content: The histopathological examination reveals large atypical cells with hallmark kidney-shaped nuclei, arranged in sheets with aggressive bone and soft tissue invasion—morphological features classic for anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL). Immunohistochemistry confirms hematopoietic origin (LCA+) and T-cell lineage (CD3+), while excluding B-cell (CD20–) and epithelial (pan-cytokeratin–) differentiation. The diffuse, strong CD30 positivity is a diagnostic hallmark of ALCL. Critically, the ALK immunostain shows diffuse nuclear and cytoplasmic positivity [Image 1], which is pathognomonic for ALK-positive ALCL, typically due to NPM-ALK translocation. MUM1 positivity [Image 2] further supports this diagnosis, as it is commonly expressed in ALK+ ALCL. The absence of EBV excludes viral-associated lymphomas. All other markers are negative, ruling out mimics such as myeloma, carcinoma, or other lymphomas. Together, the morphological, immunophenotypic, and molecular features confirm the diagnosis.
reasoning.conclusion: The femoral lesion represents a systemic anaplastic large cell lymphoma, ALK-positive, with widespread dissemination and secondary involvement of the bone and surrounding soft tissues, including potential implant site involvement.

question:
A 60-year-old man with diabetic nephropathy underwent an ABO-incompatible kidney transplant from a living unrelated donor. He received pre-transplant rituximab and plasma exchange to reduce ABO antibody titers. On postoperative day 3, he developed sudden oliguria and rising serum creatinine. To determine the cause of acute allograft dysfunction, the following investigations were performed:

- A renal allograft biopsy was analyzed using light microscopy with Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS) staining and immunohistochemical staining for C4d, with tissue sections evaluated from both cortical and medullary regions.
- Donor-specific antibody (DSA) testing, ABO antibody titers, complement levels (C3/C4), antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA), and fluorescent antinuclear antibody (FANA) tests were conducted. The results showed anti-A titer of 1:1, anti-B titer of 1:4, normal C3/C4 levels, and negative DSA, ANCA, and FANA.
- Duplex kidney ultrasound was performed, which showed no abnormalities.
- Steroid pulse therapy (methylprednisolone 250 mg q12h) was administered for three days, but no improvement in graft function was observed.
- Plasma exchange and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) were initiated, leading to partial improvement in serum creatinine. Subsequently, bortezomib was administered, after which serum creatinine declined further.

Based on these findings, what is the most likely pathophysiologic mechanism underlying the patient’s acute allograft dysfunction, and how do the clinical, histological, and therapeutic data support this mechanism?

input_logic_chain.research_context: To determine the cause of acute allograft dysfunction manifesting as sudden oliguria and rising serum creatinine on postoperative day 3 following an ABO-incompatible kidney transplant.

Dense peritubular inflammatory infiltrates composed of small, round, dark-nucleated cells are observed surrounding medullary capillaries [Image 5]. Extravasated red blood cells are present in the interstitium [Image 6]. C4d immunostaining reveals granular, discontinuous brown deposits along capillary and tubular basement membranes in both cortex and medulla [Image 1, Image 2].

The medullary findings—acute tubular injury, peritubular capillaritis, and interstitial hemorrhage—are indicative of active inflammatory damage. The presence of C4d deposits in both regions indicates complement activation via the classical pathway, a hallmark of antibody-mediated processes. The spatial restriction of inflammatory pathology to the medulla despite widespread C4d suggests compartmentalized immune effector activity.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Histological injury and inflammation are confined to the medulla, despite C4d deposition in both cortex and medulla, indicating a regionally restricted immune-mediated process.

ABO titers were 1:1 (anti-A) and 1:4 (anti-B); C3/C4 levels were normal; DSA was negative; ANCA and FANA were negative.

experiments.sub_conclusion: The absence of detectable DSA does not exclude localized antibody-mediated injury, particularly in the context of C4d positivity and histological evidence of capillaritis.

Histological evaluation revealed preserved cortical architecture but significant medullary pathology, including acute tubular injury, neutrophilic peritubular capillaritis (Banff PTC grade 3), interstitial hemorrhage, and C4d deposition in both cortex and medulla. While C4d was present in both regions, the inflammatory and structural damage was exclusively medullary, suggesting a spatially restricted immune attack. The absence of DSA and normal complement levels initially argued against systemic antibody-mediated rejection (AMR), but C4d positivity indicates local complement activation, which can occur independently of circulating DSA. The normal duplex ultrasound excluded mechanical or vascular causes. Lack of response to steroid pulse therapy ruled out typical T-cell–mediated rejection, while improvement with plasma exchange, IVIG, and bortezomib—a regimen targeting plasma cells and antibodies—strongly supports a humoral mechanism. Together, these findings indicate that the patient experienced an atypical form of AMR with pathology confined to the medulla, likely due to regional vulnerability of medullary peritubular capillaries to antibody-complement injury despite systemic desensitization.
reasoning.conclusion: The patient developed a localized form of antibody-mediated rejection (AMR) predominantly affecting the renal medulla, characterized by C4d deposition, capillaritis, and tubular injury limited to the medulla, with clinical and histological response to humoral-targeted therapies.

question: A 21-year-old male, non-smoker with no prior respiratory history, presented with progressive dyspnea, cough, and left-sided chest pain three months after beginning work in a poorly ventilated 30 m² room where perfluoroalkyl acrylic resin spray (Teximper®) was used for fabric waterproofing. He initially experienced flu-like symptoms one week after relocation to this workspace, which resolved temporarily upon leaving the site but recurred and worsened upon return. High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of the thorax was performed during the acute phase following symptom onset and the development of pneumothorax. An open lung biopsy was later conducted via thoracotomy after failed lung re-expansion with chest tube drainage, and tissue samples were processed with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining. Additional microscopic evaluation of the same H&E-stained specimen was performed at higher magnification. Pulmonary function tests, including spirometry, were conducted before and after clinical management. Serum alpha-1 antitrypsin level was also measured. The HRCT revealed a left-sided pneumothorax and bilateral, patchy ground-glass opacities, more prominent in peripheral and basal regions. The histopathological examination at low magnification (scale bar: 200 μm) showed alveolar spaces containing clusters of cells with abundant cytoplasm, mild interstitial thickening, and absence of granulomas or necrosis. At higher magnification (scale bar: 20 μm), alveolar septa were thickened and lined by pneumocytes with enlarged, hyperchromatic nuclei and abundant cytoplasm; alveolar spaces contained macrophages with foamy or granular cytoplasm, and alveolar architecture was disrupted by cellular infiltrates and proteinaceous material. Spirometry showed forced vital capacity (FVC) of 43% prior to pneumothorax, improving to 72% twelve months later. Serum alpha-1 antitrypsin level was 183 mg/dL. What can be concluded from these findings regarding the nature, etiology, and pathophysiology of the patient’s lung disease?

question: In a 27-year-old female with secondary progressive multiple sclerosis, electron microscopy was performed on twenty blood vessels located within two postphagocytic lesions from cerebellar tissue, focusing on perivascular regions at the edge of demyelinated plaques. Additionally, electron microscopy was conducted on thirty-one capillaries and larger vessels in chronic gliosed plaques from the same patient to examine astrocyte foot process morphology and membrane features. What can be concluded about astrocyte pathology in chronic multiple sclerosis based on these experiments?

reasoning.conclusion: Astrocyte loss and subsequent recovery occur in secondary progressive multiple sclerosis, indicating that astrocyte pathology is a feature of chronic MS and not restricted to acute or uncommon forms of the disease.

At 200x magnification [Image 3, Image 4], the thickened alveolar septa contain numerous spindle-shaped cells with elongated nuclei and eosinophilic cytoplasm embedded in a pink-stained fibrous matrix. The alveolar spaces are filled with a proteinaceous and cellular exudate, and the overall architecture is distorted.

What can be concluded from these histopathological findings regarding the patient's underlying lung condition and its potential impact on the clinical course of COVID-19?

question:
A patient underwent surgical resection of a cervical mass, and histopathological evaluation was performed to determine the nature of the lesion, with emphasis on distinguishing Castleman's disease from other lymphoproliferative or neoplastic conditions.

Gross examination of the en bloc resected specimen revealed a mass measuring 4.8 cm × 4.0 cm × 2.4 cm, with a tan, myxoid surface, areas of yellow tissue, and hemorrhagic changes adjacent to a thrombosed arterial segment.

Microscopic examination of the resected lymph node using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining was performed at low magnification (×40).

Additional microscopic examination using H&E staining was conducted at high magnification (×200) on a representative lymphoid follicle.

Immunohistochemical staining for CD23, cyclin D1, BCL2, CD20, CD3, CD138, CD56, kappa/lambda, CD30, and CD15 was performed, along with Congo red staining. The results showed positive staining for CD20, CD3, CD23, BCL2, and cyclin D1 in appropriate cellular compartments, balanced kappa and lambda light chain expression, and negative staining for CD15, CD30, and Congo red.

Microscopic examination was also performed on additional adjacent benign lymph nodes submitted for histology, which showed similar, though less pronounced, features such as increased vascularity and follicular changes.

What is the most likely diagnosis, and how is it supported by the findings from these investigations?

experiments.sub_conclusion: The high-magnification histology confirms the presence of the diagnostic 'lollipop lesion,' strongly supporting a diagnosis of hyaline vascular variant of Castleman's disease.

reasoning.conclusion: The patient has unicentric hyaline vascular Castleman's disease localized to the cervical lymph node, confirmed by characteristic histological architecture, immunoprofiling, and exclusion of mimics.

question:
A retrospective comparative clinicopathological and prognostic analysis was conducted on 11 female patients with papillary signet-ring cell carcinoma (PSRCC) and 50 female patients with mucinous breast carcinoma (MBC), all with stage I–III disease, based on surgical pathologic records from 1995 to 2010. 

Histological examination of hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained tissue sections was performed on primary tumors from patients with PSRCC and MBC, as well as on metastatic lymph nodes from PSRCC patients. The lymph node sections were imaged at 20x magnification.

Based on these experimental settings and the observed histological features, what conclusions can be drawn regarding the histological and biological distinctions between PSRCC and MBC?

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological examination of H&E-stained tissue sections from MBC cases.
experiments.experiment_goal: To identify the histological hallmark of MBC and differentiate it from PSRCC.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Large pools of extracellular mucin forming pale, amorphous areas that surround and separate clusters of epithelial cells arranged in glandular or cribriform patterns [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: The dominant extracellular mucin deposition is a defining feature of MBC, contrasting with the intracellular mucin in PSRCC. The epithelial clusters are less pleomorphic and more organized than in PSRCC.
experiments.sub_conclusion: MBC is characterized by abundant extracellular mucin with epithelial cell clusters embedded within mucin pools, indicating a less aggressive structural invasion pattern.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological evaluation of lymph node sections from PSRCC patients using H&E staining.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess lymph node metastasis and determine whether metastatic cells retain the primary tumor's morphology.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Clusters and sheets of atypical cells with hyperchromatic nuclei, high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, and disrupted lymphoid architecture infiltrating the lymph node; morphological similarity to primary PSRCC including signet-ring features [Image 4].
experiments.interpretation: The metastatic cells preserve the signet-ring cell morphology of the primary tumor, indicating clonal dissemination and consistent phenotypic expression in secondary sites.
experiments.sub_conclusion: PSRCC metastasizes to lymph nodes while maintaining its characteristic signet-ring cell architecture, supporting its biologically aggressive nature.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: PSRCC is histologically distinct from MBC, with intracytoplasmic mucin causing signet-ring cell morphology and loose cellular cohesion.
MBC is defined by extracellular mucin pools surrounding organized epithelial clusters, contrasting with PSRCC’s intracellular mucin and disorganized growth.
PSRCC metastases in lymph nodes retain the primary tumor's signet-ring morphology, indicating aggressive and phenotypically stable spread.

reasoning.content: The histological analysis reveals two distinct mucin-producing carcinomas: PSRCC, characterized by intracytoplasmic mucin leading to signet-ring cells with nuclear displacement and pleomorphism, and MBC, defined by expansive extracellular mucin separating cohesive epithelial clusters. The preservation of signet-ring morphology in lymph node metastases of PSRCC indicates a stable, aggressive phenotype capable of dissemination. These structural differences correlate with clinical behavior, as PSRCC shows higher rates of lymphatic spread and recurrence. The visual distinction between intracellular (PSRCC) and extracellular (MBC) mucin distribution underpins their classification as separate entities with differing biological behaviors.
reasoning.conclusion: PSRCC and MBC are histologically and biologically distinct entities, with PSRCC exhibiting a signet-ring cell architecture driven by intracytoplasmic mucin and a higher propensity for metastasis, while MBC is characterized by extracellular mucin and a more indolent architectural pattern.

question: A 72-year-old male presents with lower urinary tract symptoms and imaging reveals a large infiltrative prostate mass with hydronephrosis, but no systemic or osseous involvement on bone scintigraphy. A prostate biopsy was performed to evaluate the nature of the lesion. Histological examination of the biopsy tissue was conducted using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining, viewed at 400× magnification. Immunohistochemical analysis was performed on the same tissue using antibodies against CD45, CD20, CD79a, CD3, CD45RO, CD5, CD23, CD10, PSA, P504S, 34E12, CKpan, Syn, and CgA, with DAB chromogen detection and hematoxylin counterstain, also viewed at 400× magnification. What can be concluded regarding the diagnosis of the prostate lesion based on these studies?

input_logic_chain.research_context: Diagnosis of primary non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) of the prostate in Case 1 based on histological and immunohistochemical analysis.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological examination of prostate biopsy tissue using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining, viewed at 400× magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess cellular morphology and architectural pattern of the prostate lesion.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Dense aggregation of large lymphoid cells diffusely infiltrating the tissue, replacing normal prostatic glandular structures. Cells are round to oval with vesicular nuclei, fine chromatin, occasional nucleoli, variable nuclear size and shape, scant amphophilic or basophilic cytoplasm, and high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio. Intercellular stroma is minimally apparent and lightly eosinophilic [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The morphological features—diffuse infiltration, large atypical lymphoid cells with vesicular nuclei and high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio—are characteristic of a high-grade lymphoid neoplasm, specifically consistent with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL). The replacement of normal prostate architecture supports neoplastic infiltration rather than reactive changes.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The histological morphology supports a diagnosis of aggressive lymphoma involving the prostate.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining of the same prostate biopsy tissue using antibodies against CD45, CD20, CD79a, and other lineage-specific markers, with DAB chromogen detection and hematoxylin counterstain, viewed at 400× magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To determine the immunophenotypic profile of the neoplastic cells and confirm lymphoid origin and B-cell lineage.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Strong and diffuse brownish-yellow DAB signal localized to the cytoplasm and cell membranes of the densely packed atypical cells, indicating positive immunoreactivity. The nuclei are pale blue due to hematoxylin counterstain. The background stroma is lightly stained, allowing clear visualization of cellular staining [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: The strong, diffuse positivity for CD45, CD20, and CD79a confirms hematopoietic and B-cell lineage. The absence of T-cell markers (CD3, CD45RO), follicular markers (CD10), mantle cell markers (CD5, CD23), and epithelial/neuroendocrine markers (PSA, P504S, 34E12, CKpan, Syn, CgA) excludes other lymphomas and carcinomas.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The immunophenotype is consistent with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) and rules out prostate adenocarcinoma or other lymphoid neoplasms.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The histological morphology supports a diagnosis of aggressive lymphoma involving the prostate.
The immunophenotype is consistent with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) and rules out prostate adenocarcinoma or other lymphoid neoplasms.

reasoning.content: The histological analysis (H&E staining) revealed a diffuse infiltration of large atypical lymphoid cells with morphological hallmarks of high-grade lymphoma, including vesicular nuclei, fine chromatin, and high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, effectively replacing normal prostate architecture [Image 1]. This pattern is inconsistent with benign prostatic hyperplasia or low-grade neoplasia and strongly suggests an aggressive lymphoid malignancy. Immunohistochemical analysis confirmed this suspicion: the neoplastic cells showed strong membranous and cytoplasmic reactivity for pan-leukocyte marker CD45 and B-cell markers CD20 and CD79a [Image 2], establishing B-cell lineage. Critically, the absence of epithelial markers (PSA, 34E12, CKpan) excludes prostate adenocarcinoma, while negativity for T-cell (CD3, CD45RO), follicular (CD10), and mantle cell (CD5, CD23) markers rules out other lymphoma subtypes. The combined morphological and immunophenotypic profile is diagnostic of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL). Given the absence of systemic involvement on imaging (e.g., negative bone scintigraphy) and primary localization to the prostate, this constitutes a primary NHL of the prostate.
reasoning.conclusion: The lesion in Case 1 is a primary non-Hodgkin lymphoma of the prostate, specifically of the diffuse large B-cell type, confirmed by histomorphology and immunohistochemistry.

question:
To determine the histopathological nature of a non-encapsulated, reddish, lobulated mass excised from the head and neck region, with emphasis on confirming the diagnosis of intramuscular angiolipoma based on tissue architecture and cellular composition, the following investigations were performed:

1. Histopathological examination of the excised mass using Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) staining was conducted under light microscopy at an original magnification of ×40.

2. A second histological analysis using H&E staining was performed at a higher magnification of ×100 to examine finer structural details.

3. Clinical and intraoperative evaluation during sub-platysma dissection under general anesthesia revealed that the mass was located beneath the posterior edge of the masseter muscle, in contact with the right posterior digastric muscle and superficial parotid lobe. It was reddish, lobulated, and exhibited excessive bleeding during excision.

What can be concluded from these findings?

input_logic_chain.research_context: To determine the histopathological nature of a non-encapsulated, reddish, lobulated mass excised from the head and neck region, with emphasis on confirming the diagnosis of intramuscular angiolipoma based on tissue architecture and cellular composition.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histopathological examination of the excised mass using Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) staining, observed under light microscopy at an original magnification of ×40.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess the overall tissue architecture, encapsulation status, and spatial relationship between vascular and adipose components.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The micrograph shows a non-encapsulated mass with irregularly shaped vascular channels of varying sizes, lined by flattened endothelial cells with dark blue-purple nuclei and eosinophilic cytoplasm, embedded within a background of mature adipose tissue. The adipocytes exhibit large clear cytoplasmic vacuoles, thin rims of cytoplasm, and peripherally located nuclei. The vascular lumens contain eosinophilic material and red blood cells. There is no fibrous boundary separating the vascular and adipose elements, and the distribution appears disorganized and infiltrative [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The absence of a fibrous capsule and the intermingling of vascular and adipose tissues without clear demarcation suggest an infiltrative growth pattern. The presence of mature adipocytes and thin-walled vascular channels filled with red blood cells indicates a mixed mesenchymal tumor with prominent vascular and fatty components, consistent with angiolipoma.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The lesion lacks a capsule and demonstrates an infiltrative admixture of mature adipose tissue and vascular structures, supporting a diagnosis of non-encapsulated, infiltrating angiolipoma.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological analysis using H&E staining at a higher magnification of ×100 to evaluate cellular details and vascular morphology.
experiments.experiment_goal: To examine the structural complexity of the vascular component and the heterogeneity of the stromal environment.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The section reveals irregular, tortuous, and branching blood vessels with variable luminal dilation and endothelial lining. A central vessel shows thickened walls and uneven endothelial arrangement. The surrounding stroma contains mature adipocytes, loose connective tissue, scattered collagen fibers, and areas of hemorrhage with punctate red blood cell deposits. Hyperchromatic nuclear aggregates are present in zones of differing staining intensity, and the overall architecture lacks regularity [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: The tortuous, complex vascular network with areas of hemorrhage and thickened vessel walls indicates abnormal vascular proliferation. The coexistence of mature adipocytes with disorganized vascular elements in a non-encapsulated, infiltrative pattern further supports the diagnosis of angiolipoma, particularly the infiltrative subtype. The absence of cellular atypia or mitotic figures argues against malignancy.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The vascular component is highly developed and disorganized, consistent with the angiomatous variant of lipoma, and the lack of malignant features supports a benign diagnosis.

experiments.experimental_setting: Clinical and intraoperative evaluation during sub-platysma dissection under general anesthesia, including assessment of tumor location and bleeding tendency.
experiments.experiment_goal: To determine the anatomical location, vascularity, and surgical challenges associated with the mass.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The mass was located beneath the posterior edge of the masseter muscle, in contact with the right posterior digastric muscle and superficial parotid lobe. It was described as reddish and lobulated, with excessive bleeding encountered during excision [Context].
experiments.interpretation: The reddish color and significant intraoperative bleeding suggest a hypervascular tumor. The anatomical location within the deep musculature of the face supports an intramuscular origin. The lobulated, non-encapsulated appearance correlates with the histopathological findings of infiltration.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The clinical and surgical features—hypervascularity, intramuscular location, and non-encapsulated appearance—are consistent with an infiltrating angiolipoma.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The lesion lacks a fibrous capsule and shows an infiltrative admixture of vascular and adipose elements.
The vascular component is prominent, disorganized, and tortuous, with evidence of hemorrhage, confirming the angiomatous nature.
The tumor is located intramuscularly and exhibits high vascularity clinically, corroborating histopathological findings.

reasoning.content: The integration of histopathological and clinical findings establishes a coherent diagnostic pathway. The absence of a capsule and the interwoven distribution of mature adipocytes and thin-walled, blood-filled vascular channels observed at ×40 magnification [Image 1] indicate a non-encapsulated, infiltrative lesion. At higher magnification (×100) [Image 2], the tortuous, branching vessels with thickened walls and stromal hemorrhage confirm a significant vascular proliferation, characteristic of angiolipoma. The clinical presentation—reddish, lobulated mass with excessive bleeding during surgery—aligns with the hypervascular nature seen microscopically. The tumor's location beneath the masseter and in contact with the digastric muscle supports an intramuscular origin. Together, these findings exclude typical lipoma (which is usually encapsulated and less vascular) and rule out malignancy due to the absence of cytological atypia. The final diagnosis hinges on the combined histological pattern of mature fat with prominent, infiltrative vasculature.
reasoning.conclusion: The excised mass is a non-encapsulated, infiltrating intramuscular angiolipoma, diagnosed based on histopathological evidence of mature adipose tissue intermixed with a disorganized, hypervascular network, supported by clinical and surgical findings.

question: In a study of 26 P. plica-infected canids (13 red foxes and 13 wolves), lymphocytic or lympho-plasmacytic infiltrates were recorded in the lamina propria, submucosal blood vessels, or as perivascular infiltrates. Histological examination of urinary bladder tissue from P. plica-infected wolves and red foxes was performed using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining to assess inflammatory changes. Additionally, histological analysis was conducted on bladder tissue from five P. plica-infected wolves with moderate to severe eosinophilic cystitis using H&E staining. A separate histological evaluation focused on the bladder mucosa in P. plica-infected wolves with moderate to severe cystitis using H&E-stained sections, with a scale bar indicating 50–60 micrometers. What conclusions can be drawn from these findings and experiments regarding the histopathological response to P. plica infection in canids?

input_logic_chain.research_context: In 26 P. plica-infected canids (13 red foxes and 13 wolves), lymphocytic or lympho-plasmacytic infiltrates were recorded in the lamina propria, submucosal blood vessels, or as perivascular infiltrates. In five infected wolves with moderate or severe eosinophilic cystitis, additional histopathological features were observed, including lymphoid nodule hyperplasia, perinodular hemorrhages, hyperaemia, and microhemorrhages in the lamina propria. Lymphoid nodule hyperplasia was not observed in other species or in mild cystitis cases. Mild eosinophilic and lympho-plasmacytic infiltrates were also found around ureteral openings in two wolves with moderate and severe cystitis.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological examination of urinary bladder tissue from P. plica-infected wolves and red foxes, using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining to assess inflammatory changes.
experiments.experiment_goal: To characterize the nature and distribution of inflammatory infiltrates in the urinary bladder of P. plica-infected canids.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Lymphocytic or lympho-plasmacytic infiltrates were observed in the lamina propria, within submucosal blood vessels, or as perivascular infiltrates in 26 infected canids [Context].
experiments.interpretation: The presence of lymphocytes and plasma cells in these locations indicates a chronic inflammatory response, likely driven by persistent P. plica infection in the urinary tract.
experiments.sub_conclusion: P. plica infection in canids is associated with chronic inflammation in the urinary bladder, characterized by lympho-plasmacytic infiltration in specific tissue compartments.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological analysis of bladder tissue from five P. plica-infected wolves with moderate to severe eosinophilic cystitis, using H&E staining.
experiments.experiment_goal: To identify distinctive histopathological features associated with more severe forms of cystitis in wolves.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: A prominent, rounded lymphoid nodule is located in the submucosa, surrounded by a dense infiltration of cells with bright pink granular cytoplasm (eosinophils), along with lymphocytes and plasma cells in the lamina propria [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The dense aggregation of small, darkly stained nuclei within a defined nodule indicates organized lymphoid tissue (lymphoid nodule hyperplasia). The surrounding bright pink granular cells are morphologically consistent with eosinophils, indicating a strong eosinophilic component to the inflammation.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Wolves with moderate to severe eosinophilic cystitis exhibit lymphoid nodule hyperplasia in the submucosa accompanied by a prominent eosinophilic and lympho-plasmacytic infiltrate.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological evaluation of bladder mucosa in P. plica-infected wolves with moderate to severe cystitis, using H&E-stained sections.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess epithelial integrity and presence of microhemorrhages in severe cystitis.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The mucosal epithelium appears discontinuous with focal thinning and reduced cellular cohesion. Beneath it, numerous cells with bilobed nuclei and pink cytoplasm are densely distributed. A small hemorrhage is visible beneath the epithelium, with red blood cells outside vascular structures [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: The discontinuous epithelium suggests mucosal damage. The cells with bilobed nuclei and eosinophilic cytoplasm are morphologically consistent with eosinophils. The presence of red blood cells outside vessels confirms microhemorrhage, indicating vascular fragility or inflammation-induced damage.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Severe eosinophilic cystitis in wolves is associated with epithelial disruption, dense eosinophilic infiltration in the lamina propria, and microhemorrhages.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: P. plica infection induces chronic inflammation in canids, evidenced by lympho-plasmacytic infiltrates in the lamina propria and perivascular regions.
Lymphoid nodule hyperplasia in the submucosa, surrounded by eosinophilic and lympho-plasmacytic infiltrates, is a distinctive feature observed only in wolves with moderate to severe cystitis.
Severe cystitis in wolves is associated with structural tissue damage, including epithelial discontinuity and microhemorrhages, alongside intense eosinophilic infiltration.

reasoning.content: The histopathological findings from infected canids reveal a spectrum of inflammatory responses. While lympho-plasmacytic infiltration is common across infected red foxes and wolves, more severe pathology—specifically lymphoid nodule hyperplasia—is restricted to wolves with moderate or severe eosinophilic cystitis. The presence of organized lymphoid tissue in the submucosa (Image 1) indicates a localized adaptive immune response, possibly in reaction to persistent antigenic stimulation by P. plica. This hyperplasia is not seen in other species or in mild disease, suggesting a species-specific or severity-dependent immunological reaction. Concurrently, the disruption of epithelial integrity and presence of microhemorrhages (Image 2) reflect significant tissue injury in advanced disease. The dense eosinophilic infiltrate surrounding the lymphoid nodule and in the lamina propria underscores the prominence of eosinophils in severe inflammation, likely involved in parasite containment or immunopathology. Together, these findings demonstrate that P. plica infection in wolves can drive a distinct, severe inflammatory phenotype involving lymphoid neogenesis, eosinophilia, and tissue damage.
reasoning.conclusion: Lymphoid nodule hyperplasia in the urinary bladder is a histopathological hallmark of moderate to severe P. plica-associated eosinophilic cystitis in wolves and is not observed in other canid species or in milder forms of the disease, indicating a species- and severity-specific immune response.

question:
To investigate the differential mRNA and protein expression of TGF-β subtypes (TGF-β1, TGF-β2, TGF-β3, TGF-β4) between ovarian carcinoma and normal ovarian tissues, and to assess their prognostic significance in ovarian cancer, the following experiments were conducted:

1. mRNA expression levels of TGF-β1, TGF-β2, TGF-β3, and TGF-β4 were analyzed using data from the Oncomine database. Box plots comparing expression levels between ovarian carcinoma and normal ovarian tissues showed no significant differences for TGF-β1 (P = 0.57), TGF-β3 (P = 0.994), and TGF-β4 (P = 0.749). In contrast, TGF-β2 showed a higher mRNA expression in cancer tissues with a fold change of 1.368 and a statistically significant difference (P = 0.007).

2. Immunohistochemical (IHC) staining was performed on human ovarian carcinoma and normal ovarian tissue sections to assess protein expression of TGF-β2.

3. Immunohistochemical staining was also performed on ovarian carcinoma and normal ovarian tissue sections to evaluate TGF-β3 protein expression.

What conclusions can be drawn from these experiments regarding the expression and regulation of TGF-β subtypes in ovarian carcinoma compared to normal ovarian tissues?

input_logic_chain.research_context: To investigate the differential mRNA and protein expression of TGF-β subtypes (TGF-β1, TGF-β2, TGF-β3, TGF-β4) between ovarian carcinoma and normal ovarian tissues, and to assess their prognostic significance in ovarian cancer.

experiments.experimental_setting: mRNA expression levels of TGF-β1, TGF-β2, TGF-β3, and TGF-β4 were analyzed using data from the Oncomine database. Box plots were generated to compare expression levels between ovarian carcinoma and normal ovarian tissues (Figure 5).
experiments.experiment_goal: To determine whether there are significant differences in mRNA expression levels of TGF-β subtypes between ovarian carcinoma and normal ovarian tissues.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: [Context]: In the box plots (Figure 5), TGF-β1, TGF-β3, and TGF-β4 show overlapping distributions between cancer and normal tissues with no significant differences (P = 0.57, P = 0.994, P = 0.749, respectively). TGF-β2 shows a higher median expression in cancer tissues with a fold change of 1.368 and a statistically significant difference (P = 0.007).
experiments.interpretation: The lack of significant difference in mRNA levels for TGF-β1, TGF-β3, and TGF-β4 suggests no major transcriptional regulation of these isoforms in ovarian carcinoma. In contrast, the significantly elevated mRNA level of TGF-β2 in cancer tissues indicates selective upregulation of this isoform at the transcriptional level.
experiments.sub_conclusion: TGF-β2, but not TGF-β1, TGF-β3, or TGF-β4, exhibits significantly higher mRNA expression in ovarian carcinoma compared to normal ovarian tissues.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical (IHC) staining was performed on human ovarian carcinoma and normal ovarian tissue sections to assess protein expression of TGF-β2 and TGF-β3. Staining intensity and distribution were evaluated, and staining scores were calculated (Figure 6).
experiments.experiment_goal: To validate the differential expression of TGF-β2 and TGF-β3 at the protein level and compare their expression between ovarian carcinoma and normal tissues.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: In :fig6 a [Image 1], ovarian carcinoma tissue shows dense, irregularly arranged cells with diffuse to granular brownish-yellow cytoplasmic staining of variable intensity, with areas of strong staining interspersed with lighter regions. Nuclei are blue. In :fig6 b [Image 2], normal ovarian tissue shows heterogeneous but generally fainter brown cytoplasmic staining, primarily in stromal cells, with well-preserved architecture and no malignant features.
experiments.interpretation: The brownish-yellow chromogen indicates TGF-β2 protein presence. The higher intensity and broader distribution of staining in carcinoma tissue compared to normal tissue suggest increased TGF-β2 protein expression in cancer. The cytoplasmic localization confirms intracellular expression.
experiments.sub_conclusion: TGF-β2 protein expression is significantly higher in ovarian carcinoma tissues than in normal ovarian tissues, as evidenced by more intense and widespread cytoplasmic immunostaining.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining for TGF-β3 was performed on ovarian carcinoma and normal ovarian tissue sections (Figure 6).
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate TGF-β3 protein expression levels in ovarian carcinoma versus normal ovarian tissues.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: In :fig6 c [Image 3], ovarian carcinoma tissue displays heterogeneous brownish to brownish-yellow cytoplasmic staining with variable intensity, concentrated in densely packed, irregular cells. In :fig6 d [Image 4], normal ovarian tissue shows punctate to granular brown chromogenic deposits in a loosely organized stromal matrix with spindle-shaped cells, with lower overall staining intensity and sparser distribution.
experiments.interpretation: The brown chromogen indicates TGF-β3 protein expression localized in the cytoplasm. The increased staining intensity and density in carcinoma tissue compared to normal tissue reflect higher TGF-β3 protein expression in cancer, despite no significant mRNA difference.
experiments.sub_conclusion: TGF-β3 protein expression is significantly elevated in ovarian carcinoma tissues compared to normal tissues, suggesting post-transcriptional regulation or protein stabilization in cancer.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: TGF-β2 mRNA is significantly upregulated in ovarian carcinoma, while TGF-β1, TGF-β3, and TGF-β4 show no significant changes.
TGF-β2 protein expression is significantly higher in ovarian carcinoma tissues compared to normal tissues, consistent with its mRNA upregulation.
TGF-β3 protein expression is significantly elevated in ovarian carcinoma despite no significant change in its mRNA levels, suggesting post-transcriptional regulation.

reasoning.content: The initial mRNA analysis revealed that only TGF-β2 is transcriptionally upregulated in ovarian carcinoma, while TGF-β1, TGF-β3, and TGF-β4 show no significant differences. This selective transcriptional activation of TGF-β2 is supported by immunohistochemical evidence showing higher protein expression of TGF-β2 in cancer tissues, with intense and widespread cytoplasmic staining compared to normal tissues. Notably, although TGF-β3 mRNA levels do not differ significantly between cancer and normal tissues, its protein expression is markedly increased in carcinoma, as shown by stronger and more extensive cytoplasmic immunostaining. This discrepancy suggests that TGF-β3 expression in ovarian cancer may be regulated at the post-transcriptional level, such as through enhanced translation, reduced degradation, or protein stabilization. Together, these findings highlight TGF-β2 and TGF-β3 as functionally relevant isoforms in ovarian carcinoma, with TGF-β2 driven by transcriptional upregulation and TGF-β3 potentially regulated post-transcriptionally. These results align with the study's conclusion that TGF-β2 and TGF-β3, but not TGF-β1 or TGF-β4, are associated with poor prognosis in ovarian cancer patients.
reasoning.conclusion: TGF-β2 and TGF-β3 are significantly overexpressed at the protein level in ovarian carcinoma tissues compared to normal ovarian tissues. While TGF-β2 overexpression is driven by increased mRNA transcription, TGF-β3 overexpression occurs despite unchanged mRNA levels, suggesting distinct regulatory mechanisms. These findings support the prognostic relevance of TGF-β2 and TGF-β3 in ovarian cancer.

question:
A 30-year-old patient presents with abdominal distension and imaging reveals a large mesenteric mass. Following resection, the pathological identity of the mass must be determined based on gross, histological, and intraoperative findings. 

Gross examination of the formalin-fixed tumor revealed a multicystic structure with cyst diameters ranging from 0.3 to 2 cm; each lobule contained milky white fluid, and caseous material remained after drainage. 

Histological analysis was performed using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining at ×10 magnification. 

Additional histological evaluation was conducted using H&E staining at 40× magnification. 

Intraoperatively, the mass was observed to be yellowish, cystic, and lobulated, with a mostly complete capsule. There was tight adhesion near the descending duodenum, and visible tumor-related lymphatic vessels were seen draining toward the retroperitoneum near the head of the pancreas. 

What is the most likely pathological diagnosis, and how is it supported by the integration of these findings?

input_logic_chain.research_context: Determine the pathological identity of a large mesenteric cystic mass based on gross, histological, and intraoperative findings.

experiments.experimental_setting: Gross examination of the resected tumor following formalin fixation; measurement and visual inspection of the tumor's external and internal features.
experiments.experiment_goal: To characterize the macroscopic morphology and structural composition of the tumor.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The tumor was multicystic with cyst diameters ranging from 0.3 to 2 cm; each lobule contained milky white fluid, and caseous material remained after drainage [Context].
experiments.interpretation: The presence of multiple fluid-filled cysts with lipid-rich (milky) content and semi-solid debris suggests a lymphatic origin, as chyle is composed of乳糜 (chylomicrons, lymph, and lipids).
experiments.sub_conclusion: The gross morphology and fluid characteristics are consistent with a lymphatic-derived cystic lesion.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological analysis of the tumor tissue using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining at ×10 magnification [Image 1].
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate the cellular composition and architectural organization of the cystic structures.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Multiple rounded to ovoid clear spaces representing cystic structures, each bounded by thin walls of spindle-shaped cells with pale cytoplasm and central nuclei; internally lined by flattened, elongated cells with inconspicuous cytoplasm [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The spindle-shaped cells correspond to smooth muscle cells, and the flattened internal lining cells are endothelial cells, indicating a vascular or lymphatic endothelial-lined cystic structure supported by a muscular and connective tissue wall.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The cystic walls consist of an inner endothelial lining and an outer smooth muscle layer, supporting a congenital or developmental cystic lesion of lymphatic origin.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological analysis using H&E staining at 40× magnification [Image 2].
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess inflammatory or immune cell infiltration and stromal composition around the cystic structures.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Dense accumulation of small, round cells with dark blue to purple nuclei and scant cytoplasm adjacent to and within the cystic areas; these cells are closely packed and aligned along cyst margins and in surrounding tissue [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: The small, round, basophilic cells with high nuclear density and minimal cytoplasm are morphologically consistent with lymphocytes, indicating lymphocytic infiltration within and around the cystic spaces.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The presence of pericystic and intracystic lymphocytes supports an immunologically active lymphatic tissue environment, typical of lymphatic malformations.

experiments.experimental_setting: Intraoperative observation and dissection of the mass, including assessment of anatomical relationships and adhesions.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate the anatomical extent, encapsulation, and relationship with surrounding structures.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The mass was yellowish, cystic, lobulated, and mostly encapsulated; tight adhesion was present near the descending duodenum; visible tumor-related lymphatic vessels drained toward the retroperitoneum near the pancreatic head [Context].
experiments.interpretation: The yellowish color suggests lipid content; the lobulated, cystic appearance with partial capsule and associated lymphatic channels indicates a benign, expansive lymphatic malformation. Drainage toward retroperitoneal nodes is consistent with native lymphatic flow patterns.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The intraoperative appearance and lymphatic drainage pattern are characteristic of a benign lymphatic hygroma.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The tumor is composed of multicystic spaces filled with lipid-rich fluid, as evidenced by milky white content and residual caseous material.
The cystic structures are lined by endothelial cells and supported by smooth muscle and connective tissue, confirming a vascular/lymphatic endothelial origin.
Lymphocytic infiltration within and around the cysts indicates an active lymphatic microenvironment.
The gross and anatomical features, including color, adhesion, and lymphatic drainage, support a diagnosis of a benign lymphatic malformation.

reasoning.content: The integration of gross, histological, and intraoperative findings reveals a consistent pattern: the tumor is a multicystic, lobulated mass derived from lymphatic tissue. The presence of endothelial-lined cysts containing chylous fluid, supported by smooth muscle and connective tissue, is diagnostic of a lymphatic malformation. The additional findings of lymphocytic infiltration and retroperitoneal lymphatic drainage further confirm the lymphatic nature of the lesion. These features collectively exclude other differential diagnoses such as cystic mesothelioma, teratoma, or enteric duplication cyst, which lack the specific combination of endothelial lining, smooth muscle wall, lymphocyte infiltration, and chyle content. The formal pathological diagnosis of lymphatic hygroma is therefore fully supported by all lines of evidence.
reasoning.conclusion: The pathological diagnosis of lymphatic hygroma is confirmed based on the integration of gross morphology, histological architecture, cellular composition, and intraoperative findings.

question: A 58-year-old woman with a liver mass underwent hepatic resection to determine the histopathological characteristics of the tumor for definitive diagnosis, assessment of differentiation, and evaluation of microvascular invasion. Histopathological analysis of the resected tumor was performed using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining, with examination at ×200 magnification [Image 1]. The non-neoplastic liver tissue was also evaluated and showed preserved lobular architecture with normal hepatocytes, unremarkable portal tracts, and no fibrosis or inflammation [Image 2]. Based on these findings, what diagnosis and pathological features can be concluded regarding the resected tumor?

input_logic_chain.research_context: Determine the histopathological characteristics of the resected liver tumor to confirm the diagnosis of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and assess tumor differentiation and microvascular invasion.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histopathological examination of the resected tumor tissue using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining, viewed at ×200 magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate cellular morphology, architectural patterns, and presence of microvascular invasion in the tumor.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The tissue section is densely cellular, composed of polygonal cells arranged in trabecular and solid patterns, with occasional gland-like or pseudoglandular formations. Cells have distinct cell borders, moderate nuclear pleomorphism, hyperchromatic and variably enlarged nuclei, and occasional prominent nucleoli. Cytoplasm is eosinophilic to amphophilic. Mitotic figures are present but not abundant. Thin fibrous septa delineate nodular or lobular structures. No tumor cells are observed within endothelial-lined vascular channels [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The trabecular and solid growth patterns, nuclear pleomorphism, hyperchromasia, and mitotic activity are characteristic of hepatocellular carcinoma. The relative architectural organization and lack of diffuse infiltration suggest well-to-moderately differentiated HCC. The absence of tumor cells within endothelial-lined vascular spaces indicates no microvascular invasion.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The tumor is consistent with well-to-moderately differentiated hepatocellular carcinoma without microvascular invasion.

The degree of nuclear atypia and architectural preservation indicates well-to-moderate differentiation.
Absence of tumor cells within vascular channels rules out microvascular invasion.

These features, in conjunction with the clinical and imaging context, confirm the neoplastic nature of the lesion.
