question:
To determine the histopathological features of solitary benign lichenoid keratosis (SBLK), specifically the plaque-like variant, a series of histological evaluations were performed on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded skin biopsy sections stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E). 

- One section was examined under light microscopy at 100x magnification to evaluate epidermal architecture. 
- The same section was analyzed to characterize the inflammatory infiltrate at the dermoepidermal junction and upper dermis. 
- High-resolution examination of the basal layer and dermoepidermal interface was conducted to assess cytological changes in basal keratinocytes. 
- Intercellular connections at the dermoepidermal junction were evaluated for evidence of loss of cohesion. 
- Dermal changes and signs of solar damage were assessed in both lesional and perilesional areas. 

What can be concluded from these histopathological evaluations?

input_logic_chain.research_context: To determine the histopathological features of solitary benign lichenoid keratosis (SBLK), specifically the plaque-like variant, based on microscopic evaluation of skin biopsy specimens.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological examination of a formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded skin biopsy section stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E), viewed under light microscopy at 100x magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess epidermal architectural changes in the lesional skin.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The stratum corneum is thickened with focal areas showing retained nuclei within corneocytes; the granular layer is thickened; rete ridges are flattened, resulting in a planar epidermal-dermal interface [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: Thickened stratum corneum with retained nuclei indicates hyperkeratosis with focal parakeratosis. Increased granular layer thickness corresponds to hypergranulosis. Flattening of rete ridges suggests chronic interface dermatitis or epidermal atrophy.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The epidermis exhibits hyperkeratosis, focal parakeratosis, hypergranulosis, and flattening of rete ridges, consistent with a chronic lichenoid reaction pattern.

experiments.experimental_setting: Same H&E-stained section examined for inflammatory infiltrate distribution and morphology at the dermoepidermal junction and upper dermis.
experiments.experiment_goal: To characterize the nature, distribution, and composition of the inflammatory infiltrate.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: A dense, band-like accumulation of mononuclear cells is present at the dermoepidermal junction, forming a continuous infiltrate that obscures the basement membrane zone; the upper dermis contains scattered cells with brownish granular cytoplasmic pigment [Image 1 and Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: The band-like lymphohistiocytic infiltrate at the dermoepidermal junction is characteristic of lichenoid tissue reactions. The brownish granular pigment in cytoplasm corresponds to melanin-laden macrophages (melanophages), indicating pigment incontinence from damaged basal keratinocytes.
experiments.sub_conclusion: There is a dense band-like lymphohistiocytic infiltrate at the dermoepidermal junction with melanophages in the upper dermis, supporting a diagnosis of a lichenoid dermatitis with pigmentary changes.

experiments.experimental_setting: High-resolution examination of the basal layer and dermoepidermal interface in H&E-stained sections.
experiments.experiment_goal: To identify specific cytological changes in basal keratinocytes and the presence of apoptotic bodies.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Clear intracytoplasmic spaces within basal keratinocytes; some cells show cytoplasmic clearing and nuclear condensation; eosinophilic, rounded, amorphous structures are present at the dermoepidermal junction, one marked by an arrow [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: Clear spaces in basal cells represent vacuolar degeneration due to cytoplasmic swelling and early apoptosis. Eosinophilic rounded structures are colloid bodies (Civatte bodies), which are apoptotic keratinocytes resulting from basal cell damage.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Vacuolar degeneration of the basal layer and presence of colloid bodies confirm ongoing basal cell injury and apoptosis, hallmark features of lichenoid inflammation.

experiments.experimental_setting: Evaluation of intercellular connections at the dermoepidermal junction in H&E-stained sections.
experiments.experiment_goal: To detect evidence of loss of cohesion between basal keratinocytes.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Small clefts or microblisters are visible between basal keratinocytes at the dermoepidermal junction [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: These clefts represent Max-Joseph spaces, which result from detachment of basal keratinocytes due to immune-mediated damage, commonly seen in lichen planus and lichenoid keratoses.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Max-Joseph space formation indicates intercellular separation at the dermoepidermal junction, further supporting a lichenoid pathological process.

experiments.experimental_setting: Assessment of dermal changes and solar damage in the lesional and perilesional areas.
experiments.experiment_goal: To rule out solar elastosis and differentiate from solar lentigo.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The dermal stroma appears edematous with loose connective tissue and sparse collagen fibers; there is no accumulation of tangled, basophilic elastic fibers in the papillary dermis [Context].
experiments.interpretation: Absence of solar elastosis (degenerated elastic fibers) indicates lack of significant chronic sun damage. This helps exclude solar lentigo and other sun-induced lesions.
experiments.sub_conclusion: No solar elastosis or features of solar lentigo are present, supporting that the lesion is not primarily driven by photodamage.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The epidermis exhibits hyperkeratosis, focal parakeratosis, hypergranulosis, and flattening of rete ridges, consistent with a chronic lichenoid reaction pattern.
There is a dense band-like lymphohistiocytic infiltrate at the dermoepidermal junction with melanophages in the upper dermis, supporting a diagnosis of a lichenoid dermatitis with pigmentary changes.
Vacuolar degeneration of the basal layer and presence of colloid bodies confirm ongoing basal cell injury and apoptosis, hallmark features of lichenoid inflammation.
Max-Joseph space formation indicates intercellular separation at the dermoepidermal junction, further supporting a lichenoid pathological process.
No solar elastosis or features of solar lentigo are present, supporting that the lesion is not primarily driven by photodamage.

reasoning.content: The histopathological findings collectively demonstrate epidermal changes including hyperkeratosis, focal parakeratosis, hypergranulosis, and flattened rete ridges. A dense, band-like lymphohistiocytic infiltrate at the dermoepidermal junction is associated with Max-Joseph spaces, vacuolar degeneration of the basal layer, and colloid bodies—features diagnostic of a lichenoid tissue reaction. The presence of melanophages in the upper dermis indicates pigment incontinence secondary to basal cell damage. The absence of solar elastosis and lack of features suggestive of solar lentigo at the margins exclude a photodamaged or sun-induced etiology. These findings are consistent with the plaque-like variant of solitary benign lichenoid keratosis (SBLK), a clinicopathological entity characterized by a benign, self-limited lichenoid reaction on sun-exposed or sun-protected skin, typically in middle-aged to older adults.
reasoning.conclusion: The histopathological features observed in the biopsy are diagnostic of solitary benign lichenoid keratosis (plaque-like variant), characterized by a lichenoid interface dermatitis with epidermal hyperplasia, basal cell damage, pigment incontinence, and absence of solar elastosis.

question:
In the Robinsons grading system, six cytological parameters—cell dissociation, cell size, uniformity, nucleoli, nuclear margin, and chromatin—are each scored from 1 to 3, with total scores of 6–11, 12–14, and 15–18 corresponding to grade I, II, and III, respectively.

Microscopic evaluation of H&E-stained cytology smears was performed at 400x magnification to assess these six morphological parameters. Examination of [Image 1], [Image 2], and [Image 3] reveals significant cytological atypia across multiple fields. 

What conclusion can be drawn regarding the Robinsons grade based on this evaluation?

input_logic_chain.research_context: Robinsons grading system [7, 8] evaluates six cytological parameters—cell dissociation, cell size, uniformity, nucleoli, nuclear margin, and chromatin—each scored from 1 to 3. Total scores of 6–11, 12–14, and 15–18 correspond to grade I, II, and III, respectively.

experiments.experimental_setting: Microscopic evaluation of H&E-stained cytology smears at 400x magnification to assess six morphological parameters: cell dissociation, cell size, uniformity, nucleoli, nuclear margin, and chromatin.
experiments.experiment_goal: To determine the Robinsons grade based on cytological features.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Cells display marked pleomorphism with pronounced variation in nuclear size and shape, including angular, lobulated, and rounded forms. Nuclear membranes are irregular, chromatin is coarsely clumped and unevenly distributed with areas of clearing [Image 1]. Multiple isolated, darkly stained nuclei without cytoplasmic borders are scattered across the background [Image 2]. Heterogeneous population of cells with variably enlarged nuclei, elevated nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, coarse chromatin, and prominent nucleoli [Image 3].
experiments.interpretation: Marked nuclear pleomorphism, irregular nuclear membranes, and coarse chromatin indicate significant nuclear atypia. The presence of isolated nuclei without cytoplasm suggests extensive cell dissociation. Prominent nucleoli and high N:C ratio reflect increased metabolic and proliferative activity, typical of high-grade malignancy.
experiments.sub_conclusion: All six parameters in the Robinsons system (cell dissociation, cell size, uniformity, nucleoli, nuclear margin, chromatin) show marked abnormalities, each warranting a score of 3.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: Each of the six parameters in the Robinsons system exhibits severe morphological atypia, consistent with a score of 3 per parameter.

reasoning.content: The visual evidence shows extreme cell dissociation, as seen by the scattered, isolated nuclei without cytoplasmic borders [Image 2], supporting a score of 3 for cell dissociation. Marked variation in nuclear size and shape [Images 1, 2, 3] indicates maximal scores for cell size and uniformity. Irregular nuclear margins with angular and lobulated forms [Image 1] justify a score of 3 for nuclear margin. Coarse, clumped, and unevenly distributed chromatin with hypochromatic areas [Image 1] meets criteria for a score of 3 in chromatin. Prominent and enlarged nucleoli in multiple nuclei [Images 1, 3] support a score of 3 for nucleoli. With all six parameters scoring 3, the total score is 18.
reasoning.conclusion: According to the Robinsons grading system, a total score of 18 corresponds to grade III.

question: A case report describes a hyaline cell-rich apocrine mixed tumor with cytologic atypia, and immunohistochemical profiling is performed to characterize the tumor cell phenotype and confirm diagnosis. Immunohistochemical staining was conducted on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue sections using antibodies against S-100 protein, AE1/AE3, CAM 5.2, vimentin, epithelial membrane antigen (EMA), p63, smooth muscle actin (SMA), desmin, cytokeratin 7 (CK7), carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), Ki-67, and p53. Standard chromogenic detection with diaminobenzidine (DAB) was used, and sections were counterstained with hematoxylin. The staining patterns were evaluated using representative photomicrographs (Image 1, Image 2, Image 3, Image 4) for selected markers. For one set of markers, no brown chromogenic signal was observed in tumor cells for EMA, p63, SMA, desmin, CK7, and CEA. Additionally, atypical ‘monster’ cells showed no brown nuclear staining for Ki-67 or p53. Based on these findings, what can be concluded about the immunophenotype, cellular differentiation, and biological behavior of the tumor?

input_logic_chain.research_context: The case report presents a hyaline cell-rich apocrine mixed tumor with cytologic atypia, and immunohistochemical profiling is used to characterize the tumor cell phenotype and confirm its diagnosis.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining was performed on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue sections using antibodies against S-100 protein, AE1/AE3, CAM 5.2, vimentin, epithelial membrane antigen (EMA), p63, smooth muscle actin (SMA), desmin, cytokeratin 7 (CK7), carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), Ki-67, and p53. Standard chromogenic detection with diaminobenzidine (DAB) was used, and sections were counterstained with hematoxylin.
experiments.experiment_goal: To determine the immunophenotypic profile of the hyaline cells and assess for markers of epithelial, myoepithelial, apocrine, and proliferative differentiation.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: A dense cluster of rounded to oval cells shows brown chromogenic staining localized in both cytoplasm and nucleus, with variable intensity. Surrounding tissue shows minimal or no staining, and the background matrix is lightly counterstained, allowing clear demarcation of the stained cluster [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The brown chromogenic signal indicates positive immunoreactivity for S-100 protein. The localization in both cytoplasm and nucleus is typical for S-100. The focal concentration and variable intensity suggest heterogeneous expression within the tumor cell population, but strong reactivity supports a myoepithelial or neural crest-derived phenotype.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The hyaline cells express S-100 protein, supporting their myoepithelial lineage or differentiation potential.

experiments.experimental_setting: Same as above.
experiments.experiment_goal: To confirm epithelial origin of the tumor cells using pan-cytokeratin markers (AE1/AE3 and CAM 5.2).
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Strong brown cytoplasmic staining in densely packed epithelial cells arranged in glandular patterns, with clear contrast against unstained stroma [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: The diffuse cytoplasmic positivity for AE1/AE3 confirms the epithelial nature of the tumor cells. The glandular arrangement supports ductal or acinar differentiation, consistent with apocrine mixed tumor morphology.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The tumor cells are epithelial in origin and show ductal organization, consistent with an epithelial-myoepithelial neoplasm.

experiments.experimental_setting: Same as above.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate for additional epithelial and myoepithelial markers, particularly CAM 5.2 and vimentin.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: A cluster of cells with pale, eosinophilic cytoplasm and indistinct borders shows strong brown staining in cytoplasmic and membranous compartments, with heterogeneous intensity. Some cells are intensely positive, others weakly. Nuclei are clearly visible and vary in shape. Glandular lumina are present [Image 3].
experiments.interpretation: Positive staining for CAM 5.2 (low molecular weight cytokeratins) further confirms epithelial differentiation, particularly of ductal or secretory cells. Membranous reactivity may reflect cell adhesion or polarization. The presence of lumina supports functional ductal structures.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The tumor exhibits ductal epithelial differentiation with luminal formation, supporting apocrine differentiation.

experiments.experimental_setting: Same as above.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess for mesenchymal or myoepithelial marker expression using vimentin.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Densely packed cells with rounded to irregular morphology show brown cytoplasmic staining, variable in intensity, with some perinuclear and process-like extension. Nuclei are round to oval and lightly stained. Background stroma is pale [Image 4].
experiments.interpretation: Cytoplasmic vimentin expression is characteristic of mesenchymal, myoepithelial, or undifferentiated cells. The staining pattern, especially in cells with processes, supports a myoepithelial phenotype. Variable intensity may reflect heterogeneity in differentiation state.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Vimentin positivity supports a myoepithelial component within the tumor, consistent with mixed tumor histogenesis.

experiments.experimental_setting: Same immunohistochemical panel as above.
experiments.experiment_goal: To exclude other lineages and confirm specificity of the tumor phenotype.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: No brown chromogenic signal is observed in tumor cells for EMA, p63, SMA, desmin, CK7, and CEA [Context].
experiments.interpretation: The absence of p63 and SMA, typically expressed in myoepithelial cells, is unusual but not unheard of in hyaline cell-rich variants. Loss of these markers may reflect phenotypic shift or differentiation toward plasmacytoid myoepithelial cells. CK7 negativity helps exclude other sweat gland tumors like spiradenoma. EMA and CEA negativity argues against apocrine carcinoma or adenocarcinoma.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The immunophenotype is atypical for conventional myoepithelial cells but consistent with a hyaline (plasmacytoid) myoepithelial variant lacking typical myoepithelial markers.

experiments.experimental_setting: Same immunohistochemical panel.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess proliferative activity and p53 overexpression as markers of malignancy or atypia.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Atypical ‘monster’ cells show no brown nuclear staining for Ki-67 or p53 [Context].
experiments.interpretation: Absence of Ki-67 labeling indicates low proliferative activity, even in atypical cells. Lack of p53 staining suggests wild-type p53 status and absence of TP53 mutation-driven carcinogenesis.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Despite cytologic atypia, the tumor lacks molecular markers of aggressive behavior or malignancy.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The tumor cells express S-100, vimentin, and epithelial cytokeratins (AE1/AE3, CAM 5.2), confirming a biphasic epithelial-myoepithelial origin with plasmacytoid myoepithelial differentiation.
The absence of typical myoepithelial markers (p63, SMA) and ductal markers (CK7) supports a diagnosis of hyaline cell-rich variant, known for phenotypic divergence.
Cytologic atypia, including 'monster cells,' is present but not associated with increased proliferation or p53 mutation, indicating biological indolence.

reasoning.content: The tumor demonstrates a well-circumscribed dermal nodule composed of epithelial and myxoid stromal components, with predominant plasmacytoid hyaline cells. These cells express both epithelial (AE1/AE3, CAM 5.2) and myoepithelial (S-100, vimentin) markers, supporting the diagnosis of apocrine mixed tumor. The near-complete absence of conventional myoepithelial markers (p63, SMA) is atypical but aligns with prior reports of hyaline cell-rich variants, which often lose these markers due to plasmacytoid differentiation. The presence of cytologic atypia, including large bizarre 'monster cells,' raises concern for malignancy; however, the lack of mitotic figures, Ki-67 negativity in atypical cells, and absence of p53 overexpression indicate low proliferative activity and absence of molecular drivers of malignancy. The clinical behavior—no recurrence in 14 months—further supports benignity. Together, the histomorphology, immunoprofile, and clinical course confirm a rare variant: hyaline cell-rich apocrine mixed tumor with cytologic atypia but benign biological potential.
reasoning.conclusion: The lesion is a benign hyaline cell-rich apocrine mixed tumor with cytologic atypia, characterized by plasmacytoid myoepithelial differentiation, lack of typical myoepithelial markers, and absence of proliferative or mutational markers of malignancy.

question:
In an investigation of sclerotic dura mater lesions associated with subdural haematoma, the following studies were conducted:

- A histological section of sclerotic dura mater was stained for osteopontin using immunohistochemistry, with counterstaining and visualization under light microscopy; the image includes a 200-micrometer scale bar.
- A histological section of sclerotic dura mater was subjected to tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP) immunohistochemistry, with visualization under microscopic magnification; the image includes a 20-micrometer scale bar.
- Polarization microscopy was performed on histological sections of the calcified dural tissue, revealing an obvious lamellar structure in the calcified tissue.
- Light microscopy of hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained sections of the sclerotic dural lesions showed calcified tissues within the lesions, with cells forming a single layer observed on the surface of this tissue.

What can be concluded from these findings regarding the nature and pathological mechanisms of the sclerotic dural lesions?

input_logic_chain.research_context: Investigation of the nature and pathological mechanisms of sclerotic dura mater lesions associated with subdural haematoma, focusing on calcification, cellular infiltration, and molecular markers.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological section of sclerotic dura mater was stained for osteopontin using immunohistochemistry. The tissue was counterstained, and visualization was performed under light microscopy with a 200-micrometer scale bar for spatial reference.
experiments.experiment_goal: To determine the presence and localization of osteopontin, a protein associated with calcification and bone remodeling, in the sclerotic dural lesions.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Dark brown to brownish granular and diffuse staining localized in discrete regions surrounding denser eosinophilic material. The immunoreactive deposits are irregularly shaped, vary in size, and appear as small clusters or elongated aggregates. Arrowheads mark specific foci of staining near calcified zones. Surrounding stromal tissue shows fibrous, wavy architecture with spindle-shaped cells lightly counterstained in blue or purple [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The brown staining indicates specific immunoreactivity for osteopontin. Its localization around calcified regions suggests active involvement in the calcification process or tissue response to mineralization. The fibrous stroma with spindle-shaped cells is consistent with reactive fibrosis in the dura mater.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Osteopontin is expressed in close spatial association with calcified tissue in the sclerotic dural lesions, indicating a role in pathological calcification or mineralized tissue remodeling.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological section of sclerotic dura mater was subjected to tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP) immunohistochemistry, with visualization under microscopic magnification and a 20-micrometer scale bar. The tissue was counterstained to distinguish cellular morphology.
experiments.experiment_goal: To identify the presence of multinucleated giant cells exhibiting TRAP immunoreactivity, a marker of osteoclast-like activity, in the vicinity of calcified dural lesions.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Brown cytoplasmic staining localized within multinucleated cells, each containing multiple pale, unstained nuclei. The cells vary in shape (elongated, rounded, or irregular) and are clustered in specific regions. Three black arrows point to distinct groups of these cells. They are located near denser, structured regions consistent with calcification. The surrounding matrix is pale with fibrous structures [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: The brown cytoplasmic staining with TRAP confirms the presence of multinucleated giant cells exhibiting osteoclast-like characteristics. Their proximity to calcified areas suggests active resorption or remodeling of mineralized tissue. These cells are likely involved in localized bone-like turnover within the dura.
experiments.sub_conclusion: TRAP-positive multinucleated giant cells are present near calcified dural lesions, indicating osteoclastic activity and active remodeling of calcified tissue.

experiments.experimental_setting: Polarization microscopy was performed on histological sections of the calcified dural tissue to examine internal structural organization.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess whether the calcified tissue exhibits a lamellar structure characteristic of bone or organized mineral deposition.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: An obvious lamellar structure is demonstrated in the calcified tissue [Context].
experiments.interpretation: The presence of lamellar architecture under polarization microscopy indicates organized deposition of collagen and mineral, a hallmark of metaplastic bone formation or ossification rather than random calcification.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The calcified tissue in the dural lesions exhibits a lamellar structure, consistent with organized ossification or bone-like tissue formation.

experiments.experimental_setting: Light microscopy of hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained sections of the sclerotic dural lesions.
experiments.experiment_goal: To identify the cellular composition and structural features of the sclerotic lesions, particularly surface cell layers and calcified regions.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Calcified tissues were found in the sclerotic lesions, and cells forming a single layer were observed on the surface of this tissue [Context].
experiments.interpretation: The single-layered cells on the surface of calcified tissue may represent epithelial-like or mesenchymal-derived cells involved in the formation or encapsulation of the mineralized tissue. This is consistent with metaplastic transformation of dural cells.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The calcified lesions are covered by a monolayer of cells, suggesting a biological interface that may contribute to the formation or containment of the mineralized tissue.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The calcified dural lesions exhibit structural and cellular features resembling bone, including lamellar organization and surface epithelial-like cells.
Molecular and cellular markers (osteopontin and TRAP-positive cells) indicate active calcification and remodeling processes in the lesions.
The combined histological and immunohistochemical evidence supports the presence of ectopic bone-like tissue in the dura mater.

reasoning.content: The sclerotic dural lesions display calcified tissue with a lamellar structure under polarization microscopy, a feature typical of organized bone formation. The presence of a single-cell layer on the surface of this tissue suggests a biological boundary or epithelial-like covering, possibly derived from metaplastic dural cells. Immunohistochemistry reveals osteopontin, a non-collagenous bone matrix protein, localized around the calcified zones, indicating active involvement in mineralization. Furthermore, TRAP-positive multinucleated giant cells—characteristic of osteoclasts—are clustered near the calcified areas, demonstrating active resorption or remodeling of the mineralized tissue. Together, these findings indicate that the lesions are not merely dystrophic calcifications but represent a process of ectopic ossification or metaplastic bone formation within the dura mater. The adhesion between these bone-like lesions and cerebral superficial arteries may have contributed to vascular fragility, leading to subdural haematoma.
reasoning.conclusion: The sclerotic dural lesions represent ectopic bone-like tissue formed through metaplastic ossification, characterized by organized calcification, osteopontin expression, and osteoclast-like activity, which likely contributed to the pathogenesis of subdural haematoma via vascular adhesion and mechanical stress.

question: A patient with a history of hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) reactivation presented with recurrent fever, tachycardia, hepatosplenomegaly, and hematologic abnormalities, prompting clinical suspicion of HLH relapse. A second sternal puncture was performed for bone marrow evaluation. The first bone marrow aspirate was processed using a Romanowsky-type staining method, likely Giemsa stain, and examined microscopically. A second Giemsa-stained bone marrow sample was also examined microscopically to assess the extent of any pathological findings. What can be concluded from these experiments and the clinical context?

input_logic_chain.research_context: A patient with a history of HLH reactivation presented with systemic symptoms including fever, tachycardia, hepatosplenomegaly, and hematologic abnormalities. Due to suspected HLH relapse, the patient underwent a second sternal puncture for bone marrow evaluation, which unexpectedly revealed parasitic infection.

experiments.experimental_setting: Bone marrow aspirate was obtained via sternal puncture and stained using a Romanowsky-type staining method, likely Giemsa stain, for microscopic examination.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate the cellular composition of the bone marrow and identify potential pathological findings contributing to the patient's clinical deterioration.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Multiple macrophages are present with abundant cytoplasm and irregular, often eccentric nuclei. Within their cytoplasm, numerous small, round to oval intracellular structures are visible, each with a densely stained nucleus and an adjacent intensely stained kinetoplast. A black arrow highlights one such structure within a macrophage [Image 1]. Similar structures are observed in adjacent cells, varying slightly in size and staining intensity.
experiments.interpretation: The intracellular structures with a distinct nucleus and adjacent kinetoplast are morphologically consistent with amastigote forms of Leishmania parasites. The presence of these organisms within macrophages—cells that are natural hosts for Leishmania in human tissue—supports an active infection.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The bone marrow contains intracellular parasites morphologically consistent with Leishmania amastigotes.

experiments.experimental_setting: A second Giemsa-stained bone marrow sample was examined microscopically to confirm initial findings and assess the extent of parasitic infiltration.
experiments.experiment_goal: To corroborate the presence of Leishmania parasites and evaluate their distribution across different cells in the bone marrow.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Numerous small, dark-staining round to oval bodies are visible in the field. One is located within a larger cell with abundant cytoplasm and an eccentric nucleus, highlighted by a black arrow [Image 2]. The structure shows a densely stained nucleus and a smaller, intensely stained dot (kinetoplast) adjacent to it. Other similar bodies are seen, some clearly within host cells.
experiments.interpretation: The morphological features—small size, oval shape, dense nuclear staining, and presence of a separate kinetoplast—are diagnostic of Leishmania amastigotes. Their intracellular location within phagocytic cells such as macrophages confirms parasitism of host mononuclear phagocytes, typical of visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar).
experiments.sub_conclusion: The presence of intracellular Leishmania amastigotes in multiple macrophages confirms disseminated bone marrow infection.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The bone marrow contains intracellular parasites morphologically consistent with Leishmania amastigotes.
The presence of intracellular Leishmania amastigotes in multiple macrophages confirms disseminated bone marrow infection.

reasoning.content: The patient presented with clinical and laboratory features suggestive of HLH relapse, including fever, hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias, and prior history. However, the second sternal puncture revealed unexpected parasitic forms in the bone marrow. Microscopic examination of Giemsa-stained smears demonstrated numerous intracellular organisms within macrophages, characterized by a deeply stained nucleus and a smaller, adjacent rod-shaped or dot-like kinetoplast—hallmark features of Leishmania amastigotes. These morphological findings were consistent across both images [Image 1] and [Image 2], with clear visualization of parasites inside host cells. Given that Leishmania species (particularly L. donovani and L. infantum) cause visceral leishmaniasis, a disease known to mimic HLH through uncontrolled macrophage activation, cytokine storm, and pancytopenia, this finding explains the patient’s clinical picture. The resolution of symptoms and laboratory abnormalities following initiation of meglumine antimoniate—an antileishmanial drug—further supports that the underlying cause was infection rather than primary HLH reactivation. Therefore, the initial assumption of HLH relapse was confounded by an opportunistic infection that phenocopies HLH.
reasoning.conclusion: The patient's clinical presentation was due to visceral leishmaniasis, not HLH reactivation, as confirmed by the identification of intracellular Leishmania amastigotes in bone marrow macrophages on Giemsa-stained smears, with subsequent resolution of symptoms following specific antiparasitic therapy.

question:
A 45-year-old patient presents with asymptomatic skin lesions on the lower extremities. A skin biopsy is performed to evaluate the underlying pathology. The research context is the diagnosis of Rosai-Dorfman Disease (RDD) based on histopathological and immunohistochemical features of a skin biopsy, supported by clinical and laboratory findings.

An initial examination is conducted on a hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained section of the skin biopsy using light microscopy to assess the nature of the dermal cellular infiltrate. [Image 1] reveals a dense mixed inflammatory infiltrate involving the superficial, mid, and deep dermis, with the epidermis appearing intact and well-demarcated from the underlying dermis.

A second evaluation is performed on the same H&E-stained tissue section, focusing on specific cellular interactions within the dermal infiltrate. [Image 2] highlights distinct intracellular events involving certain large cells and smaller round cells.

Subsequently, immunohistochemical staining is performed on the biopsy tissue using antibodies against S-100, CD68, and CD1a. The histiocytes in the infiltrate show positive immunoreactivity for S-100 and CD68, while no immunoreactivity is detected for CD1a.

What is the most likely diagnosis, and what is the complete pathological reasoning supporting this diagnosis?

input_logic_chain.research_context: Diagnosis of Rosai-Dorfman Disease (RDD) based on histopathological and immunohistochemical features of a skin biopsy, supported by clinical and laboratory findings.

experiments.experimental_setting: Skin biopsy tissue section stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E), examined under light microscopy.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate the cellular composition and architectural pattern of the dermal infiltrate.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Dense mixed inflammatory infiltrate involving superficial, mid, and deep dermis, composed of cells with round to oval nuclei and dense chromatin (lymphocytes), cells with eccentric nuclei and abundant cytoplasm (plasma cells), larger cells with vesicular nuclei and pale cytoplasm (histiocytes), and cells with multi-lobed nuclei and granular cytoplasm (neutrophils). The epidermis is intact and well-demarcated [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The presence of a polymorphous dermal infiltrate with histiocytes, lymphocytes, plasma cells, and neutrophils indicates a non-specific but significant inflammatory process involving multiple cell lineages. The depth and density suggest a systemic or reactive process rather than a superficial infection or dermatitis.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The skin lesion is characterized by a deep, mixed inflammatory infiltrate consistent with a histiocytic disorder.

experiments.experimental_setting: Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained skin biopsy section analyzed for evidence of emperipolesis.
experiments.experiment_goal: To identify the hallmark histopathological feature of Rosai-Dorfman Disease—emperipolesis—defined as viable lymphocytes within the cytoplasm of histiocytes.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Two distinct instances of intact lymphocytes located within the cytoplasmic boundaries of larger histiocytes, as indicated by black arrows. The internalized lymphocytes maintain their nuclear integrity and are not undergoing phagocytic degradation [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: The presence of intact, non-degraded lymphocytes within histiocytic cytoplasm is diagnostic of emperipolesis, a phenomenon rarely seen in other histiocytic proliferations and highly characteristic of RDD.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Emperipolesis is observed, strongly supporting a diagnosis of Rosai-Dorfman Disease.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical (IHC) staining of the skin biopsy using antibodies against S-100, CD68, and CD1a.
experiments.experiment_goal: To determine the immunophenotype of the histiocytes and differentiate RDD from other histiocytic disorders such as Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH).
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The histiocytes show positive immunoreactivity for S-100 and CD68 [Context], while being negative for CD1a [Context].
experiments.interpretation: S-100 and CD68 positivity confirms the histiocytic lineage and dendritic nature of the cells. CD68 is a marker of macrophage/histiocyte differentiation, and S-100 positivity is characteristic of RDD. Absence of CD1a excludes Langerhans cell histiocytosis, which typically expresses CD1a and Langerin.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The immunophenotype (S-100+/CD68+/CD1a−) is diagnostic of RDD and rules out mimics such as LCH.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The skin biopsy reveals a deep, mixed inflammatory infiltrate with histiocytes, lymphocytes, plasma cells, and neutrophils.
Emperipolesis is present, a hallmark pathological feature of RDD.
The histiocytes express S-100 and CD68 but not CD1a, confirming the immunophenotypic profile of RDD.

reasoning.content: The histopathological evaluation of the skin biopsy demonstrates a dense, mixed dermal infiltrate involving all levels of the dermis, composed of histiocytes, lymphocytes, plasma cells, and neutrophils. This pattern is nonspecific but suggests a reactive or systemic histiocytic process. Crucially, the identification of emperipolesis—intact lymphocytes within histiocytic cytoplasm—on H&E staining [Image 2] is a defining morphological feature of Rosai-Dorfman Disease (RDD), as it reflects the unique functional property of these histiocytes to engulf viable lymphocytes without destruction. This observation differentiates RDD from other histiocytic proliferations where phagocytosis leads to degradation. Furthermore, immunohistochemical analysis confirms the diagnosis by demonstrating that the histiocytes are positive for S-100 and CD68, markers consistent with the immunophenotype of RDD, and negative for CD1a, which effectively excludes Langerhans cell histiocytosis. Together, the combination of emperipolesis and the S-100+/CD68+/CD1a− immunoprofile provides definitive evidence for RDD. Clinical correlation shows no systemic involvement on imaging, leading to the final diagnosis of primary cutaneous Rosai-Dorfman Disease (PCRDD).
reasoning.conclusion: The patient has primary cutaneous Rosai-Dorfman Disease (PCRDD), diagnosed based on characteristic histopathological findings of dermal histiocytic infiltrate with emperipolesis and confirmatory immunohistochemical profile (S-100+/CD68+/CD1a−), in the absence of extracutaneous involvement.

question:
A 35 mm × 18 mm × 14 mm skin lesion was completely excised and submitted for pathological evaluation. Grossly, the lesion was brown with a cauliflower-like surface and a narrow stalk at its inferior aspect. The cut surface was gray-white, smooth, firm, and homogeneous. 

Microscopic examination of formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue sections stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) was performed at ×4 magnification. 

Additional evaluation was carried out using higher magnification H&E staining on the same tissue section to assess nuclear and cytoplasmic details. 

Immunohistochemical staining was performed on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue sections using antibodies against cytokeratin (CK)-5, CK-14, carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), and epithelial membrane antigen (EMA). 

Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis, and how is it supported by the integrated pathological evidence?

input_logic_chain.research_context: To determine the histopathological nature of a completely excised skin lesion based on gross morphology, microscopic architecture, and immunohistochemical profile.

experiments.experimental_setting: Gross examination of the excised specimen under visual inspection and physical measurement. The specimen was observed for color, surface morphology, and cut surface characteristics.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess the macroscopic features of the excised lesion for initial characterization.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The lesion was brown with a cauliflower-like surface [Figure 1b]. A narrow stalk was visible at the inferior aspect. The cut surface was gray-white, smooth, firm, and homogeneous [Context].
experiments.interpretation: A brown, exophytic, cauliflower-like surface suggests a papillomatous or verrucous growth pattern, commonly seen in benign epithelial tumors. The presence of a stalk indicates a pedunculated morphology, often associated with benign lesions. The firm, homogeneous, gray-white cut surface suggests a solid, well-circumscribed dermal or epidermal tumor without necrosis or cystic change.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The gross morphology is consistent with a benign, pedunculated epithelial neoplasm with exophytic growth.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological examination of formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue sections stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E), viewed under light microscopy at ×4 magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate the architectural pattern, cellular morphology, and stromal characteristics of the lesion.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Proliferation of epidermal cells in the form of broad anastomosing cords extending into the dermis. The tumor cells are round to ovoid with distinct cell borders, vesicular nuclei, and moderate cytoplasm. The cytoplasm shows variable eosinophilic staining, from light pink to paler or vacuolated regions. The stroma is pale pink, less densely cellular, with loosely arranged collagen fibers, numerous blood vessels, fibroblasts, and scattered inflammatory cells. The border between epithelium and stroma is well defined. Irregularly shaped cellular aggregates are embedded in the loose stroma. [Image 1]
experiments.interpretation: The anastomosing cord-like growth pattern of uniform epithelial cells extending into the dermis is characteristic of epithelial neoplasms. The well-demarcated border and lack of infiltrative growth suggest a benign process. The loose, vascular stroma with chronic inflammation is a hallmark of reactive or inductive stroma, commonly seen in benign epithelial tumors such as epithelial proliferations with stromal interaction. The presence of duct-like structures (seen in higher detail in Image 2) supports glandular or ductal differentiation.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The histological architecture and cellular features are consistent with a benign epithelial neoplasm showing ductal differentiation and inductive stromal response.

experiments.experimental_setting: Higher magnification H&E staining (low magnification view) of the same tissue section to assess nuclear details, cytoplasmic features, and luminal structures.
experiments.experiment_goal: To identify specific cellular and structural features such as nuclear atypia, duct-like formations, and luminal content.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Tumor cells are densely packed with oval-shaped, vesicular nuclei showing finely dispersed chromatin and occasional nucleoli. Cytoplasm is lightly eosinophilic. Duct-like structures with irregular boundaries are present, some containing pink-staining (eosinophilic) material in their lumina. The overall architecture is disorganized but lacks significant nuclear pleomorphism or mitotic activity. [Image 2]
experiments.interpretation: Vesicular nuclei with fine chromatin and low nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio indicate low-grade, non-aggressive cellular kinetics. The presence of duct-like structures with eosinophilic luminal secretions suggests true ductal differentiation, a key feature in tumors of sweat gland origin. The absence of significant atypia or mitoses further supports a benign diagnosis.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The cytological features and presence of secretory duct-like structures support a diagnosis of a benign sweat gland-derived epithelial tumor.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining using antibodies against cytokeratin (CK)-5, CK-14, carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), and epithelial membrane antigen (EMA) on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue sections.
experiments.experiment_goal: To determine the immunophenotypic profile of the tumor cells and confirm epithelial and ductal differentiation.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Cytoplasmic expression of CK-5, CK-14, CEA, and EMA in tumor cells [Figure 2a–d]. [Context]
experiments.interpretation: CK-5 and CK-14 are markers of basal keratinocytes and myoepithelial cells, commonly expressed in benign epithelial tumors including those of cutaneous adnexal origin. CEA and EMA are markers of luminal epithelial differentiation and are typically expressed in ductal structures, confirming the presence of true ductal formation. Co-expression of basal and luminal markers supports a biphasic (basal and luminal) epithelial differentiation, characteristic of eccrine poroma (EP) or similar adnexal tumors.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The immunohistochemical profile confirms biphasic epithelial differentiation with both basal and ductal features, strongly supporting a diagnosis of eccrine poroma.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The gross morphology is consistent with a benign, pedunculated epithelial neoplasm with exophytic growth.
The histological architecture and cellular features are consistent with a benign epithelial neoplasm showing ductal differentiation and inductive stromal response.
The cytological features and presence of secretory duct-like structures support a diagnosis of a benign sweat gland-derived epithelial tumor.
The immunohistochemical profile confirms biphasic epithelial differentiation with both basal and ductal features, strongly supporting a diagnosis of eccrine poroma.

reasoning.content: The lesion presents with a pedunculated, exophytic, cauliflower-like appearance grossly, typical of benign epithelial tumors. Microscopically, it shows well-demarcated cords of uniform epithelial cells extending into the dermis, embedded in a loose, vascular, and chronically inflamed stroma—features characteristic of benign adnexal tumors. The presence of duct-like structures with eosinophilic luminal secretions indicates true ductal differentiation. Immunohistochemistry further confirms this with co-expression of basal cell markers (CK-5, CK-14) and luminal/ductal markers (CEA, EMA), demonstrating biphasic epithelial differentiation. These combined features—architectural, cytological, and immunophenotypic—are diagnostic of eccrine poroma, a benign tumor derived from the intraepidermal portion of eccrine sweat ducts.
reasoning.conclusion: The lesion is diagnosed as eccrine poroma based on its gross morphology, well-circumscribed anastomosing epithelial cords, ductal differentiation, and immunohistochemical expression of both basal (CK-5, CK-14) and luminal (CEA, EMA) epithelial markers.

question:
In a study evaluating the effects of a high-fat diet (HFD) and various treatments (CM, AuNPs + CM) on aortic histology in rats, with a focus on structural integrity of the aorta including endothelial layer, elastic laminae, and presence of inflammatory cells, the following experiments were conducted:

- Histological examination of descending aorta sections from rats in the Control group, stained with haematoxylin and eosin (H&E), processed for light microscopy. All images were captured at a scale of 50 µm.
- Histological examination of descending aorta sections from rats fed a high-fat diet (HFD), stained with H&E, under identical preparation and imaging conditions as the Control group. All images were captured at a scale of 50 µm.
- Histological examination of aorta sections from rats fed HFD and treated with CM, processed and stained identically to other groups. All images were captured at a scale of 50 µm.
- Histological examination of aorta sections from rats fed HFD and treated with functionalized gold nanoparticles (AuNPs + CM), processed and stained under the same conditions. All images were captured at a scale of 50 µm.

What can be concluded from these experiments regarding the impact of HFD and the treatments on aortic wall structure?

input_logic_chain.research_context: Evaluation of the effects of high-fat diet (HFD) and various treatments (CM, AuNPs + CM) on aortic histology in rats, with a focus on structural integrity of the aorta, including endothelial layer, elastic laminae, and presence of inflammatory cells.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological examination of descending aorta sections from rats in the Control group, stained with haematoxylin and eosin (H&E). The tissue was processed for light microscopy to assess general vascular morphology.
experiments.experiment_goal: To establish baseline normal aortic histological structure for comparison with experimental groups.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The luminal surface shows a slightly undulating contour with a densely stained, irregular margin. Endothelial cells form a single, mostly continuous layer with some irregularities in shape and spacing. The smooth muscle layer appears as bands of darker pink staining with elongated nuclei oriented parallel to the vessel axis. The extracellular matrix is uniformly light pink with faint wavy striations. No inflammatory infiltrates, necrosis, or structural disruption is observed [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The presence of a continuous endothelial lining, organized smooth muscle cells, and well-preserved extracellular matrix with wavy striations (indicative of elastic fibers) reflects normal aortic wall architecture. The absence of inflammatory cells or tissue damage confirms the healthy state of the vascular tissue in the Control group.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The Control group exhibits normal aortic histology, serving as a reference for identifying pathological changes in experimental groups.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological examination of descending aorta sections from rats fed a high-fat diet (HFD), stained with H&E, under identical preparation and imaging conditions as the Control group.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess the impact of HFD on aortic wall structure, particularly subendothelial changes and inflammatory infiltration.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: A darkly stained, rounded cell with a prominent nucleus is present in the subendothelial connective tissue layer, as indicated by an arrow. This cell is embedded within a loose fibrous matrix and surrounded by wavy collagenous fibers and spindle-shaped cells [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: The darkly stained rounded cell with a large nucleus in the subendothelial region is morphologically consistent with a macrophage, a key cell type involved in early atherosclerotic lesion formation. Its presence indicates immune cell infiltration in response to endothelial dysfunction or lipid accumulation induced by HFD.
experiments.sub_conclusion: HFD induces subendothelial macrophage infiltration, suggesting early vascular inflammation and endothelial disruption.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological examination of aorta sections from rats fed HFD and treated with CM (a therapeutic compound), processed and stained identically to other groups.
experiments.experiment_goal: To determine whether CM treatment mitigates HFD-induced aortic damage.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The overall layered architecture is preserved with a thin endothelial layer and a thick tunica media composed of concentrically arranged smooth muscle cells. Elastic laminae appear thin and less distinct compared to Control. No inflammatory cells are visible in the subendothelial region [Image 3].
experiments.interpretation: Preservation of vascular layering and absence of inflammatory cells suggest that CM treatment prevents HFD-induced macrophage infiltration. However, the reduced visibility and thinness of elastic laminae indicate partial structural compromise, possibly due to ongoing extracellular matrix remodeling or elastin degradation.
experiments.sub_conclusion: CM treatment prevents inflammatory infiltration but does not fully preserve elastic fiber integrity in HFD-fed rats.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological examination of aorta sections from rats fed HFD and treated with functionalized gold nanoparticles (AuNPs + CM), processed and stained under the same conditions.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate the vascular effects of combined AuNPs + CM treatment in the context of HFD.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The intima is discontinuous with irregular endothelial contours. Elastic laminae are reduced in number, fragmented, and unevenly spaced, with pale pink staining. Large, pale, acellular intercellular spaces are present within the media, disrupting the compact tissue arrangement [Image 4].
experiments.interpretation: Intimal discontinuity indicates severe endothelial damage or loss. Fragmented and rarefied elastic laminae suggest degradation or impaired synthesis of elastin. The large intercellular spaces may represent edema, matrix degradation, or loss of cell-matrix adhesion, all indicative of significant structural disorganization and potential vessel wall weakening.
experiments.sub_conclusion: AuNPs + CM treatment in HFD-fed rats is associated with severe aortic wall disruption, exceeding the damage seen in HFD alone.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The Control group shows intact aortic structure, confirming the absence of baseline pathology.
HFD induces subendothelial macrophage infiltration, indicating early vascular inflammation.
CM treatment prevents inflammatory cell infiltration but does not fully restore elastic laminae structure.
AuNPs + CM treatment leads to severe structural damage, including intimal discontinuity and elastic fiber rarefaction.

reasoning.content: Starting from the Control group, normal aortic histology is confirmed, providing a baseline for comparison. In the HFD group, the presence of a subendothelial macrophage [Image 2] indicates initiation of vascular inflammation, a hallmark of diet-induced atherosclerosis. The HFD + CM group shows preservation of overall architecture and absence of inflammatory cells, suggesting a protective effect of CM against immune infiltration. However, the thinning of elastic laminae [Image 3] implies incomplete structural protection. In contrast, the HFD + AuNPsCM group exhibits the most severe pathology: intimal discontinuity, fragmented elastic fibers, and large intercellular spaces [Image 4], indicating that the addition of AuNPs exacerbates vascular damage despite CM presence. This adverse effect is not merely a lack of protection but represents active structural deterioration, potentially due to nanoparticle-induced toxicity or disruption of matrix homeostasis.
reasoning.conclusion: While CM alone shows partial protective effects against HFD-induced vascular inflammation, the combination of AuNPs + CM leads to significant structural deterioration of the aortic wall, suggesting potential adverse vascular effects of functionalized gold nanoparticles in the context of metabolic stress.

question: To determine if CDR antigens in intact cells are available to react with Yo antibodies, surface staining was performed on HeLa cells transfected with CDR2-myc or CDR2L-myc to assess membrane accessibility of these antigens. HeLa cells were transfected with CDR2-myc or CDR2L-myc and fixed 24 hours post-transfection. Cells were either permeabilized with Triton X-100 or left untreated to assess surface exposure. The plasma membrane was labeled with WGA-Alexa Fluor 594 (red), and CDR antigens were detected using anti-myc antibody with Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated secondary antibody (green). In non-permeabilized cells, green fluorescence was observed on the cell surface only in CDR2L-myc-transfected cells, co-localizing with the red plasma membrane stain, but not in CDR2-myc-transfected cells. In permeabilized cells, strong intracellular green fluorescence was observed for both CDR2-myc and CDR2L-myc. Additionally, HeLa cells transfected with CDR2L-myc were stained with both anti-CDR2L antibody and anti-myc antibody, resulting in strong co-localization of both antibody signals on the cell surface and intracellularly. What can be concluded from these experiments regarding the potential for Yo antibodies to interact with CDR2 and CDR2L in intact cells?

input_logic_chain.research_context: To determine if CDR antigens in intact cells are available to react with Yo antibodies, surface staining was performed on HeLa cells transfected with CDR2-myc or CDR2L-myc to assess membrane accessibility of these antigens.

experiments.experimental_setting: HeLa cells were transfected with CDR2-myc or CDR2L-myc and fixed 24 hours post-transfection. Cells were either permeabilized with Triton X-100 (positive control for intracellular detection) or left untreated (to assess surface exposure). The plasma membrane was labeled with WGA-Alexa Fluor 594 (red), and CDR antigens were detected using anti-myc antibody with Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated secondary antibody (green).
experiments.experiment_goal: To determine whether CDR2 or CDR2L is exposed on the cell surface and thus accessible to extracellular antibodies like Yo antibodies.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: In non-permeabilized cells, green fluorescence (anti-myc signal) was observed on the cell surface only in CDR2L-myc-transfected cells, co-localizing with the red plasma membrane stain. In contrast, no surface green signal was detected in CDR2-myc-transfected cells. In permeabilized cells, strong intracellular green fluorescence was observed for both CDR2-myc and CDR2L-myc. [Context]
experiments.interpretation: The presence of anti-myc signal on the surface of non-permeabilized CDR2L-myc-expressing cells indicates that CDR2L is localized to or associated with the plasma membrane and is accessible to extracellular antibodies. The absence of such signal in CDR2-myc-transfected cells suggests CDR2 is not surface-exposed. Intracellular signals in permeabilized cells confirm successful expression and detectability of both proteins.
experiments.sub_conclusion: CDR2L, but not CDR2, is membrane-associated and accessible on the cell surface in transfected HeLa cells.

experiments.experimental_setting: HeLa cells transfected with CDR2L-myc were stained with both anti-CDR2L antibody and anti-myc antibody to assess specificity of surface staining.
experiments.experiment_goal: To verify that the myc-tagged CDR2L protein is specifically detected and that surface signal corresponds to the expressed protein.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Strong co-localization (yellow signal in merged channels) of anti-CDR2L and anti-myc antibodies on the cell surface and intracellularly in transfected cells. [Missing]
experiments.interpretation: Co-localization confirms that the myc-tagged protein is recognized by both antibodies, validating the specificity of the anti-myc staining for CDR2L-myc and ruling out non-specific binding.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The surface localization signal of CDR2L-myc is specific and reflects authentic protein expression and localization.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: CDR2L, but not CDR2, is membrane-associated and accessible on the cell surface in transfected HeLa cells.
The surface localization signal of CDR2L-myc is specific and reflects authentic protein expression and localization.

reasoning.content: The surface staining experiment in HeLa cells demonstrates that only CDR2L, when expressed exogenously, is accessible on the plasma membrane, as evidenced by anti-myc antibody binding without permeabilization. This surface exposure is not observed for CDR2, despite intracellular expression confirmed under permeabilized conditions. The specificity of the CDR2L surface signal is further supported by co-localization with anti-CDR2L antibodies. Together, these findings indicate that CDR2L has a unique membrane-associated localization that CDR2 lacks.
reasoning.conclusion: CDR2L is specifically localized to the cell surface in transfected cells and is therefore accessible for interaction with extracellular Yo antibodies, whereas CDR2 is not.

question:
A 54-year-old woman with clinical and biochemical evidence of adrenal Cushing's syndrome and a prior biopsy-proven metastatic lung adenocarcinoma to the liver undergoes a right adrenalectomy. The resected adrenal mass is subjected to histopathological and immunohistochemical analysis to determine its nature and origin. 

Histological examination of the mass is performed using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining under low and high magnification microscopy. 

Immunohistochemical staining for TTF-1 is conducted using chromogen detection, with nuclear localization assessed microscopically. 

Immunohistochemical staining for cytokeratin 7 (CK7) is also performed using chromogen detection, with assessment of subcellular localization. 

What can be concluded about the nature and origin of the adrenal mass based on these analyses?

input_logic_chain.research_context: Determine the nature and origin of the adrenal mass in a patient with clinical and biochemical evidence of adrenal Cushing's syndrome and a history of lung adenocarcinoma metastasis, using histopathological and immunohistochemical analysis.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological examination of the resected right adrenal mass using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining, analyzed under low and high magnification microscopy.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess the architectural and cytological features of the adrenal mass and identify distinct tissue components.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Under low magnification, two distinct regions are observed: one with densely cellular, irregular glandular structures showing pleomorphic and hyperchromatic nuclei, increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, and eosinophilic cytoplasm; the other with uniform cells arranged in nests and trabeculae, abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, round to oval nuclei, and lower nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio. A subtle transition zone exists between them. [Image 1]
experiments.interpretation: The region with pleomorphic nuclei and disorganized glandular structures is characteristic of adenocarcinoma, while the uniform, nested trabecular pattern with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm is typical of adrenal cortical adenoma. The coexistence suggests a composite tumor with both benign and malignant components.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The adrenal mass contains two morphologically distinct components: one consistent with adrenal cortical adenoma and the other with adenocarcinoma.

experiments.experimental_setting: High-magnification H&E staining of the same tissue section to evaluate cellular details and cytomorphology.
experiments.experiment_goal: To further characterize the glandular and non-glandular cell populations and confirm architectural heterogeneity.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Irregular, variably sized glandular structures with crowded lumens, hyperchromatic and pleomorphic nuclei, loss of polarity, and increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio are intermixed with polygonal cells having finely vacuolated, pale cytoplasm (foamy appearance) and small, uniform nuclei. [Image 2]
experiments.interpretation: The gland-forming epithelial cells with nuclear atypia represent adenocarcinoma. The foamy cells with uniform nuclei and vacuolated cytoplasm resemble lipid-rich adrenal cortical cells, supporting the presence of adrenal cortical tissue. Their intermingling suggests spatial proximity of neoplastic and cortical elements.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The malignant glandular component is distinct from the adrenal cortical cells, confirming a biphasic tumor with both adenocarcinoma and adrenal cortical elements.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining for TTF-1 using chromogen detection, with nuclear localization assessed microscopically.
experiments.experiment_goal: To determine the tissue origin of the neoplastic glandular cells by detecting expression of TTF-1, a marker of pulmonary and thyroid epithelium.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Brown chromogenic signal is localized within the nuclei of cells arranged in glandular or epithelial clusters. The staining is variable in intensity but confined to nuclei; no cytoplasmic staining is observed. The background stroma is lightly counterstained, providing contrast. [Image 3]
experiments.interpretation: Nuclear expression of TTF-1 is a specific immunophenotypic marker for lung adenocarcinoma. The presence of this staining in the glandular component confirms a pulmonary origin for these neoplastic cells.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The adenocarcinoma component of the adrenal mass is of pulmonary origin, as evidenced by TTF-1 immunoreactivity.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining for cytokeratin 7 (CK7) using chromogen detection, with assessment of subcellular localization.
experiments.experiment_goal: To further confirm the epithelial and likely pulmonary origin of the neoplastic cells, as CK7 is commonly expressed in lung adenocarcinomas.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Brown cytoplasmic chromogenic staining is observed in epithelial cell clusters arranged in glandular or acinar-like structures with luminal spaces. The staining is heterogeneous in intensity. Surrounding smaller stromal cells show no reactivity and appear pale yellow. [Image 4]
experiments.interpretation: Cytoplasmic expression of CK7 supports an epithelial origin, and its presence in gland-forming cells aligns with the immunophenotype of lung adenocarcinoma. The lack of staining in surrounding cells confirms specificity.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The neoplastic glandular cells express CK7, further supporting their classification as metastatic lung adenocarcinoma.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The adrenal mass contains two distinct histological components: one with features of adrenal cortical adenoma and another with malignant glandular morphology.
The malignant glandular component expresses TTF-1 and CK7, markers specific for lung adenocarcinoma.
The immunophenotype (TTF-1+ and CK7+) of the adenocarcinoma cells is consistent with a primary lung origin.

reasoning.content: The histological evaluation reveals a biphasic adrenal tumor: one component exhibits classic features of adrenal cortical adenoma, including nested and trabecular architecture with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, while the other shows gland-forming epithelial cells with nuclear pleomorphism, loss of polarity, and high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio—hallmarks of adenocarcinoma. The spatial coexistence of these components suggests either collision tumor or direct infiltration. Immunohistochemical analysis confirms the adenocarcinoma component expresses TTF-1 (nuclear) and CK7 (cytoplasmic), both well-established markers of lung adenocarcinoma. The absence of these markers in the surrounding cortical cells underscores their non-neoplastic or benign adenomatous nature. Given the patient's prior biopsy-proven metastatic lung adenocarcinoma to the liver, the adrenal adenocarcinoma component is best interpreted as metastatic disease. Therefore, the adrenal mass is not a pure adenoma but a composite lesion comprising a benign adrenal cortical adenoma with a focus of metastatic lung adenocarcinoma.
reasoning.conclusion: The right adrenal mass is a composite tumor consisting of an adrenal cortical adenoma with a focus of metastatic adenocarcinoma of pulmonary origin, confirmed by histomorphology and immunophenotypic expression of TTF-1 and CK7.

question:
An experiment was conducted to assess aortic histopathological changes in rabbits across three experimental groups (Group I: BSD+ALA, Group II: BSD+N-ORO, Group III: BSD+ORO) to evaluate the development of vascular lesions, particularly atherosclerotic plaques and wall thickening, in response to different treatments.

Histological examination of aortic tissue sections from Group I (BSD+ALA) rabbits was performed using hematoxylin and eosin (H-E) staining at 200× magnification.

Histological examination of aortic tissue sections from Group II (BSD+N-ORO) rabbits was also conducted using H-E staining at 200× magnification.

In Group III (BSD+ORO), substantial atherosclerotic plaque was detected in the aorta of two rabbits, characterized by significant fatty infiltrations, foam cells, lymphocytes, myocytes, fibres, macrophages, disrupted elastic fibres, marked wall thickening, and luminal narrowing; the other two rabbits showed less profound lesions.

Macroscopic examination of the aortas revealed focal or complete peripheral wall thickening in Group III (BSD+ORO), while no macroscopic lesions were observed in Groups I and II.

What conclusions can be drawn from these findings regarding the effects of the different treatments on aortic pathology?

input_logic_chain.research_context: Assessment of aortic histopathological changes in rabbits across three experimental groups (Group I: BSD+ALA, Group II: BSD+N-ORO, Group III: BSD+ORO) to evaluate the development of vascular lesions, particularly atherosclerotic plaques and wall thickening, in response to different treatments.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological examination of aortic tissue sections from Group I (BSD+ALA) rabbits, stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H-E), analyzed at 200× magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To detect any microscopic pathological alterations in the aortic wall structure following BSD+ALA treatment.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The aortic wall shows intact architecture with no visible lesions, disruptions, or pathological changes. The tissue exhibits a dense, uniform arrangement of elongated, spindle-shaped cells with basophilic nuclei and eosinophilic cytoplasm, organized in parallel laminar patterns. Adjacent connective tissue displays pale eosinophilic staining with evenly distributed collagen fibers. Endothelial lining is continuous, and there are no inflammatory infiltrates, hemorrhage, fibrotic deposits, or necrosis [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The presence of well-organized smooth muscle cells, intact endothelium, and absence of inflammatory or degenerative changes indicates normal aortic histology without pathological remodeling.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Group I (BSD+ALA) shows no histopathological evidence of vascular injury or early atherogenesis.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological examination of aortic tissue sections from Group II (BSD+N-ORO) rabbits, stained with H-E and analyzed at 200× magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To identify early signs of vascular wall damage or edema in response to BSD+N-ORO treatment.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The aortic wall displays three distinct layers: intima with intact endothelial lining, media composed of densely packed spindle-shaped smooth muscle cells with basophilic nuclei and eosinophilic cytoplasm, and adventitia with loose connective tissue. question: In a dataset of clinically requested Oncotype DX (ODX) tests, 71% of cases were labeled as 'do not send' based on clinicopathological features, with 98% accuracy. The 2% of cases that were discordant—predicted to have an ODX recurrence score ≤25 but with an actual score >25—were reviewed for further insight. Among these, one case had an actual recurrence score of 26 and was diagnosed with mucinous breast carcinoma. Histological analysis of the tumor was performed using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining on a tissue specimen evaluated at 200x magnification (Image 1). Additionally, immunohistochemical staining for Ki-67 was conducted on the same specimen and analyzed at 200x magnification (Image 4). Based on these findings, what can be concluded regarding the clinical interpretation of the ODX recurrence score in this case?

input_logic_chain.research_context: In a dataset of clinically requested Oncotype DX (ODX) tests, 71% of cases were labeled as 'do not send' based on clinicopathological features, with 98% accuracy. The 2% discordant cases—predicted to have ODX recurrence score ≤25 but with actual score >25—were reviewed to assess the reliability of the high recurrence scores and whether chemotherapy was warranted.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological and immunohistochemical analysis of a mucinous breast carcinoma specimen from a patient with an ODX recurrence score of 26. Tissue was processed using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining and evaluated at 200x magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess tumor morphology and proliferation characteristics that may influence ODX recurrence score.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Clusters of tumor cells are embedded in a fibrous stroma with pale pink collagen fibers and spindle-shaped stromal cells. Tumor cells form irregular glandular-like structures with nuclei displaced to the periphery by intracellular mucin vacuoles. Intracellular and extracellular mucin are present, with mucin pools visible between clusters. Nuclei are hyperchromatic with mild to moderate pleomorphism. No overt necrosis or significant mitotic figures are observed [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The morphological features are consistent with mucinous carcinoma, a subtype typically associated with low-grade histology, low proliferative activity, and favorable prognosis. The absence of necrosis and low mitotic activity further supports indolent biological behavior.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The tumor exhibits classic histological features of low-aggressiveness mucinous carcinoma, which may not justify a recurrence score of 26 or recommendation for chemotherapy.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining for Ki-67 on the same mucinous carcinoma specimen, analyzed at 200x magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate the proliferative activity of the tumor as a contributor to the ODX recurrence score.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Sparse, intensely dark brown, punctate nuclear staining is observed in isolated tumor cell nuclei, with low density across the tissue. Most nuclei remain blue without brown signal, indicating minimal Ki-67 expression [Image 4].
experiments.interpretation: The low frequency of Ki-67-positive nuclei corresponds to a very low Ki-67 labeling index (2%), consistent with low proliferative activity. This is a key factor in ODX scoring, where high proliferation increases recurrence score.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The low Ki-67 expression supports the morphological impression of low biological aggressiveness and suggests the ODX recurrence score of 26 may overestimate risk in this context.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The tumor exhibits histological and immunophenotypic features characteristic of low-risk mucinous carcinoma.

reasoning.content: The patient's tumor was classified as mucinous subtype with classic H&E features including intracellular and extracellular mucin, peripheral nuclear displacement, and absence of high-grade features such as necrosis or frequent mitoses [Image 1]. These morphological traits are associated with favorable outcomes. Additionally, Ki-67 immunohistochemistry revealed minimal proliferative activity, with only scattered positive nuclei [Image 4], confirming a low proliferation index (2%). Despite a recurrence score of 26—just above the threshold for intermediate risk—both morphology and proliferation are inconsistent with a tumor requiring chemotherapy. The slight elevation in score may stem from low PR expression, a known contributor to higher ODX scores, but this must be weighed against subtype-specific behavior. Mucinous carcinomas are known to have excellent prognosis even with moderate scores. Therefore, the clinical significance of a score of 26 in this context is questionable.
reasoning.conclusion: In mucinous breast carcinoma with very low Ki-67 and classic low-grade morphology, an ODX recurrence score of 26 likely overestimates recurrence risk, and chemotherapy may not be warranted despite the score exceeding 25.

question: A 60-year-old male presents with urinary retention and a prostatic mass on bimanual examination. His history includes prior high-grade T1 transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder. To confirm the diagnosis, a transrectal ultrasound-guided prostate biopsy was performed. Histological examination was conducted using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining at 400x magnification [Image 1]. Additional immunohistochemical analyses were performed on the biopsy specimen: one using antibodies against CD56 with brown chromogen detection and hematoxylin counterstain at 400x magnification [Image 2]; another using antibodies against synaptophysin under the same visualization conditions at 400x magnification [Image 3]. A broader immunohistochemical panel was also applied, revealing positive staining for P53, CK7, and AE1/AE3, and negative staining for chromogranin A, CK20, PSA, uroplakin III, GATA-3, and LCA. Based on these investigations, what is the most appropriate diagnosis, and how is it supported by the collective findings?

input_logic_chain.research_context: To confirm the diagnosis of small cell neuroendocrine carcinoma of the prostate in a 60-year-old male presenting with urinary retention and a prostatic mass, based on histopathological and immunohistochemical analysis.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological examination of a transrectal ultrasound-guided prostate biopsy using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining at 400x magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess the morphological features of the tumor cells for characteristics typical of small cell carcinoma.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Densely packed cells with hyperchromatic nuclei that stain dark purple, closely apposed with irregular contours and nuclear molding; nucleoli are not discernible; scant pale cytoplasm resulting in a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio; numerous mitotic figures with condensed chromatin and chromosomal alignment; sparse stroma with occasional eosinophilic fragments and small clear spaces. Three blue arrows highlight cells with these nuclear features [Image 1].
