These granulomas are located around skin appendages, a typical distribution in cutaneous sarcoidosis. The absence of caseous necrosis and negative stains for acid-fast bacilli and fungi rule out infectious mimics. Although serum ACE is normal and chest imaging is unremarkable, these findings do not exclude sarcoidosis, particularly in localized cutaneous forms. Up to 25–30% of sarcoidosis cases present with skin involvement, and in some, skin is the only organ affected. The clinical presentation, histology, and exclusion of differential diagnoses collectively support a diagnosis of specific cutaneous sarcoidosis.
reasoning.conclusion: The patient has specific cutaneous sarcoidosis, diagnosed based on clinical presentation, histopathological demonstration of non-caseating granulomas, exclusion of infectious causes, and absence of systemic pulmonary involvement.

question:
Differentiation between Keratosis Obturans (KO) and External Auditory Canal Cholesteatoma (EACC) is essential due to their clinical mimicry and divergent treatment strategies. The case presents histopathological and radiological evidence suggestive of a condition involving the middle ear and facial nerve.

A histopathological examination of tissue obtained from the attic and mesotympanum during left modified radical mastoidectomy was performed using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining and viewed under light microscopy at 200× magnification.

The same tissue sample was further analyzed using H&E staining at 40× magnification to evaluate stromal changes.

High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of the temporal bone was performed with 0.6 mm axial and coronal sections, revealing ballooning of the bony external auditory canal (EAC) with destruction, soft tissue density in the mastoid and nondependent part of the middle ear (attic), dehiscence of the facial canal, and dehiscence of the dural plate.

Preoperative otoscopic examination and intraoperative surgical exploration under general anesthesia revealed a narrow cartilaginous EAC with circumferential widening of the bony EAC, keratin debris with pus, absence of tympanic membrane, and intraoperative finding of dehiscence of the tympanic segment of the facial nerve posterior to the cochleariform process with intact sheath.

What diagnosis is supported by this collective evidence, and how do these findings collectively distinguish this condition from external auditory canal cholesteatoma?

input_logic_chain.research_context: Differentiation between Keratosis Obturans (KO) and External Auditory Canal Cholesteatoma (EACC) is essential due to their clinical mimicry and divergent treatment strategies. The case presents histopathological and radiological evidence suggestive of KO with complications involving the middle ear and facial nerve.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histopathological examination of tissue obtained from the attic and mesotympanum during left modified radical mastoidectomy, processed with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining and viewed under light microscopy at 200× magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To identify the presence and structural characteristics of keratin debris and epithelial components in the middle ear and attic region.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: A well-defined, circular structure composed of concentric layers of eosinophilic material forming a laminated keratin pearl, with amorphous, fragmented keratin debris at its center and surrounding granular eosinophilic deposits; the surrounding tissue shows fibrous stroma with scattered inflammatory cells [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The concentric, laminated architecture of the keratin pearl is characteristic of keratinized squamous epithelium with orderly desquamation, typical of keratosis obturans. The central and surrounding keratin debris indicates accumulation due to impaired clearance rather than invasive growth.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The presence of a laminated keratin pearl with central and surrounding keratin debris supports a diagnosis of keratosis obturans, as this pattern reflects generalized keratin shedding along the entire external auditory canal epithelium.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histopathological analysis of the same tissue sample using H&E staining at 40× magnification to assess inflammatory and structural changes in the stroma.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate inflammatory cell infiltration, presence of cholesterol clefts, and tissue disruption associated with chronic inflammation.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Elongated, needle-like, empty-appearing spaces with sharp, angular borders (cholesterol clefts) surrounded by cellular elements; a dense aggregate of small, round to oval cells with dark nuclei (inflammatory infiltrate); eosinophilic stroma with fibrous and disrupted architecture; scattered pale amorphous material [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: Cholesterol clefts result from the dissolution of cholesterol crystals during tissue processing and are indicative of chronic inflammation with tissue breakdown. The dense inflammatory infiltrate composed of plasma cells, lymphocytes, and histiocytes confirms chronic granulomatous inflammation, consistent with long-standing keratin retention and irritation.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The presence of cholesterol clefts and dense mixed inflammatory infiltrate reflects chronic inflammatory response to retained keratin, supporting a non-neoplastic, obstructive etiology such as keratosis obturans.

experiments.experimental_setting: High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of the temporal bone with 0.6 mm axial and coronal sections.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess bony integrity, soft tissue involvement, and extent of disease in the external auditory canal, middle ear, and mastoid.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Ballooning of the bony external auditory canal (EAC) with destruction, soft tissue density in the mastoid and nondependent part of the middle ear (attic), dehiscence of the facial canal, and dehiscence of the dural plate [Context].
experiments.interpretation: Generalized bony expansion (ballooning) of the EAC with destruction indicates chronic pressure erosion from accumulated keratin, a hallmark of KO. Dehiscence of the facial canal and dural plate suggests advanced disease with complications extending beyond the EAC into middle ear and cranial structures.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The HRCT findings of generalized EAC ballooning and attic/mastoid soft tissue with neural and dural dehiscence indicate extensive osteoclastic resorption consistent with complicated keratosis obturans rather than localized bone sequestration seen in EACC.

experiments.experimental_setting: Preoperative otoscopic examination and intraoperative surgical exploration under general anesthesia.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate the anatomical and pathological status of the external auditory canal, tympanic membrane, and middle ear structures.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Narrow cartilaginous EAC with circumferential widening of the bony EAC, keratin debris with pus, absence of tympanic membrane, and intraoperative finding of dehiscence of the tympanic segment of the facial nerve posterior to the cochleariform process with intact sheath [Context].
experiments.interpretation: Circumferential bony EAC widening with keratin accumulation and TM destruction indicates disease progression from EAC into the middle ear via the tympanic membrane, a known pathway in KO. Facial nerve dehiscence without nerve injury reflects bony erosion due to pressure from keratin debris.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The anatomical progression pattern—keratin extending from EAC through the tympanic membrane into the middle ear with bony erosion and facial nerve exposure—supports KO with secondary middle ear involvement.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The laminated keratin pearl and generalized keratin debris indicate orderly keratin accumulation along the EAC epithelium, characteristic of KO.
Chronic inflammatory response with cholesterol clefts and granulation tissue reflects long-standing keratin retention, not invasive cholesteatoma.
Generalized bony EAC ballooning and destruction with attic and mastoid involvement indicate extensive osteoclastic activity typical of advanced KO.
Disease progression through the tympanic membrane into the middle ear with facial nerve dehiscence confirms KO with complications, not primary EACC.

reasoning.content: The diagnosis hinges on distinguishing KO from EACC, which differ in etiology, progression, and management. KO is characterized by generalized keratin accumulation along the entire EAC epithelium, leading to circumferential bony erosion and potential extension into the middle ear. The histopathological identification of a laminated keratin pearl [Image 1] confirms the presence of concentric keratin layering, a hallmark of KO. The surrounding cholesterol clefts and inflammatory infiltrate [Image 2] reflect chronic inflammation due to retained keratin, not active invasion. Radiologically, the HRCT shows ballooning of the bony EAC with soft tissue in the attic and mastoid—features of extensive, pressure-induced osteoclastic resorption, not the localized bone sequestration typical of EACC. Clinically, the disease extended through the tympanic membrane into the middle ear with facial nerve dehiscence, consistent with KO progression. Although EACC may cause localized posterior EAC erosion and mastoid extension, it does not typically present with generalized EAC widening, keratin plugs, or TM destruction. The combination of laminated keratin, generalized bony destruction, and middle ear involvement via the TM confirms KO with complications, necessitating surgical intervention despite its typically conservative management.
reasoning.conclusion: The patient has keratosis obturans with middle ear and facial nerve involvement, confirmed by histopathological, radiological, and intraoperative findings, distinguishing it from external auditory canal cholesteatoma.

question: Cytological evaluation of lymph node aspirates was performed using May-Grunwald Giemsa and Hematoxylin and Eosin stained smears to identify cytomorphological patterns of tuberculous lymphadenitis, as defined by Das et al., which categorizes findings into three groups. Three separate analyses were conducted: a May-Grunwald Giemsa stained smear of a lymph node aspirate was examined under light microscopy [Image 1]; a Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) stained histological section of a lymph node aspirate was analyzed microscopically [Image 2]; and another May-Grunwald Giemsa stained smear of a lymph node aspirate was evaluated for granulomatous structures and necrotic changes [Image 3]. Based on these analyses, what conclusions can be drawn regarding the cytomorphological features of tuberculous lymphadenitis, and how do these findings collectively support the classification system proposed by Das et al.?

input_logic_chain.research_context: Cytological evaluation of lymph node aspirates was performed using May-Grunwald Giemsa and Hematoxylin and Eosin stained smears to identify cytomorphological patterns of tuberculous lymphadenitis, as defined by Das et al. These patterns were categorized into three groups: Pattern A (epithelioid granuloma without necrosis), Pattern B (epithelioid granuloma with necrosis), and Pattern C (necrosis without epithelioid granuloma).

experiments.experimental_setting: May-Grunwald Giemsa stained smear of a lymph node aspirate was examined under light microscopy to assess cellular architecture and morphological features. [Image 1]
experiments.experiment_goal: To identify the presence of epithelioid granulomas and assess for necrosis in the aspirate.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: A well-defined central cluster of epithelioid cells with purple hue, elongated morphology, granular cytoplasm, and indistinct cell borders is observed. Surrounding this cluster are smaller, darkly basophilic round nuclei corresponding to inflammatory cells. There is no amorphous, acellular debris or loss of cellular structure within the granuloma. The background stroma contains scattered individual cells with no pale acellular zones. [Image 1]

The surrounding inflammatory infiltrate is consistent with a host immune response typical of granulomatous inflammation.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The smear exhibits cytomorphological features consistent with Pattern A: epithelioid granuloma without necrosis.

experiments.experimental_setting: Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) stained histological section of a lymph node aspirate was analyzed microscopically to evaluate tissue architecture and cellular changes. [Image 2]
experiments.experiment_goal: To determine whether necrosis is present within or adjacent to epithelioid granulomas.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: A central amorphous, eosinophilic region with loss of cellular architecture and increased basophilic staining indicative of nuclear debris is surrounded by a dense layer of large polygonal epithelioid cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and indistinct borders. Multinucleated giant cells are present in the periphery. The stroma appears fibrous with scattered mononuclear cells. [Image 2]
experiments.interpretation: The central eosinophilic, acellular zone with nuclear debris is diagnostic of caseous necrosis. The surrounding epithelioid cells forming a cohesive layer represent a granulomatous reaction enclosing the necrotic core, characteristic of tuberculous lymphadenitis.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The smear exhibits features of Pattern B: epithelioid granuloma with necrosis.

experiments.experimental_setting: May-Grunwald Giemsa stained smear of a lymph node aspirate was evaluated for granulomatous structures and necrotic changes. [Image 3]
experiments.experiment_goal: To detect the presence of epithelioid granulomas and assess the extent of necrosis in the absence of organized cellular structures.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: A prominent area of amorphous, granular debris occupies the central and lower regions, lacking cellular architecture. No organized clusters of epithelioid cells are present. Scattered dark-staining punctate elements and small nuclei are distributed within the debris. The upper region shows a diffuse, washed-out background with fine granular material. [Image 3]
experiments.interpretation: The absence of epithelioid cell aggregates and presence of extensive acellular, granular debris with nuclear remnants indicates necrosis without granuloma formation. This reflects advanced tissue destruction typical of late-stage or severe tuberculous involvement.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The smear corresponds to Pattern C: necrosis without epithelioid granuloma.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: Pattern A is characterized by well-formed epithelioid granulomas in the absence of necrosis, as confirmed by the structured cellular aggregate in [Image 1].
Pattern B includes both epithelioid granulomas and central necrosis, demonstrated by the necrotic core surrounded by epithelioid cells in [Image 2].
Pattern C is defined by necrotic debris without any organized granulomatous structures, as seen in [Image 3].

reasoning.content: The three visual specimens represent distinct stages of cytomorphological evolution in tuberculous lymphadenitis. [Image 1] shows an early stage where immune cells have aggregated into a granuloma but have not yet undergone necrosis. [Image 2] represents a more advanced stage where the granuloma has developed central caseous necrosis, a hallmark of tuberculosis. [Image 3] reflects a late or destructive phase where necrosis has occurred without preservation of granulomatous architecture, possibly due to extensive tissue breakdown or sampling from a necrotic core. Together, these patterns align with the classification system proposed by Das et al., demonstrating a spectrum of disease expression from granuloma formation to necrosis-dominated pathology.
reasoning.conclusion: The cytomorphological features observed in lymph node aspirates can be classified into three distinct patterns—Pattern A (granuloma without necrosis), Pattern B (granuloma with necrosis), and Pattern C (necrosis without granuloma)—consistent with the diagnostic criteria for tuberculous lymphadenitis as defined by Das et al.

question:
A histological and immunohistochemical study was conducted on a resected facial subcutaneous mass from a ball python to determine its neoplastic nature and cell of origin. 

Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining was performed on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue sections and examined under light microscopy. The tumor was unencapsulated, poorly demarcated, and composed of neoplastic spindle cells forming loose interlacing streams and bundles within a mild fibrovascular stroma. At high power, the spindle cells exhibited cigar-shaped nuclei, moderate cytologic atypia, mitotic figures, indistinct cell borders, and moderate amphophilic granular cytoplasm. Neoplastic cells extended to the surgical margins. Prominent heterophile infiltration was noted at the inner border of the capsule. No angiolymphatic invasion was observed.

Immunohistochemistry (IHC) was performed using monoclonal mouse anti-human antibodies against desmin, smooth muscle actin (SMA), vimentin, and S-100 on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue sections, with detection via a chromogenic method (brown signal indicating positive immunoreactivity). Positive controls included smooth muscle (intestine) and striated muscle tissues. All images were captured at high magnification with scale bars for calibration. 

What diagnosis can be concluded from these findings, and what is the full pathological reasoning supporting this diagnosis?

input_logic_chain.research_context: Histological and immunohistochemical characterization of a facial subcutaneous mass in a ball python to determine its neoplastic nature and cell of origin.

experiments.experimental_setting: Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining of formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue sections from the resected mass, examined under light microscopy.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess the histological architecture, cellular morphology, and invasive behavior of the tumor.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The tumor is unencapsulated, poorly demarcated, and composed of neoplastic spindle cells forming loose interlacing streams and bundles within a mild fibrovascular stroma. High-power view shows spindle cells with cigar-shaped nuclei, moderate cytologic atypia, mitotic figures, indistinct cell borders, and moderate amphophilic granular cytoplasm. Neoplastic cells extend to surgical margins. Prominent heterophile infiltration is noted at the inner border of the capsule. No angiolymphatic invasion is observed. [Context]
experiments.interpretation: The unencapsulated, infiltrative growth pattern with extension to margins indicates locally aggressive behavior. Cigar-shaped nuclei and mitotic activity are characteristic of mesenchymal neoplasms. The spindle cell morphology and stromal pattern are consistent with a sarcoma of mesenchymal origin.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The histological features support a diagnosis of an infiltrative, moderately atypical spindle cell neoplasm consistent with a soft tissue sarcoma.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemistry (IHC) performed using monoclonal mouse anti-human antibodies against desmin, smooth muscle actin (SMA), vimentin, and S-100 on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue sections. Positive controls: smooth muscle (intestine) and striated muscle tissues (Supplementary Figure S1). Detection via chromogenic method (likely DAB), with brown signal indicating positive immunoreactivity.
experiments.experiment_goal: To determine the immunophenotype of the neoplastic spindle cells and narrow the differential diagnosis toward a specific lineage.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: No immunoreactivity to desmin [Image 1] and vimentin [Image 2], as evidenced by uniform light staining and absence of brown chromogenic signal in tumor cells. Patchy weak immunoreactivity to S-100, with faint, uneven brown signal in cytoplasmic and perinuclear regions of some spindle cells [Image 3]. Diffuse, robust cytoplasmic immunoreactivity to smooth muscle actin, shown by strong, homogeneous brown staining in the majority of tumor cells [Image 4].
experiments.interpretation: [Image 1] and [Image 2] show absence of specific staining, indicating negative results for desmin and vimentin. [Image 3] shows focal, weak positivity for S-100, which may represent nonspecific binding or minimal neural differentiation, but not diagnostic of a nerve sheath tumor. [Image 4] demonstrates strong and diffuse cytoplasmic SMA expression, a hallmark of smooth muscle differentiation.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The immunohistochemical profile—SMA-positive, desmin-negative, vimentin-negative, and S-100 focally weak—supports smooth muscle lineage and is consistent with leiomyosarcoma.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The tumor exhibits histological features of a malignant spindle cell neoplasm with infiltrative growth, cytologic atypia, and mitotic activity.
The immunophenotype shows specific expression of smooth muscle actin without expression of skeletal muscle, mesenchymal, or peripheral nerve markers.

reasoning.content: The histological evaluation reveals a poorly demarcated, infiltrative spindle cell neoplasm with moderate cytologic atypia and mitotic figures, fulfilling morphological criteria for a soft tissue sarcoma. The absence of a capsule and extension to surgical margins suggest locally aggressive behavior. Immunohistochemistry is critical for lineage determination. The tumor’s lack of desmin and vimentin expression rules out skeletal muscle origin (rhabdomyosarcoma) and broad mesenchymal nonspecificity. Focal weak S-100 staining does not support a diagnosis of peripheral nerve sheath tumor, which typically shows stronger, more diffuse reactivity. In contrast, the robust, diffuse cytoplasmic staining for smooth muscle actin is a defining feature of smooth muscle differentiation. Although desmin is often positive in leiomyosarcomas, its absence does not exclude the diagnosis, particularly in veterinary or reptilian cases where antigen expression may be variable. The combination of SMA positivity and morphological features strongly supports a diagnosis of leiomyosarcoma. The tumor’s subcutaneous facial location is rare but does not negate the diagnosis given the supportive histopathological and immunohistochemical evidence.
reasoning.conclusion: The resected facial mass in the ball python is diagnosed as a subcutaneous leiomyosarcoma based on histological morphology and immunohistochemical profile showing smooth muscle actin positivity, desmin negativity, and absence of other lineage-specific markers.

question:
A 54-year-old male presented with recurrent epistaxis and a nasopharyngeal mass in the right Rosenmüller fossa, initially diagnosed as undifferentiated carcinoma. To determine the origin of the tumor and whether it represents a metastasis from a primary lung adenocarcinoma, the following investigations were performed:

1. A biopsy from the nasopharyngeal mass was examined using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining at 40x magnification, with an inset using mucicarmine special stain.

2. Immunohistochemical staining for thyroid transcription factor-1 (TTF-1) was performed on the tumor tissue, using a chromogenic detection method and hematoxylin counterstain.

3. Additional immunohistochemical stains for CK20, PAX8, CDX2, and S100 were performed on the same tissue; the tumor showed negative immunoreactivity for all these markers.

4. A maximum intensity projection (MIP) and axial fused FDG-PET/CT scan of the head, neck, thorax, and axilla was performed, revealing the following hypermetabolic lesions: a left upper lobe lung mass with SUVmax of 13, a right nasopharyngeal lesion with SUVmax of 6.2, and hypermetabolic mediastinal (SUVmax 2.9) and left axillary lymph nodes (SUVmax 2.1).

Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis and origin of the nasopharyngeal tumor, and how can this be justified through an integrated analysis of the results?

experiments.sub_conclusion: The tumor exhibits morphological and histochemical features consistent with adenocarcinoma, particularly due to mucin production and poor cellular cohesion.

experiments.interpretation: The brown chromogen indicates specific binding of anti-TTF-1 antibody. Nuclear localization confirms expression of TTF-1, a transcription factor highly expressed in primary lung adenocarcinomas. Cytoplasmic staining may represent nonspecific or cross-reactive binding but does not negate nuclear positivity.
experiments.sub_conclusion: TTF-1 positivity supports a pulmonary origin of the tumor.

experiments.experimental_setting: Additional immunohistochemical stains for CK20, PAX8, CDX2, and S100 performed on the same tumor tissue; results described in text but not shown visually.

experiments.interpretation: Negative immunoreactivity for CK20, PAX8, CDX2, and S100 rules out common differential diagnoses including colorectal adenocarcinoma, thyroid carcinoma, renal cell carcinoma, and melanoma.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The immunoprofile (TTF-1+/CK7+/CK20-/PAX8-/CDX2-/S100-) is highly specific for pulmonary adenocarcinoma and excludes other primary malignancies.

experiments.experimental_setting: Maximum intensity projection (MIP) and axial fused FDG-PET/CT imaging of the head, neck, thorax, and axilla, assessing metabolic activity via 18F-FDG uptake.
experiments.experiment_goal: To identify primary and metastatic lesions based on glucose metabolism and anatomical localization.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Intensely hypermetabolic left upper lobe lung mass (SUVmax 13), hypermetabolic right nasopharyngeal lesion (SUVmax 6.2), and hypermetabolic mediastinal and left axillary lymph nodes (SUVmax 2.9 and 2.1, respectively) [Context].
experiments.interpretation: FDG-avid lesions indicate high metabolic activity typical of malignant tumors. The presence of a primary lung lesion with synchronous hypermetabolic nodal and distant (nasopharyngeal) involvement suggests either direct extension or metastatic spread. Given the anatomical separation, metastasis is more likely.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The PET/CT findings support a primary lung malignancy with distant metastasis to the nasopharynx and regional lymph nodes.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The nasopharyngeal tumor shows histological features of adenocarcinoma with mucin production and poor cohesion.
TTF-1 expression in tumor nuclei strongly supports a pulmonary origin.
The immunohistochemical profile excludes other common primary sites, reinforcing lung as the most likely origin.
FDG-PET/CT reveals a metabolically active lung mass with synchronous distant and nodal disease, consistent with metastatic carcinoma.

reasoning.content: The histopathological analysis of the nasopharyngeal mass reveals tumor cells with mucin-containing vacuoles and a diffuse, poorly cohesive growth pattern, characteristic of adenocarcinoma [Image 1]. The mucicarmine stain confirms intracellular mucin, supporting glandular differentiation. Immunohistochemistry demonstrates nuclear expression of TTF-1 [Image 2], a marker highly sensitive and specific for lung adenocarcinoma when combined with CK7 positivity and absence of CK20, PAX8, CDX2, and S100. This immunoprofile effectively excludes gastrointestinal, urothelial, thyroid, and melanocytic primaries. The radiological evidence from FDG-PET/CT shows a hypermetabolic lung mass with synchronous hypermetabolic lesions in the nasopharynx and lymph nodes, indicating systemic disease. Given the significant anatomical distance between the lung and nasopharynx, and the lack of local invasion patterns, the nasopharyngeal lesion is best interpreted as a metastasis rather than a primary nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Together, the histology, immunophenotype, and imaging converge to support the diagnosis of metastatic pulmonary adenocarcinoma presenting in the nasopharynx.
reasoning.conclusion: The nasopharyngeal mass represents a metastasis from a primary pulmonary adenocarcinoma, based on histomorphology, TTF-1 positivity, exclusion of other primaries, and correlative imaging findings.

question:
An investigation was conducted to study follicular dendritic cell (FDC) dynamics in hepatic lymph nodes (HLNs) and liver during *Fasciola hepatica* infection in sheep, with a focus on CNA.42+ FDC expression and germinal centre development.

Histological and immunohistochemical analyses were performed on HLNs from uninfected control (UC) and *F. hepatica*-infected sheep at 9 and 18 days post-infection (dpi) using the ABC-haematoxylin method with anti-CNA.42 monoclonal antibody.

Quantitative immunohistochemical analysis of CNA.42+ cells in germinal centres of HLNs was carried out across UC, 9 dpi, and 18 dpi groups, with cell counts normalized per germinal centre. It was observed that the number of CNA.42+ cells in germinal centres was significantly higher at 18 dpi compared to the UC group, and no CNA.42+ cells were detected in the UC group.

Immunohistochemical analysis of liver tissue from UC and infected sheep (9 and 18 dpi) was conducted using the same anti-CNA.42 mAb and staining method. In infected animals, CNA.42+ cells exhibited a stellate morphology and were located within inflammatory infiltrates that formed lymphoid follicles around portal tracts and at the periphery of granulomas. No such staining was observed in the UC group.

A quantitative assessment of CNA.42+ cells in liver tissue (per 0.08 mm²) was performed in UC, 9 dpi, and 18 dpi groups. The number of CNA.42+ cells in the liver increased significantly at both 9 dpi and 18 dpi compared to UC, although high individual variability was noted.

What conclusions can be drawn from these findings regarding the immune response to *F. hepatica* infection in sheep?

experiments.experiment_goal: To identify and localize CNA.42+ follicular dendritic cells (FDCs) within lymphoid follicles of HLNs and assess changes in their numbers during infection.

[Image 1] In Image 2, at higher magnification, reddish-brown chromogenic signal is observed in the cytoplasm and occasionally at the membrane of cells interspersed among densely packed lymphoid cells in the germinal centre. [Image 2]

Their localization within the germinal centre and morphological integration among lymphoid cells confirm their identity as follicular dendritic cells. question:
An investigation was conducted to assess the histopathological and ultrastructural effects of -CP on testicular tissue, particularly spermatogonic cells, to evaluate its potential testicular toxicity. 

Histological examination of testicular tissue from the control group was performed using Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) staining at ×10 magnification. 

Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analysis of testicular tissue from the -CP-treated group was conducted at 1.0K × magnification with negative contrast. 

A transmission electron micrograph of testicular tissue from the -CP-treated group was obtained at 2.5K × magnification. 

A comparative analysis of testicular tissue between control and -CP-treated groups was carried out using both histological and TEM data, supported by reference to prior literature (Manna et al. [12]). This analysis revealed pathological features including cell membrane damage, nuclear shrinkage, chromatin condensation, stages of apoptosis, and decreased or absent cytoplasmic organelles. 

What conclusions can be drawn from these findings, and how do the experimental observations support them?

input_logic_chain.research_context: Assessment of the histopathological and ultrastructural effects of -CP on testicular tissue, particularly spermatogonic cells, to evaluate its potential testicular toxicity.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological examination of testicular tissue from the control group using Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) staining at ×10 magnification.

Luminal spaces are prominent and pale. Nuclear morphology varies, with some nuclei larger and vesicular, others smaller and condensed. Intertubular spaces contain connective tissue, blood vessels, and scattered cells with basophilic nuclei and eosinophilic cytoplasm [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The presence of organized cellular stratification, diverse nuclear stages, and intact luminal structures indicates active spermatogenesis and normal seminiferous tubule architecture.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The control group exhibits histologically normal testicular tissue with intact spermatogenic activity and structural organization.

Numerous membrane-bound organelles with dense, electron-opaque interiors are present, some with irregular contours. Scattered granular, electron-dense deposits appear as dark punctate granules. Nuclei display reduced volume and condensed chromatin with sharply defined, irregular shapes. Cytoplasmic matrix shows variable electron density with increased granularity and dispersed particulate material. Basement membrane fragments and intercellular spaces are faintly visible. Seminiferous tubules exhibit irregular shape and size [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: Ruptured membranes indicate loss of cellular integrity. Irregular organelles and granular deposits suggest organelle degradation and cellular stress. Nuclear shrinkage and chromatin condensation are hallmark features of apoptosis. Disrupted architecture reflects widespread cellular damage.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The -CP-treated group exhibits ultrastructural evidence of cellular degeneration, including membrane rupture, nuclear condensation, and organelle disruption, consistent with apoptotic processes in spermatogonic cells.

experiments.experiment_goal: To further assess cytoplasmic and nuclear alterations in spermatogonic cells following -CP treatment.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Spermatogonic cells above the basement membrane show variable nuclear chromatin density—some nuclei are darkly stained with densely packed chromatin, others less electron-dense. Cytoplasm is electron-lucent with sparse organelles and few vesicular or membranous structures. Elongated dark profiles and small punctate dark structures are present in the extracellular matrix. Background shows variable electron density and granular texture [Image 3].
experiments.interpretation: Condensed chromatin indicates chromatin aggregation, a sign of apoptosis. Electron-lucent cytoplasm with sparse organelles reflects loss of synthetic and metabolic capacity. Extracellular dark structures may represent cellular debris or apoptotic bodies.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The treated group shows morphological evidence of advanced apoptosis and cytoplasmic degeneration in spermatogonic cells, including chromatin condensation and organelle depletion.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological and TEM-based comparative analysis of testicular tissue between control and -CP-treated groups, supported by reference to prior literature (Manna et al. [12]).
experiments.experiment_goal: To correlate observed pathological changes with known markers of testicular toxicity and validate findings.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Pathological features include cell membrane damage, nuclear shrinkage, chromatin condensation, stages of apoptosis, and decreased or absent cytoplasmic organelles [Context].

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The control group exhibits normal seminiferous tubule architecture and active spermatogenesis, as confirmed by H&E staining [Image 1].

The morphological changes observed are consistent with apoptosis and cellular degeneration, corroborated by comparison with established literature [Context].

reasoning.content: The control group's testicular tissue displays organized seminiferous tubules with normal spermatogenic cell layers and intact cellular morphology, indicating healthy spermatogenesis. In contrast, the -CP-treated group exhibits severe ultrastructural abnormalities: ruptured cell membranes, condensed chromatin, shrunken nuclei, and reduced cytoplasmic organelles—hallmark features of apoptosis. These changes are observed across multiple TEM images and are consistent with biochemical disruption. The agreement with prior studies confirms the pathological significance of these findings. Together, these observations indicate that -CP induces significant structural damage to spermatogonic cells, compromising testicular integrity and function.
reasoning.conclusion: Chronic exposure to -CP induces significant testicular toxicity, characterized by ultrastructural damage to spermatogonic cells, including apoptosis and organelle depletion, leading to disruption of spermatogenesis and potential impairment of testosterone synthesis.

question: A 60-year-old male patient presents with multiple osteolytic bone lesions initially suspected to be metastatic cancer, prompting a biopsy of the fifth lumbar vertebra to clarify the diagnosis. Histopathological examination was performed on the biopsy specimen using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining, with a scale bar of 100 μm for spatial reference. Additional immunohistochemical analyses were conducted on the same specimen using antibodies against langerin (CD207), S100 protein, and CD1a, each with a brown chromogen for detection and hematoxylin counterstain, and each slide includes a 100 μm scale bar for spatial context. Based on these studies, what is the most appropriate diagnosis, and how can it be justified through the integration of the histological and immunohistochemical findings?

input_logic_chain.research_context: To confirm the diagnosis of Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) in a 60-year-old male patient presenting with multiple bone lesions initially suspected as metastatic cancer, based on histopathological and immunohistochemical analysis of a bone biopsy from the fifth lumbar vertebra.

experiments.experimental_setting: A bone biopsy specimen was obtained from the fifth lumbar vertebra and processed for histological examination using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining. The slide was examined under light microscopy with a scale bar of 100 μm for spatial reference [Image 1].

experiments.visual_phenomenon: The H&E-stained section shows a densely cellular field with disorganized architecture, lacking clear structural boundaries. Multinucleated giant cells, eosinophils, lymphocytes, and mononuclear cells with mild nuclear atypia are present. Nuclei vary in size and shape, some with visible nucleoli, and cytoplasm is variably stained in pink and light purple [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The presence of multinucleated giant cells, eosinophils, and atypical mononuclear cells in a disorganized infiltrate is consistent with the granulomatous inflammation typical of LCH. Eosinophil-rich infiltrates are a hallmark of LCH lesions.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The histological appearance supports a diagnosis of a histiocytic disorder with features suggestive of LCH.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining was performed on the same bone biopsy specimen using antibodies against langerin (CD207), with detection via a brown chromogen and hematoxylin counterstain. The slide includes a 100 μm scale bar and is labeled 'langerin' [Image 2].
experiments.experiment_goal: To determine if the lesional cells express langerin, a specific marker for Langerhans cells.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Discrete, punctate to granular dark brown deposits are irregularly distributed throughout the tissue, indicating specific immunoreactivity. These deposits are localized in scattered cells and show variable intensity, with some clustering observed. The background is pale blue to lavender [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: The brown chromogen indicates positive immunostaining for langerin, which is expressed in the Birbeck granules of Langerhans cells. Its presence confirms the Langerhans cell lineage of the infiltrating histiocytes.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The lesional cells are of Langerhans cell origin, supporting the diagnosis of LCH.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining was performed using antibodies against S100 protein, with brown chromogen detection and hematoxylin counterstain. The slide is labeled 'S100' and includes a 100 μm scale bar [Image 3].
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess expression of S100, a protein commonly expressed in Langerhans cells and other dendritic cells.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Brown chromogenic signal is localized in scattered cells throughout the field, appearing individually and in clusters. The stained cells show heterogeneous morphology (rounded, elongated, spindle-shaped) and variable signal intensity. The background is lightly counterstained in blue or pale purple [Image 3].
experiments.interpretation: S100 protein is expressed in Langerhans cells and other neural crest-derived cells. Its expression in the lesional histiocytes further supports their identity as Langerhans cells, although it is less specific than langerin.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The lesional cells express S100, reinforcing their dendritic/Langerhans cell phenotype.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining was performed for CD1a, a classic marker for Langerhans cells, using a brown chromogen and hematoxylin counterstain. The slide is labeled 'CD1a' and includes a 100 μm scale bar [Image 4].
experiments.experiment_goal: To determine CD1a expression, a traditional diagnostic marker for LCH.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: No brown chromogenic signal is observed in any cellular or extracellular compartment. The nuclei are uniformly stained blue to lavender with hematoxylin, and the cytoplasm appears pale with no specific staining. The background is clear with minimal non-specific staining [Image 4].
experiments.interpretation: CD1a negativity is unusual but not unheard of in LCH. However, when combined with langerin positivity, it can represent a variant phenotype, as langerin is more specific and stable than CD1a. CD1a can be lost in paraffin-embedded tissues or in certain clinical variants.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Despite CD1a negativity, the presence of langerin positivity supports the diagnosis of LCH, as langerin is a more specific marker.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The H&E staining reveals a histiocytic infiltrate with eosinophils and multinucleated giant cells, characteristic of LCH.
Immunohistochemistry confirms the Langerhans cell lineage through langerin and S100 expression.
CD1a negativity does not rule out LCH when langerin is positive.

reasoning.content: The histological examination of the lumbar vertebra biopsy shows a disorganized cellular infiltrate rich in eosinophils, multinucleated giant cells, and atypical mononuclear cells—classic morphological features of LCH. Immunohistochemical analysis demonstrates positivity for langerin and S100, both markers associated with Langerhans cells. Although CD1a is negative, which may occur due to antigen loss in tissue processing or biological variation, langerin (CD207) is a more specific and reliable marker for LCH. The combination of characteristic histology and langerin positivity confirms the diagnosis even in the absence of CD1a expression. This immunophenotypic profile—langerin+/S100+/CD1a−—is a recognized variant in LCH, particularly in adult or multisystem cases.
reasoning.conclusion: The patient is diagnosed with Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) based on histopathological and immunohistochemical evidence, despite CD1a negativity, due to langerin positivity and characteristic cellular morphology.

question:
The mechanism of acridine orange (AO) monomeric binding to epichromatin DNA may involve intercalation, influenced by DNA helical conformation, with differences between epichromatin and lamina-associated domains (LADs) detectable via AO fluorescence and abolished upon DNA denaturation.

Researchers conducted the following experiments:

1. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) of rat hepatocyte nuclei using conventional fixation and heavy metal staining methods, with a scale bar of 0.25 µm for spatial calibration.

2. High-resolution TEM of rat thymocyte nuclear periphery, using conventional fixation and heavy metal staining, with a 0.25 µm scale bar.

3. Acridine orange (AO) fluorescence assay on epichromatin and LADs, comparing fluorescence color (green vs. orange-red) under native and denaturing conditions (94°C vs. 80°C), with DNase sensitivity and hydrophobicity tests. Under native conditions, AO fluorescence appears green in epichromatin and orange-red in LADs; this difference is abolished after treatment at 94°C.

4. Analysis of nucleosome occupancy and supranucleosomal structures via glutaraldehyde fixation and electron microscopy, combined with immunoprecipitation of histone H3 epigenetic marks in HL-60/S4 cells. After glutaraldehyde fixation, epichromatin reveals 30–35 nm superbeads, whereas LADs show 30 nm fibers. Immunoprecipitation shows no binding of six tested histone H3 epigenetic marks to epichromatin.

What can be concluded from these experiments regarding the structural and functional differences between epichromatin and lamina-associated domains (LADs)?

experiments.sub_conclusion: The AO fluorescence difference reflects distinct DNA helical conformations in epichromatin and LADs, which are abolished upon complete DNA melting, confirming conformational rather than sequence-only basis for differential AO binding [Context].

experiments.experimental_setting: Analysis of nucleosome occupancy and supranucleosomal structures via glutaraldehyde fixation and electron microscopy, combined with immunoprecipitation of histone H3 epigenetic marks in HL-60/S4 cells.

experiments.visual_phenomenon: After glutaraldehyde fixation, epichromatin reveals 30–35 nm superbeads, whereas LADs show 30 nm fibers; immunoprecipitation shows no binding of six tested histone H3 epigenetic marks to epichromatin [Context].
experiments.interpretation: The 30–35 nm superbeads suggest a unique, cross-link-stabilized chromatin structure in epichromatin, distinct from canonical 30 nm fibers. The absence of histone H3 marks indicates a lack of conventional epigenetic regulation in epichromatin.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Epichromatin exhibits a unique supranucleosomal architecture and lacks typical repressive or activating histone marks, further distinguishing it from LADs [Context].

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: Epichromatin forms a dense, continuous granular layer at the nuclear periphery with associated 30 nm fibrils, indicating a highly organized chromatin structure [Image 1].

reasoning.content: The visual evidence from TEM shows that epichromatin forms a uniform, electron-dense granular layer beneath the nuclear membrane with laterally projecting 30 nm fibrils, while LADs appear as patchy, irregular chromatin domains associated with the lamina and nuclear pores. These structural differences correlate with functional distinctions: AO fluorescence reveals green monomeric binding in epichromatin (indicative of constrained, GC-rich, intercalation-permissive DNA) versus orange-red dimeric binding in LADs (suggesting more open, AT-rich DNA). This difference vanishes after 94°C denaturation, confirming that the AO signal reflects DNA conformation, not just sequence. Furthermore, epichromatin’s unique 30–35 nm superbeads and absence of histone H3 modifications contrast with LADs’ 30 nm fibers and repressive marks. Together, these findings indicate that epichromatin and LADs represent distinct chromatin domains differing in structure, conformation, and epigenetic regulation.
reasoning.conclusion: Epichromatin and LADs exhibit fundamentally different DNA helical conformations and higher-order chromatin organizations, detectable by AO fluorescence and ultrastructural analysis, with epichromatin characterized by a dense, GC-rich, conformationally constrained structure lacking canonical epigenetic marks, while LADs are more heterogeneous, AT-rich, and epigenetically repressed.
