The patient has widespread osteolytic and permeative skeletal lesions with active bone turnover, consistent with extramedullary leukemic bone infiltration.

reasoning.content: The histological examination of the humerus biopsy reveals a dense infiltrate of monotonous, immature cells with high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio and scant cytoplasm, disrupting normal bone architecture [Image 1]. These morphological features are consistent with a blast cell neoplasm. The absence of LCA and MIC2 immunoreactivity in the tumor cells [Image 2, 3] excludes lymphoid leukemia and Ewing sarcoma, supporting a non-lymphoid, non-small round blue cell tumor diagnosis. Bone marrow analysis shows 64% blasts that are myeloperoxidase-negative but PAS block-positive, indicating absence of myeloid differentiation and presence of erythroid lineage markers [Context]. Flow cytometry confirms the blasts lack myeloid, lymphoid, and stem cell markers but express glycophorin A, a definitive erythroid marker, establishing the diagnosis of AML M6 (pure erythroid leukemia) [Context]. Radiological findings demonstrate multifocal lytic and permeative bone lesions with increased uptake on bone scan, confirming widespread skeletal involvement [Context]. The biopsy from the humerus shows tumor cells in sheets between bone spicules, directly linking the skeletal lesions to the leukemic process. Together, these findings confirm that AML M6 can present with extramedullary skeletal involvement, which has not been previously reported in the literature.
reasoning.conclusion: This is the first documented case of AML M6 (pure erythroid leukemia) presenting with multifocal osteolytic skeletal lesions, confirmed by histopathology, immunophenotyping, and radiological imaging, establishing that AML M6 can manifest with extramedullary bone involvement.

question: A 72-year-old male underwent radical resection of a cutaneous tumor following biopsy, with subsequent reconstruction. The clinical aim was to determine the histopathological nature and immunophenotypic profile of a cutaneous tumor exhibiting features of both squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) and mucinous adenocarcinoma (MAC)-like differentiation. Histological examination of the resected tumor was performed using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining at low and high magnification. Immunohistochemical staining was conducted for p63 and pancytokeratins using standard chromogenic detection methods. Additional immunohistochemical staining was performed for epithelial membrane antigen (EMA) and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) to assess ductal or glandular differentiation. A panel of markers including cytokeratin 7 (CK7), cytokeratin 20 (CK20), Ber-EP4 (Ep-CAM), and androgen receptor was also applied. Finally, histological assessment of resection margins and perineural invasion was carried out on H&E-stained sections. The evaluation revealed no tumor cells at the resection margins. One focus of perineural invasion was identified. The tumor cells showed no immunoreactivity for CK7, CK20, Ber-EP4, or androgen receptor. What is the most appropriate integrated pathological interpretation of these findings, and what is the likely nature of this tumor?

input_logic_chain.research_context: Determine the histopathological nature and immunophenotypic profile of a cutaneous tumor exhibiting features of both squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) and mucinous adenocarcinoma (MAC)-like differentiation following radical resection.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological examination of the resected tumor tissue using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining at low and high magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: Assess overall tumor architecture, invasion depth, cellular morphology, and presence of specific histological features such as keratinization, cystic structures, and ductal differentiation.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The histological section shows an irregular, thickened epithelial layer transitioning into a disorganized cellular mass invading the dermis, subcutaneous fat, and striated muscle [Image 1]. Tumor cells are densely packed with hyperchromatic nuclei, increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratios, and disruption of normal tissue architecture. Keratinization and intercellular bridges are present. Inflammatory infiltrates and fibrosis are observed in the stroma [Image 1]. At higher magnification, polygonal tumor cells with abundant cytoplasm, some appearing clear, form microcystic structures and micronodules. Luminal spaces contain eosinophilic material and are lined by cells showing ductal differentiation [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: The presence of intercellular bridges and keratinization supports squamous differentiation. The invasion into deep dermal, subcutaneous, and muscular layers indicates aggressive behavior. Microcystic structures filled with eosinophilic keratinous material and focal ductal-like formations suggest areas of divergent differentiation. Clear cells may represent glycogen-rich or lipid-laden tumor cells, often seen in certain SCC variants.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The tumor exhibits invasive squamous cell carcinoma with areas of clear cell morphology, microcystic change, and focal glandular/ductal differentiation, suggesting a hybrid or metaplastic phenotype.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining for p63 and pancytokeratins using standard chromogenic detection methods.
experiments.experiment_goal: Confirm squamous lineage and basal/myoepithelial cell differentiation of the tumor.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Diffuse nuclear immunostaining for p63 is observed in tumor cells, with strong dark brown signal localized to nuclei within irregular clusters and nests embedded in fibrous stroma. Surrounding stromal elements show no staining and are lightly counterstained [Image 3]. Pancytokeratin staining (not visually shown but mentioned in text) was also diffusely positive.
experiments.interpretation: p63 is a transcription factor highly expressed in basal and squamous epithelial cells. Its diffuse nuclear expression strongly supports squamous differentiation. Pancytokeratin positivity confirms epithelial origin.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The tumor is of epithelial origin with definitive squamous differentiation, as evidenced by diffuse p63 and pancytokeratin expression.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining for epithelial membrane antigen (EMA) and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) to evaluate ductal or glandular differentiation.
experiments.experiment_goal: Identify and characterize areas of glandular or ductal differentiation within the tumor.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: EMA staining shows dark brown signal localized predominantly along the luminal borders of irregular, branching glandular-like structures. The staining is membranous and outlines epithelial cells lining cystic and ductal spaces. Background stroma is pale blue, providing contrast [Image 4]. CEA staining (not visually shown) was also positive in focal ductal structures.
experiments.interpretation: EMA and CEA are markers of glandular and luminal epithelial differentiation. Their expression in membranous and luminal patterns confirms the presence of true ductal or glandular differentiation within the tumor, resembling mucinous adenocarcinoma (MAC).
experiments.sub_conclusion: Focal ductal structures within the tumor show immunophenotypic features consistent with glandular differentiation, similar to MAC.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining for cytokeratin 7 (CK7), cytokeratin 20 (CK20), Ber-EP4 (Ep-CAM), and androgen receptor to rule out other carcinomas and confirm specificity.
experiments.experiment_goal: Exclude metastatic adenocarcinoma (e.g., colorectal, breast, urothelial) and basal cell carcinoma, and assess potential hormonal influences.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Tumor cells show no immunoreactivity for CK7, CK20, Ber-EP4, or androgen receptor [Context].
experiments.interpretation: CK7/CK20 negativity argues against common metastatic adenocarcinomas (e.g., gastrointestinal, urothelial). Ber-EP4 negativity helps exclude basal cell carcinoma and some epithelial malignancies. Androgen receptor negativity suggests no hormonal driver involvement.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The tumor lacks immunophenotypic features of metastatic adenocarcinoma or basal cell carcinoma, supporting a primary cutaneous origin with divergent differentiation.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological assessment of resection margins and perineural invasion on H&E-stained sections.
experiments.experiment_goal: Evaluate completeness of resection and presence of high-risk pathological features.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: No tumor cells are observed at the resection margins [Context]. One focus of perineural invasion is identified [Context].
experiments.interpretation: Free margins indicate complete macroscopic and microscopic excision. Perineural invasion is a known risk factor for local recurrence and aggressive behavior in cutaneous carcinomas.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The tumor was completely resected, but perineural invasion suggests a higher risk of recurrence.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The tumor demonstrates unequivocal squamous differentiation with keratinization, intercellular bridges, and diffuse p63 expression.
Focal ductal structures expressing EMA and CEA indicate glandular differentiation resembling MAC.
The absence of CK7, CK20, Ber-EP4, and androgen receptor rules out metastatic adenocarcinoma and basal cell carcinoma.
The tumor is deeply invasive but completely resected, with perineural invasion as a high-risk feature.

reasoning.content: The tumor exhibits classic histological and immunohistochemical features of invasive squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), including keratinization, intercellular bridges, and diffuse p63 and pancytokeratin expression. However, it also contains distinct areas of glandular differentiation, evidenced by microcystic and ductal structures lined by EMA- and CEA-positive cells, mimicking mucinous adenocarcinoma (MAC). The lack of CK7, CK20, and Ber-EP4 expression excludes metastatic adenocarcinoma and basal cell carcinoma, supporting a diagnosis of a primary cutaneous tumor with divergent differentiation. The architectural complexity, deep invasion into subcutaneous fat and muscle, and presence of perineural invasion underscore its aggressive potential. Despite complete resection, the hybrid morphology and high-risk features necessitate close follow-up. The overall findings are consistent with a rare variant of SCC showing MAC-like differentiation, often termed 'cutaneous SCC with mucinous metaplasia' or 'MAC-mimicking SCC'.
reasoning.conclusion: The tumor is an invasive squamous cell carcinoma with areas of mucinous adenocarcinoma-like ductal differentiation, representing a metaplastic or hybrid variant of cutaneous SCC rather than a pure MAC or metastatic carcinoma.

question:
In a study on the localization and morphological characteristics of ghrelin-immunoreactive (ghrelin-IR) cells in the gastrointestinal tract of calves, with emphasis on the abomasum, duodenum, and jejunum, the following experiments were conducted:

1. Histological sections of the abomasum pars fundalis from a 13-week-old calf were stained with DAB and hematoxylin and examined at 200× magnification (scale bar: 50 μm).

2. Histological sections of the abomasum pars fundalis from a 13-week-old calf were stained with DAB and hematoxylin and examined at 400× magnification (scale bar: 50 μm).

3. Histological sections of the duodenum from a 13-week-old calf were stained with DAB and hematoxylin and examined at 400× magnification (scale bar: 50 μm).

4. Histological sections of the jejunum from a 13-week-old calf were stained with DAB and hematoxylin and examined at 400× magnification (scale bar: 50 μm).

5. Negative control samples were processed without the primary antibody and stained with DAB+.

In the negative control samples, no positive staining results were observed.

What can be concluded from these experiments regarding the presence, distribution, and characteristics of ghrelin-IR cells in the gastrointestinal tract of calves?

input_logic_chain.research_context: Localization and morphological characteristics of ghrelin-immunoreactive (ghrelin-IR) cells in the gastrointestinal tract of calves, with emphasis on the abomasum, duodenum, and jejunum.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological sections of the abomasum pars fundalis from a 13-week-old calf were stained with DAB and hematoxylin and examined at 200× magnification. Immunoreactive cells were identified based on DAB chromogen deposition (brown staining).
experiments.experiment_goal: To visualize the distribution and localization of ghrelin-IR cells in the abomasum pars fundalis.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Numerous dark brown-stained cells are scattered throughout the epithelial layer, primarily in the cytoplasm, with red arrows indicating immunoreactive cells. The nuclei appear as small, darkly stained ovoid structures, many centrally located. Cellular morphology is rounded and uniform. Scale bar: 50 μm [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The dark brown cytoplasmic staining indicates positive immunoreactivity for ghrelin due to DAB chromogen deposition. The presence of staining specifically in the cytoplasm suggests intracellular synthesis or storage of ghrelin. The uniform, rounded morphology supports epithelial origin.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Ghrelin-IR cells are present in the abomasum pars fundalis and exhibit cytoplasmic localization with epithelial cell morphology.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological sections of the abomasum pars fundalis from a 13-week-old calf were stained with DAB and hematoxylin and examined at 400× magnification to allow higher-resolution analysis of cellular details.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess the intensity, distribution, and morphological features of ghrelin-IR cells at higher magnification.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Immunoreactive cells (marked by red arrows) display intense brown cytoplasmic staining, are round to oval in shape, and are irregularly distributed among epithelial cells. Nuclei are dark blue-purple, with variable size and shape. Surrounding stroma is lightly stained. Scale bar: 50 μm [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: The intense and focal brown staining confirms strong ghrelin immunoreactivity localized to the cytoplasm. The irregular distribution suggests non-uniform expression across the glandular epithelium. The contrast with lightly stained surrounding tissue confirms specificity of staining.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Ghrelin-IR cells in the abomasum pars fundalis show strong, specific cytoplasmic immunoreactivity and heterogeneous spatial distribution.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological sections of duodenum from a 13-week-old calf were stained with DAB and hematoxylin and imaged at 400× magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To determine the presence and localization of ghrelin-IR cells in the duodenum.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: A single cell (indicated by red arrow) shows markedly darker and more intense brown cytoplasmic staining compared to surrounding cells. Other cells show variable, lighter brownish cytoplasmic staining. Glandular architecture is preserved. Scale bar: 50 μm [Image 3].
experiments.interpretation: The intensely stained single cell exhibits characteristics of a ghrelin-IR cell due to focal, strong DAB deposition in the cytoplasm. The lighter background staining in other cells may represent weak or non-specific signal, but the focal intense staining supports specific ghrelin expression in isolated cells.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Ghrelin-IR cells are sparsely present in the duodenum, with at least one clearly identifiable immunoreactive cell exhibiting strong cytoplasmic staining.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological sections of jejunum from a 13-week-old calf were stained with DAB and hematoxylin and examined at 400× magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess the presence of ghrelin-IR cells in the jejunum.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: No distinct brown-stained cells are visible. The cytoplasmic regions show only a diffuse, faint brownish signal without focal accumulation. Intercellular spaces are visible, and tissue architecture appears normal. Scale bar: 50 μm [Image 4].
experiments.interpretation: The absence of focal, intense brown staining indicates no detectable ghrelin-IR cells in this field of view. The diffuse signal likely represents background or non-specific staining rather than true immunoreactivity.
experiments.sub_conclusion: No ghrelin-IR cells are detectable in the jejunum under these experimental conditions.

experiments.experimental_setting: Negative control samples were processed without primary antibody and stained with DAB+ to assess specificity of immunostaining.
experiments.experiment_goal: To confirm the specificity of ghrelin immunoreactivity by ruling out non-specific staining.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: No positive staining results were observed in the negative control samples [Context].
experiments.interpretation: The absence of brown staining in the absence of primary antibody confirms that the observed staining in test samples is due to specific antigen-antibody interaction and not artifact or non-specific chromogen deposition.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The DAB-based immunostaining for ghrelin is specific and reliable.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: Ghrelin-IR cells are morphologically identifiable by distinct brown cytoplasmic staining via DAB and are present in the abomasum pars fundalis.
Ghrelin-IR cells are detectable but sparse in the duodenum and absent in the jejunum in the observed fields.
The immunostaining method is specific, as confirmed by negative controls.

reasoning.content: The experimental observations across multiple gastrointestinal regions show that ghrelin-IR cells are most prominently localized in the abomasum pars fundalis, where they exhibit strong cytoplasmic brown staining, round to oval morphology, and are embedded within the glandular epithelium. In the duodenum, only isolated immunoreactive cells are observed, indicating lower abundance. In the jejunum, no distinct ghrelin-IR cells are detectable, suggesting either very low density or absence. The specificity of staining is confirmed by the lack of signal in negative controls. Together, these findings establish a gradient of ghrelin expression decreasing from the abomasal fundic region to the proximal intestine.
reasoning.conclusion: Ghrelin-IR cells are predominantly localized in the abomasum pars fundalis with cytoplasmic expression, are less abundant in the duodenum, and are undetectable in the jejunum under the given experimental conditions.

question:
A 32-year-old woman presents with a well-circumscribed, un-encapsulated cervical mass, and a biopsy is performed to establish a definitive diagnosis by excluding histological mimics such as leiomyoma, aggressive angiomyxoma, and angiomyofibroblastoma. 

Histological examination of hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained tissue sections from the tumor is performed at multiple magnifications, with evaluation of cellular morphology, stromal features, mitotic activity, and necrosis. 

Immunohistochemical staining for desmin is performed on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue sections using chromogenic detection with nuclear counterstain. 

Immunohistochemical staining for CD34 is performed on tissue sections using chromogenic detection to identify antigen expression in cellular compartments. 

Immunohistochemical staining for alpha-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA) is performed on tissue sections, with internal control from vascular smooth muscle cells. 

Immunohistochemical staining for CD99 is attempted, but repeated staining shows weak positivity in only a few cells, with most of the section washed off even on repeat attempts. 

What is the most likely diagnosis, and how can it be supported by integrating the findings from these studies while excluding key differential diagnoses?

input_logic_chain.research_context: To determine the histopathological and immunohistochemical characteristics of a well-circumscribed, un-encapsulated cervical tumor and establish its diagnosis as superficial myofibroblastic tumor (MFB) by excluding mimics such as leiomyoma, aggressive angiomyxoma, and angiomyofibroblastoma.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological examination of hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained tissue sections from the cervical tumor, evaluated at multiple magnifications. The evaluation includes assessment of cellular morphology, stromal features, mitotic activity, and necrosis.
experiments.experiment_goal: To characterize the histological architecture and cytological features of the tumor.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The tumor is well-circumscribed but un-encapsulated, composed of ovoid, stellate, and spindle-shaped cells in an edematous, variably collagenized, hyalinized, and vascularized stroma. Vessels include thick-walled types and irregular stag-horn shaped vessels. No mitotic figures or necrosis are observed [Context].
experiments.interpretation: A well-circumscribed but un-encapsulated growth pattern with bland cytology, absence of mitoses, and lack of necrosis supports a benign neoplasm. The stromal vascularity and edema suggest a myxoid stromal tumor. The absence of mitotic activity and necrosis argues against malignancy.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The histological features are consistent with a benign mesenchymal neoplasm with myxoid stromal features and no evidence of aggressive behavior.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining for desmin performed on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue sections, visualized using chromogenic detection (brown signal) with nuclear counterstain.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess expression of desmin, a marker of myogenic differentiation, in lesional cells.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Diffuse brown cytoplasmic staining for desmin in spindle and stellate-shaped cells. Staining is widespread but variable in intensity, with no nuclear reactivity. Background matrix is lightly stained, enhancing contrast [Image 1], [Image 2], [Image 3].
experiments.interpretation: Cytoplasmic desmin positivity indicates myogenic or myofibroblastic differentiation. The diffuse and widespread staining across spindle and stellate cells confirms that the lesional population expresses this marker, supporting a myofibroblastic lineage.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Lesional cells show consistent myogenic immunophenotypic features via diffuse desmin expression.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining for CD34 on tissue sections, using chromogenic detection to identify antigen expression in cellular compartments.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate CD34 expression, a marker often positive in fibroblastic and myofibroblastic tumors, including superficial MFB.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Brown chromogenic staining for CD34 localized to cytoplasm and cell membranes of a large subset of spindle and stellate cells. Staining is heterogeneous, with clusters and scattered positive cells in a pale matrix. Nuclear counterstain highlights background nuclei in blue [Image 4].
experiments.interpretation: CD34 positivity in a large subset of lesional cells supports a fibroblastic or myofibroblastic origin. The co-expression with desmin is characteristic of superficial MFB and helps distinguish it from smooth muscle tumors, which are typically CD34-negative.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The tumor shows a CD34+/desmin+ immunoprofile typical of superficial MFB.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining for alpha-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA) on tissue sections, with internal control from vascular smooth muscle cells.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess for smooth muscle differentiation and distinguish from leiomyoma or other myoid tumors.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Sparse, focal brown staining for α-SMA in a small subset of spindle cells. Most lesional cells are negative. Internal control vessels show strong positivity in smooth muscle walls [Image 5].
experiments.interpretation: Limited α-SMA expression indicates only partial myofibroblastic differentiation, not dominant smooth muscle differentiation. The scarcity of SMA+ cells contrasts with leiomyomas, which typically show diffuse SMA positivity.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The immunoprofile shows only focal myofibroblastic differentiation, inconsistent with a diagnosis of leiomyoma.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining for CD99 was attempted but repeated staining showed weak positivity in only a few cells, with most of the section washed off.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate CD99 expression, which may be positive in Ewing sarcoma or other small round cell tumors, but can be variably expressed in MFB.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Weak, non-specific staining in some cells; most of the section showed loss of stain even on repeat attempts [Missing].
experiments.interpretation: The staining result is inconclusive due to technical failure. CD99 is not reliably assessed and cannot contribute to diagnostic differentiation.
experiments.sub_conclusion: CD99 staining is non-contributory and does not impact the diagnostic conclusion.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The tumor is a benign, well-circumscribed mesenchymal neoplasm with bland cytology and no mitotic activity or necrosis.
Lesional cells show diffuse desmin expression, supporting myogenic or myofibroblastic differentiation.
CD34 is expressed in a large subset of lesional cells, supporting a fibroblastic/myofibroblastic lineage and consistent with superficial MFB.
Only a small subset of cells expresses α-SMA, ruling out a diagnosis of leiomyoma or other smooth muscle-predominant tumor.

reasoning.content: The histological examination reveals a benign, well-circumscribed, un-encapsulated tumor composed of spindle and stellate cells in a myxoid stroma, lacking mitotic activity or necrosis, which excludes malignancy and aggressive mesenchymal tumors. The immunohistochemical profile demonstrates diffuse desmin positivity and strong CD34 expression in lesional cells, a combination frequently seen in superficial myofibroblastic tumors (MFB). The limited α-SMA reactivity further differentiates this tumor from leiomyoma, which typically shows diffuse SMA and desmin expression but lacks CD34 positivity. The absence of perivascular epithelioid cells and lack of diffuse SMA also argue against angiomyofibroblastoma. The CD99 result is inconclusive and does not alter the interpretation. The overall morphology and immunophenotype—particularly the co-expression of desmin and CD34 with focal SMA—are hallmark features of superficial MFB. The use of age- and site-matched non-neoplastic cervical controls (Figure 6) further supports that the observed staining is neoplasm-specific and not a stromal reactive change.
reasoning.conclusion: The tumor is most consistent with a benign superficial myofibroblastic tumor (MFB) of the cervix based on its histological features and characteristic immunohistochemical profile (desmin+/CD34+/focal SMA+), while excluding mimics such as leiomyoma, aggressive angiomyxoma, and angiomyofibroblastoma.

question: A 3-year-old girl presented with a painful, ulcerated swelling in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast. Doppler ultrasonography of the breast was performed using standard imaging protocols to evaluate the morphological and vascular characteristics of the breast mass, which revealed a well-circumscribed, hypoechoic mass with scant internal vascularity. Fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) was performed on the breast nodule, and smears were prepared and stained with May-Grünwald Giemsa (MGG) for microscopic evaluation. The excised skin nodule was grossly examined, and the specimen was processed for histopathological analysis; however, no histological description or image is provided. What can be concluded from these findings and procedures?

Scattered macrophages suggest low-grade inflammation or debris clearance.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The MGG-stained cytology supports a diagnosis of apocrine metaplasia within a benign epithelial lesion.

Cytoplasmic borders are indistinct, and the background contains cellular debris and occasional intensely stained fragments [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: The Pap stain highlights the characteristic apocrine cytoplasmic features—granularity and amphophilic staining (pink to green)—due to secretory organelles and lipid content. Bland nuclear morphology without atypia or mitotic figures rules out malignancy. The overlapping cells and cohesive clusters are consistent with intact epithelial cell sheets.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Pap staining corroborates the presence of apocrine-type epithelial cells with benign cytological features.

question: A 65-year-old male with a history of liver cirrhosis presents with gastrointestinal bleeding. Endoscopy reveals a pedunculated polypoid lesion in the stomach, which is resected via endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD). The aim is to determine the histological and immunohistochemical characteristics of the gastric tumor to confirm its origin as metastatic hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Histological examination of the resected specimen is performed using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining. Immunohistochemical staining for cytokeratin 20 (CK20) is carried out on the tumor tissue section. Additionally, immunohistochemical staining for hepatocyte paraffin 1 (HepPar-1) is performed. Finally, immunohistochemical staining for cytokeratin 7 (CK7) is performed, and lymphovascular invasion (ly, v) status is assessed via histology; surgical margins (HM0, VM0) are evaluated. The CK7 staining is negative; lymphovascular invasion is present (ly+, v+); and resection margins are negative (HM0, VM0). What can be concluded regarding the origin, histological features, immunophenotype, and clinical implications of this gastric tumor based on these findings?

input_logic_chain.research_context: Determine the histological and immunohistochemical characteristics of a gastric tumor to confirm its origin as metastatic hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological examination of the resected gastric tumor specimen using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate the cellular architecture, nuclear features, cytoplasmic characteristics, and stromal components of the tumor.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The tissue shows a dense aggregation of cells arranged in solid and sheet-like patterns with minimal glandular formation. Cells exhibit moderate to marked nuclear pleomorphism, hyperchromatic nuclei, occasional prominent nucleoli, and high nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio. Cytoplasm is eosinophilic to amphophilic, with some clear or vacuolated regions. Scattered mitotic figures are present. Fibrous stroma with desmoplastic reaction, thin-walled vascular channels, and sparse lymphocytic infiltrates is observed. Bile pigment-like inclusions are seen in isolated cells. Trabecular-like patterns are present in some areas. No prominent necrosis or hemorrhage [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The solid and trabecular architecture, nuclear atypia, eosinophilic/vacuolated cytoplasm, and presence of bile pigment-like inclusions are characteristic of hepatocellular differentiation. The absence of glandular structures argues against a primary gastrointestinal adenocarcinoma. Mitotic activity indicates proliferative potential, consistent with malignancy.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The histomorphological features are consistent with a hepatocellular neoplasm rather than a primary gastric adenocarcinoma or neuroendocrine tumor.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining for cytokeratin 20 (CK20) on the tumor tissue section.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess whether the tumor has immunophenotypic features suggestive of gastrointestinal origin, as CK20 is typically positive in gastrointestinal adenocarcinomas.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Discrete, variably sized cells show brownish-yellow staining localized to cytoplasmic and/or membranous regions, indicative of CK20 expression. Staining is irregular, with single cells and small clusters showing faint to moderate intensity. Surrounding stroma and non-neoplastic elements are largely unstained [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: Focal and variable CK20 positivity is atypical for classical gastrointestinal adenocarcinomas, which usually show diffuse and strong CK20 expression. Focal CK20 staining can occur in HCC, particularly in poorly differentiated or metastatic forms, but diffuse positivity would favor a colorectal or gastric primary.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The focal and irregular CK20 staining pattern does not support a primary gastrointestinal adenocarcinoma and is compatible with metastatic HCC.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining for hepatocyte paraffin 1 (HepPar-1 or hepatocyte marker) on the tumor tissue section.
experiments.experiment_goal: To confirm hepatocellular lineage by detecting hepatocyte-specific antigen expression in tumor cells.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Scattered discrete cells show brown to brownish-yellow chromogen deposition in cytoplasmic regions, with granular to slightly diffuse pattern. The staining is unevenly distributed, with variable intensity and density, and no organized glandular structures are seen [Image 3].
experiments.interpretation: Cytoplasmic granular staining with hepatocyte marker is a well-established immunophenotypic feature of hepatocellular differentiation. Positive immunoreactivity, even if focal, supports a diagnosis of HCC, especially when combined with morphological features.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The presence of hepatocyte marker expression confirms hepatocellular origin of the tumor cells.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining for cytokeratin 7 (CK7) was performed, and lymphovascular invasion (ly, v) status was assessed via histology; surgical margins (HM0, VM0) were evaluated.
experiments.experiment_goal: To further differentiate the tumor from other epithelial malignancies and assess resectability and aggressiveness.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: CK7 staining is negative [Context]; lymphovascular invasion is present (ly+, v+) [Context]; resection margins are negative (HM0, VM0) [Context].
experiments.interpretation: CK7 negativity is typical of HCC, which usually shows CK7(-)/CK20(-) or CK7(-)/CK20(±) profiles, whereas biliary or gastric primaries often express CK7. Lymphovascular invasion suggests aggressive behavior, but complete resection (HM0/VM0) reduces local recurrence risk.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The immunoprofile (CK7-, CK20 focal+, hepatocyte+) and lymphovascular invasion support metastatic HCC with aggressive features, but complete resection was achieved.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The tumor exhibits histological features typical of HCC, including trabecular/solid architecture, nuclear pleomorphism, bile pigment inclusions, and hepatocellular cytoplasmic features.
The immunophenotype (CK20 focal+, CK7-, hepatocyte+) is consistent with HCC and argues against a primary gastric adenocarcinoma.
The tumor was completely resected with negative margins, despite evidence of lymphovascular invasion.

reasoning.content: The histological architecture (solid and trabecular) and cellular features (nuclear atypia, bile pigment inclusions, eosinophilic/vacuolated cytoplasm) observed in H&E staining [Image 1] are characteristic of hepatocellular malignancy. The absence of glandular structures rules out primary gastric adenocarcinoma. Immunohistochemistry further supports this: while CK20 is typically associated with gastrointestinal tumors, its focal and irregular expression [Image 2] does not indicate a primary GI origin, especially in the context of CK7 negativity. In contrast, the positive hepatocyte marker staining [Image 3] confirms hepatocellular differentiation. Together, these findings establish the tumor as metastatic HCC. Lymphovascular invasion indicates hematogenous or lymphatic spread potential, but complete resection (HM0/VM0) suggests favorable local control. The solitary nature and normalization of AFP post-resection further support a metastatic HCC diagnosis with favorable response to local therapy.
reasoning.conclusion: The gastric tumor is a metastasis from hepatocellular carcinoma, confirmed by characteristic histomorphology and immunohistochemical profile (hepatocyte+, CK7-, CK20 focal+), with complete resection achieved.

question: Carbon monoxide poisoning is associated with rhabdomyolysis, and the pattern of muscle necrosis in some cases is not consistent with typical gravitational pressure-induced necrosis, suggesting a systemic toxic mechanism such as carbon monoxide toxicity. A histological examination using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining was performed on a skeletal muscle biopsy from the vastus medialis of a patient following suspected prolonged immobilization and toxic exposure. Additionally, the same H&E-stained section was examined to evaluate regenerative activity in the muscle tissue. [Image 1] and [Image 2] correspond to these analyses. Based on the research context and the findings depicted in the images, what can be concluded about the underlying mechanism of muscle injury in this patient?

input_logic_chain.research_context: Carbon monoxide poisoning is associated with rhabdomyolysis, and the pattern of muscle necrosis in this case is not consistent with typical gravitational pressure-induced necrosis, suggesting a systemic toxic mechanism such as carbon monoxide toxicity.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological examination of a skeletal muscle biopsy from the vastus medialis, stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E), obtained from a patient following suspected prolonged immobilization and toxic exposure.
experiments.experiment_goal: To identify histological evidence of muscle fiber degeneration and regeneration that may indicate the underlying cause of rhabdomyolysis.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Two muscle fibers show loss of normal striations and increased eosinophilia, with dense infiltration of small, round, darkly stained nuclei with visible cytoplasmic borders clustered around and within the affected fibers [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The increased eosinophilia and loss of striations indicate ongoing muscle fiber degeneration. The infiltrating darkly stained cells with cytoplasmic borders are consistent with inflammatory cells, particularly macrophages and lymphocytes, which are typically recruited during active muscle breakdown and phagocytosis of necrotic fibers.
experiments.sub_conclusion: There is histological evidence of active degeneration and inflammatory clearance of muscle fibers in the vastus medialis, indicating focal necrosis beyond normal post-immobilization changes.

experiments.experimental_setting: Same H&E-stained histological section of vastus medialis muscle, focusing on regenerative activity.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess whether muscle regeneration is present, which would support recent or ongoing muscle injury.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: A single muscle fiber exhibits intense basophilic cytoplasm, central and enlarged nuclei with prominent nucleoli, in contrast to surrounding fibers with peripheral nuclei and eosinophilic cytoplasm [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: Basophilic staining reflects high RNA content due to active protein synthesis. Central nucleation and prominent nucleoli are hallmark features of regenerating muscle fibers, indicating attempted repair following injury.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The presence of a regenerating fiber confirms recent myofiber injury and an active repair process in the vastus medialis.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The vastus medialis shows histological features of both degeneration (necrosis) and regeneration of muscle fibers.

The distribution and nature of the necrosis are inconsistent with typical pressure-induced rhabdomyolysis, which usually affects muscles directly under prolonged compression (e.g., gluteus maximus, quadriceps femoris near bony prominences), but not selectively involving vastus medialis with inflammatory infiltration and regeneration.

reasoning.content: The histological findings demonstrate focal muscle fiber degeneration with inflammatory infiltration and phagocytosis [Image 1], alongside a regenerating fiber with basophilic cytoplasm and central nucleation [Image 2], confirming active rhabdomyolysis and attempted repair. The involvement of the vastus medialis—a muscle not typically affected in gravitational pressure necrosis—combined with scattered necrotic changes and regeneration, suggests a systemic cause of muscle injury rather than localized ischemia from immobilization alone. Carbon monoxide poisoning is a known cause of toxic rhabdomyolysis due to mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress, which can lead to widespread myocyte damage independent of mechanical compression. Therefore, the histological pattern supports a systemic toxic etiology.
reasoning.conclusion: The histological evidence of non-pressure-related, widespread muscle fiber necrosis and regeneration in the vastus medialis is consistent with carbon monoxide-induced rhabdomyolysis, supporting the diagnosis of systemic carbon monoxide toxicity.

question:
To investigate the effect of the toluene-ethyl acetate (T-E) fraction from Cuminum cyminum on hen egg white lysozyme (HEWL) fibril formation and its consequent cytotoxicity in PC12 cells, the following experiments were conducted:

1. HEWL was incubated for 48 hours to allow fibril formation, with or without the presence of the T-E fraction. Congo red absorbance measurements were performed, and fluorescence microscopy was used to visualize fibrillar structures. Proteins incubated for 48 h formed extended networks of fluorescent fibrils.

2. The T-E fraction was added to HEWL during the fibrillation process, and fluorescence microscopic images were analyzed. The addition of the T-E fraction induced small, dense, amorphous protein particles.

3. ThT fluorescence kinetics were monitored over time during HEWL fibrillation in the presence or absence of the T-E fraction. The ThT fluorescence signal showed no significant increase for over 90 hours when the T-E fraction was present.

4. PC12 cells were treated with either: (1) 24 h-aged HEWL amyloid fibrils, (2) HEWL incubated with the T-E fraction, or (3) control conditions. Cell morphology was examined microscopically.

5. MTT assay and LDH release were measured in PC12 cells after 24 h treatment with HEWL aggregates formed in the presence or absence of the T-E fraction. Cells treated with 24 h-aged HEWL fibrils exhibited 48% cell death, while those treated with HEWL incubated with the T-E fraction showed 92% viability. LDH release in the presence of the T-E fraction was comparable to the control.

What conclusions can be drawn from these experimental findings?

experiments.interpretation: The presence of extended fluorescent fibrillar networks indicates successful amyloid fibril formation under standard incubation conditions, as confirmed by Thioflavin T (ThT) fluorescence.
experiments.sub_conclusion: HEWL forms mature amyloid fibrils after 48 h of incubation, which are structurally typical and detectable via fluorescence microscopy.

experiments.experimental_setting: The T-E fraction was added to HEWL during the fibrillation process, and fluorescence microscopic images were analyzed.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate the morphological impact of the T-E fraction on protein aggregation during fibrillation.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Addition of the T-E fraction induced small, dense, amorphous protein particles [Context].
experiments.interpretation: The absence of extended fibrillar networks and the presence of small, dense aggregates suggest that the T-E fraction disrupts the elongation and structural organization of amyloid fibrils, promoting amorphous aggregation instead.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The T-E fraction inhibits the formation of structured amyloid fibrils by redirecting aggregation toward amorphous, non-fibrillar species.

experiments.experimental_setting: ThT fluorescence kinetics were monitored over time during HEWL fibrillation in the presence or absence of the T-E fraction (Fig. 2).

experiments.experimental_setting: PC12 cells were treated with either: (1) 24 h-aged HEWL amyloid fibrils, (2) HEWL incubated with the T-E fraction, or (3) control conditions. Cell viability was assessed via MTT assay and LDH release, and cell morphology was examined microscopically (Fig. 4).

Cells treated with HEWL incubated with T-E fraction maintain intact, elongated, spindle-shaped morphology and form network-like structures [Image 3]. In contrast, cells exposed to C. cyminum essential oil show severe distortion and irregular shapes [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: Distorted cell morphology in [Image 1] is consistent with amyloid-induced cytotoxicity, while preserved, healthy morphology in [Image 3] indicates protection against toxic aggregation. The damage in [Image 2] confirms the cytotoxicity of the full essential oil, but not the T-E fraction.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The T-E fraction prevents amyloid-induced morphological damage in PC12 cells, indicating cytoprotection, whereas the full essential oil is independently cytotoxic.

reasoning.content: The experimental evidence demonstrates that HEWL undergoes fibrillation under standard conditions, forming extended β-sheet-rich fibrils that are cytotoxic to PC12 cells, causing significant cell death and morphological distortion. The addition of the T-E fraction from C. cyminum during incubation prevents the formation of these fibrils, as shown by the absence of red-shifted Congo red absorbance, lack of ThT fluorescence increase over 90 hours, and microscopic observation of amorphous aggregates instead of fibrillar networks. These structural changes correlate with a complete abrogation of cytotoxicity: cells exposed to T-E-treated HEWL show high viability (92%), minimal LDH release, and preserved spindle-shaped, network-forming morphology. In contrast, the full essential oil is cytotoxic, but the T-E fraction itself is not, suggesting that fractionation removes harmful components. Thus, the T-E fraction acts as a potent inhibitor of amyloid formation and confers cytoprotection by redirecting aggregation toward non-toxic species.
reasoning.conclusion: The toluene-ethyl acetate (T-E) fraction from Cuminum cyminum effectively inhibits the formation of cytotoxic HEWL amyloid fibrils by promoting the assembly of non-toxic amorphous aggregates, thereby preventing amyloid-induced cell death in PC12 cells.

question:
In the assessment of microvessel density (MVD) in bone marrow biopsies using CD34 immunohistochemistry to evaluate angiogenesis as a potential prognostic factor in hematologic malignancies, the following experiments were conducted:

- Bone marrow biopsy samples were processed into paraffin-embedded sections, decalcified using 10% neutral-buffered formalin, and subjected to immunohistochemical (IHC) staining for CD34 using the Ventana Benchmark XT platform with UltraView Universal DAB Detection Kit. Antigen retrieval was performed via microwave boiling in citrate buffer, followed by dewaxing, cell conditioning with CC1 buffer, incubation with primary antibody (CD34, clone QBEnd10, 1:500 dilution) for 32 minutes, counterstaining, and mounting. Imaging was performed at ×100 and ×400 magnification.

- Two independent hematopathologists manually examined slides using a Zeiss microscope to identify and count CD34-positive structures in three distinct regions per patient at 400× magnification, with each field covering 0.24 mm². The regions were selected at ×100 magnification based on increased density of stained structures. Round CD34-positive cells with distinct nuclei were excluded, as were any stained structures within trabecular bone or periosteum.

What can be concluded from these experimental procedures and observations?

input_logic_chain.research_context: Assessment of microvessel density (MVD) in bone marrow biopsies using CD34 immunohistochemistry to evaluate angiogenesis as a potential prognostic factor in hematologic malignancies.

experiments.experimental_setting: Bone marrow biopsy samples were processed into paraffin-embedded sections, decalcified using 10% neutral-buffered formalin, and subjected to immunohistochemical (IHC) staining for CD34 using the Ventana Benchmark XT platform with UltraView Universal DAB Detection Kit. experiments.experiment_goal: To specifically label vascular endothelial cells in bone marrow tissue for visualization and quantification of microvessels.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Brown DAB chromogen deposits outline thin, elongated, branching, and anastomosing structures within the bone marrow stroma, representing immunolabeled endothelial cells. These structures are embedded in a background of small, round, blue-stained hematopoietic cell nuclei. The distribution of labeled vessels is heterogeneous, with focal clusters of high vessel density. [Image 1] [Image 2]
experiments.interpretation: The brown staining corresponds to CD34 expression on vascular endothelial cells, confirming successful IHC labeling. The morphological features—branching, elongation, and network formation—are consistent with microvessels, including small arterioles and venules. The heterogeneous spatial distribution suggests variable angiogenic activity across the tissue.
experiments.sub_conclusion: CD34 IHC effectively highlights microvessels in bone marrow, enabling identification of vascular 'hot spots' for MVD quantification.

experiments.experimental_setting: Two independent hematopathologists manually identified and counted CD34-positive vessels in three 'hot spots' per patient at 400× magnification (each field covering 0.24 mm²), excluding round CD34-positive cells with distinct nuclei (hematopoietic precursors) and vessels in trabecular bone or periosteum. Slides were examined using a Zeiss microscope.
experiments.experiment_goal: To quantify microvessel density (MVD) in areas of highest vascularization in a blinded, reproducible manner.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: At ×100 magnification, a region with conspicuously increased density of brown-stained microvessels is circled, indicating a 'hot spot'. [Image 1] At ×400 magnification, individual brown-stained microvessels appear as thin, irregular, branching structures forming a network within a cellular stroma; round blue nuclei of hematopoietic cells are abundant in the background. [Image 2]
experiments.interpretation: The circled area in [Image 1] represents a region selected for high microvessel concentration, fulfilling the 'hot spot' criterion. The high-magnification view in [Image 2] confirms that the stained structures are endothelial-lined vessels, not hematopoietic cells, due to their morphology and lack of round, distinct nuclear contours typical of hematopoietic precursors.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Manual identification and counting of CD34-positive microvessels in hot spots at high magnification allow reliable and specific quantification of MVD, excluding non-vascular CD34+ cells and anatomically irrelevant regions.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: CD34 immunohistochemistry specifically labels vascular endothelial cells in bone marrow tissue, enabling visualization of microvessels.
Microvessels are heterogeneously distributed, with identifiable 'hot spots' of increased vascular density that can be reproducibly selected for quantification.
Manual MVD quantification in hot spots at 400× magnification, with exclusion criteria, ensures accurate and specific measurement of angiogenic microvessel density.

reasoning.content: The experimental workflow begins with optimized IHC staining for CD34, which selectively labels vascular endothelial cells in bone marrow biopsies. The visual evidence confirms that DAB-based staining produces clear, morphologically identifiable microvessels as brown, branching structures against a cellular background. These vessels are not uniformly distributed, and regions of high density (hot spots) are visually identifiable at low magnification [Image 1]. At high magnification [Image 2], the structural details confirm endothelial-lined vessels, distinguishing them from hematopoietic CD34+ precursors based on morphology. The quantification protocol—focusing on three hot spots per patient at 400×, excluding non-vascular CD34+ cells and anatomical regions like trabecular bone—ensures that the measured MVD reflects true microvascular angiogenesis. Together, these steps validate the methodological rigor and biological relevance of MVD as a measurable histopathological parameter.
reasoning.conclusion: Microvessel density (MVD) in bone marrow can be reliably and specifically quantified using CD34 immunohistochemistry by identifying and counting vessels in vascular hot spots under defined morphological and anatomical exclusion criteria, providing a valid basis for assessing angiogenesis in hematologic malignancies.

question:
In a study of the histopathological features of skin lesions in patients with New World Cutaneous Leishmaniasis (NUCL), the following investigations were conducted:

- Histological sections of skin lesions were prepared using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining and examined under light microscopy, with assessment of cellular composition, tissue architecture, and inflammatory aggregates. The magnification corresponds to a scale of 20 micrometers.

- Additional H&E-stained sections were evaluated for the presence of granulomatous structures and associated stromal changes. The magnification corresponds to a scale of 50 micrometers.

- Direct parasitological examination and immunohistochemical staining were performed on skin lesion biopsies to detect Leishmania amastigotes. The results showed that amastigote forms were identified in 100% (20/20) of cases by direct parasitological examination, but only in 55% (11/20) of cases by immunohistochemistry.

Based on these findings, what comprehensive pathological interpretation can be drawn regarding the nature of the inflammatory response, granuloma formation, and parasite detection in NUCL skin lesions?

input_logic_chain.research_context: Histopathological features of skin lesions in patients with NUCL (New World Cutaneous Leishmaniasis), focusing on inflammatory infiltration, parasitism, and granuloma formation.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological sections of skin lesions were prepared using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining and examined under light microscopy. The analysis included assessment of cellular composition, tissue architecture, and presence of inflammatory aggregates [Context].
experiments.experiment_goal: To characterize the nature and extent of inflammatory infiltration in dermal lesions of NUCL patients.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: A dense aggregation of mononuclear cells within the dermis, with darkly stained, hyperchromatic nuclei varying slightly in size and shape, predominantly uniform, some elongated and others rounded. Minimal intercellular space, pale pink extracellular matrix, and basophilic nuclei with eosinophilic cytoplasmic and matrix components [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The dense aggregation of cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and minimal cytoplasm is characteristic of mononuclear inflammatory infiltration, primarily composed of lymphocytes. The preservation of tissue architecture without ulceration suggests a non-ulcerative, chronic inflammatory process.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The dermal lesions exhibit mononuclear inflammatory infiltration dominated by lymphocytes, consistent with a chronic immune response in NUCL [Image 1].

experiments.experimental_setting: H&E-stained histological sections were evaluated for the presence of granulomatous structures and associated stromal changes [Context].
experiments.experiment_goal: To determine whether granuloma formation is present and its histological characteristics.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: A well-demarcated, nodular structure composed of tightly packed epithelioid cells with abundant pale cytoplasm and round to oval, centrally located dark purple nuclei, some with vesicular appearance. Interspersed small dark nuclei (lymphocytes), surrounding fibrous stroma with wavy collagen bundles indicating fibrosis [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: The presence of epithelioid cells forming a nodular structure with lymphocytic infiltration and peripheral fibrosis is diagnostic of granulomatous inflammation. This pattern is commonly associated with chronic infections such as leishmaniasis.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Granulomatous inflammation is present in the dermal lesions, characterized by epithelioid cell granulomas with lymphocytic cuffing and fibrotic stroma [Image 2].

experiments.experimental_setting: Direct parasitological examination and immunohistochemical staining were performed on skin lesion biopsies to detect Leishmania amastigotes [Context].
experiments.experiment_goal: To compare the sensitivity of direct parasitological examination versus immunohistochemistry in detecting Leishmania amastigotes.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The presence of amastigote forms was confirmed in 100% (20/20) of cases by direct parasitological exam, but only in 55% (11/20) by immunohistochemistry [Context].
experiments.interpretation: Direct parasitological methods (e.g., smear microscopy) are more sensitive than immunohistochemistry in detecting amastigotes in NUCL skin lesions, possibly due to antigen degradation or low parasite load affecting antibody binding.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Leishmania amastigotes are more consistently detected by direct parasitological methods than by immunohistochemistry in NUCL lesions [Context].

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The dermal lesions exhibit mononuclear inflammatory infiltration dominated by lymphocytes, consistent with a chronic immune response in NUCL [Image 1].
Granulomatous inflammation is present in the dermal lesions, characterized by epithelioid cell granulomas with lymphocytic cuffing and fibrotic stroma [Image 2].
Leishmania amastigotes are more consistently detected by direct parasitological methods than by immunohistochemistry in NUCL lesions [Context].

reasoning.content: The histopathological analysis reveals that NUCL skin lesions are characterized by chronic dermal inflammation with dense mononuclear infiltration, primarily lymphocytes, as evidenced by H&E-stained sections showing hyperchromatic nuclear aggregates [Image 1]. These inflammatory foci often organize into granulomatous structures composed of epithelioid macrophages, lymphocytes, and fibrotic stroma, confirming granulomatous inflammation in a subset of cases [Image 2]. Despite only discrete parasitism observed histologically, direct parasitological examination confirms Leishmania amastigotes in all cases, indicating high sensitivity of this method compared to immunohistochemistry, which detected parasites in just over half the cases. This discrepancy suggests limitations in immunohistochemical detection, possibly due to low antigen expression or technical factors. Together, these findings support the diagnosis of NUCL with a chronic granulomatous immune response and variable parasite visibility depending on detection method.
reasoning.conclusion: NUCL skin lesions are characterized by chronic granulomatous inflammation with mononuclear infiltration, predominantly lymphocytes and epithelioid macrophages, and despite low visibility in immunohistochemistry, Leishmania amastigotes are universally present as confirmed by direct parasitological examination.

question: A serval presented with an adrenal mass that caused intraoperative hypertension, prompting surgical excision and histopathological evaluation to rule out pheochromocytoma. Histological examination of the excised mass was performed using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining at 200x magnification. Additionally, immunohistochemical staining for Chromogranin A was conducted on the same specimen, with internal positive control from adrenal medullary tissue and internal negative control from adrenal cortical tissue, also viewed at 200x magnification. Based on these experiments, what can be concluded about the nature of the adrenal mass and the cause of the intraoperative hypertension?

input_logic_chain.research_context: Determine the nature of an adrenal mass in a serval that caused intraoperative hypertension, with histopathological and immunohistochemical evaluation to rule out pheochromocytoma.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological examination of the excised adrenal mass using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining, viewed at 200x magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess the architectural and cytological features of the adrenal cyst and surrounding tissue.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: An encapsulated cyst lined by a single layer of plump to attenuated, cuboidal to columnar epithelial cells with basophilic nuclei and eosinophilic cytoplasm; nuclei are basally aligned with cytoplasm extending apically. The cyst lumen contains amorphous eosinophilic (proteinaceous) debris with cholesterol clefts, macrophages, and multinucleated giant cells. Hemorrhage and mineralized debris are present at one edge. Compressed adrenal cortex forms a thin peripheral rim. Nuclei appear blue to blue-purple; cytoplasm and extracellular material are pink [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The presence of a well-demarcated, epithelial-lined cyst with proteinaceous and inflammatory contents suggests a benign epithelial cyst of the adrenal gland. The compressed adrenal tissue indicates mass effect rather than invasion. Cholesterol clefts and giant cells suggest prior hemorrhage or degeneration.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The lesion is a non-invasive, expansile, epithelial-lined adrenal cyst with features consistent with a benign process and no evidence of malignancy or medullary origin.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining for Chromogranin A on the adrenal cyst specimen, with internal positive (adrenal medulla) and negative (adrenal cortex) controls, viewed at 200x magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To determine whether the epithelial lining of the cyst is derived from neuroendocrine cells, which would support a diagnosis of cystic pheochromocytoma given the intraoperative hypertension.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The epithelial lining of the cyst shows no brown chromogenic signal, indicating absence of specific staining [Image 2]. The cyst lumen exhibits diffuse brown discoloration of the proteinaceous material, which is non-specific. Adjacent clusters of cells (*) show strong, granular, cytoplasmic brown staining (positive control). Cells in a compact region (▲) show no staining, consistent with cortical cells (negative control). Nuclei are uniformly blue [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: The lack of Chromogranin A immunoreactivity in the epithelial lining indicates that these cells are not of neuroendocrine origin. The positive staining in adjacent medullary cells confirms assay validity. Non-specific staining of cyst contents does not indicate cellular expression.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The cyst epithelium is not derived from adrenal medullary chromaffin cells, ruling out cystic pheochromocytoma as a diagnosis.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The lesion is a benign, epithelial-lined adrenal cyst with no histological evidence of neoplastic transformation or invasion.
The epithelial cells of the cyst are not neuroendocrine in origin, as demonstrated by negative Chromogranin A immunostaining.

reasoning.content: The histological features observed in the H&E-stained section [Image 1] demonstrate a well-encapsulated cyst lined by benign epithelial cells, with proteinaceous and degenerative contents, consistent with a primary epithelial adrenal cyst. The compressed adrenal cortex and lack of invasion support a non-neoplastic, space-occupying lesion. Given the intraoperative hypertension, a pheochromocytoma was a differential diagnosis, prompting Chromogranin A immunohistochemistry. The absence of specific staining in the cyst lining [Image 2], contrasted with strong positive staining in adjacent medullary cells (*), confirms the non-neuroendocrine nature of the epithelium. The non-specific staining of cyst contents does not alter this interpretation. Together, these findings exclude cystic pheochromocytoma and support a diagnosis of a non-functional, benign epithelial adrenal cyst. The resolution of hypertension post-excision may reflect mechanical or indirect effects rather than catecholamine secretion.
reasoning.conclusion: The adrenal mass is a benign epithelial cyst of non-neuroendocrine origin, not a pheochromocytoma, and the intraoperative hypertension was likely coincidental or mechanically induced rather than hormonally mediated.

question:
To determine whether the patient's cervical dorsal root ganglion (DRG) exhibited histopathological features consistent with active productive HSV-1 infection causing ganglionitis, the following studies were performed:

- Histopathological examination of resected cervical dorsal root ganglion tissue using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining was conducted at 100× magnification.
- Immunohistochemical staining for HSV-1 was performed using a polyclonal anti-HSV-1 antibody with brown chromogen and hematoxylin counterstain, visualized at ×200 magnification.
- Immunohistochemical staining for CD68, a marker of macrophages, was carried out on cervical DRG tissue at ×200 magnification with brown chromogen and hematoxylin counterstain.
- Immunohistochemical staining for CD45, a pan-leukocyte marker, was performed on cervical DRG tissue at ×200 magnification with brown chromogen and hematoxylin counterstain.

What can be concluded from these findings?

input_logic_chain.research_context: To determine whether the patient's cervical dorsal root ganglion (DRG) exhibited histopathological features consistent with active productive HSV-1 infection causing ganglionitis.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histopathological examination of resected cervical dorsal root ganglion tissue using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining at 100× magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess tissue architecture, inflammatory infiltration, and neuronal damage in the DRG.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Multifocal areas of cellular aggregation with dense inflammatory infiltrates composed of small, densely packed cells with hyperchromatic nuclei, interspersed among larger neuronal cell bodies; focal neuronophagia observed with smaller cells partially surrounding or engulfing neurons, one such instance indicated by a black arrow [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The presence of dense inflammatory infiltrates and focal neuronophagia indicates an active inflammatory process targeting sensory neurons in the DRG, a hallmark of viral ganglionitis.
experiments.sub_conclusion: There is histological evidence of active inflammation and neuronal injury in the cervical DRG, consistent with ganglionitis.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining of cervical DRG tissue using a polyclonal anti-HSV-1 antibody with brown chromogen and hematoxylin counterstain, visualized at ×200 magnification.

experiments.visual_phenomenon: Brown chromogenic staining localized within neuronal cell bodies; one arrow points to a neuron with nuclear brown staining, another to cytoplasmic brown staining; variable staining patterns among neurons, with some showing no staining [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: Brown staining indicates specific binding of anti-HSV-1 antibody to viral proteins. Nuclear and cytoplasmic localization suggests active viral protein synthesis, which occurs during productive (lytic) infection rather than latency.
experiments.sub_conclusion: HSV-1 proteins are expressed in sensory neurons of the cervical DRG, indicating active productive infection rather than latent infection.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining for CD68, a marker of macrophages, in cervical DRG tissue at ×200 magnification with brown chromogen and hematoxylin counterstain.
experiments.experiment_goal: To identify the presence and distribution of macrophages as part of the inflammatory response.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: CD68-positive cells with brown cytoplasmic staining are focally distributed within the ganglion parenchyma; one such cell is indicated by a leftward-pointing arrow adjacent to a neuronal cell body [Image 3].
experiments.interpretation: CD68-positive macrophages are key effectors in neuroinflammatory responses and their perineuronal localization suggests targeted immune activity against infected neurons.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Macrophage infiltration is present in the DRG and localized near neurons, supporting an immune response to neuronal infection.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining for CD45, a pan-leukocyte marker, in cervical DRG tissue at ×200 magnification with brown chromogen and hematoxylin counterstain.
experiments.experiment_goal: To identify the presence of lymphocytic and other leukocytic infiltration in the ganglion.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Brown-stained CD45-positive cells, round to oval with dark nuclei, are densely packed in a cluster near the center-right of the image; a black rightward-pointing arrow highlights one such cell; staining is membranous and cytoplasmic [Image 4].
experiments.interpretation: CD45 immunoreactivity confirms the presence of lymphocytes and other leukocytes within the ganglion, indicating a robust adaptive immune response to infection.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Lymphocytic infiltration is present in the DRG, further confirming an active inflammatory response to infection.
