experiments.sub_conclusion: HK31 is specifically and strongly expressed in the epithelium of onychopapilloma, particularly in the superficial layers, but not in the normal nail bed.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical analysis of multiple onychopapilloma cases for expression of hair-related keratins, including HK34, HK85, and HK86, with results summarized in Table 3. The nail bed region was specifically assessed.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate whether other hair-related keratins (HK34, HK85, HK86) are expressed in the nail bed of onychopapilloma cases.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: [Context]: Table 3 reports negative expression of HK34, HK85, and HK86 in the nail bed across all onychopapilloma cases.
experiments.interpretation: The absence of detectable immunostaining for HK34, HK85, and HK86 indicates that these hair-related keratins are not upregulated or expressed in the nail bed component of onychopapilloma.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Unlike HK31, other hair-related keratins (HK34, HK85, HK86) are not expressed in the nail bed of onychopapilloma.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: HK31 is specifically and strongly expressed in the epithelium of onychopapilloma, particularly in the superficial layers, but not in the normal nail bed.
Unlike HK31, other hair-related keratins (HK34, HK85, HK86) are not expressed in the nail bed of onychopapilloma.

reasoning.content: The visual evidence from DAB-stained sections shows a marked and specific upregulation of HK31 in the epithelium of onychopapilloma, particularly in the superficial layers exhibiting papillomatosis and acanthosis. This expression pattern is absent in normal nail unit tissue, where no concentrated HK31 signal is observed in the nail bed. In contrast, other hair-related keratins (HK34, HK85, HK86) show no expression in the nail bed of onychopapilloma cases, as confirmed by immunohistochemical data. This selective expression of HK31—while other hair keratins remain negative—suggests that HK31 may serve as a specific molecular marker for onychopapilloma among hair-related keratins. The specificity of HK31 expression in pathological epithelium, but not in normal nail bed, further supports its role in the abnormal differentiation program of onychopapilloma.
reasoning.conclusion: HK31 is uniquely and consistently expressed in onychopapilloma across both matrix-adjacent and distal nail bed regions, distinguishing it from other hair-related keratins (HK34, HK85, HK86), which remain negative, thereby establishing HK31 as a specific immunohistochemical marker for onychopapilloma.

question: A 68-year-old male presents with a white, mildly indurated subcutaneous nodule measuring 4 × 7 × 4 mm at the lateral canthus of the right eye. Clinically, the lesion is suspected to be an epidermal inclusion cyst. The tumor is resected, and the specimen is fixed in formalin for histopathological analysis. A hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained section of the formalin-fixed tissue is examined under light microscopy, revealing a cystic structure within the dermis containing eosinophilic material and refractile crystalline elements, surrounded by a dense cellular infiltrate including multinucleated giant cells and histiocytes, with overlying epidermal thinning. A high-power magnification (×20) examination of the same H&E-stained section is then performed. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis, and how can it be justified through histopathological reasoning?

input_logic_chain.research_context: To determine the histopathological nature of a subcutaneous nodule at the lateral canthus of the right eye clinically suspected to be an epidermal inclusion cyst.

experiments.experimental_setting: A formalin-fixed tissue specimen from the resected canthal tumor was processed for histopathological examination using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining and analyzed under light microscopy.
experiments.experiment_goal: To examine the microscopic architecture and cellular composition of the lesion.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: A cystic structure located within the dermis containing amorphous, pale-staining eosinophilic material and sharply defined, angular, refractile crystalline elements [Image 1]. The cyst is surrounded by a dense cellular infiltrate with multinucleated giant cells and histiocytes [Image 1]. The overlying epidermis is thinned and flattened [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The presence of a cystic space with crystalline material and a surrounding granulomatous reaction composed of multinucleated giant cells and histiocytes suggests a foreign body-type granulomatous response to non-degradable material. The amorphous eosinophilic material and refractile crystals are consistent with deposited exogenous or metabolic crystals.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The lesion represents a granulomatous inflammatory response to crystalline material within a dermal cystic structure.

experiments.experimental_setting: High-power magnification (×20) of the H&E-stained histological section was performed to analyze the morphology of the crystalline deposits and their interaction with inflammatory cells.
experiments.experiment_goal: To characterize the shape and arrangement of crystalline material and its relationship with surrounding inflammatory cells.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Needle-shaped, parallel-aligned crystalline structures arranged in a radial, spoke-like pattern within the extracellular matrix, closely associated with histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: The needle-shaped, radially arranged crystalline structures surrounded by multinucleated giant cells and histiocytes are characteristic of monosodium urate (MSU) crystal deposition, which typically induces a foreign body granulomatous reaction. This morphology is pathognomonic for gouty tophi in histological sections.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The crystalline material is consistent with monosodium urate crystals, indicative of gout.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The lesion is a dermal cystic structure with a granulomatous inflammatory reaction to crystalline material.
The crystalline material has a needle-shaped, radially arranged morphology surrounded by multinucleated giant cells, typical of monosodium urate crystals.

reasoning.content: The initial histopathological examination revealed a cystic lesion in the dermis containing eosinophilic material and refractile crystals, surrounded by a granulomatous infiltrate of histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells [Image 1]. This pattern indicates a chronic inflammatory reaction to a non-degradable substance. At higher magnification, the crystals exhibited a distinct needle-like morphology arranged in a radial, spoke-wheel pattern and were directly surrounded by multinucleated giant cells and histiocytes [Image 2], a hallmark of monosodium urate (MSU) crystal deposition. Although negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals under polarized light would confirm MSU definitively, the H&E appearance—particularly the granulomatous reaction with giant cells engulfing needle-shaped crystals—is highly characteristic of gouty tophi in routine histology. Given the clinical context of a subcutaneous nodule in the eyelid and exclusion of other cystic lesions (e.g., epidermal inclusion cyst), the histological findings override the initial clinical suspicion. Therefore, the lesion is not a simple epidermal cyst but a gouty tophus.
reasoning.conclusion: The subcutaneous nodule at the lateral canthus is a gouty tophus, representing urate crystal deposition within the eyelid dermis, confirmed by histopathological identification of needle-shaped crystalline material inducing a foreign body granulomatous reaction.

question: A 72-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of a post-traumatic, exudative plaque on the anterolateral lower third of the left leg, accompanied by extrusion of gelatinous material. She had not responded to antibiotic treatment. A punch biopsy was performed on the erythematous plaque and the tissue specimen was processed and stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) for microscopic examination. The first histological section was examined at 40x magnification. A second section from the same biopsy was examined at 100x magnification to assess finer structural details. What can be concluded from these experiments regarding the nature of the lesion?

input_logic_chain.research_context: Perforating granuloma annulare (GA) is a rare subset of GA with characteristic clinical and histopathological features that facilitate differential diagnosis. The case report presents a 72-year-old woman with a post-traumatic, exudative plaque on the left leg, and the diagnosis was confirmed through histopathological analysis.

experiments.experimental_setting: A punch biopsy was performed on the erythematous plaque located on the anterolateral lower third of the left leg. The tissue specimen was processed and stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) for microscopic examination.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate the histopathological features of the lesion for diagnostic clarification.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: A well-defined nodular infiltrate in the papillary and reticular dermis, composed of small darkly stained mononuclear cells and larger pale-staining cells with abundant cytoplasm, arranged in a palisaded pattern around central eosinophilic material [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The palisaded arrangement of histiocytes and lymphocytes around eosinophilic, amorphous material is characteristic of granuloma annulare. The eosinophilic material represents necrobiotic collagen, a hallmark of GA.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The histopathological pattern is consistent with granuloma annulare, specifically showing palisading granulomatous inflammation around necrobiotic collagen.

experiments.experimental_setting: Same H&E-stained tissue section examined at higher magnification (100x) to assess epidermal and dermal structural changes.
experiments.experiment_goal: To identify evidence of transepidermal elimination and epidermal disruption typical of the perforating variant of GA.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Disrupted epidermal architecture with a concave, crater-like depression; thin, irregular epithelial layer; and expulsion of eosinophilic material through the epidermis, accompanied by cellular debris and dermal collagen fragmentation [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: The structural distortion and extrusion of degraded dermal material through the epidermis indicate active transepidermal elimination, a defining feature of perforating GA.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The presence of transepidermal elimination confirms the perforating variant of granuloma annulare.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The lesion exhibits palisading granulomatous inflammation surrounding necrobiotic collagen.
There is clear histological evidence of transepidermal elimination of dermal material.

reasoning.content: The histopathological evaluation reveals two key diagnostic features: (1) a dermal nodular infiltrate with palisading granulomas surrounding eosinophilic, necrobiotic collagen, which is pathognomonic for granuloma annulare; and (2) epidermal disruption with crater formation and extrusion of altered dermal material, confirming the perforating subtype. These features, in conjunction with the clinical presentation of a chronic, exudative plaque with extrusion of gelatinous material, differentiate perforating GA from other granulomatous or infectious conditions such as mycobacterial infection or pyoderma. The absence of microbial organisms on staining and lack of response to antibiotics further support a non-infectious, inflammatory etiology.
reasoning.conclusion: The lesion is definitively diagnosed as perforating granuloma annulare based on the integration of clinical findings and characteristic histopathological features, including palisading granulomas and transepidermal elimination.

question:
To compare the histological features of late acute cellular rejection (LAR), recurrent HBV-associated hepatitis, and biliary complications in liver allograft recipients, with the aim of identifying distinguishing pathological patterns for differential diagnosis in the late post-transplantation period (>3 months), the following studies were conducted:

- Histological analysis of liver allograft biopsies from recipients with late allograft dysfunction (>3 months post-transplant) was performed using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining, comparing samples diagnosed with LAR, recurrent HBV hepatitis, and biliary complications.
- The same H&E-stained sections were used for further evaluation in cases of late allograft dysfunction.
- Additional H&E-stained liver tissue sections from patients with late allograft dysfunction were examined.
- Immunohistochemical staining using a chromogen-based detection method was applied to liver tissue sections to highlight ductular structures.
- A comparative histological analysis was carried out across biopsy samples from patients with LAR, recurrent HBV hepatitis, and biliary complications, focusing on lobular activity, fibrosis, cholestasis, piecemeal necrosis, and inflammatory cell composition. The following findings were observed: lobular activity was significantly lower in biliary complications compared to LAR and recurrent HBV hepatitis; piecemeal necrosis was more common in recurrent HBV hepatitis; neutrophilic infiltration was significantly more frequent in biliary complications; fibrosis and cholestasis were frequent but did not differ statistically between groups.

What conclusions can be drawn from these analyses regarding the differential diagnosis of late allograft dysfunction?

input_logic_chain.research_context: To compare the histological features of late acute cellular rejection (LAR), recurrent HBV-associated hepatitis, and biliary complications in liver allograft recipients, with the aim of identifying distinguishing pathological patterns for differential diagnosis in the late post-transplantation period (>3 months).

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological analysis of liver allograft biopsies from recipients with late allograft dysfunction (>3 months post-transplant), comparing samples diagnosed with late acute rejection (LAR), recurrent HBV hepatitis, and biliary complications. Tissue sections were stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and some with immunohistochemical (IHC) staining for ductular markers.
experiments.experiment_goal: To identify distinguishing histological features among LAR, recurrent HBV hepatitis, and biliary complications.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Bile ducts show disrupted epithelial lining, loss of normal luminal contour, and are surrounded by dense inflammatory infiltrates composed predominantly of small round lymphocytes with dark nuclei and scattered larger mononuclear cells. Inflammatory cells encroach upon and surround ductal structures. Vascular structures display endothelial swelling, perivascular cuffing of inflammatory cells, thickened walls, and intravascular inflammatory cells. Parenchyma shows increased cellular density, disrupted extracellular matrix, and edema. [Image 1]
experiments.interpretation: The presence of periductal and perivascular inflammation with endothelialitis and bile duct damage are hallmark features of acute cellular rejection. The lymphocytic infiltrate with perivascular extension and endothelial involvement supports an immune-mediated attack on both biliary and vascular components of the graft.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Image 1 demonstrates histological features consistent with late acute cellular rejection, particularly bile duct damage and vascular endothelialitis.

experiments.experimental_setting: Same as above: H&E-stained liver biopsy sections from late allograft dysfunction cases.
experiments.experiment_goal: To identify histological patterns specific to recurrent HBV-associated hepatitis.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Portal tract shows dense infiltration of mononuclear cells including lymphocytes and plasma cells with eccentric nuclei and abundant cytoplasm. Inflammatory cells extend into the interface region with spillover across the limiting plate into hepatocytes. Neutrophils are clustered around dilated bile ducts containing luminal debris. Hepatic lobules maintain overall architecture, but interface hepatocytes show swelling and cytoplasmic changes. [Image 2]
experiments.interpretation: The portal-based inflammation with interface hepatitis (piecemeal necrosis), plasma cell infiltration, and neutrophilic activity around bile ducts are characteristic of chronic viral hepatitis, particularly recurrent HBV. The presence of neutrophils and bile duct damage may mimic rejection or biliary complications but in this context reflects viral reactivation with inflammatory sequelae.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Image 2 exhibits features typical of recurrent HBV-associated hepatitis, including interface hepatitis, plasma cell-rich infiltrate, and neutrophilic involvement around bile ducts.

experiments.experimental_setting: H&E-stained liver tissue sections from patients with late allograft dysfunction.
experiments.experiment_goal: To identify histological features associated with biliary complications.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Dense cellular arrangement with disrupted hepatic architecture. Hepatocytes are densely packed with high nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio, hyperchromatic nuclei, and some cytoplasmic vacuoles. Multiple small duct-like structures lined by cuboidal to elongated epithelial cells with increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratios and occasional mitoses are seen. These are surrounded by fibrous stroma and lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates. Portal areas show mild to moderate fibrosis. [Image 3]
experiments.interpretation: The presence of ductular proliferation, fibrosis, and architectural disorganization is characteristic of biliary obstruction or injury. Ductular reaction is a regenerative response to cholestasis or biliary loss, commonly seen in biliary complications such as anastomotic stricture or ischemic cholangiopathy.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Image 3 shows histological evidence of biliary complication, particularly ductular proliferation and fibrosis in a disrupted parenchymal architecture.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining (likely cytokeratin 7 or 19) on liver tissue sections to highlight ductular structures, with chromogen-based detection (brown signal).
experiments.experiment_goal: To visualize and confirm the extent of ductular proliferation in biliary complications.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Irregular, branching, dark brown chromogenic structures form duct-like or tubular configurations, aligned along fibrous septa or at parenchymal interfaces. Staining is intense in cytoplasmic and membranous compartments of elongated cells. Proliferating ductular elements are heterogeneous in size and shape, surrounded by inflammation and fibrosis. [Image 4]
experiments.interpretation: The brown chromogenic signal specifically labels biliary epithelial cells, confirming the presence of ductular proliferation. The spatial distribution along fibrous tracts and interface zones supports a reactive biliary response to chronic injury or obstruction.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Image 4 confirms extensive ductular proliferation via immunohistochemistry, a hallmark of biliary complications.

experiments.experimental_setting: Comparative histological analysis of biopsy samples from patients with LAR, recurrent HBV hepatitis, and biliary complications, focusing on lobular activity, fibrosis, cholestasis, piecemeal necrosis, and inflammatory cell composition.
experiments.experiment_goal: To statistically differentiate histological features among the three conditions.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Lobular activity is significantly lower in biliary complications compared to LAR and recurrent HBV hepatitis [Context]. Piecemeal necrosis is more common in recurrent HBV hepatitis [Context]. Neutrophilic infiltration is significantly more frequent in biliary complications [Context]. Fibrosis and cholestasis are frequent but not statistically different between groups [Context].
experiments.interpretation: Reduced lobular activity in biliary complications reflects less parenchymal inflammation compared to immune or viral hepatitis. Increased piecemeal necrosis in recurrent HBV indicates ongoing hepatocyte destruction at the portal-parenchymal interface. Prominent neutrophils in biliary complications suggest secondary bacterial infection or cholangitis-like inflammation due to stasis.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Histological features such as lobular activity, piecemeal necrosis, and neutrophilic infiltration help differentiate biliary complications from rejection and recurrent HBV.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: Image 1 shows bile duct damage and vascular endothelialitis, which are classical features of acute cellular rejection and are significantly more frequent in LAR than in other conditions.

Image 2 demonstrates interface hepatitis, plasma cell infiltration, and neutrophilic activity around bile ducts, consistent with recurrent HBV hepatitis, supported by higher frequency of piecemeal necrosis.
Images 3 and 4 reveal ductular proliferation, fibrosis, and low lobular activity, which are characteristic of biliary complications, further confirmed by prominent neutrophilic infiltrates.

Histological parameters such as bile duct damage, vascular endothelialitis, piecemeal necrosis, and neutrophilic infiltration are differentially expressed among LAR, recurrent HBV, and biliary complications.

reasoning.content: The histological analysis reveals distinct patterns for each cause of late allograft dysfunction. Late acute rejection is characterized by bile duct damage and vascular endothelialitis, as seen in Image 1, which are significantly more frequent in this group. Recurrent HBV hepatitis shows interface hepatitis (piecemeal necrosis), plasma cell infiltration, and portal-based inflammation with spillover into parenchyma (Image 2), aligning with its viral etiology. Biliary complications are marked by ductular proliferation (Images 3 and 4), fibrosis, cholestasis, and prominent neutrophilic infiltration, with reduced lobular activity distinguishing them from inflammatory hepatitis. Although some features like fibrosis and cholestasis are common across groups, the combination of periductal/perivascular inflammation in rejection, piecemeal necrosis in HBV recurrence, and ductular reaction with neutrophilia in biliary disease allows for differential diagnosis. The immunohistochemical confirmation of ductular structures in Image 4 strengthens the diagnosis of biliary complications.
reasoning.conclusion: Late acute cellular rejection, recurrent HBV-associated hepatitis, and biliary complications exhibit distinct histological profiles that enable differential diagnosis in late allograft dysfunction: LAR is defined by bile duct and vascular injury, recurrent HBV by interface hepatitis and piecemeal necrosis, and biliary complications by ductular proliferation, fibrosis, and neutrophilic inflammation.

question: A 67-year-old male presents with acute urinary retention and hematuria. To establish a histopathological diagnosis, a bladder tissue biopsy was obtained via cold-cup cystoscopic biopsy and processed for histological examination using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining, with sections examined under light microscopy. Additionally, immunohistochemical staining for CD44 was performed on bladder tissue sections using chromogen-based detection with hematoxylin counterstain. Based on these experimental settings and the findings observed in the tissue samples, what can be concluded regarding the underlying bladder pathology?

input_logic_chain.research_context: To establish the histopathological diagnosis of eosinophilic cystitis in a 67-year-old male presenting with acute urinary retention and hematuria, based on biopsy and immunohistochemical analysis.

experiments.experimental_setting: Bladder tissue biopsy was obtained via cold-cup cystoscopic biopsy and processed for histological examination using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining. Sections were examined under light microscopy.
experiments.experiment_goal: To identify the presence and distribution of inflammatory cell infiltration, particularly eosinophils, in the bladder wall.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: In the submucosal layer, numerous cells with bilobed nuclei and bright pink granular cytoplasm are densely infiltrated beneath the urothelium. The overlying epithelium is partially preserved, with some areas appearing thinned or disrupted. [Image 1] [Image 2]
experiments.interpretation: The bilobed nuclei and bright pink granular cytoplasm are characteristic morphological features of eosinophils under H&E staining. Their dense infiltration in the submucosa, particularly in the lamina propria, indicates transmural inflammatory involvement dominated by eosinophils.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The bladder biopsy demonstrates transmural eosinophilic infiltration, consistent with the histopathological hallmark of eosinophilic cystitis.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining for CD44 was performed on bladder tissue sections using chromogen-based detection (brown signal) with hematoxylin counterstain.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate the expression pattern of CD44 across the urothelial layers, which may reflect urothelial activation or metaplastic change in the context of chronic inflammation.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: A brown chromogenic signal is observed throughout the full thickness of the urothelium, including basal, intermediate, and superficial layers, with sharp demarcation from the unstained lamina propria. The staining is cytoplasmic and membranous, and uniformly intense. [Image 4]
experiments.interpretation: CD44 is a cell adhesion molecule often upregulated in reactive or regenerative urothelium. Its full-thickness expression suggests widespread urothelial activation or phenotypic alteration due to chronic inflammatory stimuli, supporting ongoing mucosal injury and repair in eosinophilic cystitis.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Diffuse CD44 expression across all urothelial layers indicates reactive urothelial changes secondary to chronic inflammation in eosinophilic cystitis.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The bladder biopsy demonstrates transmural eosinophilic infiltration, consistent with the histopathological hallmark of eosinophilic cystitis.
Diffuse CD44 expression across all urothelial layers indicates reactive urothelial changes secondary to chronic inflammation in eosinophilic cystitis.

reasoning.content: The diagnosis of eosinophilic cystitis requires histopathological confirmation of transmural bladder inflammation with predominant eosinophilic infiltration. The H&E-stained sections ([Image 1] and [Image 2]) reveal dense submucosal accumulation of cells with morphological features diagnostic of eosinophils—bilobed nuclei and eosinophilic granules—localized beneath a partially disrupted urothelium. This fulfills the key histological criterion for EC. Additionally, immunohistochemical analysis shows CD44 expression across the entire urothelial thickness ([Image 4]), a finding not diagnostic per se but supportive of chronic mucosal injury and regenerative response, commonly seen in inflammatory bladder conditions. Together, these findings confirm the presence of active, chronic eosinophilic inflammation affecting the bladder wall. The combination of clinical presentation (hematuria, urinary retention) and these histological findings leads to a definitive diagnosis of eosinophilic cystitis.
reasoning.conclusion: The patient has a confirmed histopathological diagnosis of eosinophilic cystitis, based on transmural eosinophilic infiltration and reactive urothelial changes demonstrated in bladder biopsy specimens.

question: A 58-year-old man was found to have a liver lesion, and the clinical concern is whether this represents metastatic thymic carcinoma. To investigate this, a liver biopsy was performed. Histological examination using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining, followed by immunohistochemical staining for multiple markers, was conducted, with a chromogen producing a dark brown precipitate at antigen-antibody binding sites and hematoxylin counterstain providing blue nuclear contrast. [Image 1] shows the histological and immunohistochemical findings in the liver biopsy. Additionally, immunohistochemical staining for specific lineage markers was performed using chromogen-based detection and microscopic evaluation. The tumor cells showed immunoreactivity for cytokeratins AE1-AE3, cytokeratins 5/6, p63, and c-Kit, but no reactivity for TTF-1, WT1, CD1a, TdT, CD5, chromogranin A, or synaptophysin. What is the most likely diagnosis of the liver lesion, and what reasoning supports this diagnosis?

input_logic_chain.research_context: Determine the histological and immunohistochemical characteristics of the liver lesion to establish whether it represents metastatic thymic carcinoma.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological examination of a liver biopsy specimen using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining, followed by immunohistochemical staining for multiple markers including cytokeratins AE1-AE3, cytokeratins 5/6, p63, c-Kit, TTF-1, WT1, CD1a, TdT, CD5, chromogranin A, and synaptophysin. The chromogen used in immunostaining produces a dark brown precipitate at the site of antigen-antibody binding, with hematoxylin counterstain providing blue nuclear contrast.
experiments.experiment_goal: To characterize the cellular morphology and protein expression profile of the tumor cells in the liver biopsy to determine histogenetic origin.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Spindle-shaped cells arranged in bundles with cigar-shaped nuclei and granular chromatin; no necrosis; mitotic rate of two mitoses per ten high-power fields; cytoplasmic brown chromogenic signal in clusters of cells with variable intensity; blue nuclear counterstain highlights nuclei within and around stained regions [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The spindle cell morphology with cigar-shaped nuclei and low mitotic activity suggests a low-grade mesenchymal or epithelial-derived neoplasm. The presence of cytokeratin and p63 positivity indicates epithelial origin with squamous differentiation. Negative neuroendocrine (chromogranin A, synaptophysin), lymphoid (CD1a, TdT, CD5), and germ cell or mesothelial (WT1, TTF-1) markers excludes alternative diagnoses.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The tumor in the liver biopsy exhibits morphological and immunophenotypic features consistent with a poorly differentiated nonkeratinizing squamous cell carcinoma of epithelial origin, showing a spindle cell pattern.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining of the liver biopsy tissue for specific lineage markers using chromogen-based detection with microscopic evaluation.
experiments.experiment_goal: To determine the immunoprofile of the tumor cells and support a diagnosis of metastatic thymic carcinoma.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Positive immunostaining for cytokeratins AE1-AE3, cytokeratins 5/6, p63, and c-Kit; negative staining for TTF-1, WT1, CD1a, TdT, CD5, chromogranin A, and synaptophysin [Context].
experiments.interpretation: The immunophenotype (CK5/6+, p63+, c-Kit+) is characteristic of thymic squamous cell carcinoma. TTF-1 negativity rules out lung primary, while absence of neuroendocrine and lymphoid markers excludes small cell carcinoma and lymphoma. c-Kit expression is frequently seen in thymic carcinomas but not in most other squamous tumors.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The immunohistochemical profile strongly supports a diagnosis of metastatic thymic carcinoma rather than a primary hepatic or pulmonary neoplasm.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The liver lesion consists of spindle-shaped epithelial tumor cells with squamous differentiation based on histomorphology and cytokeratin/p63 positivity.
The immunophenotype is specific for thymic origin, particularly given the combination of CK5/6, p63, and c-Kit positivity with exclusion of other lineages.

reasoning.content: The histological examination reveals spindle-shaped tumor cells with characteristic cigar-shaped nuclei and granular chromatin arranged in fascicles within the liver parenchyma [Image 1], a pattern sometimes seen in low-grade spindle cell variants of squamous carcinoma. The absence of necrosis and low mitotic rate further support a less aggressive histological subtype. Immunohistochemistry demonstrates epithelial differentiation via positivity for broad-spectrum cytokeratins (AE1-AE3) and CK5/6, along with squamous lineage markers p63 and c-Kit. The latter is particularly notable as it is commonly expressed in thymic carcinomas but less so in cutaneous or pulmonary squamous cell carcinomas. The negative markers rule out lung (TTF-1), neuroendocrine (chromogranin A, synaptophysin), lymphoid (CD1a, TdT, CD5), and mesothelial (WT1) origins. Together, these findings confirm that the liver lesion is not a primary hepatic tumor nor a metastasis from more common carcinomas, but instead represents a metastasis from a thymic primary.
reasoning.conclusion: The liver lesion is a metastasis from a poorly differentiated nonkeratinizing squamous cell carcinoma of thymic origin, characterized by a low-grade spindle cell morphology and a thymic-specific immunophenotype.

question: A 66-year-old man presented with pain and grouped vesicles on the left scalp and trunk, corresponding to dermatomes Lt. V1 and Lt. T8. The rash was unilateral but involved two noncontiguous dermatomes. A punch biopsy was performed on vesicular lesions from the left scalp and trunk, and the tissue sections were processed and stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) for microscopic examination. Image 2 of the histological analysis was captured at 200× magnification. Additionally, polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was performed on blood samples, and serologic testing was conducted for anti-varicella-zoster virus (VZV) IgG and IgM antibodies. The results showed positive anti-VZV IgG, negative IgM, and positive PCR. What is the most likely diagnosis, and what is the full reasoning supporting this diagnosis?

input_logic_chain.research_context: A 66-year-old man presented with pain and grouped vesicles on the left scalp and trunk (dermatomes Lt. V1 and Lt. T8), suggestive of multidermatomal herpes zoster. The clinical presentation was atypical due to involvement of two noncontiguous unilateral dermatomes. Diagnosis was confirmed through histopathological and serological evaluation.

experiments.experimental_setting: A punch biopsy was performed on vesicular lesions from the left scalp and trunk. The tissue samples were processed and stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) for microscopic examination.
experiments.experiment_goal: To identify histopathological features characteristic of herpes zoster infection in lesional skin.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Intraepidermal blisters with eosinophilic intranuclear inclusion bodies in keratinocyte nuclei, acantholytic multinucleated giant cells, basal vacuolization, necrotic epidermal cells, and lymphocytic infiltration in the upper dermis [Image 1] [Image 2]. The epidermis shows loss of intercellular cohesion and cellular disarray. Image 2 shows a denuded dermal papilla beneath the blister at 200× magnification.
experiments.interpretation: Eosinophilic intranuclear inclusion bodies (Cowdry type A) and multinucleated giant cells are hallmark cytopathic effects of herpesvirus infection, particularly varicella-zoster virus (VZV). Intraepidermal blistering results from viral-induced cell lysis and loss of intercellular adhesion (acantholysis). Basal vacuolization and necrotic keratinocytes reflect viral cytopathogenicity and apoptosis. Lymphocytic infiltration indicates host immune response to infection.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The histopathological findings are diagnostic of a herpesvirus infection, specifically consistent with herpes zoster.

experiments.experimental_setting: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was performed on blood samples, and serologic testing for anti-VZV IgG and IgM was conducted.
experiments.experiment_goal: To confirm recent or past VZV infection and distinguish between primary infection and reactivation.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: [Missing]
experiments.interpretation: Positive anti-VZV IgG with negative IgM indicates prior exposure to VZV and immune memory, consistent with viral reactivation (as in herpes zoster), rather than primary varicella infection. PCR positivity from blood may suggest viremia, supporting active viral replication.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Serological and molecular results support reactivation of latent VZV, confirming the diagnosis of herpes zoster.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: Histopathological examination reveals cytopathic changes specific to herpesvirus infection, including intranuclear inclusions and multinucleated giant cells.
Serologic profile (IgG+/IgM−) and positive PCR confirm VZV reactivation rather than primary infection.

reasoning.content: The patient presented with a vesicular rash in two noncontiguous unilateral dermatomes (Lt. V1 and Lt. T8), a rare pattern known as zoster duplex unilateralis. The histopathological analysis of skin biopsies demonstrated key diagnostic features: intraepidermal blisters, eosinophilic intranuclear inclusion bodies, acantholytic multinucleated giant cells, basal vacuolization, and dermal lymphocytic infiltration—changes classically associated with VZV infection [Image 1] [Image 2]. These morphological changes result from direct viral cytopathic effects on keratinocytes. Additionally, serology showed positive anti-VZV IgG and negative IgM, indicating past infection with reactivation, typical of herpes zoster. PCR positivity further supports active viral replication. Together, these findings confirm that the patient’s condition is due to reactivation of latent VZV affecting two noncontiguous dermatomes unilaterally.
reasoning.conclusion: The patient has zoster duplex unilateralis, confirmed by histopathological and serological evidence of VZV reactivation affecting dermatomes Lt. V1 and Lt. T8.

question:
A 45-year-old patient presents with localized sharp pain in the subungual region of the right thumb. Surgical resection of a well-circumscribed tumor is performed, and the tissue is submitted for histopathological evaluation to determine if the lesion is a benign glomus tumor. The following studies are conducted:

1. Histological examination of the tumor tissue using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining at ×200 magnification reveals round and uniform cells with abundant basophilic cytoplasm, sharply defined and angulated cellular borders, and centrally located nuclei with finely granular chromatin. The tumor cells are arranged in a compact pattern around dilated vascular channels, with minimal stromal separation. There is no evidence of necrosis or mitotic figures.

2. Immunohistochemical staining for smooth muscle antigen (SMA) is performed using chromogen-based detection at ×200 magnification.

3. Immunohistochemical staining for S-100 protein is performed at ×200 magnification.

4. Immunohistochemical staining for Ki-67 is performed at ×200 magnification to assess proliferative activity.

Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis, and how do the results support this diagnosis?

input_logic_chain.research_context: Determine the histopathological and immunohistochemical characteristics of the resected tumor to confirm its diagnosis as a benign glomus tumor.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological examination of the tumor tissue using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining at ×200 magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate the cellular morphology, architectural arrangement, and presence of vascular structures in the tumor.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The cells are round and uniform in morphology, with abundant basophilic cytoplasm and centrally located, basophilic-staining nuclei with finely granular chromatin. Cellular borders are sharply defined and angulated. Dilated vascular channels, appearing as elongated, pale-staining structures, are surrounded by tumor cells. Minimal stromal separation and absence of necrosis or mitotic figures are observed [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The round, uniform cells with abundant basophilic cytoplasm and sharply defined borders are characteristic of glomus tumor cells. The perivascular arrangement of tumor cells around dilated vascular channels supports a glomus tumor histology. The absence of necrosis and mitotic activity suggests a benign biological behavior.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The histological features observed in H&E staining are consistent with a benign glomus tumor.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining for smooth muscle antigen (SMA) using chromogen-based detection at ×200 magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess the expression of smooth muscle markers in tumor cells, which is expected in glomus tumors.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Dense cellular population with uniform golden-brown cytoplasmic staining, indicating strong and diffuse immunoreactivity for SMA. Nuclei are small and centrally located, partially obscured by cytoplasmic staining. No necrosis or hemorrhage is visible [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: The strong, diffuse cytoplasmic positivity for SMA reflects the myoepithelial differentiation of glomus tumor cells, which originate from the glomus body and express smooth muscle markers.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The tumor shows immunohistochemical evidence of smooth muscle differentiation, supporting the diagnosis of glomus tumor.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining for S-100 protein at ×200 magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To exclude neural crest-derived tumors (e.g., schwannoma or neurofibroma), which typically express S-100 protein.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: No brown chromogenic staining is observed in tumor cell nuclei or cytoplasm. Tumor cells are densely packed with uniform morphology, and the background shows minimal non-specific staining [Image 3].
experiments.interpretation: The absence of immunoreactivity for S-100 protein indicates that the tumor cells do not exhibit Schwann cell or melanocytic differentiation, helping to differentiate glomus tumor from neural tumors.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The tumor is negative for S-100 protein, supporting its distinction from neural tumors and reinforcing the diagnosis of glomus tumor.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining for Ki-67 at ×200 magnification to assess proliferative activity.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate the proliferative potential of the tumor and support benign classification.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Sparse nuclear labeling with light blue-stained nuclei showing minimal brown chromogen deposition. Most nuclei lack reactivity, and only rare positive nuclei are present. The overall staining is limited in extent and intensity [Image 4].
experiments.interpretation: The very low number of Ki-67-positive nuclei indicates minimal proliferative activity, consistent with a low mitotic rate and indolent behavior.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The Ki-67 proliferative index is less than 1.0%, confirming low cellular proliferation and supporting a benign diagnosis.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The tumor exhibits classic histological features of a glomus tumor, including uniform round cells with basophilic cytoplasm, sharply defined cellular borders, and perivascular growth pattern.
The tumor expresses smooth muscle antigen, confirming myoepithelial differentiation typical of glomus tumors.
The absence of S-100 protein expression rules out neural crest-derived tumors and supports glomus tumor diagnosis.
The very low Ki-67 labeling index indicates negligible proliferative activity, consistent with benign behavior.

reasoning.content: The integration of morphological and immunohistochemical findings provides a comprehensive diagnostic profile. The H&E-stained section reveals uniform, round tumor cells with abundant basophilic cytoplasm and sharply defined, angulated borders arranged around dilated vascular channels—hallmark features of glomus tumors. Immunohistochemistry confirms smooth muscle differentiation through strong SMA positivity, while the absence of S-100 expression excludes mimics such as schwannomas. The Ki-67 index of less than 1.0% demonstrates minimal proliferative activity, reinforcing the benign nature of the tumor. Together, these findings align with the diagnostic criteria for a benign glomus tumor.
reasoning.conclusion: The resected tumor is definitively diagnosed as a benign glomus tumor based on characteristic histomorphology, immunohistochemical profile (SMA+, S-100−), and very low proliferative index.

question: A 25-year-old woman presented with normocytic normochromic anemia and nodular splenomegaly. A bone marrow biopsy was performed to investigate the underlying cause. Histopathological analysis was conducted using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining to evaluate tissue architecture and cellular morphology. Immunohistochemical staining was performed using an antibody against CD34 to assess the immunophenotype of the observed cellular proliferation. Immunohistochemical staining for CD31 showed that the spindle cells do not express CD31. Results for CD117 (c-kit) were difficult to interpret. What can be concluded from these findings?

input_logic_chain.research_context: A 25-year-old woman presented with anemic syndrome and nodular splenomegaly. A bone marrow biopsy was performed to investigate the underlying cause of her normocytic normochromic anemia and splenic enlargement, with histopathological and immunohistochemical analyses conducted to characterize a spindle cell proliferation observed in the marrow.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histopathological analysis of a bone marrow biopsy specimen using standard hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining to assess tissue architecture, cellular morphology, and presence of abnormal proliferative processes.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate the structural and cytological features of the bone marrow, particularly to identify any abnormal cellular infiltrates or architectural disruption.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The bone marrow exhibits a 'bloody' appearance with high density of erythrocytes imparting a prominent reddish-pink staining pattern. Dense aggregation of spindle-shaped cells with elongated morphology and tapered ends is observed, arranged in interlacing fascicles and loose clusters. These cells show variation in size and shape, nuclear irregularities (including enlarged and irregular nuclei), and presence of mitotic figures with condensed chromatin and distinct chromosomal alignment. The background stroma is loosely organized with pale eosinophilic matrix [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The 'bloody' appearance suggests intramedullary hemorrhage or vascular fragility. The dense proliferation of spindle cells with nuclear atypia and mitotic activity indicates a neoplastic process. The formation of interlacing fascicles and loose clusters of atypical spindle cells disrupting normal marrow architecture is consistent with a mesenchymal or vascular tumor. Mitotic figures confirm active proliferation, supporting a malignant or aggressive biological behavior.
experiments.sub_conclusion: There is a neoplastic proliferation of atypical spindle cells within the bone marrow, exhibiting cytologic atypia and mitotic activity, disrupting normal hematopoietic tissue and suggesting a malignant vascular or stromal tumor.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining of the bone marrow biopsy using antibodies against CD34, a marker associated with hematopoietic progenitor cells and vascular endothelium, with detection via chromogenic visualization (brown precipitate).
experiments.experiment_goal: To determine the immunophenotypic profile of the spindle cell proliferation, particularly its endothelial or progenitor cell lineage.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Brown chromogenic deposition is localized primarily along vascular or sinusoidal structures and within clusters of spindle-shaped cells. These stained structures form linear or branching patterns, often outlining channel-like formations. Staining is heterogeneous, with dense aggregation in some areas and sparse or discontinuous staining in others. The background hematopoietic cells show uniformly blue counterstained nuclei [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: The brown staining indicates positive expression of CD34 in the spindle cells and vascular-like structures. The localization of CD34 to both spindle cells and endothelial-like channels suggests these cells have vascular or endothelial progenitor characteristics. The heterogeneous pattern may reflect variable antigen expression within the neoplasm or sampling heterogeneity.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The spindle cell proliferation expresses CD34, supporting a vascular or endothelial lineage differentiation and reinforcing the interpretation of a vascular neoplasm.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining for CD31, a more specific endothelial marker, to further clarify the endothelial nature of the spindle cell proliferation.
experiments.experiment_goal: To confirm or exclude a definitive endothelial differentiation of the spindle cells.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The spindle cells do not express CD31 [Context].
experiments.interpretation: CD31 is a highly specific marker for mature endothelial cells. The absence of CD31 expression, despite CD34 positivity, suggests that the spindle cells are not fully differentiated endothelial cells. This pattern is characteristic of certain vascular tumors with immature or aberrant endothelial differentiation, such as epithelioid hemangioendothelioma or other CD34+/CD31− vascular neoplasms.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The spindle cells lack CD31 expression, indicating incomplete or aberrant endothelial differentiation, which narrows the differential diagnosis to vascular tumors with immature endothelial phenotype.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining for CD117 (c-kit), a receptor tyrosine kinase expressed in various cell types including mast cells, germ cells, and some sarcomas, to assess potential diagnostic overlap with other spindle cell tumors.
experiments.experiment_goal: To rule out other spindle cell neoplasms such as gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) or mast cell disease that may express CD117.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Results for CD117 (c-kit) were difficult to interpret [Context].
experiments.interpretation: Ambiguous CD117 staining limits its utility in differential diagnosis. It neither confirms nor excludes tumors such as GIST or systemic mastocytosis. The lack of clear positivity reduces the likelihood of a c-kit-driven neoplasm but does not eliminate it entirely.
experiments.sub_conclusion: CD117 expression is inconclusive and does not contribute significantly to the diagnostic clarification in this case.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: There is a neoplastic proliferation of atypical spindle cells within the bone marrow, exhibiting cytologic atypia and mitotic activity, disrupting normal hematopoietic tissue and suggesting a malignant vascular or stromal tumor.
The spindle cell proliferation expresses CD34, supporting a vascular or endothelial lineage differentiation and reinforcing the interpretation of a vascular neoplasm.
The spindle cells lack CD31 expression, indicating incomplete or aberrant endothelial differentiation, which narrows the differential diagnosis to vascular tumors with immature endothelial phenotype.

reasoning.content: The histopathological examination reveals a densely cellular spindle cell proliferation disrupting normal bone marrow architecture, with cytologic atypia and mitotic figures, indicating a neoplastic process [Exp 0]. The formation of vascular-like slits containing erythrocytes, as described in the original text and visible in Image 1, further suggests a vascular differentiation. Immunohistochemistry shows CD34 positivity in the spindle cells and channel-like structures [Exp 1], a marker commonly expressed in vascular endothelial progenitors and certain vascular tumors. However, the absence of CD31 expression [Exp 2], a more specific endothelial marker, indicates that the cells are not mature endothelial cells. This CD34+/CD31− profile is characteristic of vascular neoplasms with incomplete endothelial differentiation, such as retiform hemangioendothelioma or early-stage angiosarcoma. The medullary location and vascular-like morphology further support this interpretation. Although CD117 results are inconclusive, they do not suggest a mast cell or GIST-like process. The combination of medullary location, vascular-like slit formation, spindle cell atypia, CD34 positivity, and CD31 negativity strongly points to a rare vascular tumor of intermediate malignancy.
reasoning.conclusion: The bone marrow lesion represents a CD34-positive, CD31-negative vascular neoplasm with incomplete endothelial differentiation, most consistent with a diagnosis of retiform hemangioendothelioma or a related CD34+/CD31− vascular tumor, warranting further biopsy for definitive classification.

question:
A 46,XY patient presents with atypical genital development, prompting investigation into disorders of sex development. To explore the genetic basis, DNA sequencing of the androgen receptor (AR) and steroid 5-alpha-reductase type 2 (SRD5A2) genes was performed using the patient’s blood sample, targeting known pathogenic variants. The analysis revealed a hemizygous variant in the AR gene (c.2324G>A) and no variant in SRD5A2. 

Histopathological examination was conducted on bilateral gonadectomy specimens obtained at 8 months of age. Tissue sections were fixed, paraffin-embedded, sectioned, and stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) for microscopic evaluation at 400x magnification. 

Additionally, genetic screening of the patient’s family was carried out. The same AR variant (c.2324G>A) was detected in the patient’s mother, who is phenotypically normal. The patient’s elder sister (46,XX) did not carry the variant. 

What can be concluded from these findings?

input_logic_chain.research_context: The patient presented with 46,XY karyotype and atypical genital development, prompting investigation into the underlying cause of androgen insensitivity and testicular pathology. Genetic and histopathological analyses were conducted to determine the diagnosis and guide clinical management.

experiments.experimental_setting: Genetic sequencing of the androgen receptor (AR) gene and steroid 5-alpha-reductase type 2 (SRD5A2) gene was performed using DNA extracted from the patient's blood sample. The analysis targeted known pathogenic variants associated with disorders of sex development.
experiments.experiment_goal: To identify pathogenic mutations in AR and SRD5A2 genes that could explain the patient's phenotype.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: [Context]: A hemizygous mutation (c.2324G>A, p.Arg775His) was identified in the AR gene. No mutation was found in SRD5A2.
experiments.interpretation: The c.2324G>A variant in AR results in a missense mutation substituting arginine for histidine at position 775, a known hotspot for androgen receptor dysfunction. This mutation impairs androgen signaling despite normal or elevated androgen levels. The absence of SRD5A2 mutation excludes 5-alpha-reductase deficiency as a cause.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The patient carries a pathogenic hemizygous mutation in the AR gene, consistent with androgen insensitivity syndrome, and no defect in dihydrotestosterone synthesis.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histopathological examination of bilateral gonadectomy specimens obtained from the patient at 8 months of age. Tissue sections were fixed, paraffin-embedded, sectioned, and stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) for microscopic evaluation at 400x magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess the structural and cellular maturation of the testicular tissue and identify any abnormalities in seminiferous tubules and interstitial components.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Densely packed seminiferous tubules, each outlined by a thin basement membrane and lined with a single layer of Sertoli cells. Lumina within the tubules are indistinct and show scant to absent luminal space. Tubular epithelium contains germ cells at various stages of development, mostly immature and arrested at an early stage. Nuclear size, shape, and chromatin texture are relatively uniform. Cytoplasmic boundaries of germ cells are poorly defined. Interstitial stroma is sparse with occasional clusters of non-hypertrophied Leydig cells. No spermatozoa or advanced germ cell differentiation are evident. [Image 1]
experiments.interpretation: The absence of luminal development and stratified germ cell layers indicates failure of tubular maturation. The uniform nuclear appearance and lack of spermatocytes or spermatozoa reflect germ cell maturation arrest, a hallmark of impaired androgen signaling during testicular development. Sparse Leydig cells without hyperplasia suggest normal or near-normal testosterone production but ineffective end-organ response.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The histopathology demonstrates immature testicular architecture with germ cell maturation arrest, consistent with disrupted androgen action during development.

experiments.experimental_setting: Same as previous histopathological examination, using H&E-stained sections of gonadal tissue at 400x magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To confirm the absence of mature spermatogenesis and evaluate interstitial composition.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Multiple small, irregularly shaped seminiferous tubules with poorly defined or collapsed luminal spaces. Tubules are lined by epithelial cells with round to oval, closely packed nuclei and minimal cytoplasm. No mature germ cells or recognizable stages of spermatogenesis are present. Interstitial spaces contain fibrous stroma, scattered stromal cells, and occasional small blood vessels. No prominent Leydig cell clusters or inflammatory infiltrate. Strong contrast between basophilic nuclei and eosinophilic components. [Image 2]
experiments.interpretation: The collapsed tubular lumina and monotonous germ cell population indicate early developmental arrest, likely before the onset of true spermatogenesis. The lack of cellular diversity and structural complexity reflects failure of androgen-dependent tubular expansion and germ cell differentiation. The fibrous stroma may represent developmental immaturity or reactive change due to hormonal imbalance.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The histological findings confirm a lack of testicular maturation and absence of spermatogenic progression, further supporting defective androgen signaling.

experiments.experimental_setting: Family genetic screening was conducted using DNA sequencing of the AR gene in the patient’s mother and elder sister. The mother and sister were clinically asymptomatic and had normal external genitalia.
experiments.experiment_goal: To determine carrier status and inheritance pattern of the AR mutation for genetic counseling.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: [Context]: The same AR mutation (c.2324G>A) was found in the child's mother (heterozygous carrier). The elder sister (46,XX) did not carry the mutation.
experiments.interpretation: The presence of the mutation in the mother confirms X-linked recessive inheritance, typical of AR-related disorders. As a heterozygous female, she has one functional AR allele, sufficient for normal female development and lack of clinical symptoms. The sister, lacking the mutation, is not at risk of transmitting it.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The mutation follows an X-linked recessive inheritance pattern, with the mother as a carrier and the sister unaffected and non-carrier.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The patient has a pathogenic hemizygous mutation in the AR gene, leading to impaired androgen receptor function.
Histopathological examination reveals immature testicular tissue with germ cell maturation arrest and absent luminal development, indicative of failed androgen-dependent testicular maturation.
The AR mutation is inherited in an X-linked recessive manner, with the mother confirmed as a carrier.

reasoning.content: The patient, with a 46,XY karyotype, has a hemizygous AR mutation (c.2324G>A, p.Arg775His), which disrupts androgen signaling essential for male phenotypic development and testicular maturation. The absence of SRD5A2 mutation excludes alternative causes of undervirilization. Histopathological analysis of the gonads shows seminiferous tubules with indistinct lumina, densely packed immature germ cells, and absence of spermatozoa—findings characteristic of arrested testicular development due to androgen resistance. These structural abnormalities, including lack of tubular maturation and germ cell differentiation, are direct consequences of non-functional androgen receptors, preventing normal androgen-driven spermatogenesis and ductal development. The familial segregation of the mutation—present in the mother (heterozygous) and absent in the sister—confirms X-linked recessive inheritance, typical of complete androgen insensitivity syndrome (CAIS). Together, the genetic and histological evidence confirm that the patient has CAIS, explaining the female external phenotype despite the presence of testes and normal male karyotype.
