No caseation is observed. [Image 1]
experiments.interpretation: The presence of non-caseating granulomas composed of epithelioid histiocytes, multinucleated giant cells, and a surrounding lymphocytic cuff is characteristic of sarcoidosis. The portal tract localization is consistent with hepatic sarcoidosis, which typically affects portal areas.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The liver biopsy demonstrates histological evidence of non-caseating granulomatous inflammation consistent with sarcoidosis.

experiments.experimental_setting: Liver tissue section stained with H&E, examined at 200× magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess structural changes in the liver parenchyma suggestive of chronic venous outflow obstruction and fibrotic remodeling.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Heterogeneous liver architecture with focal hepatocyte atrophy, irregular hepatocellular nodules, fibrous septa traversing the parenchyma, inflammatory cell infiltration within septa, and entrapped regenerative hepatocellular plates (indicated by white arrow). [Image 2]
experiments.interpretation: Architectural distortion with fibrous septa, nodular regeneration, and hepatocyte atrophy indicates chronic parenchymal damage and fibrotic remodeling. The presence of regenerative nodules within fibrous septa suggests long-standing vascular insult, consistent with chronic hepatic venous outflow obstruction as seen in BCS.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The liver biopsy reveals structural changes consistent with chronic venous congestion and fibrosis, supporting a diagnosis of chronic Budd-Chiari syndrome.

experiments.experimental_setting: Abdominal ultrasound with Doppler and abdominal computed tomography (CT) scan.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate hepatic vascular anatomy and detect signs of hepatic venous outflow obstruction.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Hepatomegaly with caudate lobe hypertrophy, splenomegaly, portosystemic collateral circulation, and failure to visualize supra-hepatic veins. CT confirms absence of hepatic veins and multinodular liver contour. [Context]
experiments.interpretation: Caudate lobe hypertrophy and collateral circulation are compensatory responses to hepatic venous outflow obstruction. The inability to visualize hepatic veins bilaterally on imaging is diagnostic of BCS, particularly in its chronic form.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Radiological findings confirm chronic Budd-Chiari syndrome with complete or near-complete occlusion of hepatic veins.

experiments.experimental_setting: Skin lesion biopsy and gastric mucosal biopsy, both stained with H&E.
experiments.experiment_goal: To determine if granulomatous inflammation extends beyond the liver, supporting a systemic granulomatous disease.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Non-caseating granulomas identified in both skin and gastric mucosa biopsies. [Context]
experiments.interpretation: Extrahepatic granulomas in the skin (with predilection for scars and trauma sites) and gastric mucosa confirm systemic involvement, which is highly characteristic of sarcoidosis rather than isolated organ disease.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Multisystem granulomatous involvement of skin, gastric mucosa, and liver supports a diagnosis of systemic sarcoidosis.

experiments.experimental_setting: Laboratory testing including serum angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) level, tuberculin skin test, and bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL).
experiments.experiment_goal: To differentiate sarcoidosis from other granulomatous diseases, particularly tuberculosis.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: [Missing]
experiments.interpretation: Elevated serum ACE (201 U/L, normal 12–68) supports active sarcoidosis. Negative tuberculin test and absence of acid-fast bacilli in BAL exclude tuberculosis as the cause of granulomas.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Biochemical and microbiological findings support sarcoidosis and rule out infectious mimics.

experiments.experimental_setting: Screening for thrombophilic disorders including JAK2 mutation, antiphospholipid antibodies, factor V Leiden, protein C/S and antithrombin deficiency, homocysteinemia, and bone marrow examination.
experiments.experiment_goal: To determine whether an underlying prothrombotic condition contributed to BCS.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: [Missing]
experiments.interpretation: Absence of identifiable thrombophilia suggests that BCS is not due to a primary hypercoagulable state but is instead secondary to another process, such as inflammatory vascular compromise.
experiments.sub_conclusion: No underlying thrombophilic disorder was found, implicating sarcoidosis-related mechanisms as the likely cause of BCS.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The liver biopsy shows non-caseating granulomas in portal tracts, diagnostic of hepatic sarcoidosis.
Histopathological evidence of fibrous septa, nodular regeneration, and atrophy indicates chronic hepatic venous outflow obstruction consistent with BCS.
Radiological imaging confirms chronic BCS with absence of hepatic veins and portosystemic collaterals.
Systemic granulomatous involvement of skin, stomach, and lymph nodes confirms multisystemic sarcoidosis.
Elevated ACE and exclusion of tuberculosis support sarcoidosis as the underlying granulomatous disease.
Absence of thrombophilia suggests BCS is secondary to sarcoidosis rather than a primary clotting disorder.

reasoning.content: The patient presented with chronic anicteric cholestasis, hepatosplenomegaly, and radiological findings of hepatic vein occlusion, fulfilling diagnostic criteria for Budd-Chiari syndrome. Histopathological examination of the liver revealed two key findings: (1) non-caseating granulomas in portal tracts ([Image 1]), diagnostic of sarcoidosis, and (2) fibrous septa with nodular regeneration and atrophy ([Image 2]), indicative of chronic venous outflow obstruction. These findings, combined with imaging evidence of absent hepatic veins and collateral circulation, establish BCS as a complication of underlying liver disease. The presence of granulomas in skin and gastric biopsies confirms systemic sarcoidosis. Elevated ACE and exclusion of infections and thrombophilias rule out alternative diagnoses. Therefore, BCS in this case is not due to a primary thrombotic disorder but is a consequence of granulomatous inflammation involving or compressing hepatic veins, leading to venous stasis and thrombosis. This represents a rare multisystem manifestation of sarcoidosis where hepatic granulomatous inflammation directly contributes to vascular occlusion.
reasoning.conclusion: This case represents multisystemic sarcoidosis complicated by Budd-Chiari syndrome, where granulomatous inflammation is the likely etiology of hepatic venous occlusion in the absence of thrombophilia, confirmed by histopathological, radiological, and clinical evidence.

question: A 35-year-old male presents with cervical lymphadenopathy, prolonged fever, night sweats, and weight loss, in the setting of febrile neutropenia. Initial infectious and autoimmune workups are negative, and a core needle biopsy is nondiagnostic. An excisional lymph node biopsy is performed. Immunohistochemical staining of the lymph node tissue is carried out using a CD68 antibody with chromogenic detection and viewed under light microscopy. A second immunohistochemical stain is performed on the same tissue using a CD123 antibody with chromogenic detection and viewed under light microscopy. Additional immunohistochemical analysis is conducted for CD3, CD4, CD8, CD20, myeloperoxidase, and viral pathogens (CMV and SARS-CoV-2), revealing that lymphocytes are predominantly CD3-positive with CD8-positive T cells exceeding CD4-positive T cells, very few CD20-positive B cells, histiocytes positive for myeloperoxidase, and negative immunostains for CMV and SARS-CoV-2. Microbiological analysis of the lymph node tissue, including aerobic/anaerobic bacterial culture, fungal culture, and acid-fast bacilli culture, shows no microbial growth. Serological testing for HIV, syphilis, parvovirus, mononucleosis, CMV, adenovirus, toxoplasmosis, and Bartonella is negative, and blood cultures for bacteria, fungi, and acid-fast bacilli show no growth. Autoimmune serology, including anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith antibodies, is negative. A nasopharyngeal SARS-CoV-2 PCR test performed at the time of biopsy is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis, and how do the histopathological, immunophenotypic, microbiological, and serological findings collectively support this diagnosis?

input_logic_chain.research_context: Evaluation of lymph node histopathology to determine the underlying cause of cervical lymphadenopathy and systemic symptoms in a patient with febrile neutropenia and negative infectious and autoimmune workup.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining of excised lymph node tissue with CD68 antibody using chromogenic detection, viewed under light microscopy.
experiments.experiment_goal: To identify the presence and distribution of histiocytes within the lymph node.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Diffuse distribution of brown chromogenic signal localized within discrete, round to oval cells with distinct cytoplasmic reactivity; cells vary in size and shape, appear in clusters and scattered foci; background is lightly counterstained with pale granular and faint blue areas; no lymphoid follicles or sinuses visible [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The brown chromogenic signal indicates CD68 expression, a marker specific for histiocytes and macrophages. The cytoplasmic localization confirms cellular identity. The clustering and diffuse pattern suggest active histiocytic infiltration in the absence of normal lymphoid architecture.
experiments.sub_conclusion: There is a prominent infiltration of CD68-positive histiocytes in the lymph node, consistent with histiocytic-rich inflammation.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining of the same lymph node tissue with CD123 antibody using chromogenic detection, viewed at 100x magnification under light microscopy.
experiments.experiment_goal: To detect plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs), which are characteristically involved in Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Heterogeneous distribution of brown to brownish-red signal in discrete clusters and scattered individual cells; variable density across the field; stained cells not fully morphologically resolved; background is pale, granular, faintly eosinophilic with areas of pale blue hue; no lymphoid follicles or sinuses evident [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: CD123 is a marker for plasmacytoid dendritic cells. The presence of CD123-positive cells in clusters and scattered foci, particularly in a histiocytic-rich inflammatory background, supports the recruitment of pDCs, which are known to play a role in the immunopathogenesis of Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Plasmacytoid dendritic cells are present in the lymph node infiltrate, supporting an immune-mediated, non-malignant process typical of Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical assessment of lymph node tissue for lymphocyte subsets using CD3, CD4, CD8, and CD20 antibodies; additional stains for myeloperoxidase and viral pathogens (CMV, SARS-CoV-2).
experiments.experiment_goal: To characterize the lymphocyte composition and rule out infectious causes or myeloid malignancy.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Lymphocytes are predominantly CD3-positive; CD8-positive T cells exceed CD4-positive T cells; very few CD20-positive B cells; histiocytes are positive for myeloperoxidase, CD68, and CD4; CMV and SARS-CoV-2 immunohistochemical stains are negative [Context].
experiments.interpretation: The T-cell predominance with CD8 > CD4 skewing and paucity of B cells is a hallmark of the cytotoxic T-cell-driven immune response in Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease. Myeloperoxidase positivity in histiocytes confirms their myeloid origin. Negative viral stains rule out active CMV or SARS-CoV-2 infection in the node despite systemic SARS-CoV-2 PCR positivity.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The immune cell profile supports a benign, self-limited lymphadenitis with cytotoxic T-cell and histiocytic infiltration, not attributable to active viral infection in the node.

experiments.experimental_setting: Microbiological analysis of lymph node tissue, including aerobic/anaerobic bacterial culture, fungal culture, and acid-fast bacilli (AFB) culture.
experiments.experiment_goal: To exclude infectious etiologies such as tuberculosis, fungal infection, or bacterial abscess.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: No microbial growth reported in cultures; no organisms seen on histological stains [Missing].
experiments.interpretation: The absence of microbial growth in tissue cultures indicates no active bacterial, fungal, or mycobacterial infection in the lymph node.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Infectious causes of necrotizing lymphadenitis, such as tuberculosis or pyogenic abscess, are ruled out.

experiments.experimental_setting: Serological and blood-based infectious disease testing, including HIV, syphilis, parvovirus, mononucleosis, CMV, adenovirus, toxoplasmosis, Bartonella, and blood cultures for bacteria, fungi, and AFB.
experiments.experiment_goal: To exclude systemic infectious causes of lymphadenopathy and febrile illness.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: All serological tests negative; no growth in blood cultures [Context].
experiments.interpretation: The extensive negative infectious workup reduces the likelihood of common or opportunistic infections causing the clinical presentation.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Systemic infectious etiologies are unlikely contributors to the lymphadenopathy and fever.

experiments.experimental_setting: Autoimmune serology panel including anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith antibodies.
experiments.experiment_goal: To exclude systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), which can mimic Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease histologically.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith antibodies are negative [Context].
experiments.interpretation: Negative autoantibodies reduce the likelihood of SLE, which can present with necrotizing lymphadenitis and must be differentiated from Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Autoimmune etiology, particularly SLE, is unlikely.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The lymph node shows histiocytic and plasmacytoid dendritic cell infiltration with T-cell predominance and absence of B cells.
No evidence of infectious agents in blood or tissue supports a non-infectious inflammatory process.
Absence of autoimmune markers rules out SLE as a mimic.

reasoning.content: The histopathological findings demonstrate a necrotizing lymphadenitis characterized by CD68-positive histiocytes and CD123-positive plasmacytoid dendritic cells, which are hallmark features of Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease. The T-cell infiltrate with CD8 > CD4 skewing and minimal B cells further supports this diagnosis. Despite a positive SARS-CoV-2 PCR in the nasopharynx, the lymph node shows no evidence of viral cytopathic effect or positive immunostaining for SARS-CoV-2 or CMV, and tissue cultures are sterile, ruling out an infectious cause. The negative autoimmune panel excludes lupus lymphadenitis as a differential. The clinical response to corticosteroids with resolution of fever and symptoms further confirms the diagnosis, as Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease is typically self-limited and responsive to anti-inflammatory treatment.
reasoning.conclusion: The histopathological, immunophenotypic, and clinical findings are consistent with a diagnosis of Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease, a benign, self-limited necrotizing lymphadenitis of unknown etiology, likely triggered by a post-viral immune response in this SARS-CoV-2-positive patient.

question:
A two-month-old male presents with a firm postauricular mass present since birth, which has shown rapid regrowth despite multiple en bloc resections, including a full-thickness craniectomy. To determine whether the histological and immunohistochemical features of the resected tumor are consistent with melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy (MNTI), the following studies were performed:

1. Histological examination of the tumor tissue was conducted using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining, with sections viewed at 10x magnification.

2. Immunohistochemical staining was performed using chromogen-based detection to evaluate CD99 expression, visualized under light microscopy.

3. A comprehensive immunohistochemical panel was analyzed, revealing the following results: the large epithelioid cells are positive for cytokeratin, HMB45, and vimentin; the small round cells are positive for synaptophysin and GFAP; both cell populations are negative for chromogranin A and neurofilaments; Ki-67 shows low proliferative activity; and CD99 is positive in a subset of tumor cells, particularly in larger, pigment-containing cells.

Based on these findings, what can be concluded regarding the diagnosis and biological behavior of the tumor?

experiments.interpretation: The spindle-shaped cells with fusiform nuclei represent a mesenchymal or stromal component, while the smaller, round blue cells with hyperchromatic and fragmented-appearing nuclei are consistent with a primitive neuroectodermal cell population. The presence of two distinct cell types within a fibrous matrix aligns with the known biphasic histology of MNTI.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The H&E-stained section demonstrates a biphasic cellular population composed of spindle-shaped stromal cells and small round blue cells, morphologically consistent with MNTI [Image 1].

experiments.sub_conclusion: Immunohistochemical staining reveals CD99 positivity in a subset of tumor cells, including larger pigment-containing cells, suggesting aberrant expression that may correlate with aggressive clinical behavior [Image 2].

CD99 positivity, while atypical, is noted and may indicate increased proliferative potential.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The immunohistochemical profile is consistent with classic MNTI, with the exception of CD99 positivity, which may explain the tumor's recalcitrant and recurrent behavior.

reasoning.content: The histological evaluation reveals a biphasic tumor composed of spindle-shaped stromal cells and small round blue cells with hyperchromatic nuclei, a key morphological feature of MNTI. This is supported by immunohistochemical findings showing expression of epithelial (cytokeratin), melanocytic (HMB45), mesenchymal (vimentin), and neuroectodermal (synaptophysin, GFAP) markers in the respective cell populations—consistent with the dual differentiation seen in MNTI. Although MNTI is typically CD99-negative, the observed CD99 positivity in this case, particularly in pigment-containing cells, deviates from the norm. Given that CD99 expression has been associated with more aggressive tumor behavior in prior literature, this aberrant marker expression likely contributed to the tumor's resistance to complete surgical clearance and its rapid recurrence despite en bloc resection and craniectomy. The combination of classic histomorphology and immunoprofile—except for CD99—confirms the diagnosis of MNTI, while the atypical CD99 positivity provides a plausible biological explanation for the clinical aggressiveness.

question: A 22-year-old male presents with a progressively enlarging, ulcerated, subcutaneous nodule in the right thigh. The lesion arises in continuity with a nerve and shows focal epidermal ulceration, with preservation of native adnexal structures. Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) staining of the tissue section reveals a densely cellular tumor beneath the epidermis, with irregularly distributed dark pigmented granules. The tumor cells are arranged in fascicles and theques with nuclear palisading, and include large ganglion-like cells with abundant pigment-laden cytoplasm and vesicular nuclei. No mitotic figures, necrosis, or Verocay bodies are identified. Special staining after depigmentation shows positive reaction with Masson-Fontana stain and negative reactions with Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS) and iron stains. Immunohistochemical analysis demonstrates diffuse cytoplasmic positivity for S-100, HMB-45, and Melan-A in both spindle and ganglion-like cells, with no reactivity for cytokeratin or epithelial membrane antigen. Reticulin and laminin immunostaining reveal a biphasic pattern with prominent pericellular deposition around individual tumor cells. On assessment of tumor margins, small tongue-like projections of tumor cells are observed invading the surrounding soft tissues, and the lesion is unencapsulated. What is the most appropriate diagnosis, and how do these findings collectively support this diagnosis?

input_logic_chain.research_context: Differentiation of melanocytic schwannoma from malignant melanoma in a cutaneous/subcutaneous pigmented lesion based on histopathological and immunohistochemical features.

experiments.experimental_setting: Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) staining of a tissue section from a subcutaneous nodule in the thigh.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate the architectural and cytological features of the pigmented tumor.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: A densely cellular tumor beneath the epidermis shows irregularly distributed dark pigmented granules; tumor cells are arranged in fascicles and theques with nuclear palisading; large ganglion-like cells with abundant pigment-laden cytoplasm and vesicular nuclei are present; native adnexal structures are preserved; no mitoses, necrosis, or Verocay bodies are seen [Image 1, Image 2, Image 3, Image 5].
experiments.interpretation: The presence of pigmented spindle and ganglion-like cells arranged in fascicles and theques with nuclear palisading, arising in continuity with a nerve, supports schwannian differentiation. Lack of mitotic activity and necrosis argues against high-grade malignancy. Preservation of adnexal structures and origin from a nerve suggest a neural sheath tumor rather than a primary epidermal melanocytic lesion.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The tumor exhibits histological features consistent with a neural crest-derived neoplasm showing schwannian architecture and melanocytic differentiation, but lacks features of aggressive melanoma.

experiments.experimental_setting: Special staining with Masson-Fontana (MF), Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS), and iron stains on depigmented tissue sections.
experiments.experiment_goal: To determine the chemical nature of the intracellular pigment.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Positive staining with Masson-Fontana (black granular signal) and negative staining with PAS and iron stains [Context].
experiments.interpretation: Masson-Fontana positivity confirms the presence of melanin, while PAS and iron negativity rules out lipofuscin or hemosiderin as the source of pigmentation.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The pigment within the tumor cells is melanin, confirming melanocytic differentiation.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining for S-100, HMB-45, Melan-A, cytokeratin (CK), and epithelial membrane antigen (EMA) on depigmented sections.
experiments.experiment_goal: To identify the immunophenotypic profile of the tumor cells and differentiate from other pigmented lesions.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Diffuse cytoplasmic positivity for S-100, HMB-45, and Melan-A in spindle and ganglion-like cells; negativity for CK and EMA [Image 6, Image 7].
experiments.interpretation: S-100, HMB-45, and Melan-A positivity supports melanocytic lineage. S-100 positivity also supports schwannian differentiation. Absence of epithelial markers rules out carcinoma.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The tumor has a dual immunophenotype consistent with both melanocytic and schwannian differentiation.

experiments.experimental_setting: Reticulin and laminin immunostaining on tissue sections.
experiments.experiment_goal: To distinguish melanocytic schwannoma from malignant melanoma based on extracellular matrix deposition patterns.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Biphasic staining pattern with prominent pericellular reticulin and laminin deposition around individual tumor cells [Context].
experiments.interpretation: Pericellular reticulin and laminin staining is characteristic of schwannomas, where basement membrane material is produced by Schwann cells. In contrast, malignant melanoma typically shows reticulin around nests of cells, not individual cells.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The pericellular basement membrane pattern supports a diagnosis of schwannoma rather than melanoma.

experiments.experimental_setting: Assessment of tumor margins and invasion on H&E-stained sections.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate local aggressiveness and potential for recurrence.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Small tongue-like projections of tumor cells into surrounding soft tissues; no encapsulation; focal ulceration of overlying epidermis [Image 1b, Image 1a].
experiments.interpretation: The tumor exhibits infiltrative growth and skin ulceration, indicating locally aggressive behavior despite lack of cytologic atypia or mitoses.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The tumor shows features of local invasiveness, warranting close follow-up.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The tumor shows histological features of neural sheath origin with melanocytic pigmentation and lacks cytologic atypia or mitotic activity.
The pigment is confirmed as melanin, not lipofuscin or hemosiderin.
The immunophenotype supports dual differentiation: melanocytic (HMB-45+, Melan-A+) and schwannian (S-100+, pericellular reticulin/laminin+).
The pericellular basement membrane pattern distinguishes this lesion from malignant melanoma.
The tumor exhibits local invasiveness and ulceration, indicating potential for recurrence despite benign cytology.

reasoning.content: The lesion arises in the subcutaneous tissue of the thigh, is heavily pigmented, and shows spindle and ganglion-like cells arranged in fascicles and theques with nuclear palisading—architectural hallmarks of schwannian differentiation. The absence of Verocay bodies and microcysts does not exclude schwannoma, as these are rare in melanocytic variants. The pigment is confirmed as melanin by Masson-Fontana positivity and absence of PAS/iron staining, ruling out lipofuscin seen in conventional pigmented schwannomas. Immunohistochemistry confirms melanocytic markers (HMB-45, Melan-A) and schwannian markers (S-100), while reticulin and laminin staining show pericellular deposition—distinct from the perinest reticulin pattern in melanoma. This pattern, combined with origin from a nerve, absence of junctional activity, and lack of cytologic atypia, supports melanocytic schwannoma over malignant melanoma. Although the tumor lacks mitoses and necrosis, its infiltrative growth and ulceration suggest locally aggressive behavior. The absence of psammoma bodies, adipose tissue, and systemic findings rules out Carney syndrome. Thus, the lesion is classified as a non-psammomatous melanocytic schwannoma with locally invasive features.
reasoning.conclusion: The subcutaneous pigmented tumor is diagnosed as a non-psammomatous melanocytic schwannoma based on histomorphology, melanin pigment confirmation, dual immunophenotype, pericellular basement membrane deposition, and nerve origin, with local invasiveness necessitating close follow-up.

question:
A 62-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with vaginal bleeding. Imaging reveals a subserosal fibroid and omental nodules. She undergoes abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and excision of omental nodules. Gross pathological examination of the hysterectomy specimen reveals a fleshy mass distorting the uterine cavity with invasion extending to the serosal surface, areas of necrosis, and omental nodules containing hemorrhagic, necrotic fleshy tissue; the tubes, ovaries, and cervix appear uninvolved. Histopathological examination is performed using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining at multiple magnifications (100×, 200×, 400×), focusing on glandular architecture and stromal characteristics. Additional microscopic evaluation is conducted to assess for heterologous elements and extrauterine involvement. Focal areas within the tumor show bony tissue, malignant cartilage, and skeletal muscle. The omental tissue is infiltrated by high-grade spindle cell sarcoma with morphology similar to the uterine tumor.

Based on these findings, what is the most appropriate histopathological diagnosis, and how is it supported by the integrated analysis of the gross and microscopic features?

experiments.experiment_goal: To characterize the histological architecture and cellular features of the tumor, particularly the relationship between epithelial and stromal components, stromal cellularity, and evidence of sarcomatous differentiation.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Phyllodes-like architecture with broad, leaf-like projections composed of cellular stroma containing compressed glands lined by benign cuboidal epithelium; stroma shows variable cellularity with fibrous and loose areas; glandular spaces contain eosinophilic material or are empty; epithelial lining is thin and discontinuous [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The leaf-like architecture with compressed glands surrounded by cellular stroma is characteristic of mullerian adenosarcoma. The benign appearance of the epithelium contrasts with the atypical stroma, indicating a biphasic tumor with malignant stromal component.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The histological architecture supports a diagnosis of mullerian adenosarcoma due to the presence of phyllodes-like structures with benign epithelium and neoplastic stroma.

experiments.experimental_setting: High-power microscopic examination (H&E, ×200) of the periglandular stroma in the uterine mass.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess the degree of stromal cellularity and its spatial relationship with glandular structures.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Dense, hypercellular stroma with closely packed spindle-shaped or ovoid cells forming distinct periglandular cuffs around irregular, slit-like glandular lumens; nuclei show variable chromatin intensity; high nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: Periglandular stromal cuffing with increased cellularity indicates active stromal proliferation around residual glands. This is a hallmark of adenosarcoma and reflects the neoplastic nature of the stromal component.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The presence of hypercellular periglandular stroma confirms the stromal neoplasia characteristic of mullerian adenosarcoma.

experiments.experimental_setting: High-magnification histopathological analysis (H&E, 400×) of areas with highest stromal cellularity in the uterine mass.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate for high-grade sarcomatous overgrowth, including nuclear atypia, mitotic activity, and architectural disarray.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Dense, disorganized spindle cells arranged in haphazard fascicles and whorls; marked nuclear pleomorphism, hyperchromasia, irregular nuclear contours, and prominent nucleoli; multiple mitotic figures including those with spindle apparatus [Image 3].
experiments.interpretation: The disorganized growth pattern, nuclear pleomorphism, and high mitotic rate (>10/10 HPF) are diagnostic of a high-grade sarcoma. This represents sarcomatous overgrowth within the adenosarcoma.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The high-grade spindle cell sarcoma component confirms the presence of sarcomatous overgrowth, a feature associated with aggressive behavior in mullerian adenosarcoma.

experiments.experimental_setting: Microscopic evaluation of tumor sections for heterologous elements and extrauterine involvement.
experiments.experiment_goal: To identify the presence of non-mullerian tissue types and metastatic spread to the omentum.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Focal areas showing bony tissue, malignant cartilage, and skeletal muscle within the tumor mass [Context]; omental tissue infiltrated by high-grade spindle cell sarcoma with similar morphology to the uterine tumor [Context].
experiments.interpretation: The presence of bone, cartilage, and skeletal muscle indicates heterologous differentiation, typical of heterologous mullerian adenosarcoma. Omental involvement by identical sarcomatous tissue confirms peritoneal dissemination.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The tumor is a heterologous mullerian adenosarcoma with sarcomatous overgrowth and omental metastasis.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The tumor exhibits biphasic morphology with benign epithelium and malignant stroma, consistent with mullerian adenosarcoma.
The stroma shows progressive hypercellularity and periglandular condensation, reinforcing the neoplastic nature of the mesenchymal component.
A high-grade sarcomatous component with pleomorphism and elevated mitotic activity is present, meeting criteria for sarcomatous overgrowth.
The presence of bone, cartilage, and skeletal muscle confirms heterologous differentiation, and omental involvement indicates metastatic spread.

reasoning.content: The gross findings reveal a fleshy, necrotic uterine mass with deep myometrial invasion and omental deposits, indicating aggressive local and disseminated disease. Histologically, the tumor displays classic phyllodes-like architecture with benign epithelium overlying neoplastic stroma, diagnostic of mullerian adenosarcoma. The stroma is hypercellular with periglandular cuffing, and in areas, transitions into a high-grade spindle cell sarcoma with marked pleomorphism, frequent mitoses, and architectural disarray—features defining sarcomatous overgrowth. The identification of heterologous elements (bone, cartilage, skeletal muscle) confirms the subtype as heterologous. The omental nodules contain identical high-grade sarcoma, confirming peritoneal metastasis. Together, these findings fulfill the diagnostic criteria for heterologous mullerian adenosarcoma with sarcomatous overgrowth, deep myometrial invasion, and omental dissemination.
reasoning.conclusion: The final histopathological diagnosis is heterologous mullerian adenosarcoma with sarcomatous overgrowth, characterized by deep myometrial invasion and omental metastasis of the sarcomatous component, indicating high-risk disease with poor prognostic features.

question:
To determine the nature and cause of acute kidney injury (AKI) in a patient with hemorrhagic complications following a renal biopsy, the following studies were performed:

- A kidney biopsy specimen was stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and imaged at ×400 magnification.
- A kidney biopsy specimen was stained with H&E and imaged at ×200 magnification.
- A kidney biopsy specimen was stained with Hall's stain for bile and imaged at ×200 magnification.
- Immunofluorescence microscopy was performed for immunoglobulins (IgG, IgA, IgM), complement components (C3, C1q), and fibrinogen.
  - No specific staining was observed for IgG, IgA, IgM, C1q, C3, or fibrinogen.
- Ultrastructural examination was performed using electron microscopy on kidney biopsy tissue.
  - Moderately electron-dense inclusions were observed within proximal tubular epithelial cells. Adjacent mitochondria appeared enlarged and disorganized. Highly electron-dense particles and filamentous material were present in tubular lumina.
- Examination of the nephrectomy specimen was performed using H&E and Hall's staining.
  - Diffuse tubular epithelial necrosis and sloughing were observed, with numerous granular red and green-brown pigmented casts, particularly abundant in distal tubules and medullary collecting ducts. Hall's stain showed positive staining of the casts.

Based on these findings, what is the most likely nature and cause of the patient's acute kidney injury, and how do the experimental observations support this conclusion?

input_logic_chain.research_context: To determine the nature and cause of acute kidney injury (AKI) in a patient with hemorrhagic complications following a renal biopsy, including histopathological and ultrastructural analysis of kidney tissue.

experiments.experimental_setting: Kidney biopsy specimen stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E), imaged at ×400 magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate the presence and characteristics of pigmented material in renal tubules and tubular epithelial cells.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Intraluminal granular casts with distinct red pigmentation are visible within renal tubular structures, indicated by black arrows. Green-brown pigment is present within tubular epithelial cells, appearing finely dispersed in the cytoplasm, highlighted by yellow arrows. Tubular epithelial cells show pyknotic nuclei and dense packing. Interstitial spaces contain scattered inflammatory cells [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The red pigmentation in tubular lumens suggests the presence of hemoglobin- or myoglobin-derived pigments, while the green-brown cytoplasmic pigment is characteristic of bile pigment (bilirubin or biliverdin) deposition within tubular cells.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Pigmented casts and intracellular pigment inclusions are present in renal tubules, with visual features suggestive of both hemorrhagic and cholestatic processes.

experiments.experimental_setting: Kidney biopsy specimen stained with H&E, imaged at ×200 magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess the extent of tubular damage and the nature of sloughed cellular debris.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Renal tubules show disrupted epithelial architecture with numerous sloughed epithelial cells in the lumens, highlighted by arrows. These cells exhibit intense dark red-green discoloration. Tubular cells display cytoplasmic eosinophilia and pyknotic or fragmented nuclei. Basement membranes are partially denuded and irregular. Some tubules are dilated, others collapsed. Interstitium shows edema and scattered inflammatory cells [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: The presence of sloughed, discolored epithelial cells and denuded basement membranes indicates severe acute tubular necrosis (ATN). The dark red-green discoloration of cells is consistent with intracellular accumulation of bile pigments.
experiments.sub_conclusion: There is diffuse, severe acute tubular necrosis with pigment-laden sloughed cells, supporting a diagnosis of pigment-induced tubular injury.

experiments.experimental_setting: Kidney biopsy specimen stained with Hall's stain for bile, imaged at ×200 magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To confirm the presence of bile pigment in intraluminal casts.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: A distinct green-stained structure is present within the lumen of a renal tubule, highlighted by a black arrow. The deposit is irregular and granular, with consistent green coloration contrasting against lightly stained surrounding tissue. No green staining is seen in adjacent tubules or parenchyma [Image 3].
experiments.interpretation: Hall's stain specifically detects bile pigments, and the green coloration confirms the presence of bile in the intraluminal casts.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Bile pigment is present in the tubular lumens, confirming bile cast nephropathy.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunofluorescence microscopy for immunoglobulins (IgG, IgA, IgM), complement components (C3, C1q), and fibrinogen.
experiments.experiment_goal: To rule out immune complex-mediated glomerulonephritis or other immune-mediated kidney injury.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: No specific staining observed for IgG, IgA, IgM, C1q, C3, or fibrinogen [Context].
experiments.interpretation: The absence of immune deposits indicates no evidence of immune complex-mediated injury or glomerular disease.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The kidney injury is not due to immune-mediated mechanisms.

experiments.experimental_setting: Ultrastructural examination using electron microscopy of kidney biopsy tissue.
experiments.experiment_goal: To identify subcellular localization and morphology of pigmented inclusions.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Moderately electron-dense bile inclusions are observed within proximal tubular epithelial cells. Adjacent mitochondria are enlarged and disorganized. Highly electron-dense particles and filamentous material are present in tubular lumina, consistent with bile casts [Context].
experiments.interpretation: Electron-dense inclusions in tubular cells and lumina correspond to bile pigment accumulation. Mitochondrial abnormalities suggest cellular stress or toxicity from bile components.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Ultrastructural findings confirm intracellular and intraluminal bile accumulation with associated tubular cell injury.

experiments.experimental_setting: Examination of nephrectomy specimen with H&E and Hall's staining.
experiments.experiment_goal: To confirm and extend biopsy findings in the entire kidney, particularly regarding pigment distribution and tubular damage.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Diffuse tubular epithelial necrosis and sloughing with numerous granular red and green-brown pigmented casts. Casts are especially abundant in distal tubules and medullary collecting ducts. Hall's stain shows positive green staining of casts [Context].
experiments.interpretation: The nephrectomy specimen corroborates biopsy findings, showing widespread bile cast formation and tubular injury, predominantly in distal nephron segments.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Bile cast nephropathy is extensive and involves both proximal and distal tubules, consistent with severe cholestatic injury to the kidney.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: Pigmented tubular casts and intracellular pigment inclusions are present, with red and green-brown discoloration suggestive of hemoglobin and bile pigments.
Severe acute tubular necrosis with sloughed, discolored epithelial cells and basement membrane denudation is evident.
Hall's stain confirms the presence of bile pigment in intraluminal casts.
No immune complex deposition is detected, ruling out immune-mediated glomerular disease.
Ultrastructural findings demonstrate bile inclusions in tubular cells and lumina, with mitochondrial damage.
Nephrectomy findings confirm widespread bile cast nephropathy with severe tubular necrosis.

reasoning.content: The patient presented with AKI following a renal biopsy complicated by hemorrhage and shock. Histological examination revealed granular, pigmented tubular casts with red and green-brown discoloration, along with sloughed epithelial cells showing dark red-green pigmentation. These features, particularly the green-brown pigment in tubular cells and luminal casts, raised suspicion for bile pigment accumulation. This was confirmed by positive green staining with Hall's stain, which specifically identifies bile. Immunofluorescence showed no immune deposits, excluding immune-mediated injury. Electron microscopy revealed electron-dense bile inclusions within proximal tubular cells and lumina, along with mitochondrial abnormalities, confirming ultrastructural evidence of bile toxicity. The nephrectomy specimen demonstrated extensive bile cast formation, particularly in distal tubules and collecting ducts, with diffuse tubular necrosis. Together, these findings indicate that the AKI was primarily due to bile cast nephropathy resulting from severe cholestatic liver disease. The liver's nodular appearance during surgery further supports underlying chronic liver pathology. The absence of glomerular disease or immune complex deposition confirms that the injury is tubular and pigment-mediated.
reasoning.conclusion: The patient's acute kidney injury is due to bile cast nephropathy secondary to cholestatic liver disease, characterized by intraluminal bile casts, intracellular bile accumulation, severe acute tubular necrosis, and absence of immune-mediated mechanisms.

question:
Endocan is expressed by tumor cells in glioblastoma and pituitary tumors, and its expression is associated with tumor progression, particularly in hypoxic and high-grade regions. To investigate this, researchers conducted the following studies:

- Immunohistochemistry was performed on tissue samples from high-grade gliomas (glioblastoma) to detect Endocan expression. Hematoxylin was used as a nuclear counterstain, and a chromogenic detection method (likely DAB) produced a brown signal indicating Endocan localization.

- Immunohistochemical analysis of glioblastoma tissue sections was carried out with focus on regions of necrosis and surrounding cellular architecture, using chromogenic detection for Endocan and hematoxylin counterstaining.

- Immunohistochemical staining of pituitary tumor tissue sections was performed to detect Endocan, using chromogenic methods with hematoxylin counterstain.

What can be concluded from these experiments regarding Endocan expression and its potential role in tumor progression?

input_logic_chain.research_context: Endocan is expressed by tumor cells in glioblastoma and pituitary tumors, and its expression is associated with tumor progression, particularly in hypoxic and high-grade regions.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemistry was performed on tissue samples from high-grade gliomas (glioblastoma) to detect Endocan expression. Hematoxylin was used as a nuclear counterstain, and a chromogenic detection method (likely DAB) produced a brown signal indicating Endocan localization.
experiments.experiment_goal: To determine the cellular and spatial distribution of Endocan in glioblastoma tissue, particularly in relation to tumor and endothelial cells.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Brown chromogenic staining is observed in the cytoplasm or membranous regions of certain cells within a densely cellular tissue section. The staining appears in scattered tumor cells and in multilayered vascular structures where endothelial cells lining luminal spaces show positive signal. The overall tissue architecture shows disrupted organization and vascular proliferation [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The brown staining indicates Endocan protein expression. Its presence in endothelial cells confirms known endothelial expression, while cytoplasmic staining in parenchymal tumor cells suggests that tumor cells themselves also express Endocan in glioblastoma.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Endocan is expressed not only in endothelial cells but also in tumor cells of glioblastoma, indicating ectopic expression within the tumor parenchyma.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical analysis of glioblastoma tissue sections, with focus on regions of necrosis and surrounding cellular architecture, using chromogenic detection for Endocan and hematoxylin counterstaining.
experiments.experiment_goal: To investigate the spatial relationship between Endocan expression and hypoxic tumor microenvironments, particularly in palisading regions surrounding necrotic zones.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Brown chromogenic staining forms dense, irregular aggregates and linear arrangements, localized in a palisaded or rim-like pattern around central acellular or necrotic-appearing regions. The surrounding tissue shows lower cellularity and pale counterstaining, with the stained cells arranged in a peripheral, organized layer [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: The palisading arrangement of Endocan-positive cells around necrotic zones is a histological hallmark of hypoxia-driven tumor cell migration and pseudopalisading necrosis in glioblastoma. The co-localization of Endocan with these regions suggests its expression is linked to hypoxic stress.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Endocan expression in glioblastoma tumor cells is spatially associated with hypoxic microenvironments, suggesting hypoxia may induce or upregulate Endocan in tumor cells.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining of pituitary tumor tissue sections to detect Endocan, using chromogenic methods with hematoxylin counterstain.
experiments.experiment_goal: To determine whether Endocan is expressed in both endothelial and tumor cells in pituitary tumors.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: In one region, brown cytoplasmic staining is heterogeneously distributed among densely packed cells with round to oval nuclei, with some clusters showing intense signal and others faint or absent staining. The staining is cytoplasmic and non-uniform [Image 3]. In another region, brown signal is localized in cytoplasmic and perinuclear regions of disorganized, sheet-like tumor cells with minimal stroma and no glandular structures [Image 4].
experiments.interpretation: The heterogeneous cytoplasmic brown staining in tumor cells of pituitary adenomas indicates variable but specific Endocan expression within the tumor cell population. The presence of staining in both endothelial and tumor compartments confirms dual sources of Endocan in this tumor type.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Endocan is expressed by both endothelial and tumor cells in pituitary tumors, supporting the broader phenomenon of tumor cell-intrinsic Endocan expression across cancer types.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: Endocan is expressed in tumor cells of glioblastoma, not limited to endothelial cells.
Endocan expression in glioblastoma tumor cells is spatially linked to hypoxic palisades, a hallmark of aggressive tumor biology.
Endocan is expressed in both endothelial and tumor cells in pituitary tumors, confirming tumor cell expression in another cancer type.

reasoning.content: The immunohistochemical evidence from glioblastoma and pituitary tumors consistently demonstrates that Endocan is expressed by tumor cells themselves, not solely by endothelial cells. In glioblastoma, Endocan is detected in tumor cell cytoplasm and is specifically enriched in the pseudopalisading regions surrounding necrosis—areas known to be hypoxic and associated with aggressive tumor behavior. This spatial association suggests that hypoxia may drive Endocan expression in tumor cells. Similarly, in pituitary tumors, Endocan is detected in both vascular endothelium and tumor cell cytoplasm, confirming that tumor cell expression is not an isolated phenomenon. Together, these observations across multiple tumor types indicate that Endocan expression in tumor cells is a recurrent feature of high-grade or aggressive tumors, particularly in microenvironments of hypoxia and neoangiogenesis.
reasoning.conclusion: Endocan is expressed by tumor cells in glioblastoma and pituitary tumors, and its expression is associated with hypoxic, high-grade tumor regions, suggesting it may serve as a molecular signature of tumor progression.

question: An 18-year-old male presents with progressive ataxia and cranial nerve palsies. Imaging reveals a posterior fossa mass, and histopathological evaluation is performed. Histological examination of the tumor tissue was conducted using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining at 200× magnification. A subsequent high-magnification H&E staining (×1000 with oil immersion) was performed. Immunohistochemical staining for B-cell lineage markers (CD45, CD20, CD79a, CD10, Bcl-6) was carried out using chromogenic detection. Ki67 proliferation marker was assessed via chromogenic immunohistochemistry at ×400 magnification. Additional studies included immunohistochemical staining for synaptophysin, GFAP, INI1, Cam5.2, and SMA; in situ hybridization for EBV-encoded RNA (EBER); and FISH for IGH/MYC rearrangement. The results showed the tumor is negative for synaptophysin, GFAP, Cam5.2, SMA, and EBER; there is loss of INI1 nuclear expression with positive internal control; and FISH reveals IGH/MYC rearrangement in all nuclei. What is the most likely histopathological diagnosis, and how can it be justified through an integrated analysis of the findings?

input_logic_chain.research_context: Determine the histopathological identity of a posterior fossa mass in an 18-year-old male presenting with progressive ataxia and cranial nerve palsies.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological examination of tumor tissue using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining at 200× magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: Assess the cellular morphology and architectural pattern of the tumor.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Dense population of medium-sized discohesive cells with high nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio, poorly defined cell borders, irregular hyperchromatic nuclei (dark purple), scant eosinophilic cytoplasm (light pink), interspersed larger macrophages with vesicular nuclei and abundant pale cytoplasm, creating a speckled light-and-dark pattern; brisk mitotic activity and numerous apoptotic bodies are present [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The 'starry sky' appearance—formed by darkly stained tumor cells with scattered pale macrophages—is characteristic of rapidly proliferating lymphoid neoplasms with high turnover. The discohesiveness, high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, and frequent mitoses suggest an aggressive small round blue cell tumor of hematopoietic origin.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The tumor exhibits morphological features consistent with a high-grade B-cell lymphoma, particularly Burkitt lymphoma.

experiments.experimental_setting: High-magnification H&E staining (×1000 with oil immersion) of tumor tissue.
experiments.experiment_goal: Evaluate detailed nuclear and cellular morphology for diagnostic specificity.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Densely packed cells with squared-off, angular borders; irregularly shaped, hyperchromatic nuclei with condensed chromatin; visible mitotic figures and apoptotic bodies; minimal intercellular space and no stromal organization [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: Squared-off ('molded') cell borders are a hallmark of Burkitt lymphoma due to tight cellular packing. The presence of numerous mitotic figures and apoptotic bodies further supports an extremely high proliferative rate and rapid cell death, typical of Burkitt lymphoma.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The cytological features including molded cells and high mitotic-apoptotic index strongly support a diagnosis of Burkitt lymphoma.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining for B-cell lineage markers (CD45, CD20, CD79a, CD10, Bcl-6) using chromogenic detection.
experiments.experiment_goal: Determine the immunophenotypic profile of the tumor cells to confirm B-cell origin and subtype.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Strong and diffuse brown chromogenic staining localized predominantly to cell membranes, with some cytoplasmic reactivity; uniform distribution across all cells; no nuclear staining; clear contrast with lightly counterstained background [Image 3].
experiments.interpretation: Membranous and cytoplasmic positivity for CD20, CD79a, CD10, and Bcl-6 indicates germinal center B-cell origin. CD10 and Bcl-6 positivity further supports a germinal center phenotype, typical of Burkitt lymphoma.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The tumor is of B-cell lineage with a germinal center immunophenotype, consistent with Burkitt lymphoma.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining for Ki67 proliferation marker using chromogenic immunohistochemistry at ×400 magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: Assess the proliferative index of the tumor.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: High density of cells with intense, uniform brown nuclear staining; nearly all nuclei are labeled; pale background enhances contrast; minimal unstained nuclei [Image 4].
experiments.interpretation: Near-complete nuclear labeling for Ki67 indicates a proliferative index exceeding 95%, which is a defining feature of Burkitt lymphoma (typically >95–99%).
experiments.sub_conclusion: The tumor has an extremely high proliferation rate, strongly supporting Burkitt lymphoma.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining for synaptophysin, GFAP, INI1, Cam5.2, and SMA; in situ hybridization for EBV-encoded RNA (EBER); and FISH for IGH/MYC rearrangement.
experiments.experiment_goal: Exclude differential diagnoses and confirm molecular hallmark of Burkitt lymphoma.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Negative staining for synaptophysin and GFAP [Missing]; loss of INI1 nuclear expression with positive internal control [Context]; negative Cam5.2 and SMA [Missing]; negative EBER in situ hybridization [Missing]; FISH shows IGH/MYC rearrangement in all nuclei [Context].
experiments.interpretation: Absence of synaptophysin and GFAP rules out medulloblastoma and glioma. Retained INI1 expression (implied by negative for loss) and absence of cytoplasmic globules exclude ATRT. EBV negativity does not exclude Burkitt lymphoma (common in sporadic forms). The t(8;14) translocation involving MYC and IGH is the molecular signature of Burkitt lymphoma.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The tumor lacks features of medulloblastoma, ATRT, and glioma, and harbors the defining MYC-IGH translocation, confirming Burkitt lymphoma.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The tumor displays classic 'starry sky' histology with discohesive, high-grade small round blue cells and abundant apoptosis, indicative of an aggressive lymphoid neoplasm.
Molded cell borders and extreme mitotic activity further narrow the diagnosis to Burkitt lymphoma among aggressive B-cell lymphomas.
Immunophenotype confirms germinal center B-cell origin with CD10 and Bcl-6 positivity, typical of Burkitt lymphoma.
Ki67 labeling index >99% is a hallmark of Burkitt lymphoma and supports its diagnosis over other lymphomas.
Exclusion of mimics (medulloblastoma, ATRT, glioma) and confirmation of MYC-IGH translocation provide definitive molecular evidence for Burkitt lymphoma.

reasoning.content: The histological features—starry sky pattern, discohesive cells with high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, and molded borders—suggest a high-grade B-cell lymphoma. Immunohistochemistry confirms B-cell lineage (CD20+, CD79a+) and germinal center phenotype (CD10+, Bcl-6+), while the near-universal Ki67 positivity (>99%) reflects extreme proliferation. Critically, the tumor lacks markers of neural (synaptophysin), glial (GFAP), or rhabdoid (INI1 loss) differentiation, excluding medulloblastoma and ATRT. The detection of t(8;14) by FISH confirms MYC-IGH rearrangement, the genetic hallmark of Burkitt lymphoma. Although EBER is negative, this is expected in sporadic (non-endemic) CNS Burkitt lymphoma. Together, the morphological, immunophenotypic, and molecular findings are diagnostic of Burkitt lymphoma.
reasoning.conclusion: The posterior fossa mass is a primary central nervous system Burkitt lymphoma.

question:
A 62-year-old male presented with a large, asymptomatic, irregular yellowish plaque on the vertex of the scalp with a central crater, which had gradually expanded over one year following chronic sun exposure. The lesion showed characteristic clinical features suggestive of a rare variant of keratoacanthoma. To confirm the diagnosis, the following investigations were performed:

- A deep punch biopsy was performed on the raised lesion of the scalp. The tissue specimen was processed and stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) for microscopic examination.
- Histological examination of the upper dermis was conducted using the same H&E-stained biopsy specimen.
- Clinical examination and imaging studies, including CT scan of the brain, ultrasonography of the lesion, and systemic evaluation (haemogram, chemistry, X-ray chest and skull), were carried out. The CT scan of the brain showed no abnormality. Ultrasonography revealed an ill-defined hypoechoic mass involving epidermis, dermis, and subcutaneous tissue. No regional or systemic lymphadenopathy was observed clinically.
- Post-surgical follow-up was conducted at 9 months after complete excision with grafting, during which no recurrence of the lesion was observed.

What can be concluded from these findings?

input_logic_chain.research_context: A 62-year-old male presented with a large, asymptomatic, irregular yellowish plaque on the vertex of the scalp with a central crater, which had gradually expanded over one year following chronic sun exposure. The lesion showed characteristic clinical and histopathological features suggestive of keratoacanthoma centrifugum marginatum (KCM), a rare variant of keratoacanthoma. The goal is to confirm the diagnosis of KCM based on histopathological and clinical findings.

experiments.experimental_setting: A deep punch biopsy was performed on the raised lesion of the scalp. The tissue specimen was processed and stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) for microscopic examination.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate the histological architecture of the lesion and identify diagnostic features of keratoacanthoma centrifugum marginatum.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Exoendophytic, globular, well-circumscribed central cup-shaped crater formed by epidermal invagination, with marked hyperkeratosis and a dense, glassy-appearing keratin-filled horn cyst. The base of the crater is well-demarcated and regular. The epidermis forms a buttress over the pseudohorn cyst [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The cup-shaped crater with central keratin accumulation and hyperkeratosis is a hallmark of keratoacanthoma. The 'glassy' eosinophilic keratin and the buttressing epidermis are consistent with rapid keratinization and expansive growth, typical of fully developed keratoacanthoma lesions. The well-demarcated base without infiltration supports a benign, self-limited process.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The histological architecture is consistent with a fully developed keratoacanthoma, specifically showing features diagnostic of KCM rather than squamous cell carcinoma.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological examination of the upper dermis in the H&E-stained biopsy specimen.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess the inflammatory response associated with the lesion and its localization.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Dense, sharply demarcated nodular lymphocytic infiltrate in the upper dermis, composed of small, round, darkly stained lymphocytes with scant cytoplasm, arranged in tightly packed clusters. The infiltrate compresses surrounding collagen but does not extend into deeper dermis or subcutaneous tissue [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: The presence of a dense, nodular lymphocytic infiltrate in the upper dermis suggests a host immune response to the proliferating epithelial lesion. The absence of deeper infiltration and lack of atypia in the lymphocytes support a reactive, non-malignant process.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The inflammatory infiltrate is consistent with a benign reactive process, reinforcing the non-malignant nature of the lesion.

experiments.experimental_setting: Clinical examination and imaging studies including CT scan of the brain, ultrasonography of the lesion, and systemic evaluation (haemogram, chemistry, X-ray chest and skull).
experiments.experiment_goal: To rule out systemic involvement, metastasis, or underlying malignancy.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: CT scan of brain showed no abnormality [Context]. Ultrasonography revealed an ill-defined hypoechoic mass involving epidermis, dermis, and subcutaneous tissue [Context]. No regional or systemic lymphadenopathy was observed clinically [Context].
experiments.interpretation: The absence of intracranial extension or systemic abnormalities supports a localized cutaneous process. The hypoechoic mass on ultrasound corresponds to the full-thickness skin involvement seen histologically, but lack of metastatic signs reinforces benign behavior.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The lesion is localized without evidence of systemic spread or association with internal malignancy.

experiments.experimental_setting: Post-surgical follow-up at 9 months after complete excision with grafting.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess for recurrence and confirm the benign clinical course.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: No recurrence of the lesion was observed at 9 months post-surgery [Context].
experiments.interpretation: The absence of recurrence after complete excision is typical of benign tumors such as KCM, which do not exhibit metastatic potential or aggressive regrowth.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The clinical course supports a benign, non-aggressive tumor with excellent prognosis after excision.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The histological architecture of the lesion, including the exoendophytic cup-shaped crater, hyperkeratosis, horn cyst, and epidermal buttressing, is diagnostic of a fully developed keratoacanthoma.
The dense nodular lymphocytic infiltrate in the upper dermis reflects a reactive immune response and does not indicate malignancy.
The lesion is confined to the skin without systemic or deep tissue involvement, and there is no evidence of metastasis or association with visceral malignancy.
The absence of recurrence after complete excision supports the benign biological behavior of the lesion.

reasoning.content: The integration of clinical, histopathological, and imaging findings supports the diagnosis of keratoacanthoma centrifugum marginatum (KCM). The exoendophytic growth with a central keratin-filled crater and buttressing epidermis [Image 1] is pathognomonic for keratoacanthoma. The presence of a dense, nodular lymphocytic infiltrate in the upper dermis [Image 2] without atypia or deep extension indicates a reactive process, not malignancy. Imaging and systemic evaluation showed no abnormalities, ruling out metastasis or paraneoplastic syndromes. The lack of recurrence at 9 months post-excision further confirms the benign nature of KCM. While KCM exhibits expansive growth, it lacks the infiltrative margins and cytological atypia seen in squamous cell carcinoma. The patient’s history of chronic sun exposure aligns with known risk factors for KCM, including UV radiation. Together, these findings fulfill the diagnostic criteria for KCM as a rare, benign, self-limited epithelial proliferation with no malignant potential.
reasoning.conclusion: The lesion is definitively diagnosed as keratoacanthoma centrifugum marginatum (KCM), a rare, benign, locally expansive cutaneous tumor with characteristic histopathological features and excellent prognosis following complete surgical excision.

question: A 2011 rectal lesion in a patient with prior proctitis is under evaluation to determine whether it represents a colitis-associated colorectal carcinoma. A histological examination of the resected rectal specimen was performed using hematoxylin and eosin staining at ×200 magnification. Additionally, immunohistochemical staining for p53 protein expression was conducted on rectal mucosa tissue, visualized at ×200 magnification with a scale bar indicating 50.0 μm. Furthermore, a histological evaluation of the surrounding rectal mucosa following resection revealed the presence of dysplasia. - Clinical and electrocardiographic monitoring from admission until death, including serial ECG recordings. ECG on arrival showed broad QRS complexes with ST elevation in inferior leads. At 6 hours, the ECG resembled changes seen in myocardial infarction or pericarditis. On day 2, the ECG was indicative of severe myocardial injury.
- Post mortem gross examination of the heart followed by histopathological analysis of multiple cardiac regions. Gross examination revealed no structural abnormalities in the heart.

question: A 17-year-old patient presents with repetitive lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes involving the precentral gyrus, but lacks typical features of myoclonus epilepsy and ataxia. Histological examination was conducted using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining. Additional analyses included Gomori trichrome (GT) staining, succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) enzyme histochemistry, and cytochrome c oxidase (COX) enzyme histochemistry. Based on these experimental settings and the corresponding observations, what diagnosis is supported by the biopsy findings, and how can this be justified through a stepwise interpretation of the results?

experiments.sub_conclusion: Presence of numerous RRFs confirms mitochondrial myopathy and supports a diagnosis within the spectrum of mitochondrial encephalomyopathies.

experiments.experimental_setting: Enzyme histochemistry for succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) on iliopsoas muscle biopsy.

question:
A 52-year-old woman presented with abdominal pain and a right renal mass initially suspected to be renal cell carcinoma. She underwent radical nephrectomy with thrombectomy due to a renal vein thrombus extending into the inferior vena cava. Histological examination of the resected renal mass was performed using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining at low magnification (×10). Additional histological evaluation was carried out using high-magnification H&E staining (×40 equivalent). Immunohistochemical analysis was conducted using CD34 antibody with chromogen detection and hematoxylin counterstain. Further immunohistochemical staining was performed for Vimentin, Factor VIII, CD-99, Bcl-2, SMA, S-100, and CD-68, along with assessment of the Ki-67 proliferative index. Finally, the thrombus retrieved from the renal vein and inferior vena cava was examined histologically.

The high-magnification H&E staining revealed a dense proliferation of spindle cells with elongated nuclei, scant cytoplasm, minimal pleomorphism, hyperchromatic nuclei varying slightly in size and orientation, no visible mitotic figures, absence of necrosis, and a lightly eosinophilic fibrous stroma without significant inflammatory infiltrate. The additional immunohistochemical panel showed positive staining for Vimentin, Factor VIII, CD-99, and Bcl-2; negative for SMA, S-100, and CD-68; and a low Ki-67 labeling index. The histological examination of the thrombus showed a bland thrombus without neoplastic cells.

What can be concluded from these findings?
