experiments.visual_phenomenon: Interstitial scarring involves 20–25% of the biopsy sample, with tubular atrophy and proteinaceous casts [Context].
experiments.interpretation: Moderate interstitial fibrosis and tubular damage reflect chronicity and irreversible injury, consistent with progressive kidney disease in the setting of ongoing glomerular pathology.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The degree of chronic interstitial injury supports a sustained pathological process, temporally linked to prolonged VEGF inhibition.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The renal biopsy demonstrates histological features of collapsing FSGS, including segmental capillary collapse, pseudocrescent formation, and visceral epithelial cell hypertrophy.
Chronic thrombotic microangiopathy is present, evidenced by double contouring of the glomerular basement membrane on both silver stain and electron microscopy.
Podocyte injury (foot process effacement) and endothelial damage (double contours, fibrin thrombi) coexist, indicating dual glomerular cell involvement.

The absence of autoimmune, infectious, and paraprotein-related diseases, along with normal renal artery Doppler and suppressed renin-aldosterone axis, excludes other common causes of hypertension and renal failure.
The temporal association between intravitreal VEGF inhibitor use (first Aflibercept, then Ranibizumab) and onset of severe renal injury supports a causal relationship.

reasoning.content: The patient developed rapidly progressive kidney injury following prolonged intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy. Biopsy findings reveal two key pathologies: collapsing FSGS and chronic TMA. Collapsing FSGS is characterized by segmental capillary loop collapse, visceral epithelial cell hypertrophy, and pseudocrescent formation [Image 1], along with diffuse foot process effacement on electron microscopy [Image 3]. These are hallmarks of severe podocyte injury. Concurrently, double contouring of the glomerular basement membrane—visible on both silver stain [Image 2] and electron microscopy [Image 3]—along with fibrin thrombi [Image 1], indicates chronic endothelial damage consistent with TMA. The absence of alternative etiologies (e.g., autoimmune, infectious, paraneoplastic) and the normalization of blood pressure and partial improvement in creatinine after discontinuation of Ranibizumab support a drug-induced mechanism. VEGF is critical for both endothelial health and podocyte function; its systemic depletion due to intravitreal administration (with possible spillover or cumulative effect) can lead to glomerular endothelial dysfunction and podocyte dedifferentiation. The co-occurrence of cFSGS and TMA in this context is increasingly recognized as a manifestation of VEGF pathway inhibition. Therefore, the renal injury is best explained as secondary to intravitreal VEGF inhibitor therapy.
reasoning.conclusion: The patient’s kidney injury, characterized by collapsing FSGS and chronic TMA, is attributable to intravitreal VEGF inhibitor therapy, likely due to systemic VEGF depletion leading to combined podocyte and endothelial injury.

question: A 35-year-old male presented with right orbital swelling and diminution of vision for the past month. A biopsy of the orbital mass was performed. Histological examination of the tissue was conducted using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining, with the specimen visualized under light microscopy. Immunohistochemical staining was subsequently performed using an antibody against desmin, followed by immunohistochemical staining with an antibody against myogenin. Based on these experimental procedures and the observed findings, what is the most appropriate diagnosis, and how is this conclusion supported by the integrated results of the histological and immunohistochemical analyses?

input_logic_chain.research_context: A 35-year-old male presented with right orbital swelling and diminution of vision; biopsy and immunohistochemistry were performed to characterize the orbital mass and confirm the diagnosis of alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma (ARMS).

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological examination of an orbital mass biopsy using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining. The tissue was sectioned and visualized under light microscopy.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess the morphological features of the tumor cells and their architectural arrangement for diagnostic classification.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Small, round malignant cells arranged in densely packed nests, clearly demarcated from the surrounding stroma, with hyperchromatic nuclei and scant cytoplasm. The nests are embedded in a fibrovascular stroma with a pale, eosinophilic matrix and vascular channels [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The presence of small round blue cells in nested arrangements with high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio is characteristic of primitive neuroectodermal tumors or small round cell sarcomas, including rhabdomyosarcoma. The fibrovascular stroma with vascular channels supports a mesenchymal origin.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The histomorphology is consistent with a small round cell tumor of mesenchymal origin, suggestive of rhabdomyosarcoma.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical (IHC) staining of the tumor tissue using antibodies against desmin, a muscle-specific intermediate filament protein.
experiments.experiment_goal: To determine myogenic differentiation of the tumor cells by detecting desmin expression.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Brownish-red cytoplasmic staining in spindle-shaped and scattered cells within a pale stromal background, with variable density and disorganized arrangement [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: Cytoplasmic brown chromogen deposition indicates positive immunoreactivity for desmin, a marker of myogenic lineage. The staining pattern confirms that the tumor cells are of skeletal muscle precursor origin.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The tumor exhibits myogenic differentiation, supporting a diagnosis of rhabdomyosarcoma.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining using antibody against myogenin, a transcription factor specific to skeletal muscle differentiation.
experiments.experiment_goal: To confirm the diagnosis of alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma, as myogenin is typically strongly expressed in the alveolar subtype.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Heterogeneous brownish-orange chromogenic staining localized predominantly in the nuclei of tumor cells, with some cytoplasmic reactivity. The labeled cells appear in irregular clusters and spindle-shaped forms within a fibrous stroma [Image 3].
experiments.interpretation: Nuclear staining for myogenin indicates active transcriptional regulation of myogenic genes, which is highly specific for rhabdomyosarcoma and particularly strong and diffuse in the alveolar subtype (ARMS).
experiments.sub_conclusion: Strong nuclear myogenin expression confirms the diagnosis of alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma (ARMS).

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The tumor consists of small round cells arranged in nests within a fibrovascular stroma, consistent with a primitive mesenchymal neoplasm.
The tumor cells express desmin, confirming skeletal muscle lineage.
The tumor cells show nuclear expression of myogenin, a hallmark of alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma.

reasoning.content: The histological architecture (small round cells in nests) observed in H&E staining [Image 1] suggests a small round cell tumor. Immunohistochemistry demonstrates cytoplasmic desmin positivity [Image 2], confirming myogenic differentiation. Nuclear myogenin staining [Image 3], which is highly specific for ARMS, establishes the subtype. Together, these findings fulfill the diagnostic criteria for alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma.
reasoning.conclusion: The orbital mass is diagnosed as alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma (ARMS) based on characteristic histomorphology and immunohistochemical profile (desmin and myogenin positivity).

question:
To determine the pathological basis of respiratory failure in a fatal case of e-cigarette or vaping product use-associated lung injury (EVALI) complicated by Influenza A and secondary bacterial infection, the following investigations were performed:

- Gross examination of lung tissue obtained at autopsy from a 27-year-old male with a history of THC vaping and recent Influenza A infection was conducted under standard lighting conditions.
- Histopathological analysis was performed on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded lung tissue sections stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and examined under light microscopy.
- Special histochemical staining using Oil Red O was applied to frozen lung tissue sections, followed by light microscopic examination, with a blue/purple hematoxylin counterstain.

What can be concluded about the underlying pathological mechanisms contributing to respiratory failure in this patient?

input_logic_chain.research_context: To determine the pathological basis of respiratory failure in a fatal case of e-cigarette or vaping product use-associated lung injury (EVALI) complicated by Influenza A and secondary bacterial infection.

experiments.experimental_setting: Gross examination of lung tissue obtained at autopsy from a 27-year-old male with a history of THC vaping and recent Influenza A infection. The tissue was visually inspected under standard lighting conditions for macroscopic abnormalities.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess the overall structural and morphological changes in the lungs postmortem.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The lung tissue specimen exhibits an irregular shape and surface with a predominantly red to dark reddish-brown coloration, interspersed with darker red patches and areas of paler, discolored regions. The surface appears heterogeneous, displaying solid, firm areas alongside regions of altered texture that are rougher or uneven. Distinct zones of hemorrhage are visible as dark red, densely colored patches, while other areas show loss of normal parenchymal architecture, appearing degraded and lacking structural integrity. The cut surface lacks the spongy, aerated appearance typical of healthy lung tissue, instead presenting a consolidated and dense morphology. Scattered patches of increased discoloration and possible friability are noted, with some regions showing fluid accumulation or a more compact consistency [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The dark red to reddish-brown discoloration and hemorrhagic patches indicate pulmonary congestion and bleeding. The loss of spongy, aerated texture and presence of consolidation suggest alveolar filling with exudate or cellular material, consistent with severe inflammatory lung disease. The firm, non-compliant texture reflects extensive parenchymal damage and impaired gas exchange.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The gross morphology of the lungs demonstrates severe structural damage characterized by consolidation, hemorrhage, and loss of normal architecture, indicative of advanced lung injury.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histopathological analysis of formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded lung tissue sections stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E), examined under light microscopy.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate cellular and architectural changes within the lung parenchyma.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Alveolar spaces are filled with dense, amorphous, eosinophilic material that lines alveolar walls and forms continuous, glassy-appearing layers. This material is interspersed with small, darkly stained nuclei, fibrin strands, and cellular debris. Alveolar septa are thickened and contain increased nucleated cells. Normal alveolar architecture is disrupted, with areas of consolidation and collapse [Image 2]. Additionally, there are extensive areas of tissue disruption with amorphous eosinophilic material, pyknotic or fragmented nuclei, dense infiltrates of small round hyperchromatic cells, and alveolar exudate with necrotic debris. Some regions show vacuolated spaces and coalescing inflammatory infiltrates including neutrophil-like and macrophage-like cells [Image 3].
experiments.interpretation: The eosinophilic material filling alveoli corresponds to protein-rich edema fluid and fibrin, hallmark features of diffuse alveolar damage (DAD). Thickened septa with inflammatory infiltrates indicate interstitial inflammation. The presence of necrotic debris and pyknotic nuclei suggests widespread cell death. The combination of intra-alveolar exudate, septal thickening, and architectural collapse is diagnostic of acute-phase DAD, commonly seen in ARDS.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Microscopic findings confirm diffuse alveolar damage with proteinaceous exudation, fibrin deposition, and inflammatory infiltration, consistent with ARDS.

experiments.experimental_setting: Special histochemical staining using Oil Red O on frozen lung tissue sections, followed by light microscopic examination. Oil Red O selectively stains neutral lipids red to red-orange, with a blue/purple hematoxylin counterstain.
experiments.experiment_goal: To detect the presence and localization of lipid accumulation in lung tissue, which would support a diagnosis of lipoid pneumonia associated with vaping.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Red to red-orange staining is localized within discrete round to oval cells, corresponding to cytoplasmic lipid accumulation. These stained cells are found within alveolar lumina and alveolar septa. The staining is strictly intracellular, with variable intensity (uniform, granular, or patchy). No extracellular red-stained material is observed. The background tissue shows a light blue to purple counterstain, with darkly stained nuclei, some condensed or irregularly shaped [Image 4].
experiments.interpretation: The intracellular red-orange staining with Oil Red O confirms the presence of neutral lipids within macrophages in the alveolar spaces and interstitium. This is diagnostic of lipid-laden macrophages, a key histological feature of exogenous lipoid pneumonia. Given the patient’s history of vaping THC oil—often diluted with lipid-based carriers like vitamin E acetate—this finding strongly implicates inhaled lipid exposure as a causative factor.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The presence of intracellular lipid-laden macrophages confirmed by Oil Red O staining supports a diagnosis of exogenous lipoid pneumonia secondary to vaping.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The gross lung pathology shows consolidation, hemorrhage, and loss of normal architecture, indicative of severe pulmonary injury.
Histological examination reveals diffuse alveolar damage with protein-rich exudate, fibrin, and inflammatory infiltrates, consistent with ARDS.
Oil Red O staining confirms intracellular lipid accumulation in alveolar macrophages, diagnostic of vaping-induced lipoid pneumonia.

reasoning.content: The patient presented with respiratory failure following a dual insult: Influenza A infection and a background of chronic THC vaping. The gross pathological findings demonstrate consolidated, hemorrhagic lungs with loss of normal architecture, indicating severe parenchymal damage. Microscopically, the lungs exhibit classic features of diffuse alveolar damage (DAD), including intra-alveolar proteinaceous exudate, fibrin deposition, and septal inflammation—hallmarks of ARDS. While Influenza A and MSSA infection contributed to the acute inflammatory response, the presence of lipid-laden macrophages, confirmed by Oil Red O staining, provides direct pathological evidence of exogenous lipoid pneumonia. This lipid accumulation is not a feature of viral or bacterial pneumonia but is specifically associated with inhalation of oily substances, such as vitamin E acetate used in THC vaping products. Therefore, the pre-existing lung injury from vaping created a vulnerable substrate, allowing a common respiratory infection to progress to fulminant ARDS. The combination of EVALI and superimposed infection led to multi-organ failure and death.
reasoning.conclusion: E-cigarette or vaping product use-associated lung injury (EVALI), characterized by lipoid pneumonia and diffuse alveolar damage, served as a critical predisposing factor that enabled Influenza A infection to progress to fatal ARDS, highlighting the severe and potentially lethal consequences of vaping, particularly with lipid-containing THC products.

question: In this patient, CMV-IgM was negative, and the absence of evidence of active infection led to an uncertain causal relationship between CMV infection and various symptoms, which demanded histopathology detection for further verification. Nonetheless, the positive CMV-IgG titre was more than 4-fold in 2 weeks, and elevated CMV DNA copies provided clues for diagnosis. However, false negative IgM results can occur in immunocompromised patients and infants, and negative CMV PCR results do not rule out CMV disease. CMV pp65 antigen cannot differentiate latent from active infection, and viral culture, though a gold standard, is limited by poor sensitivity and slow turnaround time. Therefore, when gastrointestinal CMV infection is suspected, endoscopy and biopsy are necessary to obtain definitive evidence. Gastroduodenoscopy and incomplete colonoscopy were performed due to the risk of intestinal perforation and massive hemorrhage. A histopathologic examination of gastrointestinal tissue biopsy was conducted using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining at 400× magnification. Additionally, immunohistochemical (IHC) staining of the gastrointestinal tissue biopsy was performed at 400× magnification to detect CMV-specific antigens. What can be concluded from these findings and investigations?

input_logic_chain.research_context: In this patient, CMV-IgM was negative, and the absence of evidence of active infection led to an uncertain causal relationship between CMV infection and various symptoms, which demanded histopathology detection for further verification. Nonetheless, the positive CMV-IgG titre was more than 4-fold in 2 wk, and elevated CMV DNA copies provided clues for diagnosis. Nevertheless, false negative IgM results can be obtained in immunocompromised patients and infants. Negative results of CMV PCR do not rule out CMV disease. As a marker of early diagnosis, CMV pp65 antigen is not able to differentiate between latent infection and active disease. Viral culture is the diagnostic gold standard, but its poor sensitivity and slow turn-around time limit its clinical utility, while histopathology assays can provide confirmatory information for invasive disease which is highly specific (Figure 4 [Image 1] [Image 2]). Therefore, when gastrointestinal CMV infection is suspected, endoscopy and biopsy must be performed to obtain positive evidence for diagnosis.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histopathologic examination of gastrointestinal tissue biopsy using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining at 400× magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To identify morphological features indicative of cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection in gastrointestinal tissue.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Inflammatory cell infiltration within the lamina propria and surrounding stroma; stroma with lightly eosinophilic appearance and nuclei varying in size and staining intensity; cytomegalic cells that are enlarged compared to surrounding cells, containing markedly enlarged nuclei with sharply demarcated, eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions surrounded by a clear perinuclear halo; disrupted cellular architecture; high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio; minimally visible cytoplasm; and hyperchromatic, condensed nuclei in inflammatory cells. Orange arrows point to cytomegalic cells [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The presence of cytomegalic cells with eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions and perinuclear halos is a classic histopathologic hallmark of active CMV infection. These inclusions represent viral nucleocapsids accumulating within the nucleus. The inflammatory infiltration and architectural disruption suggest tissue damage due to active viral replication and host immune response.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The H&E-stained tissue shows definitive histopathologic features of active CMV infection in the gastrointestinal tract [Image 1].

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical (IHC) staining of gastrointestinal tissue biopsy at 400× magnification to detect CMV-specific antigens.
experiments.experiment_goal: To confirm the presence of CMV proteins within cells, thereby verifying active viral infection.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Scattered round to oval, dark brown intranuclear inclusions of variable size, localized within individual cells; these inclusions are sharply delineated against a light blue, granular background; some inclusions are large and associated with enlarged nuclei; characteristic 'owl's eye' morphology with basophilic inclusions and clear halos; cytoplasm appears pale blue and less intensely stained. Two inclusions are highlighted with orange arrows [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: The dark brown staining in IHC indicates specific binding of anti-CMV antibodies to viral antigens, confirming the presence of CMV proteins within the nuclei of infected cells. The 'owl's eye' appearance is pathognomonic for CMV and confirms active viral replication within these cells.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Immunohistochemical staining confirms the presence of CMV antigens within intranuclear inclusions, supporting active CMV infection in gastrointestinal tissue [Image 2].

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: H&E staining reveals morphological features characteristic of CMV-infected cells, including cytomegalic cells with eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions and perinuclear halos.
IHC staining specifically identifies CMV antigens within the intranuclear inclusions, confirming viral presence at the molecular level.
Both morphological and antigen-specific markers of CMV are present in gastrointestinal tissue, fulfilling histopathologic criteria for active CMV disease.

reasoning.content: Although serologic markers such as CMV-IgM were negative and PCR results were inconclusive—limitations acknowledged in immunocompromised patients—histopathologic evaluation was necessary to establish a definitive diagnosis. The H&E-stained tissue demonstrated classic cytopathic effects of CMV, including enlarged cells with eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions and perinuclear halos [Image 1], which are visually and morphologically consistent with CMV infection. These findings were further confirmed by immunohistochemical staining, which revealed dark brown, intranuclear, 'owl's eye'-type inclusions [Image 2], indicating specific detection of CMV antigens. The combination of morphologic abnormalities and antigen-specific staining provides high specificity for diagnosing active, invasive CMV disease. Given that viral culture is slow and PCR can yield false negatives, and that serology (especially IgM) may be unreliable in immunocompromised hosts, histopathology remains the most reliable method for confirming invasive CMV infection when clinical suspicion is high. The endoscopic biopsy, despite limitations in scope due to perforation risk, yielded tissue sufficient for definitive analysis.
reasoning.conclusion: Histopathologic examination using both H&E and immunohistochemical staining confirms invasive cytomegalovirus disease in the gastrointestinal tract of this patient, establishing a definitive diagnosis despite negative CMV-IgM and limitations of other laboratory methods.

question: In the evaluation of patients with suspected megaloblastic anemia, a peripheral blood smear was prepared from patient samples using a Romanowsky-type stain and examined under light microscopy at 100× magnification. A bone marrow aspirate was also obtained and similarly stained and analyzed at 100× magnification. Additionally, hematological parameters including mean hemoglobin and mean corpuscular volume (MCV) were measured across 93 patients, vitamin B12 levels were assessed, and pancytopenia was defined as hemoglobin <11 g/dL, WBC <4 × 10⁹/L, and platelet count <150 × 10⁹/L. The results showed a mean hemoglobin of 6.68 g/dL and a mean MCV of 103.9 fL. Fifty-one patients (54.8%) had pancytopenia, 48 of whom had vitamin B12 levels <30 pg/mL. Five patients had MCV <90 fL and were found to have coexisting iron deficiency anemia. What conclusions can be drawn from these findings and analyses?

input_logic_chain.research_context: Evaluation of hematological parameters and morphological features in patients with suspected megaloblastic anemia to confirm diagnosis and assess underlying causes.

experiments.experimental_setting: Peripheral blood smear was prepared from patient blood samples and stained with a Romanowsky-type stain (likely Wright's stain), examined under light microscopy at 100× magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To identify characteristic morphological abnormalities in red blood cells and neutrophils indicative of megaloblastic anemia.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Numerous red blood cells are present, predominantly round and uniformly stained, with several exhibiting an oval shape and enlarged size, including a distinct macro-ovalocyte [Image 1]. A hypersegmented neutrophil is prominently visible, characterized by a deeply stained nucleus with more than five lobes connected by thin chromatin filaments, surrounded by minimally visible, lightly stained cytoplasm [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: Macro-ovalocytes are abnormally large, oval-shaped erythrocytes commonly seen in megaloblastic anemias due to impaired DNA synthesis affecting erythropoiesis. Hypersegmented neutrophils (neutrophils with ≥5 nuclear lobes) are a hallmark morphological feature of megaloblastic anemia, resulting from defective nuclear maturation secondary to vitamin B12 or folate deficiency.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The presence of macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils in the peripheral blood smear supports a diagnosis of megaloblastic anemia [Image 1].

experiments.experimental_setting: Bone marrow aspirate was obtained from patients and stained with a Romanowsky-type method, analyzed under light microscopy at 100× magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate erythroid precursor morphology for evidence of megaloblastic hematopoiesis.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The bone marrow aspirate shows high cellularity with large nucleated cells displaying enlarged, irregularly shaped nuclei, coarse hyperchromatic chromatin, and nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony. The cytoplasm is basophilic and relatively abundant compared to the nucleus [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: The observed morphological features—nuclear enlargement, irregular chromatin, and nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony—are diagnostic of megaloblastic erythropoiesis. These changes arise from impaired DNA synthesis, leading to delayed nuclear maturation while cytoplasmic development proceeds normally, a hallmark of vitamin B12 or folate deficiency.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The bone marrow morphology demonstrates definitive evidence of megaloblastic hematopoiesis [Image 2].

experiments.experimental_setting: Hematological parameters including mean hemoglobin and mean corpuscular volume (MCV) were measured in 93 patients; vitamin B12 levels were assessed; pancytopenia was defined as hemoglobin <11 g/dL, WBC <4 × 10⁹/L, and platelet count <150 × 10⁹/L.
experiments.experiment_goal: To correlate clinical and laboratory findings with morphological evidence of megaloblastic anemia.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Mean hemoglobin was 6.68 g/dL and mean MCV was 103.9 fL. Fifty-one patients (54.8%) had pancytopenia, 48 of whom had vitamin B12 levels <30 pg/mL. Five patients with MCV <90 fL were found to have coexisting iron deficiency anemia [Context].
experiments.interpretation: Low hemoglobin indicates severe anemia. Elevated MCV (103.9 fL) confirms macrocytosis, consistent with megaloblastic anemia. The high prevalence of pancytopenia and extremely low vitamin B12 levels in most pancytopenic patients strongly implicates vitamin B12 deficiency as the primary cause. The少数 patients with low MCV have concurrent iron deficiency, which can mask macrocytosis.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The hematological profile—severe anemia, macrocytosis, frequent pancytopenia, and very low vitamin B12 levels—supports vitamin B12 deficiency as the predominant cause of megaloblastic anemia in this cohort [Context].

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The presence of macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils in the peripheral blood smear supports a diagnosis of megaloblastic anemia [Image 1].
The bone marrow morphology demonstrates definitive evidence of megaloblastic hematopoiesis [Image 2].

The hematological profile—severe anemia, macrocytosis, frequent pancytopenia, and very low vitamin B12 levels—supports vitamin B12 deficiency as the predominant cause of megaloblastic anemia in this cohort [Context].

reasoning.content: The peripheral blood smear reveals two classic morphological hallmarks of megaloblastic anemia: macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils [Image 1], both resulting from defective DNA synthesis. These findings are corroborated at the bone marrow level, where erythroid precursors exhibit nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony, enlarged nuclei with coarse chromatin, and basophilic cytoplasm—pathognomonic features of megaloblastic transformation [Image 2]. Together, these morphological abnormalities confirm active megaloblastic hematopoiesis. Clinically, the mean MCV of 103.9 fL indicates macrocytic anemia, and the extremely low mean hemoglobin (6.68 g/dL) reflects severe anemia. The high incidence of pancytopenia (54.8%) aligns with the bone marrow's ineffective hematopoiesis. Critically, 48 of the 51 pancytopenic patients had vitamin B12 levels <30 pg/mL, indicating profound deficiency. Although five patients had low MCV, they were identified as having coexisting iron deficiency, which can suppress MCV and mask macrocytosis. Thus, the convergence of morphological, cytological, and biochemical evidence points to vitamin B12 deficiency as the primary etiology.

question:
A ferret presented with a rapidly deteriorating clinical condition despite medical stabilization with enalapril, furosemide, oxygen therapy, and subsequent addition of prednisone. Due to the clinical urgency, a necropsy was performed 36 hours after presentation. Prior to death, an ultrasound-guided fine needle aspirate of the liver was obtained for cytological evaluation. Post-mortem, histological examination of hepatic, myocardial, and pericardial tissues was conducted using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining at 20x magnification. Additionally, gross pathological assessment and cytological analysis of pericardial fluid were performed.

The cytological examination of the liver fine needle aspirate revealed that approximately 85% of the cellular population consisted of atypical lymphocytes, with the remaining 15% composed of prolymphocytes and lymphoblasts.

Histological analysis was performed on liver, myocardium, and pericardium, with images captured at 20x magnification for each.

Gross necropsy findings included congestion of the liver, kidneys, myocardium, and pericardial tissue, along with moderate accumulation of fluid in the pericardial space. Cytological evaluation of the pericardial exudate showed it was rich in lymphocytes and plasma cells.

What comprehensive diagnosis can be concluded from these findings, and how do the results from each investigation collectively support this diagnosis?

input_logic_chain.research_context: To confirm the diagnosis of hepatic lymphoma and assess the extent of lymphoid infiltration in multiple organs (liver, myocardium, and pericardium) in a ferret with rapidly deteriorating clinical condition following failed medical stabilization.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological examination of hepatic tissue obtained post-mortem, processed for hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining and imaged at 20x magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate the presence and morphology of abnormal cell infiltrates in the liver parenchyma.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Irregularly shaped, variably sized clusters of densely packed cells with darkly stained nuclei and scant cytoplasm are observed within the hepatic parenchyma, disrupting normal tissue architecture. Surrounding hepatocytes are arranged in cords with interspersed sinusoidal spaces. The infiltrates exhibit round nuclear morphology and are composed of small to medium-sized cells with distinct cytoplasmic boundaries. Staining shows contrasting purple (nuclear) and pink (cytoplasmic) hues [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The densely packed, monomorphic population of small to medium-sized round cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio is characteristic of a neoplastic lymphoid infiltrate. The architectural disruption and nodular growth pattern are consistent with lymphoma rather than reactive hyperplasia.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The liver contains a nodular lymphoid infiltrate with morphological features diagnostic of lymphoma.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological examination of myocardial tissue obtained during necropsy, processed with H&E staining and imaged at 20x magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To determine whether lymphoid infiltration extends to the myocardium, indicating cardiac involvement by lymphoma.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Nodular aggregates of densely packed small, round cells with darkly stained, basophilic nuclei and scant cytoplasm are present within the interstitial spaces between myocardial fibers. These infiltrates disrupt the parallel alignment of striated, eosinophilically stained cardiac muscle fibers, which show cross-striations and occasional wavy appearance. The infiltrating cells are more basophilic than surrounding myocytes [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: The presence of discrete, monomorphic lymphoid nodules within the myocardial interstitium, distinct from native cardiac cells, indicates neoplastic lymphoid infiltration. The morphological disparity between the infiltrate and myocardial fibers confirms non-native cell population localization.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The myocardium harbors a nodular lymphoid infiltrate consistent with cardiac involvement in systemic lymphoma.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological examination of pericardial connective tissue obtained post-mortem, processed with H&E staining and imaged at 20x magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To assess for lymphoid infiltration in the pericardium and determine whether pericardial effusion is inflammatory or neoplastic in origin.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The pericardial stroma shows dense infiltration of small, round cells with hyperchromatic, condensed nuclei and minimal cytoplasm, forming clusters among collagen bundles and fibroblasts. Adipocytes with vacuolated cytoplasm are interspersed. Tissue architecture is preserved without necrosis or hemorrhage [Image 3].
experiments.interpretation: The diffuse but organized infiltration of monomorphic small round cells with lymphoid morphology indicates a lymphocytic infiltrate. The absence of necrosis or granulomatous features argues against infectious etiology, supporting either neoplastic or inflammatory (e.g., immune-mediated) processes. Given concurrent hepatic and myocardial lymphoma, neoplastic dissemination is more likely.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The pericardium exhibits lymphocytic infiltration consistent with secondary involvement in systemic lymphoma.

experiments.experimental_setting: Cytological examination of ultrasound-guided fine needle aspirate (FNA) of the liver, performed ante-mortem.
experiments.experiment_goal: To obtain preliminary diagnosis of hepatic pathology based on cellular morphology.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: The cytology sample consists of approximately 85% atypical lymphocytes and 15% prolymphocytes and lymphoblasts, indicating a clonal or neoplastic lymphoid population [Context].
experiments.interpretation: The predominance of atypical lymphocytes with a minor component of immature forms is highly suggestive of malignant lymphoma, particularly large cell or lymphoblastic type, though definitive classification requires histology.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Cytology supports a diagnosis of hepatic lymphoma ante-mortem.

experiments.experimental_setting: Necropsy with gross and microscopic evaluation of multiple organs, including analysis of pericardial fluid.
experiments.experiment_goal: To identify systemic manifestations of disease and confirm cause of death.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Gross findings include congestion of liver, kidneys, myocardium, and pericardial tissue, along with moderate pericardial fluid accumulation. Cytological analysis of pericardial exudate reveals abundance of lymphocytes and plasma cells [Context].
experiments.interpretation: Systemic congestion suggests poor cardiac output or circulatory failure. The lymphocyte-rich pericardial effusion, in the context of disseminated lymphoid infiltrates, indicates either neoplastic effusion or paraneoplastic inflammatory response.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The patient exhibited systemic congestion and lymphocyte-dominant pericardial effusion, consistent with multi-organ lymphoma and possible cardiac compromise.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: Cytological analysis of liver FNA revealed a clonal lymphoid population dominated by atypical lymphocytes, supporting a preliminary diagnosis of lymphoma.
Histological examination of the liver confirmed a nodular lymphoid infiltrate disrupting hepatic architecture, diagnostic of hepatic lymphoma.
Histological evidence of nodular lymphoid infiltrates in the myocardium indicates direct cardiac involvement by lymphoma.
Lymphocytic infiltration in the pericardium, combined with lymphocyte-rich pericardial effusion, supports secondary neoplastic or inflammatory involvement in the context of systemic disease.

reasoning.content: The ante-mortem cytology of the liver fine needle aspirate demonstrated a lymphoid population dominated by atypical lymphocytes (85%), strongly suggesting lymphoma. Post-mortem histological analysis confirmed this diagnosis in the liver, revealing nodular infiltrates of small to medium-sized lymphoid cells with high nuclear density and architectural disruption [Image 1]. Identical morphological patterns of densely packed, round, basophilic cells forming discrete nodules were observed in the myocardium [Image 2] and diffuse clusters in the pericardium [Image 3], indicating systemic dissemination. The myocardial infiltrates disrupt cardiac fiber alignment, confirming direct neoplastic involvement of the heart. The pericardial infiltration, while less destructive, shows a similar cellular phenotype, and the presence of lymphocyte-rich exudate further supports lymphomatous or reactive involvement. Given the multi-organ infiltration with morphologically consistent cells, the findings confirm disseminated lymphoma with hepatic, cardiac, and pericardial involvement. The rapid clinical deterioration and death within 36 hours, despite supportive therapy, are consistent with multi-organ failure secondary to widespread neoplastic infiltration and possible cardiovascular compromise.
reasoning.conclusion: The ferret suffered from disseminated lymphoma with confirmed hepatic, myocardial, and pericardial involvement, leading to systemic organ dysfunction and death. Histological and cytological evidence across multiple tissues supports a diagnosis of multicentric lymphoma with cardiac and pericardial secondary localization.

To investigate the correlation between histological features and molecular genetic mutations in vascular malformations, with a focus on identifying distinct morphological patterns associated with specific driver mutations (e.g., PIK3CA, TEK, RAS, IDH1, GNA11, GNAQ, AKT1, and co-mutations), the following studies were conducted:

- Histological examination of surgically obtained tissue samples from patients with vascular malformations, stained with hematoxylin and eosin (HE), analyzed at various magnifications. Molecular analysis included sequencing for mutations in PIK3CA, TEK, RAS family genes (KRAS, NRAS, RASA1), IDH1, GNA11, GNAQ, AKT1, PTEN, and others. [Image 1] was analyzed as part of this study.

- The same histological and molecular methods were applied to evaluate architectural complexity, endothelial morphology, stromal composition, and presence of inflammatory or fibrotic changes. [Image 2] was analyzed in this context.

- Molecular genetic analysis of tissue samples with defined histology was performed to identify activating mutations in PIK3CA, TEK, RAS pathway genes, IDH1, GNA11, GNAQ, AKT1, and others. It was observed that eight of nine KRAS, one NRAS, and one RASA1 mutation cases showed well-circumscribed capillary and/or venous/cavernous malformations; the remaining two RAS-pathway mutated cases exhibited noncircumscribed AVMs.

- Histological and molecular analysis was performed on cases with IDH1 mutations. Two of three IDH1-mutated cases showed typical spindle cell hemangioma (SCH) morphology; the third was an intramuscular venocapillary malformation.

- Cases with GNA11 and GNAQ mutations were analyzed using histology and molecular profiling. All four GNA11-mutated cases showed venocapillary morphology; of seven GNAQ-mutated cases, four were venocapillary malformations, two were venous malformations (VMs), and one had combined features including an arterial component.

- Cases with dual mutations in PIK3CA combined with GNA11 or GNAQ were evaluated. All four cases with PIK3CA mutation combined with either GNA11 (n=2) or GNAQ (n=2) mutation were venocapillary malformations.

Based on these investigations, what conclusions can be drawn regarding the relationship between specific somatic mutations and histological phenotypes in vascular malformations?

reasoning.content: The integration of histological and molecular data reveals that specific somatic mutations are strongly associated with distinct histological subtypes of vascular malformations. [Image 1] shows a classic venocapillary malformation with dilated, thin-walled vascular channels lacking muscular layers—morphology commonly seen in PIK3CA, GNA11, and GNAQ-mutated cases. In contrast, [Image 2] displays architectural complexity, heterogeneous wall thickness, and tortuous interconnections—hallmarks of AVMs, which were observed in a subset of RAS-pathway mutated cases and in dual PIK3CA/TEK-mutated contexts. The consistent venocapillary phenotype across GNA11, GNAQ, and PIK3CA co-mutated cases suggests convergence on a shared developmental pathway, likely through MAPK and PI3K signaling. Meanwhile, IDH1 mutations are tightly linked to spindle cell hemangioma, a morphologically distinct entity. Although RAS mutations mostly lead to low-flow malformations, rare AVMs indicate phenotypic plasticity. Thus, the histological architecture is not random but is systematically shaped by the underlying genetic driver.

To characterize the spatiotemporal distribution and cellular localization of equine influenza virus (EIV) antigen in the lungs of infected mice during the course of infection, with emphasis on identifying primary target cells and the progression of histopathological changes, the following experiments were conducted:

- Lung tissue sections from EIV-infected mice were collected at 1 day post-infection (dpi) and processed for immunohistochemistry (IHC) using an antibody specific to EIV antigens, with a brown chromogen (DAB) for visualization and hematoxylin for nuclear counterstaining. High-magnification (1000x) imaging was performed.

- Lung tissue sections from infected mice at 3 dpi were subjected to IHC for EIV antigen detection at 400x magnification, with brown chromogen and hematoxylin counterstain.

- High-magnification (1000x) IHC analysis of lung tissue at 3 dpi was performed using anti-EIV antibodies and brown chromogen, with hematoxylin counterstaining.

- Histopathological and IHC analysis of lung tissues from infected mice was carried out at multiple time points (1–14 dpi), with H&E and antigen-specific staining. The following observations were made: At 1 dpi, bronchiolar epithelial cells exhibited cytoplasmic blebbing, necrosis, and vacuolar degeneration, with approximately 80% of bronchial epithelial cells showing EIV antigen positivity. By 2 dpi, severe epithelial necrosis, perivascular neutrophil cuffing, and vascular congestion were evident, with EIV antigens localized in the bronchial epithelium. At 3 dpi, most alveolar and interstitial macrophages were EIV antigen-positive. By 5 dpi, pulmonary consolidation affected 50–60% of the parenchyma, with type II pneumocyte proliferation and persistent EIV antigen in macrophages and epithelial cells. At 10 dpi, bronchial changes were minimal, but type II pneumocyte proliferation persisted. By 14 dpi, lesions were mild, and bronchiolar architecture was nearly normalized.

What conclusions can be drawn from the integration of these experimental findings?

question: A 73-year-old Japanese woman with a history of never smoking was diagnosed with a lung mass and a nodule in the right middle lobe. She underwent video-assisted thoracoscopic right pulmonary lower lobectomy and segmental resection of the right middle lobe in July 2013. The study investigates the utility of ERG immunostaining in distinguishing true lymphovascular invasion (LVI) from retraction artifact in various cancers, with a focus on morphological patterns such as tumor cell protrusion, fibrocollagenous separation, kissing pattern, and hugging pattern.

Histological sections from multiple cancer types (breast, stomach, thyroid) were immunostained with ERG and CD31 markers and examined under light microscopy to assess LVI, particularly in the context of retraction artifact. The analysis included evaluation of spatial relationships between tumor cells and ERG-positive endothelial cells. In gastric carcinoma, tumor cells were observed protruding into lymphovascular spaces with clear delineation by ERG staining. In thyroid cancer, LVI was clearly distinguished from retraction artifact due to sharp contrast between ERG-positive endothelial nuclei and surrounding tumor cells. Retraction artifact was characterized by gaps between tumor and stroma without endothelial lining.

ERG immunostained tissue sections were analyzed for specific spatial configurations between tumor cells and endothelial cells, including protrusion into vascular spaces, presence of fibrocollagenous layers, kissing pattern, and hugging pattern. Pathologist concordance rates were recorded for each pattern.

ERG immunostained sections from breast, stomach, and thyroid cancers were compared to CD31-stained counterparts, with focus on areas with retraction artifact and obvious LVI. Staining intensity, contrast, and clarity of endothelial boundaries were assessed. ERG staining showed discrete, punctate brown nuclear labeling of endothelial cells with sharp contrast against a pale blue cytoplasmic and stromal background. CD31 staining exhibited less specific, more diffuse cytoplasmic labeling and lower contrast in areas of retraction.

What can be concluded from these findings?

In a study evaluating PD-L1 expression in mononuclear and cervical epithelial cells in women with HR-HPV infection and varying grades of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN), the following experiments were conducted:

1. Immunohistochemical (IHC) staining for PD-L1, Ki-67, and p16 was performed on cervical tissue samples from women categorized as HR-HPV (-) CIN 0, HR-HPV (+) CIN 0/I, and HR-HPV (+) CIN II-III. Staining was analyzed in randomly selected fields using light microscopy at ×200 magnification.

2. Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) staining was performed on cervical tissue sections and examined under ×200 magnification to assess histopathological features.

3. Correlation analysis was conducted between PD-L1 expression in mononuclear and epithelial cells and the expression levels of Ki-67 and p16, assessed via immunohistochemistry in the same tissue samples. The analysis revealed a positive correlation between mononuclear PD-L1 expression and Ki-67 staining (p = 0.0417) as well as p16 staining (p = 0.0088).

4. Ki-67 and p16 expression levels were compared between HR-HPV (+) CIN II-III, HR-HPV (+) CIN 0/I, and HR-HPV (-) CIN 0 groups using light microscopy of immunostained tissue sections. The results showed that HR-HPV (+) CIN II-III women had significantly increased Ki-67 (p < 0.0001) and p16 (p = 0.0025) expression compared to the other two groups, with no significant differences between HR-HPV (-) and HR-HPV (+) CIN 0/I women.

Based on these experimental findings, what comprehensive conclusion can be drawn regarding PD-L1 expression in the context of HR-HPV infection and cervical neoplastic progression?

A provisional diagnosis of acquired idiopathic gingival overgrowth (AIGO), combined gingival overgrowth, and irritation fibroma was made based on clinical findings. To confirm the diagnosis, an excisional biopsy of the gingival tissue was performed, and the following investigations were carried out:

- A histological section of the excised tissue was stained with Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) and examined under light microscopy at ×40 magnification.
- Immunohistochemical (IHC) staining for kappa and lambda light chains was performed on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue sections, with visualization using a chromogenic detection system, and analyzed at ×100 magnification.
- Additional immunohistochemical staining specifically for lambda light chain expression was performed and evaluated at ×100 magnification.

What definitive diagnosis can be made based on the integration of these investigative findings, and how is this diagnosis supported by the collective results?

input_logic_chain.research_context: A provisional diagnosis of AIGO, combined gingival overgrowth, and irritation fibroma was made based on clinical findings. However, histopathological and immunohistochemical analyses were required to confirm the definitive diagnosis.

experiments.experimental_setting: Histological section of excised gingival tissue was stained with Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) and examined under light microscopy at ×40 magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To evaluate the cellular composition, epithelial morphology, and stromal characteristics of the gingival overgrowth.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Proliferative stratified squamous epithelium with elongated rete ridges and areas of ulceration. The underlying stroma is fibrocellular with wavy, fibrillar collagen bundles and a patchy distribution of chronic inflammatory cells. The infiltrate consists predominantly of mature plasma cells with eccentric nuclei, coarse chromatin, and pale pink to lavender cytoplasm. Plasma cells are arranged in loose clusters and sheets within the fibrous matrix. No glandular or epithelial structures are observed [Image 1].
experiments.interpretation: The elongated rete ridges and epithelial proliferation suggest chronic irritation or inflammatory stimulus. The presence of abundant mature plasma cells in the stroma, with characteristic morphology (eccentric nuclei, clock-face chromatin), indicates a plasma cell-rich inflammatory infiltrate rather than a neoplastic process. The fibrocellular stroma with collagen bundles is consistent with reactive or inflammatory fibrosis.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The histological features support a diagnosis of a chronic inflammatory lesion dominated by mature plasma cells, suggestive of a plasma cell gingivitis (PCG) rather than a fibroma or drug-induced gingival overgrowth.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical (IHC) staining for kappa (κ) and lambda (λ) light chains was performed on the formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue section, with visualization using a chromogenic detection system (brown precipitate).
experiments.experiment_goal: To determine the clonality of the plasma cell population by assessing immunoglobulin light chain expression.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Numerous cells show cytoplasmic brown chromogenic signal for both kappa and lambda light chains. Staining is diffuse and strong in many cells, with variable intensity. Cells are densely clustered in some areas and sparsely dispersed in others. Nuclear morphology is preserved with granular chromatin. The pattern is observed at ×100 magnification [Image 2].
experiments.interpretation: The presence of both kappa and lambda light chains in the cytoplasm of plasma cells indicates polyclonal immunoglobulin production. Monoclonal plasma cell proliferations (e.g., in plasma cell neoplasms) typically show restriction to either kappa or lambda, whereas polyclonal populations express both in a balanced or mixed pattern.
experiments.sub_conclusion: The immunohistochemical pattern demonstrates polyclonal plasma cell proliferation, ruling out a monoclonal (neoplastic) process and supporting a reactive etiology.

experiments.experimental_setting: Immunohistochemical staining specifically for lambda light chain expression was performed and analyzed at ×100 magnification.
experiments.experiment_goal: To confirm the distribution and intensity of lambda light chain expression and assess clonality independently.
experiments.visual_phenomenon: Lambda light chain staining shows cytoplasmic brown precipitate in numerous plasma cells, with variable intensity—some cells show strong reactivity, others weak or negligible staining. Positively stained cells are heterogeneously distributed, forming dense clusters in some regions and appearing dispersed in others. The background stroma is lightly stained, and no follicular or glandular structures are present [Image 3].
experiments.interpretation: The heterogeneous and widespread expression of lambda light chains, combined with prior kappa positivity, confirms that multiple plasma cell clones are present. The absence of uniform strong staining in all cells and the patchy distribution further support a reactive, antigen-driven polyclonal response rather than clonal expansion.
experiments.sub_conclusion: Lambda light chain expression is non-restricted and variable, reinforcing the conclusion of polyclonal plasma cell infiltration.

intermediate_inferences.sub_conclusion: The H&E-stained section reveals a dense, non-neoplastic infiltration of mature plasma cells within a fibrocellular stroma, consistent with a chronic inflammatory gingival lesion.
Immunohistochemistry shows co-expression of both kappa and lambda light chains in plasma cells, indicating polyclonal proliferation.

reasoning.content: The initial clinical presentation suggested drug-induced gingival overgrowth or fibroma, particularly given the patient's history of amlodipine use. However, histopathological examination revealed a plasma cell-dominant infiltrate, which is atypical for those conditions. The morphological features of mature plasma cells with classic 'clock-face' nuclei and perinuclear hofs, as seen in H&E staining [Image 1], pointed toward a plasma cell lesion. To differentiate between reactive (polyclonal) and neoplastic (monoclonal) processes, immunohistochemistry for immunoglobulin light chains was performed. The observation of both kappa and lambda light chain expression in the cytoplasm of plasma cells—evident as brown chromogenic signals in IHC [Images 2 and 3]—confirmed polyclonality. In monoclonal disorders such as multiple myeloma or mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma, plasma cells typically express only one light chain type (either kappa or lambda), leading to light chain restriction. The absence of such restriction, combined with the histological pattern of diffuse but non-destructive infiltration without follicular organization, supports a diagnosis of a benign, reactive process. Clinical correlation—including resolution after withdrawal of amlodipine, strict plaque control, and no recurrence over 15 months—further supports a diagnosis of plasma cell gingivitis (PCG), a rare inflammatory condition associated with hypersensitivity or chronic antigenic stimulation.
reasoning.conclusion: A confirmatory diagnosis of plasma cell gingivitis (PCG) is established based on the integration of clinical findings, histopathological evidence of plasma cell-rich inflammation, and immunohistochemical confirmation of polyclonal plasma cell proliferation.

Extrapancreatic perineural invasion (EPNI) is associated with more advanced tumor stages and impacts resection status and patient outcomes, as evaluated through pathological staging, resection margins, and imaging findings.

To investigate this, a study was conducted with the following components:

1. Pathological staging was performed on patients with and without histologically confirmed EPNI. Tumor stages were classified according to pT, pN, and pM categories. Among patients with EPNI, 86.20% had pT3 tumors, compared to 76.47% in those without EPNI.

2. Resection status (R0, R1, R2) was recorded for all patients. CT imaging was used to identify radiological signs of perineural invasion. Signs were observed in 15 out of 31 R0 resections, 13 out of 14 R1 resections, and in the single R2 resection.

3. Histological examination of resected specimens was performed using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining. Resection margins were marked with green ink to identify the medial margin. Adjacent to this inked margin, loosely arranged tissue with scattered cellular debris and amorphous extracellular material was observed.

4. Immunohistochemical staining was performed on tissue sections to detect tumor cells in proximity to nerve bundles. A chromogen producing a brown stain was used. Cells exhibiting brown staining were observed forming a cluster around a nerve bundle.

What conclusions can be drawn from these findings, and how do they collectively inform our understanding of extrapancreatic perineural invasion in relation to tumor stage, resection completeness, and disease recurrence?
